en: The Lotus Sutra of the True Dharma.
Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
Homage to all Tathāgatas, Pratyekabuddhas, and noble Śrāvakas, and to the Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present!
The Introduction Chapter.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks.

Together with twelve hundred bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats— whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated, who were noble steeds, great elephants, who had accomplished their task, completed what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, whose fetters of existence were utterly destroyed, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states, and who were renowned great śrāvakas.
Namely: with the venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya,
the venerable Aśvajit, and the venerable Bāṣpa;
and with the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Bhadrika, and the Venerable Mahākāśyapa;
and with the venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the venerable Nadīkāśyapa,
and the venerable Gayākāśyapa.
and with the venerable Śāriputra,
the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and the venerable Mahākātyāyana;
and with the venerable Aniruddha,
the venerable Revata, and the venerable Kapphiṇa;
and with the venerable Gavāmpati,
the venerable Pilindavatsa, and the venerable Bakkula;
and with the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila,
the venerable Bharadvāja, and the venerable Mahānanda;
And with the venerable Upananda, the venerable Sundarananda, and the venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra.
Together with the Venerable Subhūti and the Venerable Rāhula,
and with these and other great śrāvakas— the Venerable Ānanda who was still in training,
and two thousand other monks, both those in training and those beyond training.
Together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs headed by Mahāprajāpatī,
the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā— the mother of Rāhula— along with her retinue,
and eighty thousand bodhisattvas, all of whom were irreversible and bound to only one more birth before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;

They had attained the *dhāraṇīs* and were established in great eloquence; they turned the irreversible wheel of Dharma; they had attended upon many hundreds of Buddhas and planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; they were praised by hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; their bodies and minds were permeated with loving-kindness (*maitrī*); they were skilled in causing others to enter the wisdom of the Tathāgata; they possessed great wisdom and had reached the further shore of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); their fame resounded through many hundreds of thousands of world-systems; and they were saviors of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings.
They were as follows: the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
Avalokiteśvara; Mahāsthāmaprāpta; Sarvārthanāman; Nityodyukta; Anikṣiptadhura; Ratnapāṇi; Bhaiṣajyarāja; Bhaiṣajyasamudgata; Vyūharāja; and Pradānaśūra.
and with Ratnacandra, and Ratnaprabha, and Pūrṇacandra, and Mahāvikrāmin, and Anantavikrāmin, and Trailokyavikrāmin, and Mahāpratibhāna,
and Satatasamitābhiyukta, and Dharaṇīdhara, and Akṣayamati, and Padmaśrī, and Nakṣatrarāja.
and with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Siṃha,
together with sixteen virtuous men headed by Bhadrapāla.
They were as follows: Bhadrapāla, Ratnākara, Susārthavāha, Naradatta, Guhyagupta, Varuṇadatta, Indradatta, Uttaramati, Viśeṣamati, Vardhamānamati,
Amoghadarśin, Susaṃprasthita, Suvikrāntavikrāmin, Anupamamati, and Sūryagarbha.
and Dharaṇīndhara;
together with eighty thousand such bodhisattvas as these leaders;
and together with Śakra, the lord of the gods, accompanied by a retinue of twenty thousand sons of the gods.
Namely: the divine son Candra, the divine son Sūrya, the divine son Samantagandha, the divine son Ratnaprabha, the divine son Avabhāsaprabha, and twenty thousand divine sons headed by these;
together with the four Great Kings and their retinues of thirty thousand divine sons.
Namely: by the Great King Virūḍhaka, the Great King Virūpākṣa,
and the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
And by the great king Vaiśravaṇa;
and by the divine son Īśvara and the divine son Maheśvara, each with a retinue of thirty thousand divine sons;
and by Brahmā Sahāmpati, together with a retinue of twelve thousand divine sons of the Brahmakāyika host.
Namely: by the Brahmā Śikhin and the Brahmā Jyotiṣprabha;
headed by these, together with twelve thousand sons of the gods from the Brahmakāyika realm;
and with eight nāga kings, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of millions of nāgas.
Namely: the naga king Nanda, the naga king Upananda, Sāgara, Vāsuki, Takṣaka, Manasvin, Anavatapta, and the naga king Utpalaka.
And with four kinnara kings, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kinnaras,
namely: the kinnara king Druma,
and the kinnara king Mahādharma.
And with Sudharma, the king of the kinnaras,
and Dharmadhara, the king of the kinnaras;
and together with four sons of the gods belonging to the gandharva host, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of gandharvas.
Namely: with the gandharva Manojña, the gandharva Manojñasvara, the gandharva Madhura, and the gandharva Madhurasvara;
and with four lords of the asuras, accompanied by retinues of many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of asuras—namely, with Bala, the lord of the asuras, and so forth.
And by the asura lord Kharaskandha,
and by the asura lord Vemacitrin,
and by the asura lord Rāhu.
And together with four lords of the *garuḍas*, accompanied by a retinue of many hundreds of thousands of millions of *garuḍas*—
namely, the *garuḍa* lord Mahātejas,
and the *garuḍa* lords Mahākāya, Mahāpūrṇa, and Maharddhiprāpta.
And together with King Ajātaśatru of Magadha, the son of Vaidehī.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One— surrounded, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated by the four assemblies— having spoken the Dharma discourse, the sūtra, the great vaipulya teaching,
the instruction for bodhisattvas, and the protection of all Buddhas, titled "The Great Exposition," while seated upon that very same great Dharma-throne.
Having sat cross-legged, he entered the samādhi called "The Foundation of Infinite Exposition," remaining with a body that was motionless and a mind that had attained imperturbability.
Immediately upon the Blessed One’s entry into this state, a great rain of divine flowers— māndārava, mahāmāndārava, mañjūṣaka, and mahāmañjūṣaka— fell from above.
They scattered them over the Blessed One and those four assemblies.
The entire buddha-field shook in six ways: it trembled, trembled violently; it quaked, quaked violently; it shuddered, shuddered violently.

Furthermore, at that time, the assembly was gathered together, consisting of monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.
They were seated together:
regional kings, powerful wheel-turning monarchs, and universal wheel-turning monarchs of the four continents.
All of them, along with their retinues, gazed upon the Blessed One, filled with wonder, filled with amazement, and filled with joy.
Then, at that moment, a single ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of the Blessed One.
It extended toward the eastern direction across eighteen thousand Buddha-fields.
All those Buddha-fields were clearly visible, illuminated by the radiance of that ray of light, reaching as far as the great Avīci hell below and as far as the peak of existence above.
And whatever beings were present in those buddha-fields within the six realms of existence, they all appeared there without exception;
and whatever Buddhas, Blessed Ones, were residing, staying, and maintaining themselves in those buddha-fields, [they too appeared].
All of them were also visible,
and whatever Dharma those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, were teaching, all of that was heard in its entirety.

And those monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen in those buddha-fields— whether they were practitioners of yoga (*yogin*), practitioners of the way of yoga (*yogācāra*), or those who had attained the fruits [of the path] or had not yet attained them—
all of them were also visible.

And those bodhisattva mahāsattvas in those buddha-fields who practice the conduct of a bodhisattva through various and manifold objects of hearing, inclinations, causes, and reasons, by means of their skill in expedient means (*upāyakauśalya*).
All of them were visible;
and those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who had entered final nirvana in those Buddha-fields, all of them were also visible.
And all the jewel-encrusted relic-stūpas of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who had entered final nirvāṇa in those buddha-fields, were also clearly visible.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ah, this great sign, this great miracle has been performed by the Tathāgata!
What could be the cause here, what the reason, that the Blessed One has performed such a great sign, such a great miracle, and that the Blessed One has entered into meditative absorption?"
And these kinds of great, wonderful, marvelous, and inconceivable miracles of great supernatural power were being displayed.
What indeed should I ask as the meaning I ought to inquire about?
Who here would be capable of resolving this matter?
This thought occurred to him: "This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has performed services under previous Victors, planted roots of merit, and attended upon many Buddhas.
This Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta has previously seen such signs from former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and he has previously experienced great discourses on the Dharma."
What if I were now to ask Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta about this matter?

When those four assemblies—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—and the many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans saw this such great sign, this manifestation of the Blessed One’s miraculous power, they were struck with wonder, filled with amazement, and seized by curiosity.
This thought occurred to them: "What indeed should we ask the Blessed One regarding this such manifestation of his great miraculous power?"

Then, at that very moment, instant, and second, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having perceived with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those four assemblies, and being himself possessed of a doubt regarding the Dharma, at that time [addressed] Mañjuśrī—

He spoke thus to the youthful Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, what is the cause, what is the condition, for this such marvelous and extraordinary manifestation of supernatural power performed by the Blessed One, and why are these eighteen thousand Buddha-fields—variegated, beautiful, most beautiful, preceded by Tathāgatas, and led by Tathāgatas—visible?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the youthful Mañjuśrī with these verses:
For what reason, Mañjuśrī, has this ray been emitted by the Leader of Men? This single ray, illuminating from between his eyebrows, has issued forth from the treasury of the *ūrṇā*. (Saddhp 1.1)
And the gods, greatly rejoicing, released a great rain of māndārava flowers,
as well as divine mañjūṣaka blossoms mixed with sandalwood powder— fragrant, delightful, and enchanting.
By this, this earth is beautified on all sides, and the fourfold assembly has attained great joy;
and this entire field trembles in six ways with a most terrifying appearance.
And that very ray of light illuminated eighteen thousand full worlds in the eastern direction in a single instant; all those worlds became as if of a golden color.

From the Avīci hell up to the highest peak of existence, and as many beings as there are in those realms existing within the six states of rebirth— those who are passing away and those who are being born there— (Saddhp_1.5)
The various and manifold karmas of those beings are seen within their destinies as both happiness and suffering;
whether inferior, superior, or middling, standing here, he beheld all of this.
And I behold the Buddhas, those lions among the lords of men, proclaiming and revealing the Dharma;
they govern many millions of beings, uttering voices with sweet tones. (Saddhp 1.7)
They emit a profound, vast, and wonderful sound throughout their respective realms,
illuminating this Buddha-dharma with millions of billions of parables and reasons.

To those beings who are tormented by suffering, whose minds are exhausted by birth and old age, and who are ignorant, he reveals the peaceful nirvana, saying: "O monks, this is the end of suffering. (Saddhp 1.9)
And those men who have attained noble power, endowed with merits and likewise with visions of the Buddhas—
to them they speak of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, extolling this method of the Dharma.
And as for those other sons of the Sugata who, seeking supreme knowledge,
perform various activities at all times— for them too they speak in praise of enlightenment.
"Mañjughoṣa, standing here, I hear and see such things as these there;
I shall describe but a small portion of the thousands of millions of other distinctions."
I see in many fields as well those bodhisattvas who are like the sands of the Ganges;
in numbers of many thousands of kotis, not few, they produce awakening through various kinds of vigor.
In that same way, some give gifts—wealth, silver, gold, pearls, gems, conch shells, stones, coral, as well as male and female slaves, chariots, horses, and sheep. (Saddhp_1.14)
With joyful minds, they give gifts such as palanquins adorned with jewels, dedicating them toward supreme enlightenment, thinking: "May we indeed become recipients of this vehicle. (Saddhp_1.15)
The Buddha-vehicle, praised by the Sugatas as the most excellent and distinguished vehicle within the three realms—
may I also quickly become an attainer of that, by giving such gifts as these.
Some give gifts of chariots yoked with four horses, complete with railings and adorned with flowered banners and victory standards made of jewels; others likewise give such gifts.
They give away their sons and likewise their daughters; some give their own dear flesh when asked;
and they give their hands and feet when solicited, seeking this supreme enlightenment.
Some give their heads, some their eyes, and some their most excellent bodies;
having given these gifts with serene minds, they indeed pray for the wisdom of the Tathāgatas.

I see, Mañjuśrī, that some, having abandoned flourishing kingdoms, as well as their harems, all their islands, and having left behind all their ministers and kinsmen, [go forth]. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 1.20.
They approach the leaders of the world and ask for the supreme Dharma for the sake of peace;
they don saffron robes and shave their hair and beards.
I see some bodhisattvas who, appearing as monks, dwell in the forest; some frequent empty wildernesses, devoted to the recitation and study of the teachings. (Saddhp 1.22)
And I see some wise bodhisattvas entering mountain caves,
cultivating this Buddha-knowledge, reflecting upon it, and clearly perceiving it.

Having completely cast off all desires, others— those whose selves are fully cultivated and whose spheres of activity are pure— having attained the five supernormal powers here, dwell in the forest as sons of the Sugata.
Standing here with feet together, some wise ones, with palms joined in reverence facing the Leaders,
having produced joy, praise the King of the Lords of Jinas here with thousands of verses.
Mindful, self-controlled, and confident, some who understand the subtle course of conduct inquire about the Dharma from the best of bipeds, and having heard it, they become upholders of the Dharma.
I see some sons of the Lord of Jinas there and there, their own selves fully cultivated,
preaching the Dharma to many millions of living beings through many tens of thousands of examples and reasons.
Filled with joy, they proclaim the Dharma, exhorting many bodhisattvas;
having struck down Māra along with his army and his mounts, they beat this drum of the Dharma.

I see some sons of the Sugata in the teaching of the Sugata, honored by humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas— those who are free from pride, humble, and whose conduct is peaceful and thoroughly tranquil.
Relying on forest groves, others appear in various forms, emitting light from their bodies; rescuing beings from the hells, they likewise encourage them toward awakening. (Saddhp 1.30)

Some sons of the Conqueror are established in vigor, while others, having abandoned drowsiness without remainder, dwell in the forest engaged in walking meditation; through their vigor, they have set out for supreme enlightenment.

And those who here always guard their pure, unbroken morality, which is like a precious jewel, and who practice it there in its fullness— by means of that morality, they are set forth toward supreme enlightenment.

Some sons of the Conqueror possess the power of patience; they endure the abuse, revilement, and threats of monks who are full of arrogance, for through patience they have set out for supreme enlightenment.
And I see some bodhisattvas who, having abandoned all delight in play and having avoided childish companions, take pleasure in associating with the noble ones and are composed in meditation.
Avoiding distracted minds, they remained one-pointed in mind within forest caves;
meditating for billions of years, they set out toward supreme enlightenment through their meditation.
Likewise, some give gifts in the presence of the Jinas and their assemblies of disciples—
edibles and foods, as well as drinks, and abundant, not meager, medicines for the sick.
Some give them hundreds of millions of garments, each worth a thousand million;
others give garments of priceless value in the presence of the Jinas and their assemblies of disciples. (Saddhp 1.37)
Having caused hundreds of millions of monasteries to be built, made of jewels as well as sandalwood,
and adorned with abundant beds and seats, they offer them in the presence of the Sugatas.

Some give pleasure groves that are clean, delightful, endowed with fruits, and variegated with flowers, for the purpose of daytime recreation for those bulls among men together with their disciples. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 1.39.
Filled with joy, they give such gifts as these—various and manifold; and having given, they generate vigor for the sake of awakening. Through their giving, they set out for supreme awakening.
And some proclaim the peaceful Dharma through many tens of millions of examples and reasons;
they teach it to thousands of millions of living beings, having set out for supreme enlightenment by means of their knowledge.
Understanding that all phenomena are devoid of agency, they proceed without duality, resembling the flight of birds;
unstained, these sons of the Sugata have set out for supreme enlightenment through wisdom.
Furthermore, Mañjughoṣa, I see that in the teachings of the Sugatas who have entered final nirvāṇa,
many wise bodhisattvas have arisen and pay honor to the relics of the Jinas.
I see thousands of millions of stupas, not few, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
by those sons of the Jinas, these millions of fields have been constantly adorned.

Exalted standards made of the seven precious gems, five thousand yojanas in height and two thousand in circumference, were raised; upon them were thousands of millions of parasols and banners. (Saddhp 1.45)
Always adorned with victory banners and constantly resounding with clusters of bells,
they were likewise worshipped with flowers, perfumes, and musical instruments by humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
The sons of the Sugata cause such worship as this to be performed here upon the relics of the Jinas,
by which the ten directions are adorned as if with the Pārijāta trees in full bloom.
I and these many millions of living beings standing here all behold this entire world, including the gods, in full bloom; this single ray has been released by the Jina.
Oh, the power of this bull among men! Oh, his vast and untainted knowledge!
For today a single ray of light emitted by him reveals thousands of many buddha-fields throughout the world.
We have been struck with wonder upon seeing this sign, so marvelous and immeasurable.
O Mañjusvara, son of the Buddha, explain this matter; dispel our curiosity!
"O Hero, these four assemblies here look up at you with uplifted minds and at me as well;
arouse their joy, dispel their doubt, and grant us an explanation, O Son of the Sugata!"
For what purpose has such a radiance been emitted by the Sugata today?
Oh, the power of the Bull among Men! Oh, his vast and pure wisdom! (Saddhp 1.52)
Since today a single ray of light has been emitted by him and reveals many thousands of fields in the world—
such will be the significance of this matter for which he has released this vast radiance.
What supreme dharmas were touched by the Sugata, that best of men, at the seat of awakening? Will the Lord of the World now teach them here, or will he prophesy [the future] for these bodhisattvas?
There must be no small cause for this, that so many thousands of fields have been shown—
so wonderfully variegated and adorned with jewels— and Buddhas of infinite vision are seen.
"Ask," said Maitreya, the son of the Jina; "these humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas long for it. These four assemblies are looking on, wondering what Mañjusvara will here prophesy."

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya and that entire assembly of bodhisattvas: "Noble sons, it is the Tathāgata’s intention to hold this discourse for the hearing of the Great Dharma;
he intends to pour down the great rain of Dharma, to beat the great drum of Dharma, and to raise the great banner of Dharma."

O sons of good family, today the Tathāgata intends to perform the kindling of the great torch of Dharma, the blowing of the great conch of Dharma, the beating of the great drum of Dharma, and the teaching of the great Dharma.
O sons of good family, this is how it appears to me.

Just as I have seen this very kind of prior sign from previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones— in the case of those previous Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, there was likewise this manifestation of the emission of rays—
I understand by this that the Tathāgata desires to engage in a discourse on hearing the Great Dharma, and desires to cause others to hear the Great Dharma.
For what reason has he manifested such a portent as this?
It is because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, desires to cause [beings] to hear the Dharma discourse that is contrary to all the world.
Thus he displayed this kind of great miracle, the radiance of the emission of rays, as a preliminary sign.

I recall, noble sons, in the past, beyond eons that were incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, limitless, and boundless— further back than that— at that time and in that age, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Candrasūryapradīpa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
The Buddha, the Blessed One,
taught the Dharma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
He fully revealed the holy life (brahmacarya), which is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine.

That is to say, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma associated with the four noble truths and proceeding by way of dependent origination, for the purpose of transcending birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair, and culminating in nirvāṇa.

And for the sake of the bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, he taught the Dharma associated with the six perfections, beginning with unexcelled perfect enlightenment and culminating in the knowledge of omniscience.

Furthermore, noble sons, after that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa, there appeared in the world another Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, also named Candrasūryapradīpa. Thus indeed, Ajita, by this succession of examples, there were Tathāgatas, Arhats [named] Candrasūryapradīpa.

There were twenty thousand Tathāgatas who were perfectly enlightened Buddhas, all sharing the same name and belonging to the same family and lineage— namely, the Bharadvāja lineage. In that regard, Ajita, from the first Tathāgata among those twenty thousand Tathāgatas up to the very last Tathāgata,
each was a Tathāgata named Candrasūryapradīpa (Moon-Sun-Lamp), an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, perfected in knowledge and conduct.
The Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—
he too taught the Dharma that is virtuous in the beginning, virtuous in the middle, and virtuous in the end;
he fully revealed the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that is meaningful, well-phrased, unique, complete, pure, and pristine.
That is to say, for the sake of the śrāvakas, he taught the Dharma associated with the four noble truths and proceeding from dependent origination,
which culminates in nirvāṇa for the purpose of transcending birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair;

and for the sake of the bodhisattvas and mahāsattvas, he taught the Dharma associated with the six perfections, beginning with unexcelled perfect enlightenment and culminating in the knowledge of omniscience.

Furthermore, Ajita, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa, while he was formerly a prince and had not yet departed from the life of a householder, had eight sons.
They were as follows: there was a prince named Mati.
There was a prince named Sumati,
and one named Anantamati,
and one named Ratnamati.
And there was one named Viśeṣamati, and one named Vimatisamuddhāṭī,
and one named Ghoṣamati.
And there was a prince named Dharmamati.
Furthermore, Ajita, those eight princes who were the sons of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa, possessed vast supernatural power;
each one had the four great continents as their domain of enjoyment.
They exercised sovereignty over those very realms;

and having learned that the Blessed One had gone forth from the household life and heard that he had awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they renounced all royal enjoyments and followed the Blessed One into the homeless life.
And all of them had set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and became Dharma-preachers;
those princes were always practitioners of celibacy and had planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas.

Furthermore, Ajita, at that time, after the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa had spoken the Dharma discourse, the sūtra, the great vaipulya teaching called *Mahānirdeśa*, which is an instruction for bodhisattvas and is embraced by all Buddhas, (Vaidya 13)

At that very moment, at that very instant, at that very second, and within that same assembly, he sat cross-legged upon that very great Dharma-throne and entered the meditative absorption named "The Foundation of Infinite Exposition," remaining with his body unmoving and his mind unmoving.
Immediately upon his entering [meditative absorption], a great rain of divine flowers—māndārava, mahāmāndārava, mañjūṣaka, and mahāmañjūṣaka—fell, covering the Blessed One and his assembly.
Furthermore, that entire buddha-field shook in six ways: it quaked, it trembled, it shook violently; it quivered, it trembled violently; it was agitated, it was agitated violently.

Furthermore, Ajita, at that time and on that occasion, there were gathered and seated in that assembly monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans;
as well as regional kings, powerful wheel-turning monarchs, and universal monarchs of the four continents.
They all, together with their retinues, gazed upon that Blessed One, struck with wonder, filled with amazement, and overcome with joy.
Then, at that very moment, a single ray of light issued forth from the circle of hair between the eyebrows of that Blessed Tathāgata Candrasūryapradīpa.
It extended toward the eastern direction, reaching across eighteen thousand buddha-fields.
And all those buddha-fields were seen, perfectly clear, by the radiance of that ray,
just as these buddha-fields are seen now, Ajita.
Furthermore, Ajita, at that time there were twenty koṭis of bodhisattvas following that Blessed One.

Those who were listeners to the Dharma in that assembly became filled with wonder, filled with amazement, filled with joy, and their curiosity was aroused upon seeing the world illuminated by that great radiance of light.
Furthermore, Ajita, at that time, under the teaching of that Blessed One, there was a bodhisattva named Varaprabha.
He had eight hundred disciples.
Then that Blessed One, having emerged from that samādhi, extensively proclaimed the Dharma discourse called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, beginning with that bodhisattva Varaprabha.
He spoke for a full sixty intermediate eons while seated upon a single seat, with his body unshaken and his mind unmoving.
And that entire assembly, seated upon a single seat, listened to the Dharma from that Blessed One for those sixty intermediate eons;
yet not even a single being in that assembly experienced any physical fatigue.
And there is no fatigue of the mind.

Then, after the lapse of sixty intermediate kalpas, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa, having taught this Dharma discourse, the Sūtrānta of the Great Vaipulya, the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka, which is an instruction for Bodhisattvas and is upheld by all Buddhas, announced his parinirvāṇa at that very moment, instant, and second.

"Monks, before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and before this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, its gods, humans, and asuras, I declare: today, in this very night, during the middle watch, the Tathāgata will attain final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder."
Then, Ajita, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa, having prophesied the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Śrīgarbha to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
addressed that entire assembly: "Monks, this Bodhisattva Śrīgarbha shall [attain] unsurpassed..."
He will fully awaken to unexcelled perfect enlightenment;
he will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Vimalanetra.

Then, Ajita, during the middle watch of that very night, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrasūryapradīpa, passed into final nirvāṇa in the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder;
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Varaprabha retained that Dharma discourse, the Lotus of the True Dharma.
For eighty intermediate kalpas after that Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, that bodhisattva mahāsattva Varaprabha upheld and proclaimed his teaching.
In that regard, Ajita, those who were the eight sons of that Blessed One, headed by Mati—
They became the disciples of that very Bodhisattva Varaprabha;
they were matured by him for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And after that, they beheld and honored many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
And they all fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment; and the last among them was the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.
Among those eight hundred disciples, there was one bodhisattva who placed excessive importance on gain, honor, and fame, and who desired renown.
For him, every word and syllable he was taught would vanish and not remain fixed;
thus, he became known by the very name "Yaśaskāma" (Desirer of Fame).
By that root of merit as well, he propitiated many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas;
and having propitiated them, he honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated them.

Now, Ajita, you might perhaps have some doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation, thinking that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Varaprabha, the Dharma-preacher, at that time and on that occasion, was someone else.
Furthermore, it should not be viewed in this way.
Why is that?
Because at that time, on that occasion, I was that very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Varaprabha, the Dharma-preacher.
And as for that bodhisattva named Yaśaskāma who had fallen into indolence—
it was you yourself, Ajita, who at that time and on that occasion were the bodhisattva named Yaśaskāma who had fallen into indolence.
Thus indeed, Ajita, having seen this prior sign of the Blessed One through this method and having observed such a ray of light being emitted, I reflected in this way:
Just as the Blessed One also desired to speak that Dharma-discourse, the Lotus of the Good Dharma, a sūtra of great vaipulya, an instruction for bodhisattvas, and the protection of all Buddhas.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, wishing to further elucidate this very matter, at that time spoke these verses:
"I recall the past, in an inconceivable and immeasurable eon, when there was a Jina, the supreme among beings, named Candrasūryapradīpa. (Saddhp 1.57)
The Leader of the people teaches the true Dharma and disciplines infinite millions of beings;
he inspires many inconceivable bodhisattvas toward the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
And those eight sons who were then his, when he was still a prince and a leader,
having seen that great sage gone forth, abandoned all desires and quickly went forth as well. (Saddhp 1.59)
And that Lord of the World speaks the Dharma, this sutra called the *Anantanirdeśavara*;
it is indeed proclaimed as this Vaipulya, which he reveals to thousands of millions of living beings.
Immediately after speaking, that Guide, the best of sages, sat cross-legged for a moment on his Dharma-seat and entered the supreme samādhi called "Infinite Exposition."
A divine rain of māndārava flowers fell, and drums resounded without being struck;
gods and yakṣas, stationed in the sky, offered worship to the Supreme among Men.
At that very moment, the entire field trembled, and there was a most wonderful and marvelous event;
the Leader emitted from between his eyebrows a single ray of light, exceedingly beautiful to behold.
Having gone to the eastern direction, that ray of light indeed fills eighteen thousand fields;
illuminating and shining throughout the entire world, it reveals to sentient beings their passing away and rebirth.
Some fields here consist of jewels, while others likewise have the luster of lapis lazuli;
they appear variegated and exceedingly beautiful through the radiance of the rays of light from the Guide.
Gods, humans, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, apsarases, and kinnaras—
those who are intent upon the worship of the Sugata are seen and perform worship throughout the world-systems. (Saddhp_1.66)
And the Buddhas, the self-existent ones, appear in person, beautiful to behold like golden sacrificial pillars;
and like a golden image set within lapis lazuli, they proclaim the Dharma in the midst of the assembly.
Therein, no calculation of the śrāvakas exists; those disciples of the Sugata are immeasurable.
Indeed, the radiance of the rays from each of the Leaders in every field reveals them all.
Endowed with vigor, possessing unbroken and flawless morality like precious jewels,
the sons of the leaders of men are seen dwelling in mountain caves.

By that very ray of light, all those many bodhisattvas— wise ones who renounce all their possessions, endowed with the power of patience, and devoted to meditation— are seen, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Unwavering and unshaken, established in patience, delighting in meditation, and composed, the sons of the Sugata are seen; through meditation, they have set out for supreme enlightenment.
Understanding the true state, which is peaceful and free from outflows, they reveal it;
by the power of the Sugata, they teach the Dharma in many world-systems—such is this activity.
And having seen this power of the Protector Candrārka-dīpa, all those four assemblies were filled with joy at that moment and asked one another, "How can this be?"

Not long after that, the Leader of the World, honored by humans, gods, and yakṣas, arose from his meditative absorption and then addressed his son Varaprabha, who was a wise bodhisattva and a preacher of the Dharma. (Saddhp 1.74)
"You are the eye and the refuge of the world; you are wise, trustworthy, and the upholder of the Dharma for me.
For you are the witness here in my treasury of Dharma as to how I shall speak for the benefit of living beings."
Having established many bodhisattvas, having gladdened, praised, and extolled them,
that Jina proclaimed those supreme dharmas for a full sixty intermediate kalpas.
Whatever supreme and most excellent Dharma that Lord of the World spoke while seated upon a single seat,
all of that was retained by that son of the Jina, Varaprabha, who was a preacher of the Dharma.
Having spoken this supreme Dharma and gladdened many people,
on that very day the Leader spoke before the world together with its gods.
I have revealed this guide to the Dharma and explained the true nature of phenomena as it is; O monks, today at this very hour, in the middle watch of the night, it is the time of my parinirvāṇa.
Be heedful, take resolve as your essence, and apply yourselves diligently to this teaching of mine;
for the Jinas, the great seers, are extremely difficult to encounter even after the passing of millions of billions of eons.

Many sons of the Buddha were born into anguish and were overwhelmed by fierce suffering upon hearing the voice of the Supreme among Men— the word that his parinirvāṇa was so imminent. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 1.81)
And having comforted those many inconceivable millions of living beings, the king of kings said:
"Do not fear, O monks; after I have entered parinirvāṇa, you shall become Buddhas following me."
This wise Bodhisattva Śrīgarbha has attained the state of untainted knowledge;
he shall touch the supreme, foremost enlightenment and become a Victor named Vimalāgranetra.
On that very night, during the middle watch, he entered final nirvāṇa like a lamp when its fuel is exhausted;
his relics were widely distributed, and there arose infinite billions of *koṭī-nayuta* of stupas.
And there were monks as well as nuns who had set out for supreme, foremost enlightenment;
they were not few, being like the sands of the Ganges, and were devoted to the teaching of that Sugata.
And that monk who was the Dharma-preacher Varaprabha, by whom that Dharma was upheld,
preached the supreme teachings within that dispensation for a full eighty intermediate eons.
He had eight hundred disciples whom he had all brought to maturity at that time;
they had seen many millions of Buddhas and had paid honor to those great seers.

Having practiced the conduct that is in accordance with the Dharma, they became Buddhas in many world-systems; and immediately thereafter, they mutually prophesied one another's attainment of supreme enlightenment.
And in the succession of those Buddhas, Dīpaṃkara was the last;
the god beyond gods, honored by the assembly of sages, he disciplined many billions of living beings.
And you were at that time a disciple of that son of the Sugata, Varaprabha, as he was preaching the Dharma—
a disciple who was indolent and greedy, seeking both gain and knowledge.
He was excessively desirous of fame and had traveled from family to family;
at that time, all his teachings and recitations did not remain when he spoke them.
And his name was thus: he was renowned throughout the ten directions by the name Yaśaskāma;
yet, by that unwholesome karma which had been performed and was now stained with impurity, [he fell].
He pleased ten million billion Buddhas and performed vast offerings to them;
he practiced the excellent and conformable conduct, and this Lion of the Śākyas has now been seen as a Buddha.
And he shall be the very last [to appear]; he will attain the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
Belonging to the lineage of Maitreya, he will become a Blessed One and will discipline many thousands of millions of living beings.
At that time, when the Sugata had entered final nirvana, he who had fallen into indolence was none other than you; and at that time, I was the Dharma-preacher.
By this causal reason, having today seen such a sign as this,
I declare that the first well-known sign of that knowledge was seen by me there.
Surely even the Lord of Jinas, the All-Seeing One, the Sovereign of the Śākyas who perceives the ultimate truth,
desires to speak that very same supreme method; today I have heard it.
Today, that very same perfect sign of the skillful means of the Leaders has been fulfilled;
the Lion of the Śākyas is establishing it and will speak the seal of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
"Be disciplined and pure in mind, with palms joined; he who is compassionate for the welfare of the world will speak.
He will rain down the Dharma like an endless shower, satisfying those who stand firm for the sake of awakening."

And whatever doubts or uncertainties there may be here, whatever hesitations exist— these shall be dispelled for the sons of the Self-Knower, those bodhisattvas who have set out here toward awakening.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Introduction," in the noble Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma. //1//
(Vaidya 21) Chapter Two: Skill in Means.
Then the Blessed One, mindful and self-possessed, arose from that samādhi.
Having arisen, he addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, the Buddha-knowledge of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas is profound, difficult to see, and difficult to realize;
it is hard for all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas to understand. Why is that?"
Śāriputra, for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have indeed attended upon many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas;

they have practiced their conduct under many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Buddhas; they have long pursued unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they have exerted heroic vigor; they are endowed with marvelous and extraordinary qualities; they are endowed with qualities difficult to understand; and they have realized those qualities that are difficult to understand.
Śāriputra, the intentional language (*saṃdhābhāṣya*) of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones is difficult to understand.
Why is that?

Because they reveal the dharmas that are their own realization through various skillful means, insights, visions, explanations of causes and conditions, supports, etymologies, and designations—by means of those skillful means for those who are attached to this or that [view].

Śāriputra, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have attained the supreme perfection of the knowledge and vision of great skill in means for the sake of liberating sentient beings. They are endowed with unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision, the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditations, the liberations, the concentrations, the attainments, and marvelous dharmas; they are the proclaimers of the various teachings.
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have attained that which is most wonderful and marvelous.
Enough, Śāriputra, let it be said only this much: 'Śāriputra, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have attained the supreme wonder.
Śāriputra, only a Tathāgata can teach the dharmas of a Tathāgata."
Śāriputra, whatever dharmas the Tathāgata knows, the Tathāgata alone teaches all those dharmas;
the Tathāgata alone knows all those dharmas.
And those phenomena, how those phenomena are, and what kind of phenomena they are—
Whatever characteristics those phenomena have, whatever intrinsic natures those phenomena have,
and what those phenomena are— in what way, of what kind, with what characteristics, and with what intrinsic natures they are.
Regarding those phenomena, the Tathāgata alone is one who perceives them directly and not indirectly.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate this very matter more extensively, at that time spoke these verses:
"In this world, including its gods and humans, there are immeasurable great heroes, the Leaders;
it is not possible for all sentient beings to know them in every respect. (Saddhp 2.1)
The powers, the liberations, the kinds of fearlessnesses,
and the kinds of Buddha-qualities that he possesses cannot be known by anyone.
In the past, he practiced the conduct in the presence of millions of Buddhas—
a conduct that is profound, subtle, difficult to understand, and very hard to see.
After practicing that conduct for inconceivable millions of eons,
I beheld the fruit upon the seat of enlightenment exactly as it is.
I know this, as do the other leaders of the world, how, what,
and of what kind it is, and what its characteristics are.
It cannot be shown; it has no verbal expression. Nor is there any such being to be found in the world. (Saddhp 2.6)
To whomsoever one should teach that Dharma, and who should understand it once taught—
except for those bodhisattvas who are established in resolute faith.
And even those disciples of the Knower of the World who have performed their duties, who are praised by the Sugata,
whose outflows are exhausted, and who bear their final bodies— even for them, there is no sphere within the knowledge of the Jinas.
Even if this entire world-system were filled with beings equal to the sons of Śāriputra,
and they were to concentrate as one and contemplate it, they would not be able to know the wisdom of the Sugata.
If these ten directions were filled with wise men like you,
and likewise filled with those who are my other disciples, it would be exactly so.
And even if they were all to become one and today contemplate the wisdom of the Sugata,
they would not be able, even together, to know my immeasurable Buddha-wisdom.
Suppose that in all ten directions there were as many Pratyekabuddhas— free from outflows, of sharp faculties, and bearing their final bodies— as there are reeds or bamboos in a forest.
Even if they were to become solitary and contemplate even a mere fraction of my supreme teachings for infinite billions of nayutas of kalpas, they would not truly understand its meaning.
Bodhisattvas who have newly set out on the vehicle, who have performed services under many millions of Buddhas,
who are well-ascertained in their meaning, and who are preachers of the Dharma in many ways— even for them, the tenth direction would be filled.
If the entire world were constantly filled without any gaps by reeds and bamboos, and they were to become one and reflect upon the Dharma that was directly perceived by the Sugata; Saddhp_2.15 //
Even after contemplating for many millions of eons, as immeasurable as the sands of the Ganges,
those who are single-minded with subtle wisdom— this [Dharma] is not within their domain.
Even those non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
if they were to contemplate with undistracted minds, would find that this domain is not within their reach.
The Buddhas’ dharmas are profound and subtle; they are beyond all ratiocination and entirely free from outflows.
I know them exactly as they are, just as those Jinas themselves do throughout the worlds in the ten directions.
"Śāriputra, have full conviction in that which the Sugata proclaims!
The Jina, the Great Seer, speaks no falsehood; he proclaims the supreme truth only after a long time. (Saddhp 2.19)
I address all these śrāvakas and those who have set out for individual enlightenment;
they have been established by me in nirvāṇa and liberated from the succession of suffering.
This supreme skill in means of mine is that by which I preach many dharmas in the world;
in various places I liberate those who are attached, and I manifest the three vehicles.

Then, indeed, those great disciples present in that assembly— headed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya, consisting of twelve hundred Arhats who had exhausted their outflows and attained mastery— as well as others belonging to the vehicle of the Śrāvakas, including monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.

And those who had set out in the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, they all thought to themselves: "What is the cause, what is the reason that the Blessed One so highly extols the skillful means of the Tathāgatas,
and extols this profound Dharma as having been fully awakened to by me?"
Why does he describe it as difficult to be understood by all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
For just as the Blessed One has declared that there is but one liberation,
so too we have obtained the Buddha-dharmas and attained nirvāṇa.
And we do not understand the meaning of this speech of the Blessed One.

Then the venerable Śāriputra, having perceived the doubts and hesitations of those four assemblies and having understood their mental reflections with his own mind, and being himself beset by uncertainty regarding the Dharma, at that time addressed the Blessed One:
"What, Blessed One, is the cause?"

What is the reason that the Blessed One repeatedly and extensively praises the Tathāgatas’ teaching of the Dharma through their skill in means and their knowledge and vision— saying, "The Dharma I have fully awakened to is profound"—
and why he repeatedly praises it as being difficult to understand and spoken with intentional ambiguity?
"O Blessed One, never before have I heard such a discourse on the Dharma from the presence of the Blessed One.
And these four assemblies, O Blessed One, have fallen into doubt and uncertainty.
Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One would explain for what purpose the Tathāgata repeatedly praises this profound Dharma of the Tathāgata."

Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses: "Today, after a long time, the Sun among Men delivers such a discourse as this: 'The powers, the liberations, and the meditations—infinite in number—have been realized by me. (Saddhp_2.22)
You proclaim the seat of enlightenment, yet no one asks you about it;
you proclaim your intentional speech, yet no one questions you.
Unasked, you speak; you describe your own conduct;
you proclaim the attainment of knowledge and you discourse upon what is profound.
Today these ones have fallen into doubt; they are self-controlled and free from outflows, yet they are set forth toward nirvāṇa—what is it that the Jina speaks?
Those seeking pratyekabodhi— monks and likewise nuns,
as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and mahoragas.
Conversing with one another, they gaze upon the Supreme among Men; full of doubt and reflection, they say: "Explain it, O Great Sage! *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 2.27.
"Whatever disciples there are here of the Sugata in every respect,
I have been designated by the Supreme Rishi as one who has reached the perfection in this regard."
O Best of Men, even I have a doubt regarding this very matter of my own station: Is my final goal in nirvāṇa, or has the practice been shown to me? (Saddhp 2.29)
Release your voice with the sound of a sublime drum; proclaim this Dharma as it is!
These sons of the Jina, born from his heart, stand here gazing at the Jina with palms joined in reverence. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 2.30)
Gods and nāgas, along with yakṣas and rākṣasas, numbering thousands of millions like the sands of the Ganges,
and those eighty thousand who stand complete and perfect, all of whom aspire to unexcelled enlightenment.

The kings who are lords of the earth, the universal monarchs who have come from thousands of millions of fields, all stand with palms joined in reverence, wondering: "How indeed shall we fulfill the course of conduct?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Enough, Śāriputra!
What is the use of speaking on this matter? For what reason?"
"Śāriputra, this world with its gods will be terrified when this matter is explained.
For a second time, the venerable Śāriputra entreated the Blessed One: "Let the Blessed One speak, let the Sugata explain this very matter!"

For what reason? Blessed One, in that assembly there are many hundreds of beings, many thousands of beings, many hundreds of thousands of beings, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of beings who have seen previous Buddhas,
and who will have faith in, believe, and take up what the Blessed One has spoken.

Then the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One with this verse: "Speak clearly, O Supreme among Victors! In this assembly there are thousands of living beings who are faithful, serene, and respectful toward the Sugata; they will understand the Dharma that you proclaim."
Then the Blessed One spoke a second time to the venerable Śāriputra: "Enough, Śāriputra, with explaining this matter.
Śāriputra, when this matter is explained, this world with its gods will be terrified, and monks who have attained conceit will fall into a great abyss."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Enough indeed with preaching the Dharma here; this knowledge is subtle and beyond ratiocination.
There are many fools who have fallen into conceit, and being ignorant, they reject the Dharma when it is taught."
A third time, the venerable Śāriputra entreated the Blessed One: “May the Blessed One speak; may the Sugata explain this very matter.”
“O Blessed One, in this assembly there exist many hundreds of living beings such as myself;

and furthermore, O Blessed One, there are many hundreds of living beings, many thousands of living beings, many hundreds of thousands of living beings, and many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings who were matured by the Blessed One in previous births.”
They will have faith in, believe, and take up what has been spoken by the Blessed One;
that will lead to their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness.
Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra spoke these verses:
"Speak the Dharma, O supreme among bipeds! I, your eldest son, entreat you.
There are here thousands of millions of living beings who will have faith in the Dharma you speak."
And all those beings whom you have constantly matured throughout very long periods in previous existences—
they too stand here with palms joined together, who will have faith in this Dharma of yours.
Seeing these twelve hundred like us, as well as those who have set out for supreme enlightenment, may the Sugata speak to them and generate in them the highest joy.

Then the Blessed One, having understood the third request of the venerable Śāriputra, said this to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, since you have now requested the Tathāgata even for a third time,
what shall I say to you, Śāriputra, who thus entreats me?"
Therefore, Śāriputra, listen; pay close and careful attention,
and I shall speak to you.
As soon as these words had been spoken by the Blessed One,
five thousand monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen of arrogant disposition from that assembly rose from their seats, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and departed from there.
The members of the assembly withdrew,
for they were possessed by the unwholesome root of conceit; regarding what was not attained as attained and what was not realized as realized,
they perceived themselves to be wounded and thus departed from that assembly.
And the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, my assembly is now free of chaff; the worthless have departed, and it is established in the essence of faith.
Well done, Śāriputra, that those who were conceited have withdrawn from here.
Therefore, Śāriputra, I shall speak on this matter.”
"Excellent, Blessed One," the Venerable Śāriputra replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this: "Śāriputra, only once in a great while does the Tathāgata deliver such a teaching of the Dharma.
Śāriputra, it is just as the flower of the udumbara tree is seen only once in a great while."
In the same way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata also speaks such a teaching of the Dharma only once in a great while. Believe me, Śāriputra; I am a speaker of truth.
I am one who speaks thus, I am one who speaks without deviation. Śāriputra, the intentional language of the Tathāgata is difficult to understand.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, I have proclaimed the Dharma through hundreds of thousands of various skillful means, by means of diverse explanations, definitions, expressions, and teachings.
Śāriputra, the true Dharma is beyond reasoning, outside the sphere of logic, and is to be realized only by a Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, it is for one single purpose, for one single task, that a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha appears in the world—for a great purpose, for a great task.

And what, Śāriputra, is that one single purpose, that one single task, that great purpose, that great task of a Tathāgata, for which purpose a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha appears in the world?

It is for the purpose of causing sentient beings to undertake the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world; it is for the purpose of demonstrating the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge to sentient beings that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world;
it is for the purpose of leading sentient beings into the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world.
It is for the purpose and cause of awakening beings to the wisdom of the Tathāgata that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world;
it is for the purpose and cause of leading beings onto the path of the vision of the Tathāgata’s wisdom that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world.
This, Śāriputra, is the Tathāgata’s single task, his single duty, his great task, his great duty, his sole purpose for appearing in the world.
For in this way, Śāriputra, that which is the Tathāgata’s single task, his single duty, his great task, his great duty— that the Tathāgata performs.
Why is that?
Śāriputra, I am indeed one who causes others to undertake the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge;
Śāriputra, I am indeed one who demonstrates the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge;
Śāriputra, I am indeed one who leads others into the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
Śāriputra, I am indeed the awakener to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
Śāriputra, I am indeed the one who leads others onto the path to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
Śāriputra, it is with reference to only a single vehicle that I teach the Dharma to sentient beings, namely, the Buddha-vehicle.
Śāriputra, there exists no second or third vehicle whatsoever.
Śāriputra, this is the nature of phenomena everywhere in the worlds of the ten directions.
For what reason?

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who appeared in the past in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake of the great mass of beings—
For the benefit and happiness of both gods and humans,

they have taught the Dharma, having understood the inclinations of beings with their various dispositions and latent tendencies, by means of skill in expedients— employing various demonstrations, explanations, diverse causes, reasons, illustrations, objective supports, and etymologies.
Śāriputra, all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have taught the Dharma to sentient beings by means of only a single vehicle;
that is to say, the Buddha-vehicle which culminates in omniscience,
which is precisely the inciting of sentient beings toward the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and the revealing of the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.

Śāriputra, those beings who heard the true Dharma from those past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, [the Buddhas] taught the Dharma solely for the purpose of causing sentient beings to enter into the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, solely for the purpose of awakening them to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and solely for the purpose of leading them onto the path of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
They all also became attainers of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who will appear in the future in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, and out of compassion for the world—

For the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great body of beings— both gods and humans— they will, having understood the inclinations of sentient beings who possess various dispositions and latent tendencies, teach the Dharma through various skillful means, including diverse explanations, instructions, manifold causes, reasons, illustrations, objective supports, etymologies, and expertise in expedient methods.

Śāriputra, all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will also teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of only one single vehicle— namely, the Buddha-vehicle which culminates in omniscience; that is to say, it is solely for the purpose of causing sentient beings to undertake the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, to demonstrate the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, to lead them into the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, to awaken them to the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, and to lead them onto the path of the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
They will teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
Moreover, Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear that Dharma from those future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, they all shall become attainers of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Moreover, Śāriputra, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who now, in the present age, reside, remain, and maintain themselves in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions,

and who teach the Dharma for the benefit of many people, for the welfare of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great mass of beings, both gods and humans—

Śāriputra, those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who— through various demonstrations, explanations, diverse causes, reasons, illustrations, objects of focus, etymologies, and skillful means— having understood the inclinations of beings with their various dispositions and various elements and intentions, teach the Dharma to those beings by means of only a single vehicle; that is to say, the Buddha-vehicle which culminates in omniscience,
which is precisely the inciting of beings toward the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, and the revealing of the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.

They teach the Dharma to sentient beings solely for the purpose of causing them to enter the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, solely for the purpose of awakening them to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and solely for the purpose of causing them to enter the path to the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.
Śāriputra, those sentient beings who hear that Dharma from those present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—
They, too, shall all become attainers of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Śāriputra, I too, at this time, as a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the sake, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings— both gods and humans— teach the Dharma after having understood the inclinations of beings with their various dispositions and intentions, by means of various demonstrations, explanations, diverse causes, reasons, illustrations, objective supports, definitions, and skillful methods.

I too, Śāriputra, teach the Dharma to sentient beings by means of only a single vehicle— namely, the Buddha-vehicle which culminates in omniscience; that is to say, it is solely for the purpose of instilling in sentient beings the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, for showing them the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, for causing them to enter the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, for awakening them to the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, and for leading them onto the path of the vision of the Tathāgata’s knowledge.
I teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
Śāriputra, those sentient beings who now hear this Dharma of mine will all likewise attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, Śāriputra, by this very method it should be understood that there is no designation for a second vehicle anywhere in the world in the ten directions, much less for a third.

Moreover, Śāriputra, when Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas arise during an aeon of corruption, or when they arise during a corruption of sentient beings, a corruption of afflictions, a corruption of views, or a corruption of lifespan—
during such corruptions of the agitation of the aeon, Śāriputra, among many sentient beings who are greedy and possess few roots of merit.
Then, Śāriputra, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, through skill in means, teach that very same single Buddha-vehicle by way of the exposition of three vehicles.

In this regard, Śāriputra, those disciples who are Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas do not hear, do not enter into, and do not understand this activity of the Tathāgata, which is the instigation toward the Buddha-vehicle.
Śāriputra, those should not be known as disciples of the Tathāgata,

nor should they be known as Arhats, nor even as Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if any monk or nun should claim to have attained Arhatship, [they should be known as having fallen into a great hell].

Śāriputra, you should recognize as one who is conceited anyone who, without having taken up the vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, should say, "I am cut off from the Buddha-vehicle," or should say, "This is the final nirvana for me in this body."

For what reason? Śāriputra, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a monk who is an arhat with out-flows exhausted would, upon hearing this Dharma in the presence of a Tathāgata, not have faith— except in the case of a Tathāgata who has already entered final nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Śāriputra, when the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa, at that time and in that moment, the śrāvakas will not be the ones who uphold or teach such sūtras as these.
However, Śāriputra, they will become free from doubt regarding other Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones.
"Śāriputra, have faith in these Buddha-qualities; believe and accept them.
For, Śāriputra, no falsehood exists in the Tathāgatas.
Śāriputra, there is only this one vehicle, namely, the Buddha-vehicle."
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate this very matter more extensively, at that time spoke these verses:
"Now there were monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who had attained overweening pride;
they were five thousand in number, not fewer, and were lacking in faith."
Failing to perceive this fault, those of childish intellect— though possessed of a training that was full of flaws and merely guarding their own wounds— have departed.
Knowing the corruption of the assembly, the Lord of the World consented [to depart],
for there was no merit in them to enable them to hear this Dharma.
My assembly is pure and free from chaff;
it is well-established, with all that is worthless removed, and this essence alone remains.
Listen to me, Śāriputra, how this Dharma of the Perfectly Awakened Ones is [taught] by the Supreme among Men,
and how the Buddhas, the Leaders, speak through many hundreds of skillful means.

Having understood their inclinations and their conduct here among billions of living beings, and having recognized their various dispositions and the diverse deeds they have performed in the past, including whatever merit they have cultivated— (Saddhp_2.43)
Through various etymological explanations and reasons, I lead these living beings to understanding;
by means of hundreds of causes and examples, I satisfy all sentient beings in whatever way is necessary.
I speak sūtras as well as verses, historical narratives, birth stories, and marvelous tales;
with hundreds of diverse introductory accounts and parables, I speak geyas and likewise instructions.
To those who delight in what is inferior, who are ignorant, who have not practiced their course under many millions of Buddhas,
who are stuck in saṃsāra and deeply afflicted— I show them nirvāṇa.
The Self-Existent One employs this skillful means for the sake of awakening the knowledge of a Buddha;
yet he never says to them, "You too shall become Buddhas here in this world."
For what reason? Because the Protector, having observed the time and seen the opportune moment, speaks only thereafter;
this very moment has somehow been obtained today, whereby I shall here declare the certainty of reality.
This ninefold teaching of mine has been revealed according to the strength and weakness of sentient beings;
this skillful means was demonstrated by me for the purpose of leading them into the knowledge of the Giver of Boons.
To those sons of the Buddha who are here always pure, manifest, clean, and gentle,
who have performed services under many millions of Buddhas— to them I speak these Vaipulya sūtras.
For they were endowed with a perfection of intention that was pure in form;
therefore, I declare to them: "In a future time, you shall become Buddhas, compassionate for the welfare of others. (Saddhp 2.51)
And having heard this, they all become suffused with joy, thinking, "We shall become Buddhas, the foremost in the world.
Furthermore, knowing their conduct, I reveal the Vaipulya sūtras to them.
And these are the disciples of the Leader, by whom this supreme teaching has been heard;
even if but a single verse has been heard or retained, there is no doubt that all of them are destined for enlightenment.
For there is indeed one vehicle; a second does not exist, nor is there ever a third in the world.
It is only as a skillful means that the Supreme Men display a variety of vehicles.
The Lord of the World appears in the world for the purpose of revealing the Buddha-knowledge;
for there is but one task, and no second—indeed, the Buddhas do not lead [beings] by means of the Inferior Vehicle.
Wherein the Self-Existent One himself is established, and what the Buddha is, and how he is—
therein indeed he establishes all beings as well, along with the powers, the meditations, the liberations, and the faculties.

For it would be a fault of stinginess for me, having touched the stainless and sublime awakening, if I were to establish even a single sentient being in the inferior vehicle; that would not be right for me.
In me there is no stinginess anywhere, nor envy, nor even desire-attachment;
all my dharmas have been cut off from evil. Therefore, because of my awakening to the world, I am a Buddha.
For just as I, adorned with the marks [of a great man], illuminating this entire world,
am honored by many hundreds of living beings and teach this seal of the intrinsic nature of phenomena.
And thus, Śāriputra, I reflect: "How indeed might all sentient beings come to possess bodies endowed with the thirty-two marks, being self-luminous, knowers of the world, and self-arisen?"
Just as I have seen, just as I have reflected, and just as my resolve was formerly, so this vow of mine has been fulfilled; I proclaim both the Buddhas and enlightenment.

Śārisuta, if I were to say, "Generate the aspiration for awakening for the sake of all beings," they would all wander in delusion because they lack understanding; they would never grasp my well-spoken words.

And knowing them to be such as these— having not practiced their conduct in previous births, obsessed with the qualities of sensual pleasure, clinging to them, and their minds bewildered by craving and delusion— I [do not teach them].* *Saddhp_2.63*
For the sake of sensual desires, they fall into miserable states, suffering weariness within the six realms of existence;
oppressed by suffering and possessing little merit, they increase the charnel grounds again and again.
Constantly clinging to the thickets of views— whether "it exists," "it does not exist," or "it both exists and does not exist"—
they remain there, relying on the sixty-two types of views and grasping at non-existent entities.

Difficult to purify, arrogant, deceitful, crooked, treacherous, and of little learning— these fools never hear the voice of the Subduer of Māra, even throughout thousands of millions of births. (Saddhp 2.66)
O Śārisuta, for their sake I declare a skillful means: "Bring an end to suffering!
Seeing beings oppressed by suffering, I likewise point out nirvāṇa even there.
And thus I speak: all these phenomena are eternally extinguished and primordially tranquil;
having fulfilled the course of practice, that son of the Buddha shall become a Victor in a future age.
Such is my skill in means that I manifest three vehicles;
for there is indeed but one vehicle and one path, and this is the singular teaching of the Leaders.
Dispel your doubt and likewise your uncertainty; whoever here possesses any doubt, [know that] these leaders of the world speak nothing otherwise: this is the one vehicle, there is no second.
And those Tathāgatas who existed in the past, many thousands of Buddhas who have entered final nirvana during incalculable eons in the past— their number can never be known.
By all those Supreme Men, many pure dharmas have been revealed through parables,
reasons, causes, and numerous hundreds of skillful means.
And they all demonstrate the single vehicle and cause them to enter that one vehicle;
upon this single vehicle, they bring to maturity inconceivable thousands of millions of living beings.
The Jinas have various other skillful means by which they reveal this supreme Dharma;
having understood the inclinations as well as the dispositions of those in the world, including the gods, the Tathāgatas [teach accordingly].
And those beings who, in his presence, hear the Dharma, or those who have heard it before,
who have given gifts, practiced ethical discipline, and perfected all their conduct through patience— Saddhp_2.75.
Those who have performed their duties through vigor and meditation, or by whom these dharmas have been contemplated through wisdom,
and by whom various merits have been performed— they have all become attainers of enlightenment.
And those beings who, during the teachings of those Jinas who have entered final nirvāṇa,
were patient, self-controlled, and disciplined— every one of them became attainers of enlightenment.
And those who also perform worship of the relics of the Jinas who have entered final nirvana,
constructing many thousands of stūpas made of jewels, of gold, silver, and crystal;
And those who have built stupas of emerald, some of sapphire and pearl,
and likewise of the finest lapis lazuli and indranīla— all of them have attained awakening.
And those who build stūpas out of stone, and some who [build them] out of sandalwood or aloeswood;
those who build stūpas out of deodar cedar, and some who [build them] from a collection of various woods.
With joy, they build stūpas for the Jinas, made of bricks or constructed from piles of earth;
even those who, in forests or difficult terrains, erect heaps of dust for their sake [attain great merit]. (Saddhp 2.81)
Furthermore, those children who, here and there, while playing, built mounds of sand as stupas dedicated to the Jinas— all of them became attainers of enlightenment.
Likewise, some have caused images made of jewels to be fashioned, bearing the forms of the thirty-two marks;
those by whom these were commissioned have all become attainers of enlightenment.
Those who had images of the Sugatas made there, whether out of the seven precious gems, or of copper, or likewise of bronze— all of them became attainers of enlightenment.
Those who had images of the Sugatas made from lead, iron, or clay,
or those beautiful ones fashioned from cloth-work— all of them became attainers of enlightenment.

Those who create images on variegated walls, with limbs complete and endowed with the marks of a hundred merits— whether they paint them themselves or cause others to paint them— all of them have attained awakening.
And furthermore, those who there were training, even while amusing themselves with play,
made figures with their fingernails or wood— whether men or boys— upon the walls.
And they were all compassionate; they all delivered millions of living beings.
By exhorting many bodhisattvas, they all became attainers of enlightenment.
And those who, toward the relics of the Tathāgatas, or toward stūpas, or toward clay images, or even on painted walls, or toward a stūpa made of dust, have offered flowers and incense; (Saddhp_2.89)
And those who there played musical instruments, whether they sounded kettledrums, conchs, drums, or sweet-sounding cymbals,
or those who beat large drums as an act of worship for the sake of the supreme and foremost enlightenment— Saddhp_2.90.
Those who played lutes, cymbals, and drums, as well as those who played mṛdaṅgas, flutes, and charming tuṇavas,
whether they were performers at festivals or delicate youths— all of them became attainers of awakening.
Even those by whom cymbals were made to resound, or water-drums or flat drums,
have offered well-sung, sweet, and pleasing songs for the sake of honoring the Sugatas.
And all of them became Buddhas in the world after having performed that manifold worship of the relics;
how much more so for one who has caused even a very small musical instrument to be played before the relics of the Sugatas?
Even by worshipping with a single flower images of the Sugatas painted on a wall,
even those with distracted minds, having performed such worship, will in due course behold tens of millions of Buddhas.

And those who there made an añjali-gesture toward the stūpa— even if it were only a single full gesture or a mere joining of palms; or who for a moment raised their heads, or likewise bowed their bodies even once— (Saddhp_2.95)
Those who, even with distracted minds, have uttered "Homage to the Buddha" but once at those reliquaries— every one of them has attained this supreme enlightenment.
At that time, whether those Sugatas had already entered parinirvāṇa or were still remaining,
all those beings who heard even the name of the Dharma became attainers of enlightenment.
Furthermore, many future Buddhas, inconceivable in number and beyond all measure—
those Jinas, the supreme protectors of the world— they too shall proclaim this very skillful means.
The skill in means of those leaders of the world shall be infinite,
by which they will guide billions of living beings here into the stainless wisdom of a Buddha.
Not even a single sentient being, having heard their Dharma, would ever fail to become a Buddha;
