for this is the vow of the Tathāgatas: "Having practiced for enlightenment myself, may I cause others to practice as well."
In the future age, they will illuminate many thousands of millions of gateways to the Dharma;
demonstrating this single vehicle, they shall indeed preach the Dharma for the sake of Tathāgatahood.
For this guidance of the Dharma is ever-abiding, and the nature of phenomena always shines forth. Having realized this, the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds, shall proclaim my Single Vehicle.
The stability of phenomena and the fixed order of phenomena, which are eternally established and unshakable in this world—
the Buddhas shall reveal this awakening at the seat of enlightenment on earth through their skill in means.
In the ten directions there dwell Buddhas, honored by gods and men, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
for the sake of bringing happiness to all living beings here, they too proclaim this supreme enlightenment.
They manifest skillful means and display various vehicles;
yet the Buddhas illuminate this single vehicle, this supreme state of peace.
Having understood the conduct of all embodied beings, their inclinations, and what they have practiced in the past;
having recognized their vigor and strength, and knowing their resolute convictions, they reveal [the Dharma].
By the power of their knowledge, the Leaders display many examples and reasons, along with numerous causes;
having understood the diverse inclinations of sentient beings, they manifest various methods of accomplishment.
I too, the Leader and Lord of Jinas, have now appeared for the sake of bringing happiness to sentient beings;
I manifest this awakening of a Buddha through many thousands of millions of diverse means.
I teach the Dharma in many ways, having understood the inclinations and inner dispositions of living beings;
I gladden them through various means—this is my own power of personal gnosis.
I too behold those impoverished beings, utterly destitute of wisdom and merit;
fallen into the cycle of existence, obstructed in the difficult path, they are submerged once again in a succession of sufferings.
Like a yak caught in a snare, O fool, you are blinded at all times by sensual desires;
you do not seek the Buddha of great majesty, nor do you seek the Dharma that leads to the end of suffering. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 2.111.

With their minds confined within the six realms of existence, remaining unshakable in their adherence to wrong views, they rush from suffering to further suffering; toward them, my compassion is powerful.
Having understood this, I remained at that seat of awakening for a full seven days and three nights,
contemplating this very matter while gazing up at that tree.
I gaze unwinkingly at that king of trees and pace back and forth beneath it;
yet this supreme and wondrous knowledge remains [hidden], while these beings are blinded by delusion and lack understanding.
At that time, Brahmā entreated me, as did Śakra, the four world-protectors,
Maheśvara, Īśvara, and ten trillion hosts of Maruts.
All stand with palms joined in reverence, and I reflect upon their welfare: "How shall I act? I speak the praises of awakening, yet these beings are overwhelmed by sufferings. (Saddhp 2.116)
They will revile my Dharma as the speech of a fool; having reviled it, they shall go to the states of woe.
It would be better for me never to have spoken at all; may my peaceful nirvana occur this very day.
Recalling the Buddhas of the past and how they were skilled in means, [he thought]: "What if I too were to reveal this awakening of a Buddha here by dividing it into three parts? (Saddhp 2.118)
And as I was reflecting thus on this Dharma, the other Buddhas in the ten directions revealed their own bodies to me and uttered the sound: "Excellent! *Saddhp_2.119*

Excellent, O Sage, foremost leader of the world! Having realized here this unsurpassed knowledge, you contemplate skillful means and follow the training of the leaders of the world. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 2.120.
We too shall then proclaim that supreme state of a Buddha, having divided it into three parts;
for men who are ignorant and of inferior inclinations would not believe that they could become Buddhas.
Then, by means of a compendium of causes and practicing skillful means, we, proclaiming the desire for the fruit, have encouraged many bodhisattvas. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 2.122.
At that time, having heard the charming voice of those bulls among men, my heart was uplifted; I spoke to those Protectors: "The supreme Great Seers do not speak with delusion."
I too shall conduct myself in this way, just as the wise leaders of the world declare;
I too shall bring about an upheaval in this dreadful age when beings have arisen amidst the five corruptions.
Then, O Śāriputra, having understood this, at that time I set out for Vārāṇasī;
there, by means of skillful methods, I proclaimed the Dharma— the ground of perfect peace— to the group of five monks.
Then my Wheel of Dharma was set in motion, and the word "nirvāṇa" appeared in the world;
likewise, the word "arhat," the word "Dharma," and the word "Saṅgha" arose there.
I have been speaking for no small number of years, and I reveal the ground of Nirvana;
"This is the end of the suffering of saṃsāra"—thus do I speak at all times.
And at that time, Śāriputra, I saw thousands of millions, no small number, of sons of the Supreme among Men who had set out for the highest, foremost enlightenment. (Saddhp 2.128)
Having approached me, they all stood before me with palms joined in reverence;
by them had been heard the Dharma of the Jinas, consisting of many various kinds of skillful means.
Then, at that moment, this thought occurred to me: "Now is the time for me to speak the supreme Dharma;
I shall here proclaim that foremost enlightenment, for the sake of which I was born into this world."

It will be difficult for those of childish intellect here today to have faith in these signs; for they are ignorant, possessed of overweening pride, and lacking in wisdom. But these bodhisattvas shall indeed hear them.
Then, confident and greatly rejoicing, having abandoned all concealment,
I speak in the midst of the sons of the Sugata and likewise encourage them toward enlightenment.
Having beheld such sons of the Buddha, even your own doubt shall be dispelled;
for these twelve hundred who are free from outflows shall all become Buddhas in this world.

Just as was the nature of the Dharma of those former Protectors and of the future Victors, so too is this my own nature, free from conceptual construction; in that very same way, I shall teach it to you today.
Sometimes, somewhere, and in some way, there occurs the arising of the bulls among men in the world;
and having arisen in the world, those of infinite vision sometimes teach such a Dharma as this.
Such a supreme Dharma is extremely difficult to encounter even in tens of millions of billions of eons;
and such beings as those who, having heard this supreme Dharma, place their faith in it, are likewise extremely rare to find.

Just as the udumbara flower is difficult to find, appearing only at some time, in some place, and in some way; and just as its form would be pleasing to people, it would be a marvel to the world together with its gods.

Therefore, I declare this even more wonderful: having heard this well-spoken Dharma, if one rejoices in it or speaks even a single word of approval, it shall constitute an offering made to all the Buddhas.
"Dispel your hesitation and doubt here; I declare myself the King of Dharma. I exhort you toward supreme enlightenment; there are no śrāvakas here who belong to me."
Śāriputra, let this be your secret, as well as that of all my other disciples;
and may these preeminent bodhisattvas also uphold this secret of mine. (Saddhp_2.140)
For what reason? Because in this age of the five corruptions, sentient beings have become petty and wicked;
their infantile intellects are blinded here by sensual desires, and they never set their minds upon awakening.
And having heard that this single vehicle was revealed by that Jina, beings in a future age might wander astray; by rejecting this sutra, they would go to hell.
To those beings who are modest and pure, and who have set out for supreme, foremost enlightenment,
I speak with confidence of the infinite praises of that single vehicle.
Such is the teaching of the Leaders; this is their most excellent skill in means.
It is expressed through many intentional words, for it is difficult to understand by those who have not trained.
Therefore, understand the intentional speech of the Buddhas, the protectors and teachers of the world;
having abandoned hesitation and cast aside doubt, you shall become Buddhas—arouse joy!
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Skill in Means," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble Lotus of the True Dharma.
(Vaidya 44) Chapter 3: The Parable.
Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra was satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.

Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, facing the Blessed One and gazing intently at him, he said this to the Blessed One: "I have attained a state of wonder and amazement, O Blessed One; I am filled with rapture, having heard such a voice as this from the presence of the Blessed One."
For what reason?

Lord, even before I had heard such a Dharma as this from the presence of the Blessed One, upon seeing other bodhisattvas and hearing that those bodhisattvas would have the name of Buddha in a future age,
I grieved exceedingly and was consumed with intense distress.
"I have indeed fallen away from such a range of Tathāgata-knowledge and from such vision of knowledge.

And whenever, Blessed One, I frequently go to mountains, mountain caves, forest thickets, groves, riverbanks, the roots of trees, or solitary places for my daytime rest, even then, Blessed One, I mostly dwell by means of this very same dwelling."
"Since the entry into the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is indeed equal, we have been led away by the Blessed One by means of an inferior vehicle.
And so, Blessed One, at that time it occurred to me: 'This is our own fault; it is certainly not the fault of the Blessed One.'"

For what reason? Because if we had waited for the Blessed One while he was delivering a preeminent teaching of the Dharma concerning this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, [we would have attained it].
"O Blessed One, we would have attained deliverance through those very same teachings.

However, O Blessed One, because the Bodhisattvas were not present, and because we did not understand the Blessed One’s intentional terminology (*saṃdhābhāṣya*), we— being in haste— heard, took up, retained, cultivated, reflected upon, and attended to the Tathāgata’s very first discourse on the Dharma."
Therefore, Blessed One, I spend most of my days and nights in self-reproach alone.
Today, Blessed One, I have attained nirvāṇa;
today, Blessed One, I am completely extinguished.
"Today, Blessed One, I have attained arhatship.
Today, Blessed One, I am the Blessed One’s eldest son, born from his heart, born from his mouth, born of the Dharma, fashioned by the Dharma, an heir to the Dharma, and produced by the Dharma.
Today, Blessed One, I am free from all burning anguish, having heard from the presence of the Blessed One this kind of marvelous teaching, a sound never heard before."
Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Blessed One with these verses:

“I have attained a state of wonder, O Great Guide, and am filled with joy upon hearing this sound. No further doubt remains for me; I have been brought to maturity here in the supreme vehicle. (Saddhp 3.1)
The voice of the Sugatas is marvelous; it removes the doubt and sorrow of living beings.
For me, whose outflows are exhausted, all sorrow has vanished upon hearing this voice. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 3.2)
While wandering for my midday rest through forest groves, parks, and the roots of trees,
or frequenting mountain caves, I reflected upon this very thought. (Saddhp 3.3)
"Alas! I have been deceived by my evil thoughts regarding the equal, untainted dharmas, in that I shall not teach the supreme dharma within the three realms in the future."
The thirty-two marks have been lost to me, and my golden-colored skin has vanished;
all these powers and liberations have been forsaken. Alas, I am a fool regarding these equal dharmas!
The eighty excellent and distinguished secondary marks of the Great Sages, and the eighteen unique qualities—these too have been lost; I am ruined, I am deceived.
And having seen you, who are compassionate for the welfare of the world, as you were alone wandering for your midday rest, I thought:
"Alas, I have been deceived," because of that inconceivable, unattached knowledge.
O Lord, I spend my days and nights thinking almost exclusively of this;
I shall therefore ask the Blessed One whether I have indeed fallen away or not. (Saddhp 3.8)
And so, O Lord of Jinas, as I reflected thus, days and nights passed for me constantly,
having seen many other bodhisattvas praised by the Leader of the World.
And having heard this Buddha-dharma, which was indeed spoken for the sake of the Saṅgha,
I understand that the Jina, at the seat of enlightenment, brought forth a wisdom that is beyond reasoning, subtle, and free from outflows.
"In the past, I was indeed stuck in views, a wandering mendicant esteemed by the heretics.
Then the Protector, knowing my disposition, spoke of nirvāṇa for the sake of liberating me from those views. (Saddhp 3.11)
Having completely abandoned all those fabricated views and having personally realized that all phenomena are empty, I then understood: "I am extinguished," yet this is not called Nirvana.
But when he becomes a Buddha, the supreme being, honored by humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas,
and possesses a body endowed with the thirty-two marks, there he attains complete nirvāṇa.
Having heard this sound, all my conceits have been removed, and today I am at peace,
since you have prophesied my supreme enlightenment before the world together with its gods.
And great was my trepidation upon first hearing the voice of the Guide, lest this be Māra, the harasser, who had conjured up on earth the appearance of a Buddha. (Saddhp 3.15)

But when that supreme enlightenment of the Buddha was demonstrated through reasons, causes, and millions of billions of similes, and was well-established, then, having heard the Dharma, I became free from doubt.

And when I shall proclaim the names of those thousands of millions of Buddhas, those Jinas who have entered final nirvana, and how this Dharma was taught by them, having established themselves in skillful means; (Saddhp_3.17)
There are many Buddhas yet to come who abide in the world, those who perceive the ultimate truth;
through hundreds of skillful means, they will demonstrate and now do teach the Dharma.
And thus, such was the conduct of yours as it was praised from the time you went forth;
such was the wheel of Dharma of yours regarding the Buddha, and such was your established teaching of the Dharma.
And so I know that this is not Māra; the Lord of the World shows me his true conduct, for indeed no way for Māras exists here. It was only my own mind that had fallen into doubt.
But when I was gladdened by the Buddha’s voice, which is sweet, deep, and beautiful,
then all my doubts were shattered, my uncertainty vanished, and I stood firm in knowledge.
Without doubt, I shall become a Tathāgata, honored in this world including its gods;
I shall proclaim this awakening of a Buddha to the Saṅgha, inciting many bodhisattvas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "I announce to you, Śāriputra;
I declare to you, before this world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and before this generation of recluses and brahmins:
I, Śāriputra, have brought you to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in the presence of twenty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Buddhas."
And you, Śāriputra, have been my disciple for a long time.
You, Śāriputra, were born here in my teaching through the counsel of the bodhisattvas and the secret of the bodhisattvas.
Yet, Śāriputra, because of the empowerment of the bodhisattvas, you do not remember that former vow of conduct, the counsel of the bodhisattvas, and the secret of the bodhisattvas.
"You think, 'I have attained final nirvana.

Śāriputra, desiring to cause you to remember the awakening to the knowledge of your former conduct and vows, I proclaim to the disciples this Dharma discourse, this sūtra, this great vaipulya text, this instruction for bodhisattvas, which is upheld by all the Buddhas: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, in a future time, after immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable eons, you shall uphold the true Dharma of many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Tathāgatas, perform various kinds of worship, and bring this very bodhisattva practice to fulfillment.
"You shall become in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmaprabha—
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One."

Furthermore, Śāriputra, at that time, the Buddha-field of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Padmaprabha, shall be named Viraja; it will be level, delightful, pleasing, most beautiful to behold, utterly pure, prosperous, flourishing, secure, well-supplied with food, and crowded with many hosts of men and women.
It will be strewn with celestial flowers and made of beryl, laid out in a checkerboard pattern of gold threads;
and upon those squares there will be jewel-trees, perpetually and constantly provided with the flowers and fruits of the seven precious gems.
Moreover, Śāriputra, that Tathāgata Padmaprabha, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will teach the Dharma by means of precisely three vehicles.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, although that Tathāgata will not appear during an age of degeneration,
he will nevertheless teach the Dharma through the power of his former vows.
Śāriputra, that eon shall be named Mahāratnapratimaṇḍita (Adorned with Great Jewels). What do you think, Śāriputra? For what reason is that eon called Mahāratnapratimaṇḍita?
Śāriputra, in a Buddha-field, "jewels" refers to bodhisattvas.

At that time, in that world-system Virajā, there will be many bodhisattvas— immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, unfathomable, and beyond all calculation, except by the calculation of a Tathāgata. For that reason, that eon is called Mahāratnapratimaṇḍita (Adorned with Great Jewels).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, at that time, the bodhisattvas in that buddha-field will for the most part be those who stride upon jewel lotuses;
they will be bodhisattvas who are not beginners,
having long cultivated roots of virtue and having practiced the holy life under many hundreds of thousands of buddhas.

Praised by the Tathāgatas, devoted to the wisdom of the Buddhas, perfected through the cultivation of the great superknowledges, skilled in the methods of all dharmas, gentle, and mindful— Śāriputra, that buddha-field will for the most part be filled with such bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, the lifespan of that Tathāgata Padmaprabha will be twelve intermediate kalpas, excluding the period of his youth.
And the lifespan of those beings will be eight intermediate kalpas.

Then, Śāriputra, at the conclusion of those twelve intermediate kalpas, that Tathāgata Padmaprabha, having prophesied the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Dhṛtiparipūrṇa to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
He will attain parinirvāṇa.
Monks, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Dhṛtiparipūrṇa will, immediately after me, realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
he will become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmavṛṣabhavikrāmin in the world, endowed with knowledge and conduct.

The Sugata, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One— Śāriputra, the Buddha-field of that Tathāgata Padmavṛṣabhavikrāmin shall also be of such a nature.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, after that Tathāgata Padmaprabha has passed into parinirvāṇa, his true Dharma will remain for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
Then, when that true Dharma of his has perished, a semblance of the true Dharma will remain for thirty-two intermediate kalpas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "O Śārisuta, in a future age, you too shall become a Jina, a Tathāgata."
Named Padmaprabha and possessing universal vision, you shall discipline tens of billions of living beings.
Having performed acts of veneration toward many millions of Buddhas and having acquired the power of conduct therein,
and having generated the ten powers, you shall touch the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
In an inconceivable and immeasurable eon, there will then be an eon called Prabhūtaratna;
at that time, the world-system of that supreme among bipeds will be a pure field named Virajā.
The ground was likewise strewn with lapis lazuli and adorned with golden threads;
it was endowed with hundreds of beautiful jewel-trees, decorated with fruits and flowers.
In that field there are many bodhisattvas endowed with mindfulness, who are highly skilled in accomplishing the conduct;
those who have trained in the conduct under hundreds of Buddhas are born in that realm.
If, in his final existence, that Jina, having passed through the stage of youth,
shall renounce desires and go forth into homelessness, he will realize the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
At that time, the lifespan of that Jina will be twelve intermediate kalpas;
the measure of the lifespan of those humans there will be eight intermediate kalpas.
Even after that Jina has entered parinirvāṇa, his true Dharma will remain for a full thirty-two intermediate kalpas; at that time, it shall exist for the benefit of the world, including its devas.
When the True Dharma has perished, its semblance will remain for thirty-two intermediate eons;
the body of that Protector will be widely disseminated and constantly honored by humans and gods. (Saddhp_3.31)
Such will that Blessed One be; therefore, O Śārisuta, be filled with joy!
You yourself shall become such a one—the unsurpassed among bipeds, invincible.

Then indeed, those four assemblies—the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; and the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—having heard from the presence of the Blessed One this prophecy of the Venerable Śāriputra regarding his unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; they covered the Blessed One with their respective robes.
Śakra, the lord of the gods, and Brahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, along with hundreds of thousands of millions of other sons of the gods, covered the Blessed One with divine garments;
they scattered divine māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers over him,
and they caused divine robes to flutter in the air above.
Hundreds of thousands of divine musical instruments and drums resounded in the sky above;

and having rained down a great shower of flowers, they spoke these words: "Formerly, the Blessed One turned the wheel of Dharma at Ṛṣipatana in the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī; but today, the Blessed One has once again turned this unsurpassed second wheel of Dharma."
And at that time, those sons of the gods spoke these verses:
"O Peerless One in the world, O Great Hero, you have set in motion the Wheel of Dharma in Vārāṇasī, [revealing] the arising and passing away of the aggregates."
The first was set in motion there, O Leader; this second one, which you have taught today, O Guide, is difficult for them to believe.
We have heard many teachings in the presence of the Lord of the World,
yet never before have we heard a teaching such as this.
We rejoice, O Great Hero, in the intentional discourse of the Great Seer;
for this confident Śāriputra has indeed been prophesied according to the truth.
"May we too become such supreme Buddhas in the world,
teaching the unsurpassed enlightenment of a Buddha through intentional speech."
Whatever we have heard or done in this world or in another, and whatever way we have pleased the Buddha— may this aspiration be for the sake of awakening.

Then, indeed, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, I am free from doubt and have transcended all uncertainty, having heard directly from the presence of the Blessed One this prophecy concerning myself regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."

And as for these twelve hundred who have attained mastery, O Blessed One, whom the Blessed One previously established on the stage of training and instructed thus, and exhorted thus: "Monks, this is the culmination of my Dharma and Vinaya, namely, the complete transcendence of birth, old age, sickness, death, and sorrow, and the convergence upon Nirvana."

And these two thousand bhikṣus, O Blessed One— both those in training and those beyond training, the disciples of the Blessed One, all of whom were free from the view of self, the view of existence, the view of non-existence, and all views,
and who considered themselves to be established on the plane of nirvāṇa—
upon hearing this kind of Dharma, never heard before, from the presence of the Blessed One, have fallen into a state of doubt.
Therefore, may the Blessed One please speak for the sake of dispelling the remorse of these monks, so that, O Blessed One, these four assemblies may become free from doubt and free from uncertainty.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, have I not already explained to you that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, having understood the dispositions of beings who possess various inclinations and various elements and intentions, teaches the Dharma through various demonstrations, explanations, diverse causes, reasons, illustrations, objective supports, etymologies, and skillful means?"
Starting from this very unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, he causes [beings] to take up the Bodhisattva vehicle alone through all his teachings of the Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, I shall provide you with a parable for the sake of further illustrating this very point.
Why is that?
In this world, some wise persons understand the meaning of what has been spoken through a simile.

It is just as if, Śāriputra, there were here in some village, city, town, district, region, kingdom, or capital a householder who was aged, elderly, advanced in years, and having reached old age, yet he was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments.
And his residence would be large, lofty, and extensive; it would have been built long ago and was dilapidated, serving as a dwelling for two, three, four, or five hundred living beings;
that residence had but a single door and was thatched with grass.
The palace would be crumbling;
its pillars and foundations would be rotten; and its walls and plaster would be completely decayed.
And suddenly, by means of a great mass of fire, the entire dwelling would be set ablaze on all sides;
and that man would have many young children— perhaps five, ten, or twenty—
and that man would have gone out from that dwelling.

Then, Śāriputra, that man, seeing his own house set ablaze on all sides by a great mass of fire, would become afraid, terrified, and anxious in mind, and he would reflect thus: "I am capable of quickly escaping from this burning house through the gate in safety, remaining untouched and unburnt by this great mass of fire."
To run out! But these young children of mine, these boys, who are playing, sporting, and diverting themselves with various toys right here in this very house that is on fire,
do not know, do not perceive, do not understand, do not realize, and do not feel alarm regarding this burning house.
Though being scorched by this great mass of fire and touched by this great mass of suffering, they do not attend to the suffering in their minds,
nor do they give rise to the thought of escaping.
And that man, Śāriputra, would be strong and possessed of great physical strength;
he would think to himself: "I am strong and possessed of great physical strength."
"What if I were to gather all these boys together into one mass, take them up in my lap, and lead them out of this house?
He would then reflect further: "This dwelling indeed has but a single entrance, and its door is closed;
moreover, the boys are fickle, restless, and of a childish nature."
Lest they wander about and,
by means of this great mass of fire, meet with misfortune and ruin;
what if I were now to urge them on?
Having reflected thus, he addressed those young boys: "Come, sirs, young boys!
Come out!
This house is ablaze with a great mass of fire."
"Lest you all be consumed right here by this great mass of fire and fall into ruin and calamity.

Yet those boys did not understand what that man, desiring their welfare, had said; they were not alarmed, they were not terrified, they were not frightened, they did not tremble, nor did they fall into a state of panic.
They do not reflect upon it, nor do they run away;
they neither know nor understand what this "blazing" actually is.
Instead, they merely run and rush about here and there.
Again and again they look toward their father;
for what reason?
Because of their state of childhood.
Then that man would reflect thus: "This house is on fire, set ablaze by a great mass of flames.
Let it not be that I and these children shall meet with calamity and disaster right here through this great mass of flames.
What if I were to use skillful means to get these children out of this house?"
And that man would know the disposition of those boys and understand their inclinations;
for those boys would have many kinds of various playthings, diverse, delightful, desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing.
And those would be difficult to obtain.
Then that man, knowing the disposition of those boys, said this to them: "Boys, those toys of yours which are delightful, wonderful, and marvelous—
those for the lack of which you were distressed—
which are of various colors and many kinds,"
They were as follows: ox-carts, goat-carts, and deer-carts—
those which were desirable, lovely, dear, and pleasing to you—
and all of these have been placed by me outside the gate of the residence for the purpose of your play.
"Come, sirs, and emerge from this dwelling!
Whatever anyone among you may require or have need of, I shall give that very thing to each of them."
"Come quickly for their sake; run out!
Then those boys, for the sake of those delightful toys—desirable, as they had imagined, and pleasing—[rushed out].

Hearing the names of their beloved, dear, and charming women, they immediately exerted their vigor from that burning house and, with great speed, not waiting for one another— each thinking "Who will be first? Who will be even sooner?"— they crowded against one another with their bodies and quickly rushed out from that burning house.

Then that man, seeing those boys had come out safely and well, and perceiving that they had attained fearlessness, sat down in the open air at the village crossroads; filled with joy and gladness, free from grasping, with hindrances gone, he became one who had attained fearlessness. Then indeed those boys approached where their father was.

Having approached him, they would say: "Father, give us those various delightful toys, such as little bullock-carts, goat-carts, and deer-carts. Then, Śāriputra, that man [gave] to his own sons those [carts] endowed with the speed of the wind.
He should provide small chariots made of the seven precious gems, equipped with railings and hung with networks of tinkling bells;
they are lofty, grasped by handles, adorned with wonderful and marvelous jewels, beautified with strings of gems, decorated with flower garlands, furnished with cushions of cotton and wool,
spread with fine cloth coverlets, provided with red pillows on both sides, and yoked to white, bright, swift-running oxen.
He would give to each individual boy ox-carts that are attended by many men, adorned with victory banners, endowed with the speed and power of the wind, and of various colors and types.
For what reason?
For instance, Śāriputra, that man might be wealthy, possess great riches, and have abundant storehouses.
He would think to himself: "It is enough for me to give these boys other vehicles.
And why is that?
All these young boys are indeed my own sons; all are dear and pleasing to me.
And I possess such great vehicles as these.
I must regard all these children equally, not unequally;
for I possess many treasuries and storehouses,
and I would give such great vehicles as these to all sentient beings as well.
How much more so, then, for his own sons?
And at that time, those children, having mounted those great vehicles, would experience something marvelous and extraordinary.
What do you think, Śāriputra, could there be any falsehood in that man’s words?
"How is it that, having first shown those boys three vehicles, you subsequently gave them all only Mahāyānas— indeed, only sublime vehicles?
Śāriputra said, "Certainly not so, Blessed One."
Indeed, Sugata,

for this very reason, O Blessed One, that man would not be a speaker of falsehood, since by means of his skill in upāya those children were led out from that burning house and provided with their lives.
For what reason?
Blessed One, by the very acquisition of their own bodies, all toys have already been obtained.
Even if, Blessed One, that man were not to give even a single chariot to those children, [they would still be satisfied].
Nevertheless, Blessed One, that man would not be a speaker of falsehood.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, that man had previously reflected thus: "By means of skillful artifice, I shall deliver these children from that great mass of suffering."
By this reasoning also, O Blessed One, there would be no falsehood for that man;

how much less so when that man, considering his own great treasury and storehouses to exist and out of love for his sons, being full of praise, gave them vehicles of a single color, namely, the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna)?
"O Blessed One, there is no falsehood on the part of that man."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Śāriputra: "Excellent, excellent, Śāriputra!
It is so, Śāriputra; it is just as you say."

In the same way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has turned away from all fears; he is entirely and in every respect liberated from all calamities, distresses, misfortunes, suffering, dejection, and the veils of the darkness, gloom, and cataracts of ignorance.

Endowed with the powers of knowledge, the grounds of self-confidence, and the unique qualities of a Buddha, the Tathāgata is exceedingly powerful through the power of his supernormal faculties; he is the Father of the world.

Having attained the supreme perfection of the knowledge of great skillful means, he is one of great compassion, whose mind is untiring, who seeks their welfare, and is full of pity. He appears within the triple world— which is like a dwelling with a roof and walls that are old and ablaze with a great mass of suffering and dejection— for the sake of beings who are established in the darkness, gloom, and cataracts of ignorance, and who are enveloped by birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair.

For the sake of liberating [beings] from passion, hatred, and delusion, and for the sake of inciting them toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; as soon as he was born, he saw beings being burned, cooked, tormented, and consumed by birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.

For the sake of enjoyment and on account of the cause of sensual desire, they experience many kinds of suffering. On account of seeking and on account of grasping, they will experience many kinds of suffering pertaining to this life and the future life in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama;
they also experience the sufferings of poverty among gods and humans, as well as the suffering of union with the unpleasant and separation from the pleasant.
And while revolving within that very mass of suffering, they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves;
they do not tremble, they are not terrified, they do not fall into fear; they do not awaken, they do not perceive, they are not distressed, and they do not seek an escape.
And therein, within this triple world which resembles a house on fire, they take their delight.
They run about in various ways,
and though struck by that great mass of suffering, they do not produce the perception of mental attention directed toward suffering.
In this regard, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata perceives thus: "I am indeed the father of these beings;
for by me these beings must be liberated from this very great mass of suffering, and by me the immeasurable and inconceivable bliss of the Buddha-knowledge must be bestowed upon these beings."
By means of which these beings will play, rejoice, enjoy themselves, and perform various sports.

In this regard, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata perceives thus: "If, thinking 'I possess the power of knowledge' and thinking 'I possess the power of supernatural transformations,' I were to [teach] these beings the powers and fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata's knowledge without employing skillful means, these beings would not depart by means of these dharmas.
Why is that?
For these beings are intent upon the five strands of sensual pleasure and the delights of the three realms;
they are not liberated from birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
they are burned, cooked, tormented, and consumed by anguish.
"How will these [beings] enjoy the wisdom of a Buddha, having not yet escaped from the triple world, which is like a dwelling with a roof and walls that are burning and dilapidated?

In this regard, Śāriputra, just as that man, though possessing great physical strength, sets aside his physical strength and instead uses skillful means to lead those children out from that burning house; so too does the Tathāgata act.
Having caused them to emerge, he would subsequently give them magnificent great vehicles;

in the very same way, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One— endowed with the powers and fearlessnesses of Tathāgata-knowledge, yet setting aside those powers and fearlessnesses for a time— through the knowledge of skillful means, displays three vehicles, namely the Śrāvaka-vehicle, for the purpose of causing sentient beings to emerge from the triple world, which resembles a house that is burning, dilapidated, and covered in thatch.
[He teaches] the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas and the vehicle of the Bodhisattvas.

With these three vehicles, he entices sentient beings and speaks to them thus: "Sirs, do not take delight in this triple world, which is like a house on fire, nor in inferior forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles."
For here you are delighted in the triple world; you are burned, tormented, and consumed by craving accompanied by the five strands of sensual pleasure.
Run forth from this triple world!
You shall attain the three vehicles, namely: the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas.
I am your guarantor in this matter;
I shall give you these three vehicles.
Exert yourselves for the sake of escaping from the triple world.
And thus I entice them: "O beings, these things are noble and praised by the noble ones, and are endowed with great delight.
With these, you shall play, rejoice, and enjoy yourselves without meanness;
and through the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments, you shall experience great joy."
And you shall be endowed with great happiness and mental well-being.
In that regard, Śāriputra, those beings who are of a wise nature place their deep faith in the Tathāgata, the Father of the World.
Having placed their faith in the teaching of the Tathāgata, they apply themselves and exert effort.

Among them, some beings, desiring to follow after hearing the voice of another, apply themselves to the teaching of the Tathāgata for the sake of their own parinirvāṇa and for the realization of the Four Noble Truths;
these are said to be those who, desiring the Śrāvaka vehicle, flee from the triple world.
It is just as if, from that burning house, some children had run out desiring deer-carts;

likewise, other beings, desiring knowledge without a teacher, self-control, and tranquility, and for the sake of their own parinirvāṇa and the realization of causes and conditions, apply themselves to the teaching of the Tathāgata—
they are said to run out from the triple world desiring the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas.
It is just as if, from that burning house, some children had run out seeking a goat-cart;
yet other beings, desiring the knowledge of omniscience, the knowledge of a Buddha, self-arisen knowledge, and knowledge that is without a teacher,
act for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings.
For the sake of the parinirvāṇa of all beings— both gods and humans— and for the realization of the Tathāgata’s knowledge, powers, and fearlessnesses,
they apply themselves to the teaching of the Tathāgata.
They are said to be those who, desiring the Mahāyāna, rush forth from the triple world.
For that reason, they are called bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas.
It is just as if, from that burning house, some of the children had run out desiring ox-carts;
it is just as if, Śāriputra, that man [were to see] those boys having run out from that burning house.
Having seen that they were completely liberated through safety and well-being and had attained fearlessness, and knowing himself to be possessed of great wealth,

he would bestow upon those children a single, magnificent vehicle; even so, Śāriputra, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, perceives many millions of beings [liberated] from the triple world...

They were completely liberated; they were freed from suffering, fear, terror, and calamity, having emerged through the gateway of the Tathāgata’s teaching and been released from all the wildernesses of fear and misfortune. They had attained the bliss of nirvāṇa, having reached the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra, at that time, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— knowing that he possesses an abundant treasury of the power of great wisdom and fearlessness,
and knowing that all these beings are indeed his own sons— causes those beings to attain final nirvāṇa by means of the Buddha-vehicle alone;
yet he does not speak of a personal, individual nirvāṇa for any being whatsoever.
And he brings all those sentient beings to final nirvana through the Tathāgata’s great parinirvāṇa;
and those sentient beings, Śāriputra, who have become fully liberated from the triple world—
To them the Tathāgata gives the noble, supreme blisses of the meditations, liberations, concentrations, and attainments as their playthings and delights,
all of which are of a single color. Śāriputra, it would be as if that man were not speaking falsely.

Just as that man, having displayed three vehicles, gave to all those children only a single Great Vehicle— one made of the seven precious gems, adorned with every ornament, uniform in appearance, a magnificent vehicle, indeed the foremost vehicle for all— so too, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is not a speaker of falsehood.
By means of which skill in means he first displays three vehicles and subsequently leads sentient beings to final nirvāṇa by the Great Vehicle alone—
for what reason? Because,

Śāriputra, the Tathāgata is endowed with a vast treasury and storehouse of the power of knowledge and the grounds of self-confidence, and is thus capable [of bestowing] upon all sentient beings that which is accompanied by the knowledge of the All-Knowing One.
In order to demonstrate the Dharma,
Śāriputra, by this method also it should be understood that the Tathāgata, through the accomplishment of the knowledge of skillful means, teaches only the single Great Vehicle.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Just as if a man should have a house that is old, vast, and very weak;
its upper stories would be crumbling, and the pillars would be rotten at their bases."
The palace had its windows and upper stories with parts fallen away, its walls crumbling and its plaster peeling;
it was dilapidated, with its raised platforms overgrown and torn out, and its thatched roof falling down on all sides.
There would be the dwelling place for no fewer than five hundred living beings;
moreover, there would be many cramped courtyards filled with excrement and loathsome.
All the rafters there have fallen away, and likewise the walls and partitions have collapsed;
tens of millions of vultures dwell there, as do pigeons, owls, and other birds.
In those various regions there are fierce venomous serpents, terrible with potent poisons;
there are also vicitrikas, scorpions, and mice—these are the dwellings of such extremely wicked creatures.
In various places, moreover, they were infested by non-human beings and defiled by excrement and urine;
they were filled with worms, insects, and fireflies, and resounded with the howling of dogs and jackals.
There are fierce bheruṇḍakas there, devouring human corpses,
and many dogs and jackals dwell there, waiting for their exit.
Weak and constantly overcome by hunger, they roam from place to place devouring one another; quarreling and shouting, they make that house sound most terrifying. (Saddhp 3.46)
Even yakṣas with extremely fierce minds dwell there, tearing apart human corpses;
in various places throughout that region, centipedes, *gonasaka* snakes, and wild beasts also reside.
In various regions, they build dwellings for their young ones and deposit them there;
yet, as soon as they are deposited, those yakṣas devour them once again.

And when those yakṣas, having devoured other beings with their most fierce minds, become satiated and their bodies are fully satisfied with the flesh of other beings, they then engage in violent quarreling there.
In those ruined dwellings there dwell kumbhāṇḍas of cruel and fierce mind;
measuring a span, a cubit, or two cubits in height, they wander about.
And they too, seizing the dogs by their legs and throwing them onto the ground on their backs,
and likewise choking them by the necks, take delight there in threatening and harassing them.
Pretas of various kinds—black as well as weak, tall and large—dwell there;
hungry and searching for food, they cry out with piteous voices here and there.
Some with needle-like faces and some with ox-like faces, the size of humans or even dogs,
with disheveled hair, they utter cries while being tormented by the thirst for food.
And here, those yakṣas, pretas, piśācas, and vultures, constantly looking out through the windows and lattice openings in all four directions, are searching for food.
Such would be that terrifying house— vast, lofty, yet very weak,
dilapidated, fragile, and transient— and it would be the possession of a single man.
And suppose that man were outside the house, and that dwelling were set ablaze,
suddenly and on all four sides, blazing with thousands of flames.
The bamboo and the timbers, scorched by the fire, produce a heavy and most terrifying sound;
likewise, the pillars and the walls are ablaze, while yakṣas and pretas let out their cries.
Scorched by flames, hundreds of vultures and many kumbhāṇḍas with singed faces wander about;
and all around, hundreds of beasts of prey, being burned, roar and shriek there.
Many Piśācas of little merit wander there, tormented by fire;
tearing one another with their teeth, they drench each other with blood while burning.
There, bheruṇḍaka beasts and those who have passed away devour one another;
excrement burns, and a foul odor wafts through the four directions of the world.
Centipedes flee in all directions, while *kumbhāṇḍas* devour them;
and hungry ghosts with flaming hair wander about, burning with the heat of hunger. (Saddhp 3.61)
O Bhairava, such was that dwelling, with thousands of flames indeed issuing forth;
and that man, the master of that house, stood at the door, looking on.
And there he hears his sons, their minds intent on play, playing with toys;
they delight themselves, intoxicated by their playthings, just like children who do not understand.
Having heard this, he quickly entered there for the sake of liberating his children,
lest all these young children of mine be burned and perish instantly.
He speaks to them of the defects of that house: "O noble sons, this is a terrible suffering!
There are various beings here, and this great fire—a succession of miseries indeed. (Saddhp 3.65)
Vipers, yakṣas with most fierce minds, many kumbhāṇḍas and pretas dwell there;
as well as packs of bheruṇḍakas, dogs, and jackals, and vultures seeking food.
Many such beings dwell here, which is extremely terrifying even without fire;
this suffering is of such a nature alone, yet this fire is blazing on all sides.
Thus being exhorted, those children of immature intellect, distracted by their playthings, did not consider what their father was saying, nor did they pay any attention to him. (Saddhp 3.68)
And that man, being deeply distressed there at that time, would think: "I am suffering greatly here with anxiety for my sons;
what use have I for these sons who are childless? Let it not be that they are burned here by this fire."
At that time, he devised this skillful means: "These children are greedy for toys;
yet there is no play nor any delight here at all—alas, such is the deluded nature of children! (Saddhp_3.70)
He said to them, "Listen, young men! I have various kinds of vehicles:
yoked with deer, goats, and excellent oxen; they are lofty, large, and well-adorned."
"Run out from this dwelling; with those [toys], do what you need to do!
For your sake I had them made; come out together, having met with joyful minds! ||| Saddhp_3.72 |||
Having heard of such vehicles, they all exerted their vigor and, becoming swift, rushed out at that very moment; freed from suffering, they stood in the open air.
And that man, having seen the boys come out, stood in the middle of the village at the crossroads;
sitting upon his lion-throne, he said to them: "O friends, today I have attained peace!"
Those twenty young sons of mine, my beloved legitimate children, whom I obtained with great difficulty through my asceticism—
they were in a dreadful, dilapidated house, filled with many creatures and most terrifying.
While that house was ablaze, filled with thousands of flames, you were devoted to your pleasures and amusements;
yet today I have liberated you all, by which you have now attained nirvāṇa.
Knowing that their father was dwelling in comfort, those children approached him and spoke thus: "Father, give us the three kinds of delightful vehicles, just as you promised."
If all that was spoken by you there in that house, dear father, is indeed true, then I shall bestow the three kinds of vehicles; give them now, for this is the time for them here today.
And that man would possess a treasury of great strength, consisting of gold, silver, jewels, and pearls;
he would have abundant gold and slaves, and various kinds of vehicles would be provided for him.
There were excellent ox-carts made of jewels, provided with railings and draped with networks of tinkling bells;
they were adorned with parasols and banners, and covered with lattices of pearls and gems.
With garlands made of golden flowers hanging down in every region, they were covered with noble cloths and spread over with excellent white fine fabrics.
Likewise, those chariots there were spread with soft silken cloths and excellent cotton mattresses;
they were further covered with choice blankets worth thousands of millions, marked with the figures of geese, cranes, and swans.
White, well-nourished, powerful oxen, of great size and beautiful to behold—
those yoked to those jewel-adorned chariots were attended by many men. (Saddhp 3.83)
That man bestows such excellent and distinguished boons upon all his sons;
and they too, satisfied and joyful in mind, go about playing in every direction and intermediate quarter.
In the same way, Śārisuta, I am the great seer who is the protection and the father of sentient beings;
and all these living creatures, those fools clinging to desires within the triple world, are my sons.
And just as that dwelling was most terrifying, strewn with hundreds of sufferings, so too is the triple world ablaze on all sides without exception by many hundreds of births, old age, and diseases.
I am liberated from the triple world, peaceful, dwelling alone in the forest;
yet this triple world is my domain, for those who are burned therein are my sons.
I perceived the danger therein and recognized that I alone was their protector;
yet all those fools did not listen to me, for their intellects were so entangled in sensual desires.
I employ skillful means and proclaim these three vehicles for them;
having recognized the manifold faults within the triple world, I teach this method for the sake of their escape.
And those sons who rely upon me— those of great majesty possessing the six supernormal powers and the three types of knowledge,
as well as the pratyekabuddhas here and the bodhisattvas who are irreversible in this world. (Saddhp_3.90)

O wise one, at that very moment, by means of this excellent parable, I declare to those sons who are equal [to me]: "This single Buddha-vehicle is what you must all embrace; you shall all become Jinas."

And that knowledge of the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds, is most excellent, delightful, and distinguished in form throughout all the world; it is of noble character and likewise worthy of homage. (Saddhp 3.92)
The powers, the meditations, as well as the liberations, and many hundreds of millions of concentrations—
such is this most excellent chariot, in which the sons of the Buddha always delight.
Playing with this, they pass nights and days, fortnights, seasons, and months;
they pass years, intermediate eons, and even thousands of millions of eons.
By means of this most excellent vehicle made of jewels, many bodhisattvas who sport here at the seat of enlightenment, as well as those disciples of the Sugata who hear it, proceed.
Understand this now, Tiṣya: there is no second vehicle anywhere here, even if one were to search all ten directions, except for the skillful means of the Supreme Men.
"You are my sons, and I am your father; by me you have been delivered from suffering—having been scorched for many millions of eons within this triple world, which is so terrifying and fearsome."

And thus I declare there that you have attained nirvana, even though you are not yet truly liberated; you are freed here from the sufferings of saṃsāra, but the Buddha-vehicle must still be sought. (Saddhp 3.98)
And whatever bodhisattvas are here, let them all hear my guidance as a Buddha—
this skillful means of the Jina, by which he leads many bodhisattvas.
When sentient beings here take delight in base and loathsome desires,
then the Leader of the World, whose speech is never otherwise, proclaims the Noble Truth of suffering.
Furthermore, those of childish intellect who, not understanding suffering, do not perceive its root here—I show them the path; for craving is the origin and the source of suffering.
The cessation of craving, which is forever non-reliant—this is my third truth, the truth of cessation.
By means of this, which is unchanging, a person is liberated; for by cultivating the path, one becomes emancipated.

And from what are they liberated, O Śārisuta? They are liberated from grasping at the unreal; yet they are not yet liberated in every respect. The Leader declares here that they are not yet in final nirvāṇa.
For what reason do I not speak of his liberation, until he has attained this supreme, foremost enlightenment?
This is my wish: that I, as a King of Dharma, have been born here in this world for the sake of bringing happiness.

This, Śāriputra, is my Dharma-seal, which I have spoken today in this final age; for the benefit of the world including its gods, teach it in all directions and intermediate directions. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 3.105)
And if any being should speak to you, saying, "I rejoice in this," and should accept this sutra upon their head, you should regard that person as irreversible.
He has seen former Tathāgatas and has rendered them honor;
he has heard this very kind of Dharma, which one who has faith in this sūtra would hear.
Both you and I shall be seen, as will this entire community of my monks;
and all these bodhisattvas shall be seen by whoever has faith in what I have spoken.
This sutra, which deludes foolish people, has been spoken here for those with the knowledge of supernormal powers;
for this is not the domain of the śrāvakas, nor is it the range of the pratyekabuddhas.
Śāriputra, even my resolve is based on faith; how much more so these other disciples of mine?
They too proceed by faith alone toward me, for they do not possess personal, individual knowledge.
Do not speak this to those who are arrogant or conceited, nor to those who are not practitioners of yoga;
for fools, always intoxicated by sensual desires, being ignorant, would reject the Dharma as it is spoken.
Having rejected my skill in means— which is the guidance of the Buddhas that always abides in the world—
and having cast it aside with a frown, hear now of the intense retribution for that act.

Having rejected a sūtra of this kind while I am still present or after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, or having harbored malice toward those monks— listen here to the ripening of their karma. (Saddhp 3.113)
Having passed away from among humans, they shall dwell in the Avīci hell for a full kalpa;
thereafter, having died again and again for many intermediate kalpas, those fools fall back into that same place.
And when they have passed away from the hells, they go further into the realm of animals;
becoming extremely weak dogs or jackals, they become playthings for others.
Because of that, their complexion becomes black, mottled, scarred, and itchy;
they become hairless and exceedingly weak, as they harbor hatred toward my supreme enlightenment.
They are constantly despised among living beings, beaten by blows from clods of earth and weeping;
terrified here and there by the staff, they are struck by hunger and thirst, their limbs withered.

Furthermore, those of childish intellect who reject the guidance of the Buddha will become camels or donkeys, carrying heavy burdens while being beaten with whips and sticks, constantly preoccupied with thoughts of food.
Furthermore, they become jackals there, loathsome, one-eyed, and crippled;
these fools are tormented by village boys and struck with clods of earth.
Then, having passed away from there, those fools again become beings with bodies fifty yojanas long; they are dull, deluded, and continue to wander in saṃsāra.
They become footless creatures that crawl on their bellies, being devoured by many millions of living beings;
they experience most terrible sensations because they have rejected a sūtra such as this. (Saddhp 3.121)

And when they obtain a human body, they become crippled, deformed, hunchbacked, one-eyed, dull-witted, and wretched there—those who have no faith in this sūtra of mine. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 3.122.
They become untrustworthy in the world, and a foul odor blows from their mouths;
the spirit-grasping Yakṣa enters their bodies because they lack faith in this awakening of the Buddha.
They are poor, they are grinders [of grain], and they are constant attendants to others; being weak, many afflictions befall them, and they dwell in the world as those who have become protectorless.
To whomever they offer their service there, he becomes unwilling to give them anything; even what has been given perishes very quickly—such indeed is the fruit of evil.

Moreover, whatever medicine they obtain there, even if it is of the most appropriate kind and administered by skilled practitioners, by that very means their ailment increases further; that disease never reaches its end.
Furthermore, thefts committed by others, as well as riots, civil commotions, and conflicts, and the plundering of property by others, fall upon that person of evil karma. (Saddhp 3.127)
He shall never behold the Lord of the World, the King of Men who rules the earth;
for by rejecting this guidance of my Buddhahood, he will indeed dwell only in the states of no opportunity. (Saddhp 3.128)
Furthermore, that fool does not hear the Dharma; he becomes deaf and senseless.
Having rejected such enlightenment as this, he never attains peace.
For many thousands, nayutas, and even more millions of eons, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one becomes dull-witted and impaired; this is the evil fruit of having rejected this sutra.
For him, the pleasure groves become hell; his dwelling place is the realm of misery.
When he is established here, there are always wild boars, pigs, jackals, and earth-worms.
Even having attained human status, he falls into blindness, deafness, or dull-wittedness;
he becomes a servant to others and is constantly poor—these are his ornaments at that time.
And his garments will become diseased; there will be millions of billions of sores upon his body, as well as scabies, itching, ringworm, leprosy, vitiligo, and a putrid stench.
His view of a self-existent body becomes dense, and the power of his anger is aroused;
his passion becomes exceedingly intense, and he always delights in the wombs of animals.
If today, Śārisuta, I were to speak of the faults of one who would revile this sutra of mine for an entire eon,
it would not be possible to reach the end of those faults.
Perceiving this very purpose, Śāriputra, I instruct you:
do not ever speak a sūtra of this kind in the presence of foolish people. (Saddhp_3.136)
But those here who are manifest, of great learning, possessed of mindfulness, wise, and endowed with knowledge—
those who have set out for supreme, foremost enlightenment— to them you should cause this ultimate truth to be heard.
To those who have seen many millions of Buddhas, who have planted immeasurable roots of merit,
and whose resolute intention is firm— to them you should proclaim this ultimate truth.
To those who are energetic and always possess a mind of loving-kindness, who cultivate loving-kindness here for a long time,
and who have renounced both body and life— to them you should recite this sutra in their presence.
They share mutual intentions and are full of reverence; they have no intimacy with the young.
You should cause those who are content in mountain caves to hear this auspicious sutra.
Attending upon spiritual friends and avoiding evil companions—
reveal this sutra to those sons of the Buddha whom you see who are such as these.

Those sons of the Buddha who possess faultless morality, who are like precious jewels, and who are established in the upholding of the Vaipulya sutras— when you see such ones, recite this sutra in their presence.
To those who are never angry and are always upright, who are endowed with compassion for all living beings,
and who possess reverence toward the Sugata— in their presence you should recite this sutra. (Saddhp_3.143)
To him who, having attained non-attachment, speaks the Dharma in the midst of the assembly with a disciplined mind,
you should present this sutra with many millions of billions of parables.
He who, joining his palms above his head and seeking the state of omniscience, should wander through the ten directions as a monk searching for the well-spoken word; ||| Saddhp_3.145 ||
One should uphold the Vaipulya sūtras, and never take pleasure in others;
one should not hold even a single verse from elsewhere—teach this supreme sūtra to them.
Just as a man might search for a relic of the Tathāgata, so too is he who searches for such a sūtra; having found it, he should bear it upon his head.
Have no concern for other sūtras, nor for the Lokāyata or other such treatises;
such are the spheres of activity of fools—you should avoid them and proclaim this [sūtra].
Śāriputra, even if I were to speak for an entire eon, I could describe thousands of millions of aspects;
you should preach this sutra before those who have set out for the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Parable," in the Dharma-discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 71) Chapter Four: On Resolute Belief.
Then, indeed, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Mahākātyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, and the venerable...

Having heard this kind of Dharma, never before heard, from the presence of the Blessed One, and having heard the prophecy concerning the Venerable Śāriputra regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, Mahāmaudgalyāyana was struck with wonder, struck with amazement, and filled with joy; at that moment, he rose from his seat and approached the Blessed One.

Having approached, they arranged their upper robes over one shoulder, placed their right knees upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, they gazed up at the Blessed One with bodies bent forward, stooped, and deeply inclined. At that time, they said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we are indeed aged and decrepit."
"Blessed One, we are elders in this community of monks, esteemed as seniors; worn out by old age, we have thought, 'We have attained nirvāṇa.
Thus, Blessed One, we are without exertion regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; we lack the power for it and lack the undertaking of vigor."
Even when the Blessed One teaches the Dharma and has been seated for a long time, we remain present throughout that teaching of the Dharma.

Even then, Blessed One, as we have sat for a long time and attended upon the Blessed One for a long time, our limbs and members ache, and our joints and articulations ache. Therefore, Blessed One, while the Blessed One is teaching the Dharma, we manifest everything— emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
We did not conceive a longing for these Buddha-qualities, nor for the arrays of Buddha-fields, nor for the playful displays of bodhisattvas, nor for the playful displays of Tathāgatas.
Why is that?
Because, Blessed One, we had fled from this triple world with the notion that it was nirvāṇa.
And we ourselves have grown old with age;
therefore, Blessed One, we too have exhorted other bodhisattvas toward unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment,
and have instructed them.
And, Blessed One, not even a single thought of longing arose in us regarding that.

But now, Blessed One, having heard from the presence of the Blessed One that even for the śrāvakas there is a prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, we have attained what is marvelous and extraordinary; we have attained a great gain.
"Blessed One, having today suddenly heard this kind of voice of the Tathāgata, never heard before, we have obtained a great jewel.
Blessed One, we have obtained immeasurable jewels.
Blessed One, this kind of great jewel has been obtained by us, Blessed One, without being sought, without being searched for, without being thought of, and without being prayed for."
"It occurs to us, Blessed One; it occurs to us, Sugata.
It is just as if, Blessed One, some man were to depart from the presence of his father."
He would depart and go to another region of the country;
there he would dwell for many years—twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty.
Then, Blessed One, that man would become great.
He would be poor;
and while seeking a livelihood for the sake of food and clothing, wandering through various directions and intermediate points, he would go to a certain region.
Meanwhile, his father would have departed for yet another country.
He would possess abundant wealth, grain, gold, treasuries, and granaries;
he would be endowed with much gold, silver, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, native copper, and silver;
and he would have many female and male slaves, laborers, and servants.
He would possess many elephants, horses, chariots, cattle, and sheep;
he would have a vast retinue,
and he would be a wealthy man in great kingdoms.
And he would possess abundant wealth derived from loans, investments, agriculture, and trade.

Then, O Blessed One, that poor man, wandering through villages, towns, market towns, districts, countries, and royal capitals for the sake of seeking food and clothing, eventually arrived at the place where his father— the man possessing vast wealth, gold, silver, treasuries, and storehouses— was living.
He would arrive at that city.

Then, O Blessed One, the father of that poor man—who possessed great wealth, gold, treasuries, and granaries—while living in that city, would constantly and perpetually remember his son who had been lost for fifty years; and though remembering him, he would tell no one of it, but would only grieve within himself alone.
And he should think thus: "I am aged, old, and advanced in years;
I possess abundant gold, bullion, wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses, yet I have no son whatsoever."
"Lest my death should occur, lest all this should perish unused. He would then remember his son again and again: "Oh, how happy I would be if that son of mine were to enjoy this mass of wealth!"
Then, Blessed One, that poor man, while searching for food and clothing,

would eventually arrive at the residence of that wealthy man who possessed abundant gold, silver, wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses. Then, Blessed One, that father of the poor man was at the gate of his own residence, surrounded by a great assembly of Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras.

Surrounded and honored, he would be seated upon a great lion-throne provided with a footstool, adorned with gold and silver; conducting business with hundreds of thousands of millions of pieces of gold, fanned by a yak-tail whisk, he would be seated in great splendor upon a vast area of ground covered by a spread canopy, strewn with loose flowers, and hung with strings of jewels.

O Blessed One, that poor man saw his own father sitting right at the gate of his own residence with such splendor, surrounded by a great multitude of people, performing the duties of a householder. Upon seeing him, he was terrified, trembling, agitated, his hair standing on end, and his mind filled with distress; he thought to himself: "I have suddenly encountered here either a king or one of high royal rank."
"We have no work here;
let us go to the street of the poor, for there food and clothing will arise for us with very little difficulty."
Enough of my lingering here for long;
let it not be that I am seized as a prisoner here, or that I incur some other calamity.
Then, O Blessed One, that poor man, terrified by the fear of contemplating a succession of sufferings, would depart in haste and flee;
he would not remain there.
Then, O Blessed One, that wealthy man, seated upon his lion-throne at the gate of his own residence, would recognize his own son at the very sight of him.

And having seen him, he would become satisfied, elated, joyful, glad, and filled with a sense of pleasure and well-being; and he would think: "How wonderful! It is truly marvelous that a consumer of this great wealth of gold, bullion, money, grain, treasuries, and storehouses has been found.
And yet, I have been constantly remembering this very person again and again."
And he has come here of his own accord,
while I am worn out, aged, and advanced in years.
Then, O Blessed One, that man, tormented by longing for his son, at that very instant, moment, and second, would dispatch swift messengers, saying: "Go, sirs, and bring that man back quickly!
Then, O Blessed One, those men, all running with great speed, would seize that poor man.
At that moment, the poor man—frightened, terrified, agitated, his hair standing on end, and his mind overwhelmed—would let out a terrible cry of distress, wailing and crying out.
He would say, "I have committed no offense against you at all," yet those men would forcibly drag that poor man away even as he cried out.
Then indeed, that poor man—afraid, terrified, agitated, and with a distressed mind—would think: "May I not be executed or punished;
let me escape! He would faint and fall to the ground.
And he would be unconscious;
meanwhile, his father were nearby, and he would say to those men: "Sirs, do not bring this man here."
Having sprinkled him with cool water, he would not speak to him again.
Why is that?
Because that householder knows the poor man’s inferior inclinations and his own noble capacity.
And he knows that "this is my son."
Then, O Blessed One, that householder, through skillful means, would not tell anyone, "This is my son.
Then, O Blessed One, that householder would address another man: "Go, good man, and say this to that poor man: 'Go, good man, wherever you wish.'"
"You are free.
Having said this and given his promise to him, that man would go to where the poor man was.
Having approached him, he would say to that poor man: "Go, my good man, wherever you wish."
"You are free!
Then, upon hearing these words, that poor man would be struck with wonder and amazement;
he would rise from that spot on the earth and go toward the street of the poor for the sake of seeking food and clothing.
Then that householder, for the purpose of attracting that poor man, would employ a skillful means.

He would dispatch two men there who were ill-favored and of little majesty, saying: "Go, sirs; having hired by my own word that man who came here, paying him double the daily wage, you should have him perform work here in my residence."
If he were to say, "What work must be done?",
you two should say to him, "The refuse heap is to be cleared together with us.
Then those two men, having sought out that poor man, would engage him in that task.

Then those two men and that poor man, having received their wages from that wealthy man, would clear away the heaps of refuse in that very house; they would take up residence in a small hovel near the grounds of that same wealthy man’s home. And that rich man, through a window or an air-vent, would see his own son clearing away the heaps of refuse.
And having seen it, he would again be struck with wonder.
Then that householder, having descended from his own residence, removed his garlands and ornaments,
took off his soft garments,
and put on soiled clothes that were clean and noble.
Taking the basket with his right hand and defiling his own body with dust, he would approach the place where that poor man was while speaking from a distance.
Having approached him, he would say: "Carry these baskets, sirs; do not stay."
"Take away the dust! By this means he would address and converse with that son, saying to him:
'Come here, my good man, and do work right here.'"
"Do not go elsewhere again;
I shall give you a special wage, and whatever you may need for your purpose, I shall provide."
"Therefore, ask me confidently for it—

whether for the price of a bowl, or the price of a water-pot, or the price of a cooking-pot, or the price of wood, or the price of salt, or for food, or for clothing; for I have, O man, an old garment."
If you have need of those,
ask for them; I shall give them to you.
"Whatever kind of requisites you require for your needs, O man, I shall provide all of those to you.
Be at ease, O man."
As your father is, so am I to be regarded by you.
For what reason? Because I am [your father]. (Vaidya 74)
I am old and you are young;
yet much work has been performed by you for me while cleaning this heap of refuse.
Furthermore, my good man, while performing this work here, you have never before displayed deceit, crookedness, guile, pride, or hypocrisy, nor do you do so now.
"In every respect, my good man, I do not perceive even a single evil deed in you,
such as these faults that are found in other men who perform [such] actions.
You are like a son of my own body."
From this day forward, you shall be such as that to me.
Then, Blessed One, that householder would give the name "son" to that poor man;
and that poor man would conceive the notion of his father toward that householder.
In this manner, Blessed One, that householder, longing for a son, would have that son clean the heap of refuse for twenty years.
Then, after the passing of twenty years, that poor man would become confident in entering and leaving the householder’s residence,
and he would make his dwelling right there in that very straw hut.
Then, indeed, O Blessed One, if illness were to befall that householder,
and he were to perceive that the time of his own death had arrived,
he would say this to that poor man: "Come here, my good man!"
"I possess this vast quantity of gold, bullion, wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses;
I am gravely ill.
I wish [to designate] that to whom this should be given, from whom it should be taken, and how it should be deposited."
You should recognize it all.
For what reason?
Because I am the owner of this property exactly as it is.
You, too, are such as that;
do not cause me to lose anything from this.
Then, Blessed One, by this means that poor man would come to recognize all that abundant gold, bullion, wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses belonging to the householder;
yet he himself would remain without desire for them and would not request anything from them.
Even for as little as the price of a prastha of barley meal,
he would dwell right there in that very hut of straw,
constantly brooding over that same state of poverty.
Then, O Blessed One, that householder, having recognized that his son was capable, a protector, and fully matured;

and having perceived that he was distressed, ashamed, and disgusted by his former state of poverty— despite his mind being subdued and possessed of noble conceptions— summoned that poor man at the time when death was imminent, and [brought him] from the great...
Having presented him before the assembly of kinsmen, or in the presence of the king or a royal minister, and before the merchants and countryfolk, he should proclaim thus: "Listen, sirs!
This is my own legitimate son, begotten by me myself."
There is a city named so-and-so;
from there this man, who is fifty years old, went missing;
he is known by the name so-and-so.
I too am named so-and-so;
and from that city, seeking this very person, I have come here.
This is my son.
"I am his father;
whatever enjoyment I possess,
I bestow all of that upon this person."
Whatever personal wealth I possess,
he alone knows it all.

Then, O Blessed One, at that time, having heard such a voice as this, that poor man would be struck with wonder and amazement, and he would think to himself: "All of a sudden, I have obtained this very much gold, silver, wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses!"
In the same way, Blessed One, we are like sons of the Tathāgata;
and the Tathāgata speaks to us thus: "You are my sons."
Just as that householder did,
O Blessed One, we too were oppressed by three kinds of suffering.
