By which three?
Namely, by way of the suffering of suffering, the suffering of conditioned formations, and the suffering of change;
and those whose inclinations are inferior within saṃsāra— therefore,
we have been led by the Blessed One to contemplate many inferior dharmas that are like a heap of refuse.
And we were applied to them, striving and exerting ourselves;
O Blessed One, seeking only nirvāṇa, we searched for it as one seeks the seal of day.
And having obtained that nirvāṇa, O Blessed One, we were satisfied.
"We consider that we have gained much from the Tathāgata by being devoted to, striving in, and exerting ourselves in these teachings;
yet the Tathāgata knows our inferior inclinations, and for that reason, the Blessed One has neglected us."
He does not divide it,
nor does he declare: "This very treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom shall be yours."
And through his skillful means, the Blessed One establishes us as heirs to this treasury of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
Yet we were without desire for it, O Blessed One;
therefore, we understood it thus: that it was a great gain for us to receive from the presence of the Tathāgata even a single day’s wage, as it were, in the form of nirvāṇa.
"Lord, we provide a sublime teaching of the Dharma for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, beginning with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
we reveal, show, and demonstrate the Tathāgata’s knowledge. Yet, Lord, we ourselves remain free from desire for it."
For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata, through his skill in means, knows our inclinations;
yet we did not know or understand that which the Blessed One has now declared—that we are the true sons of the Blessed One.
And the Blessed One reminds us that we are heirs to the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
For what reason? Because we are indeed the true sons of the Tathāgata.
Moreover, we are indeed of inferior inclinations;
yet, if the Blessed One were to perceive the strength of our resolve,
the Blessed One would address us with the title "Bodhisattva."

Furthermore, we have been made to perform two tasks by the Blessed One: first, we were told to be those of inferior inclination in the presence of the Bodhisattvas, and they were encouraged toward the sublime enlightenment of a Buddha; and now, having recognized our power of inclination, the Blessed One has uttered this.

"By this method, O Blessed One, we say: suddenly, by us who were free from longing, the jewel of omniscience has been obtained—without being sought, without being searched for, without being pursued, without being thought of, and without being prayed for—just as it was by the sons of the Tathāgata."

Then, at that time, the venerable Mahākāśyapa spoke these verses: "We have become filled with wonder and amazement, and we have attained great joy upon hearing this sound. Suddenly, today, we have heard this such delightful voice of the Guide. (Saddhp 4.1)
This vast heap of distinguished jewels has been obtained by us today in a mere moment;
it was neither thought of nor ever prayed for. Having heard this, we have all been struck with wonder. (Saddhp 4.2)
Just as if there were a foolish man who, being led astray by foolish people,
should depart from his father's presence and go to another land very far away.
And at that time, the father, knowing that his own son had fled, grieved for him;
he searched throughout the cardinal and intermediate directions for no fewer than fifty years.
And so, while searching for his son, he went to another great city, built a residence there, and lived on, provided with the fivefold array of sensual pleasures.
Abundant gold and silver, grain, wealth, conch shells, crystals, and coral;
as well as elephants, horses, infantry, cattle, livestock, and even sheep.
He possessed capital and investments, as well as fields, female and male slaves, and a vast multitude of servants;
he was highly honored by many thousands of millions of living beings and was always a favorite of the king.
The city-dwellers and those villagers who live in the countryside stand before him with palms joined in reverence;
many merchants, having business to attend to, come into his presence for various matters.
Such a man, though possessed of supernatural powers, would become worn out, aged, and decrepit;
constantly brooding over grief for his son, he would pass his time day and night.
Such was my foolish son, who had been wandering away for fifty years; yet here is this vast treasury of mine, and my time of death has now arrived. (Saddhp 4.10)
And at that time, his son was likewise a fool— poor, wretched, and always [in such a state]—
wandering from village to village, seeking food and clothing.
Though searching, he might sometimes obtain something, yet at other times he obtains nothing at all;
that fool with his limbs smeared [with filth] withers away in the refuge of others, scratching his scabies and itching.
And he would go to that city where his father had gradually gone;
seeking food and clothing, he would come to the dwelling of his own father.
And that wealthy man, possessing great riches, was seated upon a lion throne at the gate,
surrounded by many hundreds of living beings, while a canopy was spread over him in the air.
And his trustworthy people stood all around him; some were counting wealth and gold, while others were having documents written out, and some were engaging in lending on interest.
And that poor man, having seen the householder’s residence thus adorned, thought:
"Where have I come today? This must be a king or a high official."
"Lest I now incur blame here, or be seized and made to perform forced labor," thinking thus,
that man flees, inquiring for the street of the poor.

And that wealthy man, seeing his own son seated upon the lion throne, would be overjoyed; he would dispatch messengers to his presence, saying, "Bring this poor man here! *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 4.18.
Immediately those men seize that man; as soon as he is seized, he falls into a swoon:
"Surely my executioners have arrived; what use have I for clothing or food? (Saddhp 4.19)
And having seen him, that wise man of great wealth thought: "This fool is of inferior inclination and poor intellect;
he will not believe this splendor of mine, nor will he believe that 'this is my father. (Saddhp 4.20)
And there he would employ men who were crooked, one-eyed, or lame; poorly dressed, dark-skinned, and of low character, saying: "Search for that man who is to do the work."
"This heap of refuse of mine is putrid and ruined by excrement and urine;
perform the work of cleaning it, and I shall give you double wages. (Saddhp 4.22)
Having heard such a cry, that man came and thoroughly cleaned that place;
right there he would build a dwelling within this corner of the house.
And that wealthy man would constantly watch that man even through the window-opening, thinking:
"This son of mine has inferior aspirations; he is cleaning the heap of refuse."
Having descended, taking a basket and putting on soiled garments, he approached that man, threatening him, "Do not perform this work! (Saddhp 4.25)
"I shall give you double wages, and likewise double the foot-ointment;
I shall provide you with salted food, and furthermore, I shall give you vegetables and a garment."
Having thus rebuked him at that time, the wise man would then reconcile with him once more:
"Truly, you perform your work well here; you are clearly my son, there is no doubt about this."
He should have that man enter the house little by little and have him perform work;
when twenty years have been fully completed, he would gradually gain the confidence of that man.
He would settle there in that residence gold, pearls, and crystal;
he would make an inventory of everything and reflect upon all its wealth.
That fool, dwelling alone in a small hut outside that house,
would dwell on the thoughts of a pauper, thinking, "I have no such possessions as these."
And having recognized that my son has come to possess such noble conceptions,
I shall bring together a multitude of friends and kinsmen and bestow upon him his entire inheritance.
Having assembled the king, the citizens, the townspeople, and many merchants,
he spoke thus in the midst of the assembly: "This is my son, who was lost for a long time."
"Fifty full years have passed, and for another twenty since I last saw him. He was lost to me from such-and-such a city, and I have come here searching for him."
He is the master of all my wealth; let him take it all without exception.
Let him perform his duties with his father’s riches, for I give this entire household to him.

And that man would be filled with wonder, remembering his former state of poverty and his low inclinations toward his father; yet, having obtained those virtues and the family estate, he thinks, "I am happy today. (Saddhp 4.35)
In the very same way, our Leader, having recognized our inferior inclinations,
did not proclaim to us, "You shall become Buddhas," but rather said, "You are indeed my disciples, my sons."
And the Lord of the World exhorts us who have set out for supreme, foremost enlightenment:
"O Kāśyapa, speak to them of the unsurpassed path, that path by cultivating which they shall become Buddhas. (Saddhp_4.37)
And we have been sent by the Sugata to those many bodhisattvas of great power;
we demonstrate the unsurpassed path through millions of billions of examples and reasons.
And having heard this, the sons of the Jina cultivate the supreme, excellent path toward awakening;
at that very moment, they receive their prophecy: "You shall become Buddhas in this world."
We perform such service for the Protector, guarding this treasury of the Dharma and revealing it to the sons of the Jinas, just like that man who was his trusted confidant. (Saddhp 4.40)
While distributing this treasury of the Buddha, we contemplate the anxieties of the poor;
yet we do not ourselves aspire for the wisdom of the Jina, even as we reveal the wisdom of the Jina.
We imagined our own individual nirvāṇa to be attained by this much; we thought there was no further knowledge beyond this.
Even when we heard of the magnificent arrays of the Buddhas' fields, we never felt any joy. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 4.42)
"All these dharmas are indeed peaceful, untainted, and devoid of both cessation and arising;
yet herein no dharma whatsoever exists. Having reflected thus, faith does not arise.
For a long time we have been free from longing for the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha;
we never made a vow for that, yet this supreme goal was spoken of by the Jina.
In this final body, which culminates in nirvāṇa, we have cultivated emptiness for a long time;
liberated from the suffering and oppression of the three realms, we have fulfilled the teaching of the Jina.
For whatever we may reveal to the sons of the Jinas who have set out here for supreme enlightenment,
and whatever Dharma we speak to them, we never feel any longing for that.
And yet our Teacher, the Self-Existent One, overlooks him while awaiting the proper time;
he does not speak of the connection between the true state of things, seeking instead our own inclinations.

Just as that man of great wealth, through his skill in means, at the proper time constantly disciplines those of inferior inclinations, and having disciplined them, bestows his wealth upon them. (Saddhp 4.48)
The Lord of the World performs what is most difficult to do, manifesting skillful means;
he tames his sons who are inclined toward inferior things, and having tamed them, he bestows this knowledge.
Today we have suddenly attained what is marvelous, just as a poor man might obtain wealth;
and here, within the teaching of the Buddha, we have obtained the first fruit, which is distinguished and free from outflows.
O Protector, that morality which we have guarded for a long time in the teaching of the Knower of the World—
today we have obtained the fruit of that morality practiced in the past.
The supreme and utterly pure celibacy that was practiced within the teaching of the Leader—its distinguished fruit has been obtained today: peaceful, sublime, and untainted.
"O Protector, we who have become disciples shall now proclaim the supreme enlightenment;
we shall make the sound of enlightenment resound, and for that reason we are called 'terrible' disciples."
O Protector, having become Arhats today, we deserve to receive worship from the world including its gods, its Māras, and its Brahmās, and from the presence of all sentient beings. (Saddhp_4.54)
Who indeed, even if they were to exert themselves for many millions of eons,
would be able to repay you for such extremely difficult deeds as these that you perform here in the world of mortals?
Indeed, it is difficult to perform a service in return with hands, feet, or even the head;
for one might carry [the Buddha] on the head or on the shoulders for as many full eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges. (Saddhp 4.56)
One should give food, clothing, drink, and bedding with spotless covers;
one should cause monasteries made of sandalwood to be built and offer them spread with pairs of fine cotton cloths.

One might constantly offer various kinds of medicine for the sick as an act of worship to the Sugata for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges; even so, it would never be possible to repay his kindness.

O Great King, the Buddhas—great-souled ones of incomparable majesty and great supernatural power, established in the strength of patience, the Victors free from outflows—endure such things from fools. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 4.59.
Thus, always acting in accordance with the signs [of the times], he proclaims the Dharma;
he is the Lord of Dharma, the Sovereign in all the world, the Great Lord, the Chief Guide of the World.
Understanding the various stations of sentient beings, he demonstrates the practice in many ways;
and having known their diverse inclinations, he teaches the Dharma by means of thousands of causes.
The Tathāgata, fully understanding the conduct of all beings and individuals,
indeed teaches the Dharma in many ways, demonstrating this supreme enlightenment.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "Resolute Faith," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 84) Chapter Five: The Herb.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Mahākāśyapa and those other elder great disciples: "Excellent, excellent, Mahākāśyapa!"
"It is indeed excellent, Kāśyapa, that you speak of the true qualities and praises of the Tathāgata.
These, Kāśyapa, are the true qualities of the Tathāgata; beyond these, there are others that are immeasurable and incalculable."
It is not easy to reach the end of these [teachings], even if one were to speak for immeasurable eons;
Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata is the Lord of Dharma,
the King, the Master, and the Sovereign of all dharmas.
And, Kāśyapa, whatever Dharma the Tathāgata deposits in a particular context,
it remains exactly so;
for the Tathāgata, Kāśyapa, deposits all dharmas through logical reasoning.
He deposits them by means of the Tathāgata’s wisdom so that those phenomena proceed precisely to the stage of omniscience; furthermore,
the Tathāgata thoroughly perceives the course of the meaning of all phenomena.

Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained mastery over the meaning of all dharmas; he has attained the resolute intention toward all dharmas; he has attained the supreme perfection of the knowledge of skill in the definitive discernment of all dharmas; he is the one who demonstrates the knowledge of the All-Knowing One, the one who causes entry into the knowledge of the All-Knowing One, and the one who bestows the knowledge of the All-Knowing One.

Kāśyapa, it is just as if, in this great trichiliocosm, there were as many grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees— of various colors, various kinds, and various names— as grow upon the earth, or in the mountains, peaks, and caves; and then a cloud, filled with great water, should rise up.
Having raised it up, he would cover the entire great trichiliocosm;
and having covered it, he would release water everywhere at the same time.
In that regard, Kāśyapa, whatever grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest trees there are in this great trichiliocosm,
Therein, those young grasses, shrubs, herbs, forest trees, trees, great trees, and massive trees— possessing tender stalks, branches, leaves, and foliage—
all of them drink in the element of water from the rain released by that great cloud, according to their strength and according to their respective domains.
And by means of that abundant water of a single flavor released by the cloud, they attain growth, sprouting, and expansion in accordance with their seeds and their natures.
And thus they produce flowers and fruits,
and each receives its own distinct name;
yet all those clusters of medicinal herbs and groups of seeds are established upon the same earth and are moistened by water of a single flavor.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, appears in the world. Just as a great cloud rises,
so too the Tathāgata, having appeared, makes himself known by his voice to the entire world, including its gods, humans, and asuras.
Just as, Kāśyapa, a great cloud covers the entire trichiliocosm,

even so, Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, utters this sound and makes this proclamation before the world with its gods, humans, and asuras: "O you, gods and humans, I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One."
Having crossed over, I help others cross;
being liberated, I liberate others; having found rest, I give rest to others.
I have attained final nirvāṇa; I lead others to final nirvāṇa.
With right wisdom, I understand this world and the world beyond as they truly are; I am all-knowing and all-seeing.
Let the venerable gods and humans approach me to hear the Dharma.
"I am the proclaimer of the path, the guide of the path, the knower of the path, and the one skilled in the path.

Therein, Kāśyapa, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings approach the Tathāgata to hear the Dharma. Then the Tathāgata [discerns] the diversity of those beings' faculties, their vigor, and their various degrees of excellence."

Having understood those various Dharma-discourses, he brings them together; he delivers this or that Dharma-talk— abundant, diverse, gladdening, satisfying, inspiring joy, and conducive to welfare and happiness—
by which talk those beings become happy in this very life.
And having passed away, they are reborn in happy realms,
where they enjoy abundant sensual pleasures and hear the Dharma.
Having heard that Dharma, they become free from hindrances;
and they apply themselves progressively to the qualities of omniscience according to their strength, according to their scope, and according to their station.
Kāśyapa, it is just as if a great cloud were to cover the entire trichiliocosm and release water evenly, satisfying all the grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees with that water;
those grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees drink the water according to their respective strength, capacity, and power.
And each attains its own specific measure of birth.

In the very same way, Kāśyapa, whatever Dharma the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims, all that Dharma is of a single flavor— namely, the flavor of liberation, the flavor of dispassion, the flavor of cessation, which culminates in the knowledge of the All-Knowing One.
In this regard, Kāśyapa, those beings who hear the Dharma as the Tathāgata speaks it, retain it, and apply themselves to it, do not know, feel, or awaken to a self by means of a self.
Why is that?
Kāśyapa, only the Tathāgata knows those beings— both who they are and how they are.
Whoever they are,
what they think, and how they think—
That by which they think, that which they cultivate, and the manner in which they cultivate it—
That by which they cultivate,
that which they attain,
and the manner in which they attain it.
And by what means they attain [their respective states],
Kāśyapa, only the Tathāgata is there directly present and directly seeing— just as he sees those beings established in their various stages, like grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees,
whether inferior, superior, or middling.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, having realized the single-flavored Dharma— namely, the flavor of liberation, the flavor of cessation, which culminates in nirvāṇa,

is eternally parinirvāṇized, belongs to a single stage, and has the nature of space— I do not suddenly reveal the knowledge of an omniscient one, out of regard for the inclinations of sentient beings.
"You have attained what is marvelous, Kāśyapa; you have attained what is wonderful, in that you are unable to penetrate the intentional speech (*saṃdhābhāṣita*) of the Tathāgata.
For what reason?
Because, Kāśyapa, the intentional speech of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, is difficult to understand."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate this very matter more extensively, spoke these verses:
"I am the King of Dharma, arisen in the world as the crusher of existence. Having understood the inclinations of sentient beings, I proclaim the Dharma. (Saddhp 5.1)
Those of steady intellect and great heroism long protect what has been spoken;
they maintain the secret and do not disclose it to living beings.

Moreover, that knowledge is difficult to understand; if the foolish and the dull-witted hear it suddenly, they will harbor doubts, and consequently, having fallen away from it, they will wander in delusion.
I speak according to the capacity of each person and whatever strength they possess; through various means, I bring their vision to rectitude. (Saddhp 5.4)
Just as, Kāśyapa, a cloud arises over the world-system,
covering the entire earth and bringing all moisture, so too is it with the Tathāgata.
And that great cloud, garlanded with lightning, completely filled with water,
gladdens all living beings by making a thundering sound.
Having warded off the rays of the sun and made the circle cool,
standing within arm's reach, he would release water on all sides.
And that very [water] of mine would release a vast mass of water,
flowing everywhere and satisfying this earth.
Whatever medicinal herbs there may be here on earth,
whether they be grasses, shrubs, forest plants, trees, or great trees;
Whatever various crops there may be, or whatever else is green, whether on the mountain, in the ravine, or in the groves— Saddhp_5.10.
Just as a cloud satisfies all grasses, shrubs, and forest trees,
so too does it quench the parched earth and drench the medicinal herbs.
And that water, released from the cloud and remaining here, is of a single taste;
the grasses and shrubs drink it according to their strength and according to their capacity.
Whatever trees there are—great trees, small ones, and those of middle size, according to their age—all drink the water according to their strength; they drink and grow according to their desires.

Just as great medicinal herbs grow by means of their stalks, stems, and bark, as well as their branches and sub-branches, and likewise by their leaves, flowers, and fruits, when rained upon by the clouds.
According to their strength, according to the nature of the soil, and according to whatever kind of seed each possesses,
they each produce their own respective growth, even though the water released is of a single flavor.
In the same way, Kāśyapa, the Buddha also appears in this world like a rain-cloud appearing in the world;
having appeared, the Lord of the World speaks and reveals the true course of conduct for living beings. (Saddhp_5.16)
And thus the Great Seer, honored in this world together with its gods, proclaims:
"I am the Tathāgata, the Jina, the supreme among bipeds; I have arisen in the world just like a cloud. (Saddhp 5.17)
I shall satisfy all sentient beings whose limbs are withered and who are clinging to the three realms of existence;
drying up through suffering, I shall establish them in happiness, and I shall grant them both their desires and nirvana.
Listen to me, you multitudes of gods and humans; come into my presence to see me.
I am the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the Unconquered, born here in this world for the sake of delivering beings.
And I preach the pure and beautiful Dharma to thousands of millions of living beings;
yet its equality and suchness is one, namely: liberation and final extinction.
And with a single voice I preach the Dharma, always making enlightenment its foundation;
for this is equal and there is no inequality—neither hatred nor passion is found therein.
I have no partiality whatsoever, nor do I harbor either affection or aversion toward anyone;
I proclaim the Dharma equally to all embodied beings, just as I would to a single being, so too to another.
With no other task, I proclaim the Dharma— whether they are walking, standing, or sitting;
even when seated or reclining upon a bed or seat, I never experience weariness.
I shall satisfy this entire world, releasing water equally like a cloud,
with an even mind toward the noble and the lowly, and toward those who are immoral as well as those who possess virtue.
Likewise, those men whose conduct is ruined and those who are endowed with virtuous conduct;
those established in [wrong] views and those whose views are ruined; those with right view and those with impure views.
Whether among those of inferior or superior intellect, or those with dull faculties, I preach the Dharma;
having abandoned all weariness, I rightly pour down the rain of the Dharma.
Having heard me according to their strength, they establish themselves upon various stages—
among gods and mortals who find delight, as Śakras, Brahmās, or even universal monarchs (cakravartins).
These herbs here in the world are minor and very minor;
listen as I shall reveal all those others that are middling and great.

Those people who, understanding the untainted Dharma, dwell having attained nirvāṇa, and those who possess the six supernormal powers and the three types of knowledge—they are called the "minor medicinal herbs" that have arisen. (Saddhp 5.29)
Those people who dwell in mountain caves and yearn for the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—
those whose intellects are of middling purity— are like the medicinal herb that has arisen as the middle one.

Those who aspire to the state of a bull among men, thinking "I shall become a Buddha, a lord of gods and men," and who cultivate vigor and meditation— they are said to be like this supreme medicinal herb. (Saddhp_5.31)
And those sons of the Sugata who are disciplined here, who practice loving-kindness and peaceful conduct,
having attained freedom from doubt regarding their status as bulls among men— such a tree is said to be like this.
For those wise ones who set in motion the irreversible wheel and stand firm in the power of supernatural faculties,
liberating many millions of living beings— he is indeed called the Great Tree.
And that Dharma taught by the Jina is equal, like water released equally from a cloud;
these various supernormal powers are just like the medicinal herbs situated upon the surface of the earth.
By this illustration and demonstration, understand the skillful means of the Tathāgata;
and how he speaks a single Dharma through various explanations, like drops of water.
May the rain of Dharma fall for me as well, so that this entire world may be satisfied;
and according to their respective capacities, they shall contemplate the well-spoken word, even though the Dharma is of a single flavor.
Just as grasses and shrubs, or even the herbs in the midst [of the forest], or likewise trees and great trees, all shine beautifully in the ten directions when it rains; so too does this [light].
This nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which always benefits the world, satisfies this entire world with the Dharma;
and once the entire world has been satisfied, it releases medicinal herbs and flowers.

It also causes the intermediate medicinal herbs to flourish—those Arhats who abide in the destruction of the outflows, and the Pratyekabuddhas who wander in the forest groves; it brings to fulfillment this well-spoken Dharma. (Saddhp 5.39)
Many bodhisattvas, mindful and steadfast, who have reached the depths of all states within the triple world,
seeking this supreme enlightenment, grow constantly like trees.

Those who possess supernatural powers, who meditate on the four dhyānas, and who, having heard of emptiness, give rise to joy—emitting thousands of rays of light—they too are called "great trees" here. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 5.41.
Such, Kāśyapa, is this teaching of the Dharma, released like water from a cloud:
many great medicinal herbs grow, as do the infinite flowers of humanity. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 5.42.
I proclaim the Dharma based on my own realization, and in due time I manifest the enlightenment of a Buddha;
this is my supreme skill in means, shared by all the leaders of the world.
In this way, I have spoken according to the ultimate truth: all those disciples do not enter into final nirvāṇa;
they practice the supreme conduct of awakening, and all these disciples shall become Buddhas.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, the Tathāgata is equal in the discipline of sentient beings and not unequal.

Just as, Kāśyapa, the light of the moon and sun illuminates the entire world— whether one who performs wholesome deeds or one who performs unwholesome deeds, whether situated above or situated below, whether fragrant or foul-smelling—
their light falls equally upon all things and not unequally.

In the same way, Kāśyapa, the light of the mind of omniscient wisdom of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas proceeds equally toward all beings born in the five realms of existence, teaching the True Dharma according to their respective inclinations— whether they belong to the Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, or the Śrāvakayāna.
Furthermore, there is neither deficiency nor excess in the radiance of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, corresponding to the way it arises from the accumulation of merit and knowledge.
Kāśyapa, there are not three vehicles; it is only that sentient beings have various different dispositions.
By means of that, the three vehicles are designated.

When this had been said, the venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One as follows: "If, Blessed One, there are not three vehicles, for what reason is the designation of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas established in the present time?"
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, it is just as when a potter makes vessels from lumps of clay that are all the same;
among them, some become vessels for molasses, and some become vessels for ghee."
Some vessels for curd and milk become inferior and impure vessels,
yet there is no difference in the clay itself.
And yet, by the mere addition of different substances, the diversity of the vessels is perceived.
In the very same way, Kāśyapa, there is only this one vehicle, namely the Buddha-vehicle;
no second or third vehicle exists.

When this had been said, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, although there are beings of various inclinations who have emerged from the triple world, do they have one single nirvāṇa, or two, or three?
The Blessed One replied: "Kāśyapa, nirvāṇa arises indeed from the awakening to the equality of all phenomena."
And that is one, not two, nor three.
Therefore, Kāśyapa, I shall give you a simile;
for by means of a simile, some wise people here understand the meaning of what has been spoken.
It is just as if, Kāśyapa, there were a man born blind who were to say: "There are no forms that are beautiful or ugly, nor are there any perceivers of forms that are beautiful or ugly."
The sun and moon do not exist; the constellations do not exist; the planets do not exist.
There are no seers of the planets.
Then, other people might say this very thing in the presence of that man blind from birth: "There are forms, both beautiful and ugly; there are seers of forms, both beautiful and ugly."
The sun and moon exist; the constellations exist; the planets exist.
There are those who see the planets;
yet that man blind from birth would not believe those people, nor would he accept what they said.
Then suppose there were a certain physician who knew all diseases; he might see that man blind from birth and think to himself: "This man's disease has arisen due to his past sinful karma."

Whatever diseases arise, they are all of four kinds: those caused by wind (vātika), those caused by bile (paittika), those caused by phlegm (ślaiṣmika), and those caused by a combination of the humors (sāṃnipātika).
Then that physician, for the sake of alleviating that disease, should repeatedly contemplate the appropriate remedy.
It might occur to him: "Indeed, this disease cannot be cured by these medicinal substances that are currently available;
however, there are four medicinal herbs on Himavat, the king of mountains."
Which four?
They are as follows: the first is named "Accompanying All Colors, Tastes, and Bases," and the second is named "Liberator from All Diseases."
The third is named "Destroyer of All Poisons," and the fourth is named "Bestower of Happiness Remaining in One's Own Place. These are the four medicinal herbs.
Then that physician, having conceived compassion for that person blind from birth, would devise such a means by which he might be able to go to Himavat, the king of mountains;
and having gone there, he would even ascend upward.
He might descend even below and search even across;
searching in this manner, he would find those four medicinal herbs.
Having prepared some by chewing it with his teeth, he should give it;
some by grinding it, he should give it;
and some, having mixed it with other substances and cooked it, he should give it.
He might give some [medicine] after mixing it with raw substances;
he might give some after piercing the site on the body with a needle;
he might give some after cauterizing it with fire.
Having combined some of these with one another’s substances—even applying them to food, drink, and so forth—he might give them to him;
then, by means of that application of skillful methods, that man born blind would regain his sight.
Having regained his sight, he would see externally and internally, far and near, the light of the moon and sun, the stars, the planets, and all forms.
And he should speak thus: "Alas, how foolish I was,
that I did not have faith in those who were speaking before me, and did not accept what was said!"
Thus, I now see everything;
I am liberated from blindness,
and I have regained my sight.
And [he thinks], "There is no one superior to me.

At that time, there might be sages possessing the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), who are skilled in the divine eye, the divine ear, the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of recollecting past lives, and the performance of supernatural powers and liberations;
they would say to that man: "O man, you have merely obtained eyes!"
But you do not know anything at all;
from where has this conceit of yours arisen? You possess no wisdom.
And you are not wise.
They would say this to him: "O man, when you are sitting inside a house, you do not see other forms outside, nor do you know them."
Nor do you recognize those beings who are either friendly-minded or hostile-minded; you do not discern the speech of people standing at a distance of five yojanas,
nor do you perceive or hear the sounds of drums, conchs, and the like.
"You are unable to travel even a distance of one krośa without lifting your feet;
moreover, you were born and raised within your mother's womb,
yet you do not remember that experience."
How then are you wise?
And how do you say, "I see everything"? Therefore, O man, it is well that you perceive darkness as light.
And that which is light, you perceive as darkness.
Then that man would speak thus to those sages: "What is the means,
or what auspicious deed must I perform, so that I might obtain such wisdom as this,
and through your favor, obtain these qualities?"
Then those sages would say this to that man: "If you so desire, dwell in the forest;
or, seated in mountain caves, contemplate the Dharma."
"And those afflictions must be abandoned;
likewise, endowed with the qualities of ascetic purification (dhūtaguṇa), you will attain the superknowledges (abhijñā).
Then that man, having grasped this matter, went forth into the religious life.

Dwelling in the forest with a one-pointed mind, having abandoned craving for the world, one may attain the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). Having attained these superknowledges, one should reflect: "Whatever other karma I performed in the past, by that no quality whatsoever has been acquired by me."
Now I shall go as I have intended;
previously, I was of little wisdom, of little realization, and I was as if blind.
Thus, Kāśyapa, this parable has been made for the sake of making this matter known.
Furthermore, this is the meaning to be understood here:
"one born blind," Kāśyapa, is a designation for sentient beings dwelling in the saṃsāra of the six realms of existence.
Those who do not know the true Dharma increase the blinding darkness of the afflictions;
they are blinded by ignorance.
Blinded by ignorance, they accumulate volitional formations;
with volitional formations as condition, there is name-and-form,
and so on, until there is the arising of this entire great mass of suffering.
Thus do sentient beings remain blinded by ignorance within saṃsāra.

But the Tathāgata, having generated compassion, has emerged from the triple world; like a father toward a beloved only son, he generates compassion and, descending into the triple world, beholds the sentient beings wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra.
And they do not understand the escape from cyclic existence (saṃsāra). Then the Blessed One beholds them with the eye of wisdom (prajñācakṣus);
having seen them, he knows: "These beings, having previously performed wholesome deeds, have weak aversion but intense passion."
Some have weak passion but intense hatred;
some have little wisdom, while others are learned.
Some have attained purity through ripening, while others hold wrong views;
for those sentient beings, the Tathāgata teaches three vehicles through his skill in means.
In that regard, just as those sages possessed the five superknowledges and the purified eye,
so too do bodhisattvas, having generated the thought of awakening and attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this regard, just as that great physician is, so should the Tathāgata be viewed.
Just as that person blind from birth is, so should sentient beings blinded by delusion be regarded;
and just as wind, bile, and phlegm are, so are passion, hatred, and delusion.
The sixty-two types of speculative views are to be regarded [as such].
Just as there are four medicinal herbs, so too are emptiness, the signless, the wishless, and the gateway to nirvāṇa to be regarded.
Just as substances are employed [according to their specific needs],...
In this way, as [the remedies] are applied, the diseases are pacified.
Likewise, by cultivating the gateways to liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—sentient beings bring ignorance (*avidyā*) to cessation.
From the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
In this way, there comes to be the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering;
and thus his mind abides neither in the wholesome nor in the unwholesome.
Just as a blind person regains their sight,
so should one regard those belonging to the vehicles of the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha;
they sever the bonds of the afflictions of saṃsāra.
Freed from the bonds of the afflictions, he is liberated from the three realms and the six states of existence.
Therefore, one who follows the vehicle of the śrāvaka understands thus and speaks these words: "There are no further dharmas to be fully awakened to."
"I have attained nirvāṇa.
Then the Tathāgata teaches him the Dharma by which no dharmas are attained.
"How can there be nirvāṇa for such a person?
To him, the Blessed One inspires [him] toward awakening. Having generated the thought of awakening, he neither remains in saṃsāra nor has he attained nirvāṇa.
Having realized this, he perceives the triple world in the ten directions as empty, like a magical creation, like an illusion, and like a dream, a mirage, or an echo;
he perceives all phenomena as unarisen and unceasing, neither bound nor liberated, neither darkness nor light.
He who perceives the dharmas thus deeply—
By means of non-seeing, he perceives the entire triple world as filled with the various inclinations and dispositions of sentient beings toward one another.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate this very matter more extensively, at that time spoke these verses:
"Just as the light of the moon and sun falls equally upon all men— whether upon the virtuous or upon the wicked— there is no deficiency or excess in its radiance."
The light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is indeed equal to that of the sun and moon;
it disciplines all sentient beings, neither deficient nor excessive.
Just as a potter, while fashioning earthenware vessels from clays that are all alike, produces containers for molasses, milk, ghee, and water; ||| Saddhp_5.47 |||
Some of those [materials] there are impure, while others are made of curd;
that potter, O Bhārgava, takes a single portion of clay when fashioning his vessels.
Just as a vessel is characterized by the kind of substance that is poured into it,
so too do the Tathāgatas [appear] due to the difference in the inclinations of sentient beings, even though there is no distinction among those beings.
They describe a distinction between vehicles, yet the Buddha-vehicle is certain; due to ignorance regarding the wheel of saṃsāra, they do not understand nirvāṇa. (Saddhp_5.50)
But he who understands that phenomena are empty and devoid of self knows, in accordance with reality, the awakening of the Blessed Buddhas.
Because they are established in the midst of wisdom, they are called Pratyekajinas;
because they lack the knowledge of emptiness, they are declared to be Śrāvakas.
But because of his awakening to all phenomena, he is called a Samyaksambuddha;
therefore, by means of hundreds of skillful methods, he constantly teaches the Dharma to living beings.
Just as a certain person born blind, not seeing the sun, the moon, the planets, or the stars, might say: "There are no forms whatsoever."
But the great physician, having established compassion for those born blind,
went to the Himalayas, as well as to the regions below, above, and across.
He obtained medicinal herbs from the mountains that possessed all colors, tastes, and potencies;
then he applied these four [herbs] in the following manner.
Having crushed some with his teeth and likewise ground others,
he would pierce them with the point of a needle and apply them to the body of one blind from birth.
Having gained his sight, he would behold the sun, the moon, the planets, and the stars;
and thus, from his previous knowledge, it would be described to him in this way.
Thus beings, possessing great ignorance and born blind, wander in saṃsāra due to their lack of knowledge regarding the wheel of dependent origination, the path of suffering. (Saddhp 5.59)
Thus, when the world was utterly deluded by ignorance, the Tathāgata— the supreme among all-knowers, the great physician whose very nature is compassion— appeared.
The Teacher, skilled in means, teaches the true Dharma;
he teaches the unsurpassed awakening of a Buddha to those who belong to the foremost vehicle.
The Leader reveals the Middle Way to those of middling wisdom;
moreover, he praises another awakening for those who are terrified of cyclic existence.
For the Śrāvaka who has emerged from the triple world and possesses such understanding, it occurs thus: "By me has been attained the stainless and auspicious Nirvāṇa."
I reveal that very thing there; this is not called Nirvana.
However, through the awakening to all dharmas, the deathless Nirvana is attained. (Saddhp 5.64)
Just as the great seers, having indeed established compassion for him, say: "You are deluded; let it not occur to you that 'I am possessed of knowledge. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 5.65.
When you are situated inside the inner chamber,
you of little intelligence do not know at all what exists outside.
But he who remains inside does not even now know what has been done or left undone outside; how then will you, O one of little intelligence, know it?
If a sound were to issue forth here at a distance of only five yojanas,
you would not even be able to hear it, let alone any other sound from further away.
Those who harbor evil thoughts toward you, or others who are well-disposed—these you are unable to know; how then can you have such pride?
Even when one must travel only a single *krośa*, there is no movement without a path;
yet you have forgotten everything that occurred within your mother’s womb.
He who possesses these five superknowledges is called "omniscient" here;
yet out of delusion, you, knowing nothing at all, declare yourself to be omniscient.
If you seek omniscience, you must bring forth the superknowledges;
staying in the forest, contemplate that bringing forth of the superknowledges,
for by means of that pure Dharma, you will attain the superknowledges.
Having grasped that meaning, he went to the forest and, with a well-composed mind, reflected upon it;
endowed with virtuous qualities, he attained the five supernormal knowledges before long.
In the same way, all the śrāvakas have the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa; then the Jina teaches them: "This is merely a rest, not final extinction."
This is the skillful means of the Buddhas; they say that there is no nirvāṇa apart from omniscience. Therefore, apply yourselves to that.
The infinite knowledge of the three times, the six auspicious perfections,
emptiness, the signless, and that which is free from aspiration.
The thought of awakening and all other dharmas that lead to nirvāṇa—
whether with outflows or without outflows, peaceful— all are like space.
The four Brahma-vihāras and those means of integration (saṃgraha) which have been proclaimed were taught by the supreme ṛṣis for the sake of disciplining sentient beings. (Saddhp 5.78)
And whoever understands that phenomena have the nature of an illusion and a dream, that they are as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree, and equal to an echo— (Saddhp 5.79)
He knows the intrinsic nature of the triple world in its entirety as neither bound nor liberated, yet he does not perceive a final extinction.
All phenomena are equal, empty, and devoid of any inherent differentiation;
he does not perceive them, nor does he discern even the slightest phenomenon.
That one of great wisdom perceives the Dharma-body in its entirety;
there is no such thing as three vehicles here, for there is only the single vehicle.
All phenomena are equal; all are equal, always equally equal.
Knowing this, one understands the deathless peace that is nirvāṇa.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Chapter on the Medicinal Herbs," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 97) Chapter Six: The Prophecy.

Then, having spoken these verses, the Blessed One addressed the entire community of monks: "I announce to you, monks, I declare to you: I prophesy that all of you shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas."
I declare this: my disciple, the monk Kāśyapa, will perform acts of respect, veneration, honor, worship, adoration, and reverence toward thirty thousand koṭis of Buddhas.
He will uphold the true Dharma of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. In his final existence, in the world-system Avabhāsaprāptā, during the eon Mahāvyūha,
he will appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Raśmiprabhāsa, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata.
He will be a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. His lifespan will be twelve intermediate kalpas,
and his True Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.
The semblance of the True Dharma will remain for exactly twenty intermediate kalpas.
Furthermore, that Buddha-field of his will be pure and clean, free from stones, pebbles, and gravel; free from chasms and precipices; and free from drains, sewers, and cesspools.
It will be level, delightful, serene, beautiful to behold, composed of lapis lazuli, adorned with jewel-trees, laid out like a chessboard with golden threads, and strewn with flowers.
And many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas will arise there;
there will also be immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of śrāvakas there,
and Māra the Evil One will find no opportunity for interference there.
And the retinue of Māra will not be perceived;
yet indeed, Māra and his retinue will exist there.
Nevertheless, in that world-system, they will be devoted to upholding the true Dharma within the teaching of that very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Raśmiprabhāsa.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "O monks, with my Buddha-eye I see that this elder Kāśyapa shall indeed become a Buddha in a future age, after incalculable eons, having performed worship to the Supreme among Bipeds. (Saddhp 6.1)
"O monks, this Kāśyapa shall indeed behold thirty thousand full koṭis of Jinas;
and there he shall practice the holy life for the sake of the wisdom of a Buddha."
Having made offerings to the supreme among bipeds and having fully realized this unsurpassed knowledge,
he will later become a Lord of the World, an incomparable great seer.
And his field shall be preeminent—wondrous, pure, auspicious, and beautiful to behold;
it shall be pleasing in form, ever-lovely, and adorned with golden threads. (Saddhp 6.4)
O Bhikṣu, in that field there will be various trees made of jewels, each one upon a checkerboard square, emitting delightful fragrances.
Adorned with various kinds of flowers and graced by manifold blossoms,
it shall be level, auspicious, beautiful to behold, and free from pits or precipices.
There will be many thousands of millions of bodhisattvas— thousands upon thousands— who have well-subdued minds, possess great supernormal powers, uphold the Vaipulya sūtras, and are protectors.
Those disciples of the King of Dharma who possess the final body and are free from outflows—
no measure for them can ever be found, even if one were to calculate their number with divine knowledge throughout the eons.

He shall remain for twelve intermediate kalpas; his True Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas, and its Counterfeit shall remain for twenty intermediate kalpas—such will be the array of the Radiance of Rays.

Then indeed, the elder Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Subhūti, and the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, with their bodies trembling and their eyes fixed unblinking upon the Blessed One, gazed at him. And at that moment, each individually, they spoke these verses in mental concert:
O Arhat, O Great Hero, Lion of the Śākyas, Supreme among Men!
Out of compassion for us, please utter the word "Buddha."
O Supreme among Men, O Lord, having surely recognized the opportune moment, please sprinkle us as if with nectar and grant us your prophecy. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 6.11)
Suppose a man who has come from a famine, having obtained excellent food, were told: "Wait; the food is already within reach of your hand. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 6.12.
In this very way, we are eager; having contemplated the Lesser Vehicle, may we,
like beings who have eaten during a time of famine, obtain the wisdom of a Buddha.
The Great Sage, the Fully Awakened One, does not yet grant us a prophecy,
just as one would not eat food placed directly into the hand.
And thus, O Hero, having heard this unsurpassed proclamation, we were filled with longing; when we are prophesied, then we shall be at peace.
Please grant an explanation, O Great Hero, you who desire our welfare and are compassionate;
O Great Sage, may there be an end even to the state of poverty in our minds. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 6.16.
Then the Blessed One, having known with his own mind this very reflection in the minds of those elder great śrāvakas,
addressed the entire community of monks once again: "Monks, this elder great śrāvaka of mine, Subhūti, will pay honor to three hundred thousand myriads of kotis of Buddhas."
He will show respect, honor, worship, veneration, and reverence;
and therein he will practice the holy life and fully realize awakening.

Having performed such meritorious deeds, in his final existence he will become in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śaśiketū, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
And that buddha-field of his shall be named Ratnasaṃbhava;
that eon shall be named Ratnāvabhāsa;
and that buddha-field shall be level.
It will be delightful, made of crystal, adorned with various jewel-trees, free from chasms and precipices, devoid of filth and refuse-heaps, charming, and strewn with flowers;
and there, men shall take up residence in the enjoyment of gabled chambers.
Furthermore, he will have many disciples, immeasurable in number.
It will not be possible to reach the limit of their number through calculation;
there will be many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas here,
and the lifespan of that Blessed One will be twelve intermediate kalpas.
The true Dharma shall remain for twenty intermediate eons;
the semblance of the true Dharma shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate eons.
And that Blessed One, standing in the sky above, will constantly teach the Dharma.
And he will discipline many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas and many hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"I announce it today, O monks; I declare it today—listen to me!
This elder Subhūti, my disciple, shall become a Buddha in a future age. (Saddhp 6.17)
And having beheld thirty full nayuta-koti of Buddhas of great majesty,
he will then practice the conduct that is in accordance with this wisdom, for the sake of this very knowledge.
In his final existence, O Hero, that great seer will bear a body endowed with the thirty-two marks, resembling a golden pillar, compassionate and intent on the welfare of the world.
And that excellent field shall be beautiful, desirable, and pleasing to the great multitude,
where that Friend of the World will dwell after having delivered millions of billions of living beings.
Many bodhisattvas of great majesty here shall set in motion the irreversible wheel;
those of sharp faculties within the teaching of that Jina will adorn his buddha-field.
His śrāvakas are many; there is never any number or measure of them.
They possess the six superknowledges and the three types of knowledge, have great supernatural powers, and are established in the eight liberations.
And his power of supernormal transformation will be inconceivable as he proclaims this supreme enlightenment;
gods and humans, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, will constantly stand before him with palms joined in reverence.
Thus, his true Dharma shall remain for twelve intermediate eons,
and its semblance shall likewise remain for twenty intermediate eons of the Supreme among Men.
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire community of monks once more: "I announce to you, monks; I declare to you:
this elder Mahākātyāyana, my disciple, shall pay homage in the presence of eight hundred thousand million Buddhas."
He will show respect, honor, worship, veneration, and reverence [to them].

And after those Tathāgatas have passed into parinirvāṇa, he will construct stūpas for them, one thousand yojanas in height and fifty yojanas in circumference, made of the seven precious substances—namely:
gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald, and the seventh precious substance, musāragalva.
And he will perform worship to those stūpas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags,
and victory-pennants. Furthermore, beyond that and even further beyond, he will likewise perform such honor toward twenty koṭis of Buddhas,
rendering them respect, reverence, veneration, worship, adoration, and homage.

In his final existence, in his final acquisition of a physical body, he will appear in the world as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Jāmbūnadaprabhāsa— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.

And his buddha-field will be completely pure— level, delightful, serene, beautiful to behold, made of crystal, adorned with various jewel-trees, interlaced with golden threads, strewn with carpets of flowers, free from the realms of hell-beings, animals, the world of Yama, and the hosts of asuras;
it will be filled with many humans and gods, graced by many hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas, and embellished by many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
The lifespan of his life will be twelve intermediate kalpas;
his True Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate kalpas,
and the semblance of the True Dharma will likewise remain for twenty intermediate kalpas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Listen now, all you monks, to my words as I speak them today, which are not otherwise.
This elder Kātyāyana, my disciple, shall perform worship for the Leaders."
He will offer manifold and diverse honors to those leaders of the world,
and he will cause stupas to be built for those who have entered nirvana, worshipping them with flowers and perfumes.
Having attained his final physical existence, he will become a Jina in a perfectly pure field;
having fulfilled this very wisdom, he will teach it to thousands of millions of living beings.
Honored in the world including its gods, he shall become a Buddha, a radiant and all-pervading light;
known by the name Jāmbūnadābha, he will be the deliverer of millions of gods and humans.
Many bodhisattvas as well as śrāvakas—immeasurable and innumerable—will adorn the Buddha’s teaching in that field; they will all have abandoned existence and are free from becoming.
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire community of monks once again: "I announce to you, monks;
I declare to you."

"This disciple of mine, the Elder Mahāmaudgalyāyana, will please twenty-eight thousand Buddhas; he will perform various acts of service toward those Blessed Buddhas, and he will offer them honor, respect, veneration, worship, and reverence."
And for those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who have entered final nirvāṇa, he will cause stūpas to be made consisting of the seven precious substances—
namely, gold, silver, beryl, crystal, red pearl, emerald, and musāragalva—
measuring one thousand yojanas in height and five hundred yojanas in circumference.

And he will perform various kinds of worship for those stupas with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory-pennants. Furthermore, beyond that and even further beyond, he will likewise perform such honor, reverence, respect, worship, adoration, and veneration for two million billion buddhas.
And in his final acquisition of a physical body, there will appear in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Tamālapatracandanagandha—
one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed,
a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
And that buddha-field of his shall be named Manobhirāma; that eon shall be named Ratiprapūrṇa;
and that buddha-field of his shall be perfectly pure.
It will be level, delightful, pleasing, beautiful to behold, made of crystal, variegated with jewel-trees, strewn with loose flowers,
filled with many humans and gods, and frequented by hundreds of thousands of ṛṣis— namely, by both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas. Furthermore, his lifespan will be twenty-four intermediate kalpas.
The True Dharma shall remain for forty intermediate eons;
the Counterfeit Dharma shall likewise remain for forty intermediate eons.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"This disciple of mine, Maudgalyāyana by clan, having cast off his human body,
shall behold twenty thousand Tathāgatas, Protectors, as well as eight other stainless Victors."
And there he will practice the holy life of a Buddha, seeking this very knowledge;
at that time, he will pay manifold honor to those leaders, the supreme among bipeds.
Having upheld their vast and sublime True Dharma for thousands of millions of eons,
they will then perform worship at the stupas of those Sugatas who have entered final nirvana.
They will construct stūpas made of jewels and adorned with victory banners for those supreme Jinas,
worshipping those who are compassionate toward the welfare of the world with flowers, perfumes, and musical instruments. (Saddhp 6.33)
And to the west of that very mountain, in a delightful field within that lovely landscape,
there shall be one who pities and benefits the world, named Tamālapatracandanagandha.
The lifespan of that Sugata will be a full twenty-four intermediate kalpas,
as he constantly proclaims this guidance of the Buddha among humans and gods.
There, that Jina had many thousands of millions of śrāvakas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
they possessed the six superknowledges, the three types of knowledge, and great supernatural powers, having attained higher knowledge within the teaching of the Sugata.
And there were many thousands of irreversible bodhisattvas there, who had initiated vigor, were always possessed of clear comprehension, and were devotedly engaged in the teaching of the Sugata.
Even after that Jina has entered parinirvāṇa, his true Dharma will remain during that time;
for twenty full intermediate kalpas, such shall be the duration of its semblance.

These five disciples of mine, who possess great supernatural powers and whom I have designated for supreme enlightenment, shall become self-arisen Victors in a future age; hear from me concerning their conduct.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Prophecy," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 104) Chapter 7: The Previous Deeds.
Once upon a time, monks, in the past, incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, inconceivable, limitless, and boundless eons ago—thereafter...
Long ago, in a time even further back than that— at that time, at that moment— a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū appeared in the world.

He was endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One, in the world-system Saṃbhavā during the eon Mahārūpa.
"Monks, how long has it been since that Tathāgata first appeared?
Monks, suppose a man were to take all the earth-element within this great trichiliocosm world-system and grind it all into powder."
He would make ink.
Then, that man, having taken a single atom of dust from that world-system, would cross over a thousand world-systems in the eastern direction and deposit that single atom of dust there.
Then, that man, having taken a second atom of dust, would cross over another thousand world-systems beyond that and deposit the second atom of dust.
In this manner, that man might deposit the entire earth-element in the eastern direction.
What do you think, monks, would it be possible by calculation to reach the end or the limit of those world-systems?
They said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."

"Certainly not, Sugata. The Blessed One said: "But, monks, it might be possible for some mathematician, or a great master of calculation, to reach the limit of those world-systems by means of calculation—in which those atoms were deposited."
Or those in which they were not deposited;

yet it is not possible, even by means of calculation, to reach the limit of those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons that have passed since the parinirvāṇa of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.
Monks, that period of time was thus inconceivable and thus immeasurable;
yet, through this empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge and vision, I remember that Tathāgata who entered parinirvāṇa so long ago as if he had entered parinirvāṇa today or yesterday.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"I remember many billions of past eons the Supreme among Bipeds, the Great Sage Abhijñājñānābhibhū; at that time, there was an unsurpassed Jina. (Saddhp 7.1)
Suppose someone were to reduce the three-thousandfold world system to dust particles of atomic size;
then, taking a single atom from that mass, he would travel a thousand fields and deposit it there. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 7.2.
And if he were to deposit a second and even a third [particle], he would deposit every single one of those motes of dust;
this world-system would become empty, and all that dust would be exhausted.

Whatever amount of dust might exist in those world-systems, such that its measure is inexhaustible— having reduced all that dust to nothingness, let that be the mark given when a hundred kalpas have passed. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 7.4)
Even after immeasurable many millions of eons have passed since that Sugata entered parinirvāṇa, all those atoms would not even be perceptible; so many eons will have been exhausted.
For so long that Guide remained in parinirvāṇa—those disciples and those bodhisattvas—I remember such wisdom of the Tathāgatas as if it had occurred today or yesterday. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 7.6)
O monks, such is this knowledge, and it is the infinite knowledge of the Tathāgata;
for many hundreds of eons, I have cultivated through subtle and untainted mindfulness the state of a Buddha.
Furthermore, monks, the lifespan of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was five million four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of kalpas.

And previously, before he had attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, while still at the most excellent seat of awakening, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, utterly shattered and defeated the entire army of Māra.
"Having shattered and defeated them, I shall realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment"—yet even so, those dharmas did not yet become manifest to him.
He remained at the seat of awakening at the foot of the Bodhi tree for one intermediate kalpa; he remained there for a second intermediate kalpa as well.
Yet he did not yet fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. For a third, a fourth, a fifth, a sixth, a seventh, an eighth, a ninth, and even a tenth intermediate kalpa,
he remained at the foot of the Bodhi tree at the seat of awakening, sitting cross-legged once and never rising from it in the interim.
With a mind that was unshakable, he remained with a body that was unmoving and unwavering;
yet, those dharmas did not yet become manifest to him.

Furthermore, monks, when that Blessed One had reached the most excellent seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), a great lion-throne was prepared for him by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, measuring one hundred thousand yojanas in height;
it was upon this that the Blessed One sat and fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. And as soon as that Blessed One had sat down at the seat of enlightenment,

Then the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahmakāyika realm rained down a divine shower of flowers. For a hundred yojanas all around the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), they released winds from the sky that swept away those withered flowers.
And that rain of flowers, once it had begun to fall, poured down unceasingly upon the seat of awakening where the Blessed One was seated;
for ten full intermediate kalpas, they showered that Blessed One.
And they continued to pour down that rain of flowers in such a manner until the time of the Blessed One’s final nirvāṇa, showering that Blessed One throughout.
And the sons of the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings sounded divine celestial drums;

for the sake of honoring the Blessed One who had reached the supreme seat of enlightenment, they sounded them without interruption for ten full intermediate kalpas while that Blessed One remained seated.
Beyond that, those divine musical instruments were sounded continuously and incessantly until the time of the Blessed One’s great final nirvana.
Then, monks, at the end of ten intermediate kalpas, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And having known that he had just attained it, those who were the sixteen legitimate sons of that Blessed One while he was still a prince existed;
among them, the eldest was named Jñānākara.

Furthermore, monks, each of those sixteen princes possessed various playthings and delightful objects, diverse and beautiful to behold. Then, monks, those sixteen princes, having cast aside those various playthings and delightful objects,
and having learned that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, [approached him].
Surrounded and preceded by their weeping mothers and nurses, and surrounded and preceded by that great universal monarch,

the noble grandfather Mahākośa, as well as by many royal ministers and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings, they proceeded toward where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was at the most excellent seat of enlightenment.
They approached him;
they approached for the sake of honoring, respecting, revering, worshiping, adoring, and paying homage to that Blessed One.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of that Blessed One, having circumambulated that Blessed One three times to the right, and having joined their palms in reverence, they addressed that Blessed One face-to-face with these verses:
They praised him with words of like meaning:
"You are the Great Physician; you are unsurpassed; you have attained perfection through infinite eons.
For the sake of delivering all embodied beings here, this auspicious resolve of yours has been fulfilled."
Having sat down upon a single seat, he performed these ten extremely difficult practices for ten intermediate kalpas;
yet during that time, his body was never moved, nor his hands or feet, nor any other limb.
Your mind, too, has reached peace; it is well-established, immovable, and forever unshakable.
There is never any distraction for you; you abide in ultimate tranquility, free from outflows.
"By good fortune, you have arrived safely and in well-being, unharmed, having attained this supreme enlightenment!
Such is the supernatural power we possess; by good fortune, O Lion among Men, we flourish! (Saddhp 7.11)
This entire population is leaderless, suffering, and deprived of happiness like one whose eyes have been plucked out;
they do not know the path that leads to the end of suffering, nor do they exert effort for the sake of liberation. (Saddhp 7.12)
The states of woe increase for a long night, and even the divine bodies are subject to decline;
the voice of the Jinas is never heard, and this entire world is shrouded in blinding darkness.
O Knower of the World, today you have attained here the auspicious, supreme, and untainted state;
both we and the world have been graced, and we come to you for refuge, O Protector.
Then, monks, those sixteen princes, while still youths and children,
having praised that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhimukha, face-to-face with these appropriate verses, entreated that Blessed One to turn the wheel of Dharma.
“May the Blessed One teach the Dharma;

may the Sugata teach the Dharma for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, for the welfare, the benefit, and the happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
And at that time, they spoke these verses:
Teach the Dharma, O Great Seer, Guide endowed with the marks of a hundred merits and peerless!
You have attained the most excellent and distinguished wisdom; reveal it to the world, including its devas.
Deliver us and these beings as well; reveal the wisdom of the Tathāgatas, so that we too may attain this supreme enlightenment, as shall these beings.

You know all conduct and wisdom, as well as the resolute intention and the merit previously performed; you know the inclinations of all living beings—set in motion the unsurpassed, supreme wheel of Dharma! (Saddhp 7.17)
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, monks, at that time, when that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was awakening to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, five million billion nayutas of world-systems in each of the ten directions shook in six ways.
And they were suffused by a great radiance.
Furthermore, in all those world-systems, in the intermediate spaces between worlds— which are filled with unfavorable conditions and shrouded in blinding darkness,
where even these two, the sun and the moon, though possessing such great supernatural power, such great majesty, and such great splendor, do not even reach with their light— [all were suffused].
They did not perceive his color even with their own color, nor his radiance even with their own radiance;
yet at that time, a great light appeared even in those intermediate spaces between worlds where beings had been born.
They also see one another in this way and perceive one another in this way: "Aha! Indeed, there are other beings born here; aha! Indeed, there are other beings born here!
And in all those world-systems, whatever celestial abodes and divine palaces there are,
As far as the Brahma-world, the earth shook in six ways and was suffused with a great radiance that surpassed the divine majesty of the gods.
Thus, monks, at that time, there appeared in those world-systems a great earthquake and a great, manifest radiance throughout the world.
Then, in the eastern direction, among those five hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems, whatever Brahma palaces there were,
they shone, blazed, and gleamed exceedingly,
being magnificent and full of splendor.
Then, monks, it occurred to those Great Brahmās: "Indeed, these celestial palaces of the Brahmās are exceedingly radiant, glowing, resplendent, glorious, and majestic.
Of what could this be the precursor?"
Then indeed, monks, all those Great Brahmās in those five hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems went to one another’s abodes and announced [the matter].
Then, monks, the Great Brahmā named Sarvasattvatrātā addressed that great assembly of Brahmās in verses:
"Today we are all exceedingly joyful; these most excellent celestial palaces are ablaze.
They are beautiful with splendor and radiance; what is the cause for such a thing as this occurring today?"
"Excellent! Let us now investigate this matter: which son of the gods has been reborn today, whose power is of such a kind as this, never seen before, yet is seen here today? (Saddhp 7.19)
Or perhaps a Buddha, a king among men, has appeared somewhere in the world today, for whose sake such a sign as this exists, so that the ten directions are ablaze with splendor today. (Saddhp 7.20)
Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās who were in those five hundred thousand quintillion world-systems,

having gathered together in harmony, each mounted his own divine Brahmā-palace and, taking divine baskets of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru, they walked and roamed about in the four directions toward the west.
They departed toward that direction.
Then, monks, those Great Brahmās beheld in those five hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems, in the western direction, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.

He saw the Perfectly Awakened One at the supreme and most excellent seat of awakening, seated upon a lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, surrounded and honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; and he was being entreated by those sixteen sons, the royal princes, to set the wheel of Dharma in motion.
Having seen him, they approached the place where the Blessed One was;

having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated that Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered those flower-baskets, as large as Mount Sumeru, over the Blessed One.
They scattered [them] over that Bodhi tree, which measured ten yojanas in extent;
having strewn them, they offered those Brahma-palaces to the Blessed One, saying: "May the Blessed One accept these Brahma-palaces out of compassion for us."
May the Sugata enjoy these Brahma-palaces out of compassion for us.
Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having offered their respective celestial palaces to that Blessed One, at that time praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
"The Jina, the immeasurable, has appeared as a wonder in the world, compassionate for the welfare [of beings]."
You are our protector, you are our teacher, you are our guru; today the ten directions have been graced by your birth.
There are fifty thousand full billions of world-systems from here,
from which we have come to pay homage to the Jina, having completely abandoned our most excellent celestial palaces.
Indeed, these celestial palaces are variegated and wonderful because of deeds performed in the past;
O Knower of the World, please accept them for our benefit and enjoy them as you wish.

Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having praised the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, face to face with these appropriate verses, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
May the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma;
may the Sugata turn the wheel of Dharma in the world.
May the Blessed One teach the state of final liberation.
May the Blessed One ferry across all sentient beings!
May the Blessed One favor this world!
May the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, teach the Dharma to this world with its Māras and Brahmās, to this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, monks, those five million billion nayutas of Brahmās, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Blessed One with these appropriate verses:
"Teach the Dharma, O Blessed One! Teach it, O Supreme among Men!
Teach the power of loving-kindness and deliver the suffering beings! (Saddhp 7.24)
The Illuminator of the World is as difficult to encounter as the flower of the udumbara tree;
O Great Hero, you have now appeared—we entreat the Tathāgata.
Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those Great Brahmās by remaining silent.
