Furthermore, monks, at that time, in the southeastern direction, within those five million billion nayutas of world-systems, the Brahma palaces were exceedingly radiant, glowing, brilliant, majestic, and powerful.
Then, monks, it occurred to those Brahmas: "Indeed, these Brahma palaces are exceedingly radiant, glowing, brilliant, majestic, and powerful."
"Of what, indeed, will this be the precursor?
Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās in those five hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems went to one another's abodes and announced it.
Then, monks, the Great Brahmā named Adhimātrakāruṇika addressed that great assembly of Brahmās in verses:
"Friends, by whose omen is this seen?
All the celestial palaces of those possessed of great glory are shining with exceeding brilliance."
Or perhaps a meritorious son of the gods has come here today,
by whose power all these celestial palaces are thus adorned.
Or rather, the Buddha, the supreme among bipeds, has appeared in this world;
by his majestic power, these celestial palaces have become such as these today.
"Let us all search together; this cause cannot be a minor one.
Indeed, such a portent as this has never been seen before. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 7.29)
We travel in the four directions, going through millions of lands;
it is evident that today the appearance of a Buddha will take place in the world.

Then, monks, those fifty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Brahmās also ascended their respective divine Brahma-palaces and, taking up divine baskets of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru, [proceeded] in the four directions.
Wandering and roaming through the quarters, they proceeded toward the northwestern direction. Then, monks, those Great Brahmās beheld in the northwestern direction that Blessed One,
the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, who had reached the most excellent and supreme seat of awakening.

Seeing him seated upon a lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, surrounded and honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, and being entreated by those sixteen royal princes, his sons, to set the wheel of Dharma in motion,
they approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of that Blessed One, they circumambulated the Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times and scattered and strewed those flower-baskets, as large as Mount Sumeru,
over the Blessed One and over the Bodhi tree, which measured eighty yojanas in height.
Having scattered them, they offered those Brahma palaces to the Blessed One, saying: "May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us;
may the Sugata enjoy these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us."
Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having offered their respective celestial palaces to that Blessed One, at that time praised the Blessed One face-to-face with these appropriate verses:
"Homage be to you, O peerless Great Sage, God of gods, with a voice as sweet as the kalaviṅka bird!"
O Vināyaka, in this world including its devas, I pay homage to you, who are compassionate for the welfare of the world. (Saddhp 7.31)
O Protector, you have appeared today in this world after a very long time; you are a marvel, having somehow arisen now.
For a full eighty hundred kalpas, this world of living beings has been devoid of Buddhas.
It was empty of the best of bipeds, and at that time the realms of misery were overflowing;
meanwhile, the divine hosts were declining for a full eight thousand eons.

He has now arisen in the world as one who is compassionate for our welfare—the eye, the path, the shelter, the protection, the father, and likewise the kinsman; by our merits, this King of Dharma has appeared here.

Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having praised the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, face-to-face with these appropriate verses, said this to the Blessed One:
May the Blessed One set in motion the wheel of Dharma;
may the Sugata set in motion the wheel of Dharma in the world;
may the Blessed One teach the state of nirvāṇa.
May the Blessed One deliver sentient beings;
may the Blessed One favor this world;
may the Blessed One teach the Dharma to this world with its Māras and Brahmās, to this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas, humans, and asuras.
That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, monks, those five million billion nayutas of Brahmās, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Blessed One with these two appropriate verses:
"O Great Sage, set in motion the supreme wheel; reveal the Dharma in the ten directions!
Rescue beings who are oppressed by the nature of suffering; produce joy and gladness for all embodied beings."
Having heard this, they shall become attainers of awakening and go to divine realms;
all the hosts of asuras shall diminish, and they shall become peaceful, self-controlled, and happy.
Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those Great Brahmās by remaining silent.
Furthermore, monks, at that time, in the southern direction, within those five million billion trillion world-systems, the Brahma palaces were exceedingly radiant,
glowing, resplendent, glorious, and powerful.
Then, monks, it occurred to those Great Brahmās: "Indeed, these Brahmā palaces are exceedingly radiant, glowing, resplendent, glorious, and powerful.
Of what could such a portentous sign be the precursor?"
Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās in those five million billion trillion world-systems went to one another’s abodes and announced [the news].
Then, monks, the Great Brahmā named Sudharma addressed that great assembly of Brahmās with these two verses:
"Friends, it cannot be without cause or without reason that all these celestial palaces are blazing here today.
They surely portend some sign in this world; let us thoroughly investigate the meaning of this."
Indeed, throughout hundreds of past eons, such a sign has never occurred before—
whether it be a son of the gods born here, or whether a Buddha has appeared in this world.
Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās in those five million billion nayutas of world-systems, having gathered together in harmony, mounted their respective divine Brahmā palaces and,
taking divine baskets of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru, walked and roamed about in the four directions toward the north.
They departed toward the northern quarter. Then, monks, those Great Brahmās beheld the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,
who had reached the most excellent seat of awakening and was seated upon a lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Seeing him surrounded and honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans,
and being entreated by those sixteen royal princes, his sons, to set in motion the wheel of the Dharma,
they approached the Blessed One.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of that Blessed One, they circumambulated the Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times. Then, with those flower-baskets as large as Mount Sumeru, they scattered and strewed them over that Blessed One and over the Bodhi tree, which measured ten yojanas in height.
Having scattered those divine Brahma palaces, they offered them to the Blessed One, saying: "May the Blessed One accept these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us;
may the Sugata enjoy these Brahma palaces out of compassion for us."
Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having offered their respective celestial palaces to that Blessed One, at that moment praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
"The sight of the Leaders is very difficult to obtain; you have come well, O crusher of the passion for existence!"
It has been a very long time since you were seen in this world; you are seen today after hundreds of complete eons.
Satisfy the thirsty beings, O Lord of the World! You have never been seen before; somehow you are now visible.
Just as the flower of the Udumbara tree is difficult to find, so too have you been seen, O Leader, by some rare chance.
"O Leader, by your power these celestial palaces of ours have been made radiant today;
O All-Seeing One, accept them and enjoy them for the sake of showing us favor."

Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having praised the Blessed One Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, face-to-face with these appropriate verses, said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma in the world!"
May the Blessed One teach the state of nirvāṇa; may the Blessed One deliver all beings;
may the Blessed One favor this world.

May the Blessed One teach the Dharma to this world with its Māras and Brahmās, to this generation with its śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, its gods, humans, and asuras. That will be for the benefit of many, for the happiness of many, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of a great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, monks, those five million billion nayutas of Brahmās, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Blessed One with these two appropriate verses:
"Teach the Dharma, O Blessed One, O Guide; set in motion the wheel consisting of the Dharma!
Resound the drum consisting of the Dharma, and blow that conch shell of the Dharma! (Saddhp 7.42)
Rain down the rain of the true Dharma upon the world; speak with a melodious voice and utter well-spoken words.
Being thus entreated, proclaim the Dharma and liberate millions of billions of beings.
Then, monks, that Blessed One consented to those Great Brahmās by remaining silent...
[and so on] ...likewise in the southwestern direction.
Thus in the western direction, thus in the northwestern direction,
and thus in the northern direction.
In this same way in the northeastern direction, and likewise in the downward direction.

Then, monks, in the upward direction, within those five million billion trillion world-systems, whatever Brahmā-palaces there were, they shone exceedingly, blazed, gleamed, were glorious, and were full of majesty.
Then, monks, this thought occurred to those Great Brahmās: "Indeed, these Brahmā-palaces are shining exceedingly, blazing, gleaming, glorious, and full of majesty."
"To whom indeed will this kind of omen belong?
Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās in those five hundred thousand quintillion world-systems went to one another's abodes and announced it.

Then, monks, the Great Brahmā named Śikhin addressed that great assembly of Brahmās in verses: "Friends, what is the cause of this? For what reason are these celestial palaces so completely filled, and why have they increased so excessively in vigor, color, and radiance? What is the cause of this?"
"Never before have we seen anything like this, nor have we heard of such a thing as it was in the past.
These [trees] are now suffused with splendor and shine with exceeding brilliance; what is the cause of this?"
Or perhaps some son of the gods, endowed with virtuous karma, has been born here; this is his majestic power, or else it may be that a Buddha has appeared in the world at some time. (Saddhp 7.46)

Then, monks, all those Great Brahmās who were in those five million quintillion world-systems, having gathered together in unison, mounted their respective divine Brahmā palaces and took up divine baskets of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru; wandering and roaming through the four directions, they approached the downward direction.
Furthermore, monks, those Great Brahmās beheld in the lower direction that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,

who had reached the most excellent seat of awakening and was seated upon a lion throne at the foot of the Bodhi tree, surrounded and honored by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans.

Seeing him being entreated by those sixteen princes, the sons of the king, to turn the wheel of Dharma, they approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One hundreds of thousands of times, and scattered over the Blessed One heaps of flowers as large as Mount Sumeru.

They scattered [flowers] over that Bodhi tree to the extent of ten yojanas. Having strewn them, they offered their respective divine Brahma-palaces to the Blessed One, saying: "May the Blessed One accept these Brahma-palaces out of compassion for us;
may the Sugata enjoy these Brahma-palaces out of compassion for us."
Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having presented their respective celestial palaces to that Blessed One, at that time praised the Blessed One to his face with these appropriate verses:
"Excellent is the sight of the Buddhas, the protectors and lords of the world!"
Indeed, within the three realms, the Buddhas are those who truly liberate sentient beings.
The World-Leaders with their all-seeing eyes survey the ten directions;
having opened the door to the Deathless, they cause many beings to enter.
Inconceivable eons have passed in the past which were empty;
because the Lords of Jinas were not seen, the ten directions were blind.
The fierce hells increase, as do the animal realms and the asuras;
and thousands of millions of living beings are reborn among the pretas.
Divine bodies decay, and having fallen from them, they go to an evil destiny;
for those who have not heard the Dharma of the Buddhas, their destination becomes wretched. (Saddhp 7.51)
The purity of conduct, the destinies, and the wisdom of all living beings decline;
their happiness perishes, and their perception of happiness is destroyed. (Saddhp 7.52)
They will be of improper conduct and established in false dharma; unsubdued by the Lord of the World, they will fall into the miserable destinies. (Saddhp 7.53)
You have been seen, O Light of the World; you have come after a very long time.
You have arisen out of compassion for the sake of all sentient beings.
"By good fortune, you have safely attained the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha;
we rejoice in you, as does the entire world together with its gods."
"O Lord, through your majestic power, we offer you these most variegated celestial palaces; accept them, O Great Hero, O Great Sage! (Saddhp 7.56)
O Leader, please partake [of this] out of compassion for us,
so that we and all sentient beings may touch supreme enlightenment.

Then, monks, those Great Brahmās, having praised the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, face-to-face with these appropriate verses, said this to the Blessed One:
"May the Blessed One turn the wheel of Dharma!"
May the Sugata set the wheel of Dharma in motion;
may the Blessed One teach the state of nirvāṇa;
may the Blessed One deliver all sentient beings.
May the Blessed One favor this world;
may the Blessed One teach the Dharma to this world with its Māras and Brahmās, to this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods, humans, and asuras.

That will be for the benefit of many people, for the happiness of many people, out of compassion for the world, and for the welfare, benefit, and happiness of the great multitude of beings, both gods and humans.
Then, monks, those five million billion nayutas of Brahmās, with one voice and in unison, addressed the Blessed One with these two appropriate verses:
"Turn the supreme, unsurpassed wheel! Beat the drum of the Deathless!
Liberate beings from hundreds of sufferings and show them the path to Nirvāṇa! (Saddhp 7.58)
We entreat you: speak the Dharma and favor us as well as this world;
release that beautiful and sweet voice which has been perfected through ten million billion eons.

Then, monks, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, having understood the entreaty of those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Brahmās and of those sixteen royal princes,
at that time set in motion the Wheel of Dharma— threefold in its revolutions and twelvefold in its aspects— which had never before been set in motion.
Neither by a śramaṇa, nor by a brāhmaṇa, nor by a deva, nor by Māra, nor by Brahmā, nor by anyone else in the world, can this be overturned in accordance with the Dharma:
namely, that "this is suffering" and "this is the origin of suffering."
"This is the cessation of suffering;
this is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.
And he extensively proclaimed the process of dependent origination: "Thus, monks, conditioned by ignorance are the volitional formations," and so forth.
With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises;
with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise.
With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact;
with contact as condition, there is feeling; with feeling as condition, there is craving;
with craving as condition, there is clinging.
With grasping as condition, existence arises; with existence as condition, birth arises;
and with birth as condition, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering:
from the cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of volitional formations;
from the cessation of volitional formations comes the cessation of consciousness.
With the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease;
with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases.
With the cessation of contact, feeling ceases;
with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases;
with the cessation of craving, grasping ceases.
With the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases;
with the cessation of birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.

And as soon as this Wheel of Dharma had been set in motion, monks, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, it was done in the presence of the assembly consisting of gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and of the generation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, including gods, humans, and asuras.
Then, at that very instant, moment, and second, the minds of sixty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of living beings were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging;
and they all became possessors of the three knowledges, the six superknowledges, and meditators on the eight liberations.
Furthermore, monks, in due course, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, gave a second teaching of the Dharma.
He gave a third discourse on the Dharma, and he also gave a fourth discourse on the Dharma.

Then, monks, during each individual teaching of the Dharma by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, the minds of hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging. Thereafter, monks, the community of disciples of that Blessed One became beyond calculation.
Furthermore, monks, at that time those sixteen princes, while still in their youth, out of faith went forth from the home to the homeless life.

They all became novice monks (*śrāmaṇera*), wise, discerning, intelligent, skillful, and experienced in the conduct of many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas; they were seekers of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Then, monks, those sixteen novices [approached] that Blessed One, Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū...
They said this to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: "Furthermore, Blessed One,

these many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of the Tathāgata’s disciples— possessing great supernatural power, great majesty, and great renown— have been brought to perfection through the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dharma."

Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, out of compassion for us, were to teach the Dharma starting from unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
so that we too may train in accordance with the Tathāgata. O Blessed One, we are seekers of the vision and knowledge of the Tathāgata.
The Blessed One alone is our witness in this very matter;
and you, O Blessed One, who know the inclinations of all sentient beings, know our own resolute intention.

Furthermore, monks, at that time, having seen those foolish children, the princes who had gone forth as novices, half of all the retinue of that universal monarch likewise went forth— eighty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of living beings.
Then, monks, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,

having understood the resolute intention of those śrāmaṇeras, after the passing of twenty thousand kalpas, [taught] the Dharma discourse named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, a sūtra of great vaipulya, an instruction for bodhisattvas, and the protection of all Buddhas.
He proclaimed it in detail for all those four assemblies.
Furthermore, monks, at that time those sixteen royal princes, who were novice monks (śrāmaṇera), took up, retained, mastered, and fully comprehended what was spoken by that Blessed One.

Then, monks, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, gave a prediction (vyākaraṇa) to those sixteen novice monks regarding their unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, monks, while that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū was preaching this Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the Good Dharma, those sixteen novices and many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of living beings fell into doubt.
Then, monks, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū,
having preached this Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma for eight thousand eons without ceasing, entered his dwelling to retire in solitude.
And so, monks, remaining thus in seclusion, that Tathāgata remained established in his dwelling for eighty-four thousand kalpas.
Then, monks, those sixteen novices, having perceived that the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, was in retreat, each individually prepared lion-thrones as Dharma-seats;
having sat upon them and paid homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, they [addressed] that *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*...
They extensively proclaimed this Dharma discourse for eighty-four thousand kalpas before the fourfold assembly.

Therein, monks, each individual novice bodhisattva ripened, exhorted, gladdened, inspired, delighted, and established hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of living beings— equal in number to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers— in unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.

Then, monks, at the conclusion of those eighty-four thousand eons, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, mindful and clearly comprehending, arose from that samādhi. Having arisen, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, approached that Dharma-seat.
Having approached, he sat down on the very seat that had been prepared.

Monks, as soon as the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, had sat upon that Dharma-seat, he immediately surveyed the entire circle of the assembly and addressed the community of monks: "It is wonderful!"

"Monks, these sixteen novices have attained the marvelous; they are wise, having attended upon many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, having practiced their conduct, serving the wisdom of the Buddhas, receiving the wisdom of the Buddhas, entering into the wisdom of the Buddhas, and manifesting the wisdom of the Buddhas.
Monks, attend upon these sixteen novices again and again."

Whosoever among the monks— whether belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas— shall not reject nor oppose the Dharma teaching of these sons of good family.
They shall all swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and they shall all realize the wisdom of the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, monks, by those sixteen sons of good family, this Dharma-discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was repeatedly proclaimed under the teaching of that Blessed One.

Moreover, monks, by each one of those sixteen bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who were śrāmaṇeras, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of beings, equal to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers, [were established in the supreme enlightenment].
They were incited toward enlightenment,

and all of them subsequently went forth into homelessness together with those very same individuals throughout various successive births; beholding them alone, they heard the Dharma from their very presence.
By them, forty thousand koṭis of Buddhas have been propitiated;
some even now continue to propitiate them.
I announce to you, monks; I declare to you:
those sixteen princes who, while still youths, were novice monks and Dharma-preachers under the teaching of that Blessed One—
They have all fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and they all currently abide, remain, and maintain themselves,
teaching the Dharma to many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas in various buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.
Namely, monks, in the eastern direction, in the world-system Abhirati, there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Akṣobhya; and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Merukūṭa.
In the southeastern direction, monks, there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Siṃhaghoṣa; and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Siṃhadhvaja.

Monks, in the southern direction there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Ākāśapratiṣṭhita, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Nityaparinirvṛta; and in the southwestern direction, monks, there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Indradhvaja, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Brahmadhvaja.
Monks, in the western direction there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Amitāyus; and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvalokadhātūpadravodvegapratyuttīrṇa.
Monks, in the northwestern direction there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Tamālapatracandanagandhābhijña; and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Merukalpa.
In the northern direction, monks, there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Meghasvaradīpa, and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Meghasvararāja.
In the northeastern direction, monks, there is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvalokabhayacchambhitatvavidhvaṃsanarakara.
And I, monks, am the sixteenth Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni, who has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment right here in the midst of this Sahā world-system.

Furthermore, monks, those beings who at that time heard the Dharma from us while we were novices under the teaching of that Blessed One— of each one of those bodhisattva mahāsattvas there are many [lives] equal to the sands of the river Gaṅgā.
"O monks, those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of beings whom we have exhorted toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— even now they remain only on the level of the śrāvakas;
yet they are being brought to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
This very sequence leads them to the full awakening of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Why is that?
Because, monks, the wisdom of the Tathāgata is thus difficult to resolve with faith.

And who, monks, were those beings whom I, as a bodhisattva, under the teaching of that Blessed One, caused to hear the Dharma of omniscience— beings numbering in the hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis, immeasurable and incalculable, equal to the sands of the river Ganges?
You, monks, were those beings at that time, in that age.
And those who, after I have entered final nirvana, will become my disciples in a future time and hear of the bodhisattva practice,
yet will not realize, "We are bodhisattvas," [will fall into error].

Furthermore, monks, although all those monks will pass into final nirvana with the perception that they have attained final nirvana, nevertheless, monks, in whatever other world-systems I dwell under various names, there they shall be reborn, seeking the wisdom of a Tathāgata.
And there they will again hear this teaching:
that for the Tathāgatas there is only one parinirvāṇa;
there is no other second nirvāṇa outside of this.
Monks, this should be understood as the skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) and the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas.
Monks, at whatever time the Tathāgata perceives that it is the time for his own final nirvana (*parinirvāṇa*),

and he sees that the assembly is completely pure— possessing the essence of resolute faith, having entered the course of the Dharma of emptiness, endowed with meditative concentration, and possessing great meditative concentration— [then he acts accordingly].
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, knowing that this was the time, gathered all the bodhisattvas and all the śrāvakas together and subsequently proclaimed this matter:
"Monks, there is no second vehicle or parinirvāṇa whatsoever in the world; what need is there to mention a third?"

"Monks, this indeed is the skillful means of the Tathāgatas, the Arhats: having perceived that the realm of sentient beings has long been lost, delighting in what is inferior and sunk in the mire of sensual desires, the Tathāgata, monks, then proclaims to them that nirvāṇa which they are inclined toward."

"Monks, it is just as if there were here a wilderness forest five hundred yojanas in extent, and a great multitude of people had set out upon it to go to an island of jewels. Among them, there would be a single guide who was experienced, wise, skillful, intelligent, and truly adept in the difficult terrains of the wilderness."
And he would lead that caravan through the forest.

Then, indeed, that great multitude of people—exhausted, weary, afraid, and terrified—would speak thus: "O noble guide and leader, you should know this: we are indeed exhausted, weary, afraid, terrified, and find no rest."
"We shall turn back once more;

this wilderness is too far from here. Then, monks, that guide, being skillful in means, perceiving that those men wished to turn back, thought thus: "Lest these poor wretches [fail to reach] such a great island of jewels..."
Thinking, "Let them not go [further]," he would employ skillful means out of compassion for them;
having traversed a hundred yojanas, or two hundred yojanas, or three hundred yojanas into the midst of that wilderness, he would magically create a city made of supernatural power (*ṛddhimaya*).
Then he should speak thus to those men: "Do not be afraid, sirs;
do not turn back.
This is that great country."
Rest here!
Perform here all whatever duties you have to perform.
Attain nirvana here and dwell here, having found rest.
Furthermore, whoever shall have business there will go to that great island of jewels.
Then, monks, those beings who had reached that wilderness would be struck with wonder and amazement, thinking: "We have been delivered from the forest wilderness;
here we shall dwell having attained nirvāṇa.
Then, monks, those men would enter that city made of magical power.
They would have the perception that they have arrived, and they would have the perception that they have crossed over;
they would think, "We are extinguished; we have become cooled."
Then, knowing that they were rested, the guide would cause that city made of magical power to disappear.
Having caused it to disappear, he would say to those men: "Come, sirs, beings!
This great island of jewels is now near."
"But this city has been conjured by me for the sake of your rest."
"In the same way, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is the guide for you all and for all sentient beings.
Then, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, spoke thus:"
He perceives: "This great wilderness of afflictions must be traversed, escaped from, and abandoned;
lest these beings, upon hearing this single Buddha-knowledge, should turn back in mere haste and never approach it."
"This wisdom of a Buddha must be accomplished through much hardship.

In that regard, the Tathāgata, perceiving that sentient beings have weak aspirations, creates a city made of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)—just as that guide did—for the sake of providing rest to those beings;
and once they have rested, he says to them: "This indeed is a city made of supernatural power."

In the same way, monks, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened one, through his great skill in means, teaches and proclaims two intermediate stages of nirvāṇa for the sake of providing rest to sentient beings— namely, the stage of the śrāvaka and the stage of the pratyekabuddha.

And at whatever time, monks, those beings are situated there, then indeed, monks, the Tathāgata also proclaims to them in this way: "Monks, you have certainly not yet accomplished your task nor finished what was to be done;
rather, monks, you must continue your practice."
"O monks, look upon the wisdom of the Tathāgata; investigate it! That which you consider to be nirvāṇa is not actually nirvāṇa at all.
Rather, O monks, this is the skillful means of the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, that they proclaim three vehicles."
Then the Blessed One, wishing to further elucidate this very matter, at that time spoke these verses:
"When the Leader of the World, Abhijñājñānābhibhū, sat upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa),
he, the seer of ultimate truth, did not attain awakening for ten full intermediate eons (antarakalpa)."
Then the gods, nāgas, asuras, and guhyakas exerted themselves for the sake of honoring that Jina;
they released a rain of flowers there upon the Buddha, this Leader of Men, and upon his enlightenment.
And in the sky above, drums resounded for the sake of honoring and worshiping that Jina;
yet there, the Jina remained deeply distressed because he was taking so long to awaken to the unsurpassed state.
And after ten intermediate kalpas had passed, that Blessed One, Anābhibhū, touched enlightenment;
at that time, all the gods, humans, bhujagas, and asuras were joyful and exultant.
Then his sixteen heroic sons, the princes of that leader of men, who were rich in virtues,
approached that foremost of bipeds, preceded by thousands of millions of living beings.
Having bowed at the feet of the Guide, they entreated him: "Reveal the Dharma!
Satisfy us and this world with your well-spoken words here, O lion among the lords of men! (Saddhp 7.65)
After a long time, you have become known throughout these ten directions; you have arisen, O Great Guide.
For the sake of exhorting living beings by means of signs, the celestial palaces of Brahmā tremble.
In the eastern direction, fifty thousand koṭis of realms were shaken;
there too, those supreme Brahmā palaces became exceedingly radiant.
Having recognized such a prior sign, they approached the Lord of the World-Leaders;
having scattered flowers here over the Guide, they offered all their celestial palaces to him.
They entreated him to turn the wheel [of Dharma] and praised him with songs of verse;
yet that king of men remained silent, thinking: "It is not yet time for me to preach the Dharma."
In this way, from the southern direction, and then from the western, the nadir, the northern, the zenith,
and likewise from the intermediate directions, thousands of millions of Brahmās arrived.
Having scattered flowers over the Leader and having bowed at the feet of the Guide,
and having offered all the celestial palaces and praised him, he made this request once again.
Set in motion the wheel, O you of infinite vision! You are extremely difficult to encounter even in many millions of eons.
Display the power of loving-kindness practiced in the past; open the door to the deathless!
Knowing the request, the one of infinite vision reveals the Dharma in many ways;
he explains in detail the Four Truths, [showing] that all these existents have arisen in dependence [upon causes].
The One with Vision, having made ignorance the primary cause, declares that suffering ends with death;
know that all these faults are born from birth, and that these very things constitute human mortality.
Immediately after he had spoken the Dharma in its many forms, various and infinite,
eighty *nayuta*-koṭis of beings, having heard it, quickly established themselves on the level of the śrāvakas.
In another moment, as that Jina was teaching many dharmas,
those pure beings, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, became śrāvakas in an instant.
Thereafter, the assembly of that Leader of the World was incalculable;
even if one were to count for tens of millions of billions of eons, one would not reach the end of them.
And those sixteen princes, all of whom had become monks like Cailaka, as novices (śrāmaṇera), spoke to that Jina: "O Leader, reveal the supreme Dharma!"
"O Knower of the World, may we become just as you are, the supreme among all Victors;
and may all these beings likewise become just as you are, O Hero of pure vision."
And that Victor, having understood the aspirations of those sons who were still youths,
revealed the supreme, foremost enlightenment through many millions of billions of parables.
Demonstrating through thousands of causes and setting forth the knowledge of supernormal powers,
the Lord of the World reveals the true course of conduct, according to which wise bodhisattvas practice.
The Blessed One spoke this very Vaipulya Sūtra, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,
with no small number of thousands of verses, the measure of which is like the sands of the Ganges.
And having spoken this sutra, the Jina entered his dwelling and remained there for eighty-four full eons, the Lord of the World absorbed in a single meditative concentration.
When those novices realized that the Leader was staying in his dwelling and had not yet departed,
they proclaimed this stainless, auspicious Buddha-knowledge to many millions of living beings.
Having prepared separate seats for each, he spoke this very sutra to them: "In the teaching of that Sugata, they shall perform a service such as mine. (Saddhp 7.85)
Just as the sands of the Ganges are immeasurable, so too did those sixty thousand sons of that Sugata each lead forth no small number of sentient beings.

After that Jina had passed into parinirvāṇa, they practiced their conduct and beheld tens of millions of Buddhas; together with those who had been their disciples, they then made offerings to those supreme among bipeds. (Saddhp 7.87)
Having practiced a vast and distinguished course of conduct, those Buddhas attained enlightenment in the ten directions;
they were the sixteen sons of that Jina, two Jinas in each of all the directions.
And those who were then proclaimed as disciples by all those Jinas— they too,
by means of various skillful methods, gradually lead them toward this very enlightenment.
I too was among them; by me you were all made to hear [the Dharma].
Therefore, you are my disciples today; I lead you all here toward awakening by means of this skillful method.
This indeed was the cause and this the condition by which I have preached the Dharma;
I lead you toward my supreme enlightenment—O monks, do not be afraid at this point.

Just as a forest might be fierce and dreadful, empty, without support or refuge, filled with many beasts of prey and lacking water—it would be terrifying to the foolish. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 7.92.
And suppose there were many thousands of men who had set out for that forest;
and that forest would be empty and vast, extending for a full fifty yojanas.

And there would be a man who is wealthy, mindful, discerning, steadfast, humble, and confident—one who would serve as their guide through that difficult and most terrifying wilderness. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 7.94.
And those many millions of beings, being exhausted, spoke to that guide at that time: "We are weary, O Noble One; we are not able to proceed. We prefer to turn back here today. (Saddhp 7.95)
Then that wise and skillful leader would reflect upon this skillful means:
"Alas, what a pity! All these fools are losing themselves as they turn back from these jewels. (Saddhp 7.96)
"What if I were now, by the power of my supernatural might, to create here today a vast city, adorned with tens of millions of dwellings and beautified by monasteries and gardens? (Saddhp 7.97)
I would create ponds and rivers, adorned with the flowers of groves,
beautified by walls and gates, and filled with incomparable men and women.
Having created these emanations, he would say to them: "Do not fear; rather, rejoice!
You have reached the most excellent city; enter it and quickly attend to your business."
With uplifted hearts, speak here that you have found peace; tell us that you have completely crossed the entire wilderness without exception.
Speak these words for the sake of our encouragement: "How is it that none of us has returned?"
Having perceived that all were fully rested, he gathered them together again and said:
"Come, listen to me as I speak; this city has been created through my miraculous power."
"Knowing your exhaustion and that you would not turn back, I have employed this skillful means; therefore, generate the vigor to go to the island. (Saddhp 7.102)
In the same way, O monks, I am the guide and leader of thousands of millions of living beings;
I see those living beings suffering in just that manner, unable to break through the shell of the egg of the afflictions. (Saddhp 7.103)
Then I thought about this matter: "These states of nirvāṇa have been made into a place of rest;
this is the cessation of all suffering. You have accomplished what was to be done on the stage of an Arhat."
But when, at this very time, I am staying here in this place and see you all there as Arhats,
then, having gathered everyone here together, I shall declare the true meaning, such as this Dharma is.
The skillful means of the Leaders, by which the Great Sages teach three vehicles—there is indeed only one vehicle, and no second; the two vehicles were taught merely for the sake of providing rest.
Therefore, monks, I say to you today: generate supreme and noble vigor!
By means of the wisdom of the Omniscient One, no mere limited nirvāṇa shall be yours. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 7.107)
But when you touch the wisdom of the omniscient one— the ten powers and those qualities of the Victors—
having become Buddhas who bear the form of the thirty-two marks, you shall attain final nirvana.
Such is the teaching of the Leaders: they proclaim nirvana for the sake of providing rest.
And knowing that they have rested in that nirvana, they lead them all toward the wisdom of the Omniscient One.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Previous Life," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 128) Chapter Eight: The Prediction for the Five Hundred Monks.
Then, the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, in the presence of the Blessed One, [heard] this very kind of skillful means, knowledge, and vision.

Having heard this explanation of intentional speech, having heard the prophecy concerning these great śrāvakas, having heard this discourse connected with their former lives, and having heard of the Blessed One’s preeminence as a bull among men, he was struck with wonder and filled with amazement;
and with a mind free from worldly desire, he became suffused with joy and rapture.
With great joy and gladness, and with great reverence for the Dharma, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and conceived this thought: "It is marvelous, Blessed One!
It is marvelous, Sugata!
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas perform what is supremely difficult."

Those who conform to this world of diverse elements and teach the Dharma to sentient beings through many demonstrations of skillful means and wisdom, and who, by means of skillful means, liberate those sentient beings who are attached to this or that [object], [are the Tathāgatas].
“Blessed One, what can we do in this matter?
Only the Tathāgata knows our disposition and our former course of conduct.
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he stood to one side, paying homage to the Blessed One and gazing at him with unblinking eyes.
Then the Blessed One, perceiving the mental disposition of the venerable Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, addressed the entire community of monks: "Monks, do you see this disciple Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra,
whom I have designated as the foremost among the preachers of the Dharma in this community of monks?"
He has been praised for his many qualities by many beings,
and in many ways he is devoted to upholding the true Dharma within this teaching of mine;
he gladdens, inspires, rouses, and delights the fourfold assembly with his tireless preaching of the Dharma.
He is a sufficient expounder of this Dharma and a sufficient benefactor of his fellow celibates;
monks, apart from the Tathāgata, no one else is able to surpass Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, whether in meaning or in phrasing.
"What do you think, monks? Is this one who upholds my true Dharma only me?
Indeed, monks, you should not view it in this way. For what reason?"
"Monks, I recall that in the past, during the time of ninety-nine billion Buddhas,
he upheld the True Dharma within the teachings of each of those Blessed Buddhas.
Just as he is now my foremost among all preachers of the Dharma,"
And he had attained mastery over emptiness in all respects;
he had obtained the analytical knowledges in all respects; and he had attained mastery over the superknowledges of a bodhisattva in all respects.

He was a teacher of the Dharma who was well-ascertained, a teacher of the Dharma free from doubt, and a teacher of the Dharma that was perfectly pure. Throughout his life, he practiced the holy life under the teachings of those Blessed Buddhas,
and in every instance, he was known by the designation of "disciple" (śrāvaka).
Indeed, by this means he accomplished the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of beings,
and he brought immeasurable and incalculable beings to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and everywhere he remained present for beings through his buddha-activity.
And everywhere he purified his own buddha-field and was devoted to the ripening of sentient beings.
Monks, this was true even for these seven Tathāgatas headed by Vipaśyin, of whom I am the seventh.
He indeed became the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
Furthermore, monks, in the future time, during this Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), there will be one thousand Buddhas less four;
in the teaching of those [Buddhas] as well, this very Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra will be the foremost among those who preach the Dharma.
And he will be a sustainer of the true Dharma;

thus, in the future time, he will uphold the true Dharma of immeasurable and incalculable Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and he will accomplish the welfare of immeasurable and incalculable sentient beings.
He will bring immeasurable and incalculable beings to maturity for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and he will be constantly and continuously devoted to the purification of his own buddha-field and to the maturing of sentient beings.
Having fulfilled such a course of conduct of a bodhisattva, after immeasurable and incalculable eons, he will manifest complete awakening to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

A Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Dharmaprabhāsa will appear in the world— endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One—
and he shall arise in this very same buddha-field.
Furthermore, monks, at that time, trichiliocosm world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges will become a single buddha-field.
It will be level like the palm of a hand, composed of the seven precious jewels, free of mountains, and filled with gabled palaces made of the seven precious jewels;
and the celestial mansions of the gods will remain suspended in the sky.
The gods will see humans,
and humans will also see the gods. Furthermore,
monks, at that time this buddha-field will be free from evil and devoid of women.
And all those beings will be of miraculous birth, practicing celibacy, with mind-made bodies, self-luminous,
possessing supernormal powers, traveling through the air, vigorous, mindful, and wise; their forms will be adorned with golden-colored bodies and the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Furthermore, monks, at that time in that buddha-field, those sentient beings will have two kinds of nourishment.
Which two?
Namely, the nourishment of the joy of the Dharma and the nourishment of the joy of meditative concentration.

There will be immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas, all of whom have attained the great superknowledges, have mastered the analytical knowledges, and are skilled in instructing sentient beings;
his disciples will also exceed all calculation, possessing great supernatural power and majesty, and being meditators on the eight liberations.
Thus, that buddha-field will be endowed with such immeasurable qualities.
That eon shall be named Ratnāvabhāsa,
and that world-system shall be named Suviśuddhā;
and his lifespan shall last for immeasurable and incalculable eons.
And after that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Dharmaprabhāsa has entered parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma will endure for a long time.
That world-system will be filled with stūpas made of jewels.
Monks, in this way, that buddha-field of that Blessed One will be endowed with such inconceivable qualities.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke as follows:
"Listen, O monks, to this matter: how the conduct was practiced by my son."
And how this bodhisattva practice was carried out by one well-trained in skillful means. (Saddhp_8.1)
Knowing that these beings have inferior inclinations and are terrified of the Great Vehicle,
those bodhisattvas become śrāvakas and manifest the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. (Saddhp 8.2)
By means of many hundreds of skillful methods, they bring many bodhisattvas to maturity;
and thus they speak: "We are indeed śrāvakas; we are far from the supreme, foremost enlightenment."
By training themselves in this very practice toward them, millions of beings indeed reach full maturity;
even those of inferior inclinations and indolent nature all eventually become Buddhas.
They practice the conduct of ignorance, thinking, "We, indeed, are disciples with few duties;
we are weary of all deaths and rebirths, and we purify our own fields. (Saddhp 8.5)
They manifest passion within themselves, as well as hatred and delusion;
and having recognized that sentient beings are stuck in false views, they even adopt those very views for their sake.
My many disciples who practice in this way liberate sentient beings through skillful means;
otherwise, ignorant men would fall into madness if he were to reveal his entire conduct.
"O monks, this Śrāvaka Pūrṇa has practiced in the past under thousands of millions of Buddhas;
seeking this Buddha-knowledge, he upheld their true Dharma. (Saddhp_8.8)
And everywhere he was the foremost disciple, one of great learning, a versatile speaker, and confident;
he was always an inspirer, untiring, and ever-present with the work of a Buddha.

He has always attained mastery in the great superknowledges and has become a possessor of the analytical knowledges; knowing the range of the faculties of sentient beings, he always teaches the perfectly pure Dharma. (Saddhp_8.10)
Proclaiming the most excellent True Dharma, they bring to maturity many billions of beings,
purifying their own supreme field within this unsurpassed, foremost vehicle.
And likewise in the future age, he will worship billions of Buddhas;
he will uphold the supreme True Dharma and purify his own field.
Confident and fearless, he will always teach the Dharma through thousands of millions of skillful means;
and he will bring many beings to maturity in the untainted knowledge of omniscience.
Having performed worship for the leaders of men and always upheld the supreme True Dharma,
he will become a self-arisen Buddha in the world, renowned in all directions as Dharmaprabhāsa.
And his field shall become perfectly pure, always distinguished by the seven kinds of jewels;
that eon shall be called Ratnāvabhāsa, and that world-system shall be perfectly pure.
Many thousands of millions of bodhisattvas, highly skilled in the great supernormal powers—
by whom this world-system will be filled, being utterly pure with those who are pure and possess great supernatural might.
Then, there will be a community of the Leader’s disciples numbering thousands of koṭis—
those of great supernatural power, who meditate on the eight liberations, and who have attained mastery in the analytical knowledges.
And all beings in that buddha-field will be pure and practitioners of the holy life;
they will all be of miraculous birth, golden-colored, and endowed with bodies possessing the thirty-two marks.
There, the notion of food will not exist, except for delight in the Dharma and the joy of meditative concentration;
there shall be no women, nor any fear of the states of woe or miserable rebirths.
Such will be the excellent field of Pūrṇa, endowed with all perfect qualities;
it will be filled with most auspicious beings—this much has been revealed here.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those twelve hundred who had attained mastery: "We have reached a state of wonder;
we have reached a state of amazement!
If only the Blessed One would grant us a prophecy just as he has granted them to these other great śrāvakas."
"In this way, the Tathāgata would grant a separate prediction to each of us as well.

Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those great śrāvakas, addressed the Venerable Mahākāśyapa: "Kāśyapa, these twelve hundred who have attained mastery, in whose presence I am now manifest..."
"Kāśyapa, I shall now prophesy for all these twelve hundred who have attained mastery.

Among them, Kāśyapa, the monk Kauṇḍinya, a great śrāvaka, after sixty-two hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of Buddhas have passed, will appear in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Samantaprabhāsa."
He will be one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One.
In that regard, Kāśyapa, there will be five hundred Tathāgatas under this single name.
Furthermore, all five hundred great disciples will, immediately thereafter, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
All of them shall bear the name Samantaprabha.
They are as follows: Gayākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Urubilvakāśyapa, Kāla, Kālodāyin, Aniruddha, Revata, Kapphiṇa, Bakkula, Cunda, Svāgata, and so forth—these five hundred who have attained mastery.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"This disciple of mine, of the Kauṇḍinya clan, shall become a Tathāgata, a protector of the world.
In a future age, after infinite eons, he will discipline many thousands of millions of living beings. (Saddhp_8.21)
He shall become a Victor named Samantaprabha, and his field shall be completely pure;
for in the future, after infinite eons, he will have seen many, indeed infinite, Buddhas.
Radiant and endowed with the power of a Buddha, his fame proclaimed throughout the ten directions,
honored by thousands of millions of living beings, he shall teach the supreme, foremost enlightenment.
Then those bodhisattvas, appearing diligent, having ascended their most excellent celestial palaces,
dwell there and constantly reflect, being pure in virtue and always upright in conduct.
Having heard the Dharma from the Best of Bipeds, they always go to other realms as well;
paying homage to thousands of Buddhas, they perform vast offerings for them.
In an instant, they too will then return to this field of that Leader, Prabhāsa by name, the best of men; such will be the power of his conduct.
The lifespan of that Sugata will be a full sixty thousand kalpas;
and after the Protector has entered parinirvāṇa, his Dharma shall remain here for twice that length of time.
Furthermore, his counterfeit [teaching] will likewise endure for three times that same duration;
when the True Dharma has vanished, at that time, men and gods shall suffer under the protection of that Savior.
Of those Jinas who share the same name, Samantaprabha, the Supreme Men,
these will become fifty complete leaders in succession.
The arrays of all these [Buddhas] shall be such as this, and likewise their power of supernatural faculties and their Buddha-fields;
their assemblies and true Dharma shall be exactly like this, and the abiding of the true Dharma shall be equal.
Then, in this world including its devas, all shall have such a name as that which was previously proclaimed by me for Samantaprabhāsa, the Supreme among Men.
Out of compassion for their welfare, they will explain it to one another in succession;
today there shall be no obstacle for me, just as I myself am teaching the entire world.

In this very way, Kāśyapa, you should today maintain that there are no fewer than five hundred here; and as for my other disciples who have attained mastery, speak of them also to the other disciples.
Then those five hundred arhats, having heard their own predictions from the presence of the Blessed One, were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.

They approached the Blessed One, prostrated with their heads at his feet, and spoke thus: "Blessed One, we confess our transgression, O Blessed One, by which we have constantly and continuously cultivated our minds with the thought:
'This is our final nirvāṇa.'"
"We have attained final nirvāṇa," [they thought], O Blessed One, because they were unskilled, unlearned, and ignorant of the proper method. Why is that?
"O Blessed One, we who were supposed to fully awaken to the wisdom of a Tathāgata have instead found satisfaction with such limited wisdom.

It is just as if, O Blessed One, some man had entered the house of a friend while intoxicated or asleep, and that friend, thinking, 'May this jewel belong to him,' were to tie a priceless gem into the hem of his garment."
Then indeed, Blessed One, that man would rise from his seat and depart;
he would reach another region,
and there he would fall into distress.
For the sake of seeking food and clothing, he would fall into hardship;
and with great exertion, he might somehow obtain some food,
and by means of that, he would be content, joyful, and delighted.
Then, O Blessed One, that man who was his old friend— the one by whom that priceless jewel had been tied in the hem of his garment—
should see him once again and say to him: "O man, why do you undergo such hardship for the sake of seeking food and clothing?"
"O man, when I bound this priceless jewel—a gem that fulfills all desires—for the sake of your comfort and well-being within the hem of your garment;
O man, I have bestowed this jewel upon you.
Thus, O man, the jewel remains fastened right there within the hem of your garment."
And yet, O man, you do not reflect: "What is it that binds me, or by what am I bound? What is the cause, or what is the condition for this bondage?
You are of a childish nature, O man, in that you find satisfaction while seeking food and clothing with such great hardship.
"Go, my good man! Take this precious gem, go to the great city, and trade it.
With that wealth, perform all the necessary financial transactions."
In the same way, Blessed One, when the Tathāgata was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, he caused us to generate the thoughts of omniscience;
yet, Blessed One, we did not know them and we did not realize them.
We, Blessed One, perceived ourselves as having attained extinction on the level of an Arhat.
We live in hardship,
Blessed One, in that we find satisfaction with such limited knowledge,
while our aspiration for the wisdom of the omniscient one remains forever undestroyed.
"O Blessed One, being thus awakened by the Tathāgata, we [realized]: 'O monks, do not think that this is your final nirvāṇa.
O monks, there exist within your continuums roots of merit which were previously ripened by me.
And now, it is my very skill in means, expressed through the terminology of teaching the Dharma, that you now think to be "nirvāṇa. "
And thus, having been awakened by the Blessed One, we have today been prophesied for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then, at that time, those five hundred who had attained mastery, headed by Ājñātakauṇḍinya, spoke these verses:

"Filled with joy and great delight, we have heard this unsurpassed consolation. Since we have been prophesied for supreme, foremost enlightenment, homage be to you, O Leader of infinite vision! (Saddhp 8.34)
We confess our transgression before you, just as fools, ignorant and unwise,
were content with mere personal liberation within the teaching of the Sugata.
Suppose, for instance, that some man enters here into the house of a friend,
and his friend, who is wealthy and affluent, gives him much food and drink.
Having satisfied him with food, he would give him a jewel of manifold value,
tying it in a knot within the hem of his inner garment, and having given it, he would be well-pleased with him here.
And that fool, having departed, would rise and go to another city;
fallen into distress, wretched and searching, he seeks food while suffering.
Seeking food, he would be satisfied with whatever meal he obtained without thinking of anything noble;
and yet that jewel, having been tied within his inner garment, would have been forgotten, for he had no recollection of it. (Saddhp 8.39)
He sees that very former friend by whom the jewel was given to him in his own house;
having reproached him thoroughly, he shows him the jewel within the fold of his garment.
And having seen it, he is filled with supreme bliss; such is the power of that jewel.
He becomes immensely wealthy and possessed of a great treasury, and is endowed with the five strands of sensual pleasure.
In the same way, O Blessed One, we too, being unaware of such a thing, have [acted] preceded by a vow;
for this was indeed given by the Tathāgata himself to us throughout the long night of previous existences.
And we, O Blessed One, were of childish intellect and ignorant here in the teaching of the Sugata;
for we were satisfied with mere nirvāṇa, nor did we pray for or even think of anything higher. (Saddhp 8.43)
And we have been awakened by the Kinsman of the World: "This is not such a nirvāṇa;
this is the sublime knowledge of the Supreme Men, which is nirvāṇa and the highest bliss. (Saddhp 8.44)
Having heard this sublime, vast, manifold, and unsurpassed prophecy,
O Lord, we have become joyful, elated, and filled with great joy as we were prophesied one after another.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Prophecy Concerning the Five Hundred Bhikṣus," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble Lotus of the True Dharma.
(Vaidya 137) Saddhp_9: The Chapter on the Prophecy for Ānanda and Others.
Then, at that time, the venerable Ānanda thought to himself: "Would that we too might receive such a prophecy as this!"
Having thus reflected, deliberated, and made his request, he rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One;

and the Venerable Rāhula, having likewise reflected, deliberated, and made his request, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke these words: "O Blessed One, let there be an opportunity for us as well."
O Sugata, let there be an opportunity for us as well;
for the Blessed One is our father, our progenitor, our shelter, and our protection.

O Blessed One, we are exceedingly honored in the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, being regarded as "these sons of the Blessed One," "attendants of the Blessed One," and "those who uphold the Dharma-treasury of the Blessed One."
Therefore, Blessed One, it would be truly fitting if the Blessed One were to grant us a prophecy regarding our unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And two thousand other disciples, both those still in training and those beyond training, rose from their seats, draped their upper robes over one shoulder, and with palms joined, stood facing the Blessed One,
gazing up at him while reflecting upon this very thought: namely, "May we too receive a prophecy regarding this very Buddha-knowledge."
May we attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata named Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha,
endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, and a teacher of gods and humans."
And for the sake of human beings, the Buddha, the Blessed One,
having performed acts of hospitality, reverence, honor, and worship toward sixty-two million Buddhas, [attained this state].
Having upheld the true Dharma of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and having performed the protection of their teachings, you will realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Once you have awakened to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, Ānanda, you will bring to maturity hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of twenty Ganges rivers, for unexcelled [enlightenment].
Regarding your perfect enlightenment, your buddha-field will be prosperous and composed of lapis lazuli;
that world-system shall be named Anavanāmitavaijayantī.
That eon shall be named Mano-jña-śabdābhigarjita (Resounding with Pleasing Sounds).

The lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña, shall last for immeasurable eons, such that it is impossible to reach its limit through calculation.
The lifespan of that Blessed One will be incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons.

Ānanda, for as long as the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña shall be, twice that length the True Dharma will remain after he has passed into parinirvāṇa.
For as long as the true Dharma of that Blessed One shall remain, twice that long shall the semblance of the true Dharma remain.

Furthermore, Ānanda, in the ten directions there will be many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of the river Ganges, [who will hear of] that Tathāgata Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña.
They will speak in praise.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"I announce to the assembly of monks: the auspicious Ānanda is my upholder of the Dharma."
In a future age, he will become a Victor after having honored sixty koṭis of Sugatas.
There he was renowned by the name Sāgarabuddhidhārī, one who had attained the superknowledges (abhijñā),
in the pure field Sudarśanīya, in the city Anonātā, [under the tree] Dhvajavaijayantī.
There he will further bring to maturity Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
that Jina will possess great supernatural power, his fame resounding throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
And the lifespan of him who shall remain, out of compassion for the welfare of the world, will then be immeasurable;
and even after that Protector, the Jina, has entered final nirvana, his True Dharma shall remain for twice as long.
A counterfeit [teaching] shall further arise within the dispensation of that Jina, doubling [in extent].
Even then, beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges will produce the causal roots for the awakening of a Buddha here.

Then, indeed, this thought occurred to eight thousand bodhisattvas in that assembly who had newly set out in the vehicle: "We have not even yet received such a sublime prophecy for ourselves as bodhisattvas, let alone for the śrāvakas.
What, indeed, will be the cause for this?"
"What is the condition for this?
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those bodhisattvas, addressed those bodhisattvas:
"Noble sons, at the same time, in a single moment, in a single instant, both I and Ānanda [set our minds] upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
He generated the thought of enlightenment in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dharmagaganābhyudgatarāja.
In that regard, noble sons, he was constantly and continuously devoted to great learning,
while I was devoted to the exertion of vigor.
By that means, I have more swiftly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, Ānanda, this noble son Bhadra has always been a keeper of the treasury of the true Dharma of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—namely, for the sake of the full accomplishment of bodhisattvas;
such, O sons of good family, was the vow of this noble son.

Then, indeed, the venerable Ānanda, having heard from the Blessed One his own prophecy regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, and having heard of the magnificent array of qualities of his own buddha-field, and having heard of his former conduct in making vows, [was filled with joy].
He became satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness.
At that time, he recollected the true Dharma of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas,
as well as his own former vow.
Then, at that time, the venerable Ānanda spoke these verses:
"O Jina, it is marvelous and immeasurable how you cause me to remember my own teaching of the Dharma."
For I remember the Jinas, the Protectors, who have entered parinirvāṇa as if they were today or tomorrow. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 9.6)
I have attained freedom from doubt and am established in enlightenment; such is my skill in means.
I am an attendant to the Sugata and I uphold the True Dharma for the sake of awakening.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Rāhulabhadra: "Rāhulabhadra,

in a future time you shall become a Tathāgata named Saptaratnapadmavikrāntagāmin— Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men."

And among humans, you shall always be the eldest son of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— having honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and venerated Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as numerous as the atoms in ten world-systems— just as you are mine now.
Furthermore, Rāhulabhadra, the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Saptaratnapadmavikrāntagāmin, will be exactly like this,

and his perfection of all kinds of qualities will be exactly like this— just as the array of qualities of the Buddha-field endowed with every kind of excellence belonging to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña, shall be.
"Rāhula, you alone shall become the eldest son of that Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sāgaravaradharabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña;
thereafter, you will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
“Rāhula, this is my eldest son, who was my own biological son during my youth;
even now that I have attained awakening, he is my son, the great seer who upholds the inheritance of the Dharma.”
In the future age, you shall behold many tens of millions of Buddhas whose measure is beyond reckoning;
seeking awakening, you will indeed become the son of all those Victors.
"This is Rāhula’s practice of living incognito; I know this to be his vow:
that he shall praise me among the friends of the world, saying, 'I am indeed the son of the Tathāgata. (Saddhp 9.10)
The millions of billions of his immeasurable virtues have never had any limit;
for Rāhula here, my own legitimate son, stands thus for the sake of awakening.

Then the Blessed One indeed beheld those two thousand disciples—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—gazing toward the Blessed One with faces turned forward, their minds serene, gentle, and pliant.
Thereupon, at that time, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, do you see these two thousand disciples, both those in training and those beyond training?
He replied, "I see them, Blessed One."
"I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "Ānanda, all these two thousand monks shall together accomplish the conduct of a bodhisattva;
they shall honor, revere, and respect as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are atoms of dust in fifty world-systems."
Having honored, worshipped, and venerated [them], and having upheld the True Dharma, in their final existence, in a single instant, a single moment, a single fraction of time, and a single assembly,

they shall fully awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment in various world-systems throughout the ten directions, each in their own Buddha-field. They shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Ratnaketurāja.
The lifespan of these [bodhisattvas] will be a full eon;
the arrays of qualities of their buddha-fields will be equal,
and their assemblies of śrāvakas and assemblies of bodhisattvas will be equal.
Their final nirvana will be simultaneous,
and their True Dharma will endure for an equal duration.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"O Ānanda, these two thousand disciples who stand here before me—I now prophesy that these wise ones shall become Tathāgatas in a future age. (Saddhp 9.12)
Having performed the supreme worship of the Buddhas with infinite illustrations and comparisons,
they shall realize my highest enlightenment while remaining in their final physical bodies.
In a single moment and likewise in a single instant, throughout the ten directions,
they shall sit at the foot of the most excellent trees and, having touched supreme gnosis, become Buddhas.
And they shall have a single name; they will be renowned in this world as "Jewel-Banners.
Their excellent fields shall be equal, and their assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas shall be equal.
Abounding in supernatural powers here in all this world throughout the ten directions,
even when they have entered parinirvāṇa after proclaiming the Dharma, their True Dharma will remain for exactly the same length of time.

Then indeed, those disciples, both those in training and those beyond training, having heard their respective prophecies directly from the presence of the Blessed One, were satisfied, elated, joyful, delighted, and filled with gladness and happiness; they addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"O Lamp of the World, we are satiated having heard this prophecy."
O Tathāgata, they are as happy as if they had been sprinkled with nectar.
We have no doubt or uncertainty that we shall become the supreme among men;
having heard this prophecy, we have attained happiness today. (Saddhp 9.18)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Prophecy for Ānanda, Rāhula, and Two Thousand Other Monks," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 142) Chapter Ten: The Chapter on the Dharma-preachers.
Then, O Blessed One, the Blessed One addressed those eighty thousand bodhisattvas, beginning with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja.

"Bhaiṣajyarāja, do you see in this assembly the many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as the monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen— those belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, those belonging to the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and those belonging to the vehicle of the bodhisattvas— who have heard this Dharma discourse in the presence of the Tathāgata?"
He said, "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "Bhaiṣajyarāja, all these are indeed bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas."
Those in this assembly who have heard even a single verse, or have heard even a single word, or who have, at the very least,
rejoiced in this sutra with even a single thought of resolve;
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I grant the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment to all these four assemblies.
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, whoever shall hear this Dharma discourse after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa— even if they hear but a single verse— [they too shall attain it].
Bhaiṣajyarāja, even those who rejoice with but a single thought of resolve, I prophesy that those sons of good family or daughters of good family shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will have attended upon hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of fully perfected Buddhas.

Those sons of good family or daughters of good family, Bhaiṣajyarāja, who will uphold, recite, proclaim, cause others to grasp, or write down even a single verse from this Dharma-discourse, should be known as those who have made vows before hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions of Buddhas, and who have been reborn among humans in this Jambudvīpa out of compassion for sentient beings.
Having written it down, they will keep it in mind, and from time to time they will look upon it;
and toward that book, they will generate reverence for the Tathāgata.
Out of reverence for the Teacher, they will honor, revere, respect, and worship [this teaching].

They will worship that book with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, musical instruments, and so forth, as well as with acts of salutation and joining their palms in reverence.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, whatever sons of good family or daughters of good family shall uphold even a single verse from this Dharma-discourse, or shall rejoice in it—
Bhaiṣajyarāja, I prophesy that all of them shall attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

In that regard, Bhaiṣajyarāja, if any man or woman should say, "What indeed will those beings be like who, in a future time, will be Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas? then, Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be shown to that man or woman.
Whoever from this Dharma-discourse should memorize, cause others to hear, or teach even a single four-line verse, or who possesses reverence for this Dharma-discourse—
this son of good family or daughter of good family shall indeed become a Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha in a future age.
View it thus. For what reason?
Because, Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be regarded as a Tathāgata by the world together with its gods.
