And such honor should be rendered to that Tathāgata by anyone who, from this Dharma-discourse, should memorize even a single verse;
how much more so for one who would take up, memorize, recite, master, proclaim, write, or cause to be written this Dharma-discourse in its entirety and completion?
Having written it down, one should keep it in mind;

and toward that book, one should show honor, respect, reverence, worship, veneration, and homage with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, music, joined palms, prostrations, and salutations.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be known as one who is fully perfected in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and they should be known as one who sees the Tathāgata.

Out of compassion for the welfare of the world, he has been born among humans in this Jambudvīpa by the power of his vow, for the purpose of fully proclaiming this Dharma-discourse. Having himself established a sublime performance of Dharma and a sublime rebirth in a Buddha-field, it is for the sake of proclaiming this Dharma-discourse that, after my parinirvāṇa, he acts for the benefit and out of compassion for sentient beings.
And it should be understood that one who has been reborn here is a messenger of the Tathāgata;
Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be so understood.

Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family who, after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa, should proclaim this Dharma-discourse— even if only in secret or by stealth to a single being— should be known as one who performs the work of the Tathāgata and is sent forth by the Tathāgata. Or they might explain it.
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, suppose there were some being with a wicked mind, an evil mind, or a fierce mind who, in the presence of the Tathāgata, were to speak dispraise for an eon;
and suppose another were to address even a single unpleasant word— whether true or false— to such Dharma-preachers who uphold this sūtra, whether they be householders or renunciants.
I say that this is an even more grievous evil deed.
For what reason?
Bhaiṣajyarāja, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be known as one who is adorned with the ornaments of the Tathāgata.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, he who, having written down this Dharma-discourse and made it into a book, carries it on his shoulder, carries the Tathāgata on his shoulder;
wherever he may go, he goes with the Tathāgata.

By those very beings, he is to be saluted with joined palms, honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, adored, and venerated with divine and human flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, musical instruments, food, edibles, meals, drinks, vehicles, and with supreme, divine heaps of jewels.
That Dharma-preacher should be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshipped;
and divine heaps of jewels should be presented to that Dharma-preacher.
Why is that?
May he indeed cause this Dharma-discourse to be heard even once,
hearing which immeasurable and incalculable beings would swiftly attain perfection in unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"By one who wishes to abide in Buddhahood and desires self-arisen wisdom, those beings who uphold this method should be honored. (Saddhp 10.1)
And whoever should desire how omniscience might be attained quickly, he should uphold this sūtra or even honor its upholder. (Saddhp 10.2)
Sent by the Lord of the World for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, he shall recite this sutra out of compassion for all beings. (Saddhp 10.3)
Having abandoned a glorious rebirth, that steadfast one has come here for the sake of compassion toward sentient beings—he who would uphold this sutra. (Saddhp 10.4)
By the power of his rebirth, he is seen there, preaching this unsurpassed sūtra in the final age. (Saddhp 10.5)
One should honor him with divine flowers and indeed with all kinds of human perfumes;
one should cover the Dharma-preacher with divine garments and scatter jewels over him. (Saddhp 10.6)

One should always stand with palms joined to such a person, just as one would to the Jina, the Self-Existent One himself—whosoever, in this most terrifying final age, should uphold this sūtra after [the Buddha] has passed into parinirvāṇa. (Saddhp_10.7)

One might give food, soft and hard edibles, as well as drink, and millions of monasteries, beds, seats, and garments for the sake of worshipping a son of the Jina; yet one who would even once recite this sutra [is superior]. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 10.8.
He performs the work of the Tathāgatas, and he has been sent by me into this human existence—
he who, in the final age, would write down, uphold, or even hear this sutra.
And if someone, standing here in the presence of the Jina, were to utter a single harsh word for a full kalpa with a corrupted mind and a frowning face, that person would produce much evil.
And whoever should speak dispraise or abuse toward those who uphold the sūtras while they are proclaiming this sūtra here— I declare that his evil is even greater than that.
And suppose a person were to praise me face-to-face with joined palms for an entire kalpa,
seeking this supreme enlightenment with many millions of billions of verses.
Indeed, he would obtain much merit there by praising me with a heart full of joy;
yet a person who should proclaim their praises would obtain even more than that. (Saddhp 10.13)

For eighteen thousand koṭis of kalpas, whoever performs worship toward those images with divine sounds, forms, and tastes, as well as with divine fragrances and divine tactile objects; Saddhp_10.14 //
If one were to perform such worship of books for eighteen thousand million *kalpas*, yet hear this sutra even once, the gain of wonder for that person would be great indeed. (Saddhp_10.15)
I announce this to you, Bhaiṣajyarāja;
I declare this to you: indeed, many Dharma-discourses have been spoken by me, Bhaiṣajyarāja.
I have spoken and I shall speak;
and among all those Dharma-discourses, Bhaiṣajyarāja, this very Dharma-discourse is the one most opposed by the whole world and the one least believed in by the whole world.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this is an internal secret of the Dharma of the Tathāgata, protected by the powers of the Tathāgata—a matter never before disclosed, never before declared, and never before explained.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, this Dharma discourse is rejected by many people even while the Tathāgata remains;
how much more so after he has passed into parinirvāṇa?
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, those sons of good family or daughters of good family should be known as being covered by the robes of the Tathāgata;
they are beheld and sustained by the Tathāgatas residing in other world-systems,
and they shall possess an individual strength of faith.
They will possess the power of the roots of merit and the power of their vows;
Bhaiṣajyarāja, those sons of good family or daughters of good family will dwell in the same place as the dwelling of the Tathāgata,
and their heads will be stroked by the hand of the Tathāgata.
Those who, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, shall have faith in this Dharma-discourse, read it, write it, honor it, revere it,
and cause others to hear it— furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, in whatever region of earth this Dharma-discourse is spoken, taught, written, recited, or chanted in chorus,
in that region of earth, Bhaiṣajyarāja, a stūpa for the Tathāgata should be erected, vast, made of jewels, lofty, and magnificent.
Furthermore, it is not necessary that the relics of the Tathāgata be enshrined within it.
Why is that?
Because the body of the Tathāgata is deposited within it as a single, solid mass.

In whatever place on earth this Dharma-discourse is spoken, taught, recited, chanted, or written, or where it remains written as a book, that stupa must be honored, revered, respected, worshipped, adored, and venerated with all kinds of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory-pennants; and worship must be performed with all manner of songs, instrumental music, dances, musical instruments, cymbals, and the sounding of orchestral ensembles.
Furthermore, Bhaiṣajyarāja, those beings who should obtain that stūpa of the Tathāgata for the purpose of salutation, worship, or even sight—
Bhaiṣajyarāja, all of them should be known as having drawn near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Why is that?
Bhaiṣajyarāja, many householders and renunciants practice the conduct of a bodhisattva,
yet they do not obtain this Dharma discourse for the purpose of seeing it, hearing it, writing it down, or honoring it.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, those bodhisattvas are not yet skilled in the bodhisattva practice as long as they do not hear this Dharma-discourse;
however, those who hear this Dharma-discourse [are so skilled].
Having heard it, they will have faith, enter into it, understand it,
and take it up; at that time, they will be standing near and close to unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is just as if there were a certain man who, needing water and seeking water,
were to dig a well in a parched region of the earth for the sake of water;
and he would see dry, white dust being brought up.
He would know: "Water is this far from here.
Then, at a later time, that man might see moist earth, adjacent to water, turned into mud and mire, being carried along by flowing drops of water.

And seeing those men digging the well, their limbs smeared with mud and mire, then indeed, Bhaiṣajyarāja, that man, having seen that prior sign, would become free from doubt and free from uncertainty, thinking: "Surely this water is near.
In the very same way, Bhaiṣajyarāja, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas are far from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
As long as they do not hear this Dharma-discourse,

nor take it up, nor enter into it, nor fathom it, nor reflect upon it; but when, O Bhaiṣajyarāja, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas hear this Dharma-discourse, take it up, bear it in mind, recite it, enter into it, study it, and reflect upon it—
Then they will have drawn near to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, it is from this Dharma discourse that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is born for sentient beings.
Why is that?
For this Dharma discourse is the elucidation of the ultimate intentional language spoken by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
it is declared as the hidden place of the Dharma for the sake of the full accomplishment of the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, whatever Bodhisattva should be startled, terrified, or fall into a state of terror regarding this Dharma discourse—
Bhaiṣajyarāja, that bodhisattva mahāsattva should be known as one who has newly set out on the vehicle.

However, Bhaiṣajyarāja, if a follower of the śrāvaka vehicle should be startled, terrified, or fall into fear at this Dharma discourse, that person following the śrāvaka vehicle should be known as one who is conceited.
Bhaiṣajyarāja, whatever bodhisattva mahāsattva, in the final period, in the final time after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, should proclaim this Dharma-discourse to the fourfold assembly—
by that bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja, having entered the Tathāgata’s dwelling, having donned the Tathāgata’s robe,
and having sat upon the Tathāgata’s seat, this Dharma-discourse must be proclaimed to the fourfold assembly.
And what, Bhaiṣajyarāja, is the dwelling place of the Tathāgata? Indeed, Bhaiṣajyarāja, the dwelling place of the Tathāgata is the abiding in loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
therein that son of good family should enter.
And what, Bhaiṣajyarāja, is the robe of the Tathāgata?
Indeed, Bhaiṣajyarāja, the robe of the Tathāgata is great patience and gentleness;
that is what should be worn by that son of good family or daughter of good family.
And what, Bhaiṣajyarāja, is the Dharma-throne of the Tathāgata?
Indeed, Bhaiṣajyarāja, the entrance into the emptiness of all phenomena is the Dharma-throne of the Tathāgata;
thereon that son of good family should sit.
Having sat down, this Dharma-discourse should be proclaimed to the fourfold assembly.
With an undaunted mind, a bodhisattva should proclaim it before a host of bodhisattvas and to the fourfold assembly who have set out in the bodhisattva-vehicle.
And, Bhaiṣajyarāja, even while remaining in another world-system, I shall [be present] for that son of good family through my emanations.
I shall cause the assembly to gather;
I shall also dispatch emanated monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen to listen to the Dharma.
They will not oppose what that Dharma-preacher says.
They will not reject it. Furthermore, if he should go to the forest,
there too I shall send many gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas to hear the Dharma from him.
And I, Bhaiṣajyarāja, staying in another world-system, will show my face to that son of good family;
and whatever words or syllables from this Dharma-discourse he may have forgotten, I will recite them back to him as he studies.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Having abandoned all forms of indolence, one should listen to a sūtra such as this.
Indeed, hearing it is difficult to obtain, and even faith in it is difficult to find. (Saddhp 10.16)
Just as someone seeking water might dig a well in a desert, and while digging again and again, should see only dry dust; 10.17.
Seeing this, he would think there: "Water must be far from here;
this sign of dry dust being cast up indicates that it is at a distance. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 10.18)
But when he repeatedly sees the soil moist and damp, his conclusion will be: "There is water here; it is not far off. (Saddhp 10.19)
In the very same way, those who do not hear this sutra and fail to cultivate it again and again remain far from the wisdom of a Buddha.
But when they hear or even once contemplate this profound king of sūtras, the definitive teaching for the śrāvakas, (Saddhp_10.21)
Those wise ones are indeed close to the wisdom of a Buddha, just as when there is damp soil, it is said that water is near. (Saddhp 10.22)
Having entered the dwelling of the Jina and put on my robe,
the wise one sat upon my seat and spoke fearlessly.
The power of loving-kindness is my shelter, patience and gentleness my robe, and emptiness my seat; having established myself therein, I shall indeed teach the Dharma.
Whether it be a clod of earth, a staff, or even a spear; whether it be verbal abuse or threats—when these are spoken, one should endure them there while recollecting me.
Throughout thousands of millions of fields, my physical body remains firm;
for inconceivable millions of eons, I teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
I too shall dispatch many emanations to that hero who, after my parinirvāṇa, shall proclaim this sūtra.
Monks and nuns, laymen and laywomen, as well as their assemblies, will likewise pay him honor. (Saddhp 10.28)
Clods of earth, sticks, as well as verbal abuse, threats, and reproaches—
those who would give these to him were also created by transformation to ward them off.
And even when he dwells alone, reciting [the scriptures] in a place devoid of people, whether in the forest or on the mountains; Saddhp_10.30.
Then I shall show him my radiant body,
and I shall cause his faulty recitation to be uttered again and again.
And while he dwells there alone as a forest-dweller,
I shall dispatch numerous gods and yakṣas to be his companions.
Such are the qualities of one who illuminates the four assemblies:
even when he is alone in a monastery or in forest caves, practicing recitation, my son, he would see me.
He possesses unimpeded eloquence and understands many explanations of the dharmas;
he satisfies thousands of millions of living beings because he is sustained by the Buddha. (Saddhp 10.34)
And all those beings who rely upon him quickly become bodhisattvas;
by cultivating association with him, they behold Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Preacher of the Dharma," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 149) Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra, Chapter 11: The Appearance of the Stūpa.
Then, from that spot of earth before the Blessed One, in the midst of the assembly, a stūpa made of the seven precious gems rose up, five hundred yojanas in height and proportionate thereto.
And in its circumference,

it rose up into the sky and remained suspended in mid-air— variegated and beautiful to behold, well-adorned with five thousand flower-canopied platforms, embellished by many thousands of archways, and hung with thousands of banners and victory-flags.
It was hung with thousands of jewel garlands and hung with thousands of silk bells, emitting the fragrance of *tamāla* leaves and sandalwood;
by that fragrance, this entire world-system became suffused.
And its series of parasols, made of the seven precious gems, rose up as high as the abodes of the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings.
That is to say: gold, silver, beryl, musāragalva, emerald, red pearl, and karketana.
And upon that stūpa, the sons of the gods belonging to the Trāyastriṃśa realm scattered, showered, and strewn divine māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers over that jeweled stūpa;
and from that very jeweled stūpa, such a sound issued forth: "Excellent, excellent, Blessed One Śākyamuni!"
This Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma has been well-spoken by you.
So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
Then, indeed, those four assemblies, seeing that great jeweled stupa standing in the sky in mid-air,
were filled with joy; having attained a state of gladness, rapture, and serene faith, they rose from their seats at that moment and stood with their palms joined in reverence.
Then, at that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Mahāpratibhāna, perceiving that the world with its gods, humans, and asuras was filled with curiosity, addressed the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition?"
"For what purpose has such a great jeweled stūpa appeared in the world?
And who, Blessed One, is emitting such a sound from this great jeweled stūpa?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna: "Mahāpratibhāna, within this great jeweled stūpa resides the physical body of the Tathāgata, solid and compact."
This is his stūpa;
it is this very one that utters the sound:
"O Mahāpratibhāna, there is, in the direction below, beyond incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems, a world-system named Ratnaviśuddhā."
In that [world], there was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Prabhūtaratna.

This Blessed One had made this former vow: "While I was formerly practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, I did not emerge into unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until I had heard this Dharma discourse, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which is an instruction for bodhisattvas."
But when I heard this Dharma discourse, the Lotus of the True Dharma,
then I subsequently became perfected in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Mahāpratibhāna, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhūtaratna—

At the time of his final nirvāṇa, he made this proclamation before the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, and before this generation including śramaṇas and brahmins: "O monks, after I have passed into final nirvāṇa, a single great stūpa of precious jewels must be constructed for this physical body of the Tathāgata."
Furthermore, other stupas should be constructed in my honor.
Moreover, Mahāpratibhāna, this was the empowerment of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhūtaratna:
"This stupa of mine shall appear in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions, in whichever Buddha-fields [this teaching occurs]."
Wherever this Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma is proclaimed,
this stupa containing my own physical body shall emerge there.
While those various Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are preaching this Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma, it shall stand suspended in the air above the circle of the assembly.
And whenever those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, preach this Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, this stupa containing my own physical body shall give its approval.
Therefore, Mahāpratibhāna, this is the relic-stupa of that Blessed One, Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.

While this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma discourse was being spoken by me in this Sahā world-system, [the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gadgadasvara], having emerged from the midst of this assembly and standing in the air above in the sky, gave his approval, saying, "Excellent!"
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, by the power of the Blessed One, let us behold this form of the Tathāgata.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna:
"Furthermore, Mahāpratibhāna, regarding that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Prabhūtaratna..."
His vow was weighty.

This was his vow: "Whenever the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in other Buddha-fields should preach this Dharma-discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, then may this stūpa containing my physical body go into the presence of those Tathāgatas in order to hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
Furthermore, when those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, desire to reveal and show my own physical form to the fourfold assembly,

then those Tathāgatas— in the various Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions— who are emanations of their own bodies and bear various names, and who teach the Dharma to sentient beings in those respective Buddha-fields, [will likewise manifest it].

Having assembled them all, together with those Tathāgata-forms created from my own body, this stūpa containing the form of my own body should later be opened and shown to the fourfold assembly. Mahāpratibhāna, many Tathāgata-forms have also been created by me.
Those who in the ten directions, in various other buddha-fields and thousands of world-systems, teach the Dharma to sentient beings—
all of them indeed shall be brought here.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, [I wish to see] even all those bodies of the Tathāgata, those emanations of the Tathāgata.
Thereupon, at that very moment, the Blessed One emitted a ray of light from the circle of hair between his eyebrows;

by that ray, as soon as it was emitted, [he illuminated] those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who were dwelling in the five hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of world-systems in the eastern direction, equal in number to the sands of fifty Ganges rivers.
All of them were clearly visible;
and those buddha-fields appeared to be made of crystal,
and they appeared adorned with jewel-trees.
Adorned with garlands of fine cloth, filled with many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, covered with canopies, and draped with nets of the seven precious gems and gold,
the Blessed Buddhas were seen in those various places teaching the Dharma to sentient beings with sweet and beautiful voices;
and those buddha-fields were seen to be completely filled with hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas.
Thus in the southeastern direction;
thus in the southern direction;
thus in the southwestern direction.
Thus in the western direction;
thus in the northwestern direction;
thus in the northern direction.
Thus in the northeastern direction; thus in the downward direction;
thus in the upward direction.

Thus, in each of the ten directions all around, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, and the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who reside in many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of world-systems, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges— all of them became visible.
(Vaidya 151) Then indeed, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the ten directions addressed their respective assemblies of bodhisattvas: "O sons of good family,
we must indeed go to the Sahā world-system."
[They came] into the presence of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha,

in order to pay homage to the reliquary stūpa of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, the Arhat and Samyaksaṃbuddha. Then indeed those Blessed Buddhas, each accompanied by their own attendants— two or three persons including themselves— came to this Sahā world-system.
Thus, at that time, this entire world-system was adorned with jewel-trees;

it consisted of lapis lazuli, was covered with nets of gold and the seven precious gems, was perfumed with the incense of great precious fragrances, strewn with *māndārava* and *mahāmāndārava* flowers, decorated with networks of tinkling bells, laid out in an eightfold checkerboard pattern with golden threads, and was devoid of villages, towns, market towns, provinces, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
It was free from the Kāla mountains; free from the Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda mountains; free from the Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla mountain ranges;
free from Mount Sumeru; free from all other great mountains; free from the great oceans; and it was devoid of rivers and great rivers.
It was free from the hosts of gods, humans, and asuras, and free from the realms of hell, the animal kingdom, and the world of Yama.

For at that time, all those beings who were born within the six realms of existence in this Sahā world-system were transferred to other world-systems, with the exception of those who had assembled in that assembly.
Then indeed those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, arrived in this Sahā world-system accompanied by two attendants or three attendants.
As they arrived, those Tathāgatas sat down upon lion-thrones at the foot of jeweled trees and remained there.
Each individual jeweled tree was five hundred yojanas in height, with branches, leaves, and foliage spreading out in regular proportion, and it was adorned with flowers and fruits.
And at the foot of each jewel tree, a lion throne was prepared, five hundred yojanas in height and adorned with great jewels. Upon each of these, a Tathāgata sat cross-legged.
In this manner, throughout the entire great trichiliocosm, Tathāgatas sat cross-legged at the foot of every jewel tree.
Furthermore, at that time, this great trichiliocosm was completely filled with Tathāgatas.
Yet, not even from a single direction had all those emanated bodies of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, arrived.
Then, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, created space for those forms of the Tathāgatas as they continued to arrive.

On all sides from the eight directions, there were two million billion nayutas of buddha-fields, all made of lapis lazuli, covered with nets of gold and the seven precious gems, adorned with networks of tinkling bells, strewn with *māndārava* and great *māndārava* flowers, overspread with celestial canopies, hung with celestial flower garlands, and perfumed with celestial incense and fragrances.
And all those two hundred thousand *nayuta* billion buddha-fields were devoid of villages, cities, towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals;

they were devoid of the Kāla mountains, devoid of the Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda mountains, devoid of the Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla mountain ranges, devoid of Mount Sumeru, devoid of all other great mountains, devoid of the great oceans, and devoid of rivers and great rivers.
He established them, free from the bodies of gods, humans, and asuras, and devoid of the realms of hell, animals, and the world of Yama;
and he established all those many buddha-fields as a single buddha-field, a single region of earth— level, delightful, and adorned with trees made of the seven precious gems.
The height and circumference of those jewel-trees were five hundred yojanas, and they were endowed with branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arranged in due proportion.
At the foot of every jewel-tree, there was prepared a lion-throne made of divine jewels, five hundred yojanas in height and circumference, variegated and beautiful to behold.
As each Tathāgata arrived, he would sit upon those lion-thrones at the roots of the jewel-trees, having assumed the cross-legged posture.
In this manner, furthermore, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni purified another two million billion nayutas of world-systems in each direction to provide space for those Tathāgatas who were arriving;

in each of those two million billion nayutas of world-systems in every direction, there were no villages, towns, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, or royal capitals, and they were devoid of Mount Kāla, devoid of the Mucilinda and Mahāmucilinda mountains, and devoid of the Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla mountain ranges.
He establishes [the world-systems] as being devoid of Mount Sumeru, devoid of other great mountains, devoid of great oceans, and devoid of rivers and great rivers;
they are also devoid of the hosts of gods, humans, and asuras, and devoid of the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama;
and all those sentient beings have been transferred to other world-systems.
Those buddha-fields, too, were made of lapis lazuli, covered with nets of gold and the seven precious gems, adorned with networks of tinkling bells,

strewn with *māndārava* and great *māndārava* flowers, overspread with celestial canopies, hung with celestial flower garlands, perfumed with celestial incense and fragrances, and graced by jewel-trees.
And all those jewel-trees were five hundred yojanas in height;
lion-thrones five yojanas in height were manifested,
and then those Tathāgatas sat down individually upon the lion-thrones at the roots of the jewel-trees, having assumed the cross-legged posture.

Then, at that time, all those Tathāgatas who had been emanated by the Blessed One Śākyamuni to teach the Dharma to sentient beings in the eastern direction— numbering as many as the sands of the river Gaṅgā—
all gathered from the ten directions.
Having arrived, they sat down in the eight directions.
Furthermore, at that time, in each of the eight directions, three million billion world-systems were pervaded on all sides by those Tathāgatas.
Then those Tathāgatas, seated upon their respective lion-thrones, dispatched their own attendants to the presence of the Blessed One Śākyamuni.
Giving them baskets of precious flowers, they spoke thus: "Go, you, to Vulture Peak Mountain."

Having gone there, you should again pay homage to that Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and on our behalf inquire after his freedom from ailment, his slight illness, his strength, and his well-being,
together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and the assembly of śrāvakas.
"Sprinkle this heap of jewels and speak thus: 'The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, indeed grants his consent for the opening of this great jewel stūpa.
In this way, all those Tathāgatas dispatched their respective attendants.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, having perceived that all his own emanations had assembled without exception,
and having perceived that they were seated individually upon their respective lion-thrones,
and having perceived that the attendants of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas had also arrived;
Having understood that this aspiration had been proclaimed by those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones,
at that moment he rose from his own Dharma-seat and stood in the open air in the sky.
And all those four assemblies, having risen from their seats and joined their palms in reverent salutation, stood gazing up at the face of the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One,
with the finger of his right hand, opened in the middle that great jeweled stūpa standing in the sky;
having opened it, he caused the two walls to separate.

Just as, for example, at the gates of a great city, two large door-panels swing wide open when released from their bolts, even so did the Blessed One, with his right hand, lift up and open in the middle that great jeweled stūpa standing in the air.
Immediately upon the opening of that great jeweled stūpa,

Then indeed, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, was seen seated upon the lion throne, having assumed the cross-legged posture, with his body dried up and his limbs joined together, appearing exactly as if he had entered into meditative absorption;
and he spoke these words: "Excellent, excellent, Blessed One Śākyamuni!"
Well-spoken by you is this Dharma-discourse, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
It is indeed excellent, O Blessed One Śākyamuni, that you proclaim this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma-discourse in the midst of the assembly.
It is for the sake of hearing this very *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma-discourse, Blessed One, that I have come here.

Then indeed, those four assemblies, seeing the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha— who had entered final nirvāṇa many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of eons ago— speaking in such a manner,
were struck with wonder and filled with amazement.

At that time, they scattered divine and human heaps of jewels over the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and over the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Then indeed, the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, [sat] upon that very same lion-throne within that great jeweled stūpa of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and spoke thus: "Let the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, sit right here."
Then, indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, sat down upon that half-seat together with that very Tathāgata.
And both those Tathāgatas were seen seated upon lion-thrones in the midst of that great jeweled stūpa, staying suspended in the sky above.
Then, indeed, this thought occurred to those four assemblies: "We are far removed from these two Tathāgatas;
what if we too, through the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, were to rise up into the air?
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those four assemblies, [acted accordingly].
At that time, by the power of his supernatural faculties, he established those four assemblies in the air above in the sky.
Then, at that very moment, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, addressed those four assemblies:
"O monks, who among you is able [to go] to that Sahā world-system to [promote] this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?"
To fully proclaim this Dharma discourse—
this is the time, this is the occasion.
The Tathāgata is present before you, monks; desiring to enter final nirvāṇa, the Tathāgata entrusts this Dharma discourse, the Lotus of the True Dharma.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"This Great Sage, the Leader who has entered parinirvāṇa, has come here, having entered this stūpa made of jewels.
O monks, for the sake of hearing this Dharma, who would not generate vigor for the sake of the Dharma? (Saddhp 11.1)
Although he has entered parinirvāṇa many millions of kalpas ago, he still hears the Dharma even today;
for the sake of the Dharma he goes here and there, for such a Dharma as this is extremely difficult to find. (Saddhp 11.2)
This was the vow that this Guide cultivated in his previous existence:
even though he has entered final nirvana, he continues to seek out this entire world in all ten directions.
And all these my own bodies, numbering thousands of millions like the sands of the Ganges,
have come for the sake of performing the work of the Dharma, and to behold this Protector who has entered final nirvana.
Having abandoned their respective fields, as well as all their disciples and gods,
they have all come for the sake of protecting the true Dharma, so that the eye of the Dharma may endure for a long time.

For the sake of providing seats for these Buddhas, I have, by the power of my supernatural faculties, transported thousands of millions of world-systems and likewise all the sentient beings therein, and have purified them.
How shall this such eagerness of mine be manifested, and how this guidance of the Dharma? And these immeasurable Buddhas remain at the foot of the trees like a mass of lotuses.
At the foot of ten million trees, the Guides, seated upon lion thrones with no small body,
shine and remain there at all times, like fire amidst the darkness.
The delightful fragrance of the Leaders of the World wafts through the ten directions,
by which all these beings here are constantly made to faint whenever the wind blows.
When I have entered parinirvāṇa, whoever shall uphold this Dharma discourse,
let them quickly speak these words in the presence of the Lords of the World.
For the Perfectly Awakened One, the Sage Prabhūtaratna, has indeed entered parinirvāṇa;
yet one who makes a firm resolve shall hear his lion’s roar.
"I am the second, and these many millions of leaders who have come;
I shall listen with resolve to the son of the Jina, whoever might venture to proclaim this Dharma. (Saddhp 11.12)
And I, as well as the self-arisen Victor Prabhūtaratna, shall always be honored by him who constantly goes in every direction and intermediate direction to hear this very kind of Dharma.
And these Lords of the World who have arrived, by whom this earth has been made variegated and adorned—
for them too, vast and no small worship would be performed by the proclamation of this sutra.
I am seen here upon this seat, as is the Blessed One who stands within the stupa;
and these other many lords of the world who have arrived from hundreds of various realms.
Reflect on this, O sons of good family, out of compassion for all sentient beings:
"This state is extremely difficult to perform, yet the Leaders venture to undertake it."
If someone were to proclaim many thousands of sūtras, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, that would not be difficult to do.
If one were to grasp Mount Sumeru with the hand and, forming a fist,
hurl it across millions of buddha-fields, that would not be difficult to do.
And whoever should cause this triple-thousandfold world system to tremble with the big toe of his foot, or cast it across millions of buddha-fields— that would not be difficult.
If a person were to stand at the peak of existence and preach the Dharma here,
even thousands of other sūtras, that would not be so difficult to do. (Saddhp 11.20)
But when the Lord of the World has entered parinirvāṇa, in the future time that will be most dreadful,
whoever should uphold or speak this sūtra— this is exceedingly difficult to do.
If someone were to take the entire realm of space and place it into a single fist,
and having thrown it in, were to depart, that would not be difficult to do.
But whoever, after I have entered parinirvāṇa, should write down such a sūtra as this at a later time—this indeed is difficult to do. (Saddhp 11.23)
If one were to take the entire earth element and place it upon the tip of a fingernail, and having cast it forth, go on to ascend even to the Brahma-world; Saddhp_11.24.
Indeed, he would not perform what is difficult, nor would it require such great vigor;
yet, having performed that which is difficult, he stands here at the forefront of the entire world.
Even more difficult than that, when I have entered parinirvāṇa,
will be for someone to speak this sutra for even a single moment in the future time.
It is not difficult in this world for a man to go through the midst of a conflagration at the end of an eon and carry away a load of straw without being burned. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 11.27)
Even more difficult than this, after I have entered parinirvāṇa, would it be for someone to uphold this sutra and cause even a single being to hear it. (Saddhp 11.28)
He shall uphold eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma and teach them, exactly as they were spoken, along with their instructions, to tens of millions of living beings.
For it is not difficult for monks at that time to discipline my disciples and establish them in the five supernormal powers.
This is even more difficult for him: that he should uphold this sutra, believe in it, be resolved upon it, or indeed speak of it again and again.
One might establish many thousands of millions of beings in arhatship—
those highly fortunate ones possessing the six supernormal knowledges— as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therefore, that best of men performs a far greater deed who, after my parinirvāṇa, upholds this excellent sūtra. (Saddhp 11.33)
In thousands of world-systems, many Dharmas have been taught by me;
even now I continue to teach them for the sake of the Buddha-knowledge.
This sūtra, however, is declared to be the foremost among all sūtras;
whoever upholds this sūtra upholds the body of the Jina.
"Speak, O sons of good family! The Tathāgata is present before you;
whoever among you has the resolve to uphold [this teaching] in the future time."
One who would uphold this sutra for even a moment performs a great service that is dear to all the Lords of the World in every respect. (Saddhp 11.37)
And he is always praised by the Lords of the World as one who is heroic,
courageous, and swift in attaining the higher knowledges for the sake of awakening.
And he becomes a bearer of the yoke, a legitimate son of the Lords of the World,
having reached the stage of the tamed, who upholds this sutra.
And having proclaimed this sutra after the Leader of Men has entered parinirvāṇa, he becomes like an eye for the world, including its gods and humans. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 11.40.
That wise one shall become worthy of veneration by all sentient beings,
who in the final age speaks this single sutra for even a moment.
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas and the world with its gods, asuras, and humans, saying:
"In the past, monks, in ages long gone, for immeasurable and incalculable eons, I sought the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra without weariness and without rest."

And formerly, for many eons, for many hundreds of thousands of eons, I was a king who had made a vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; yet my mind never turned back from it. I was devoted to the fulfillment of the six perfections, bestowing immeasurable gifts: gold, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, native gold, silver, and emeralds.

I have renounced villages, towns, cities, market-towns, districts, kingdoms, and capitals; I have given away my wife, sons, daughters, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, elephants, horses, and chariots—indeed, I have sacrificed even my own body, giving away my hands, feet, head, limbs, minor members, and life itself.
Yet, at no time has a mind of attachment ever arisen in me.
And at that time, this world was long-lived;
with a lifespan of many hundreds of thousands of years, I ruled the kingdom for the sake of the Dharma, not for the sake of sensual pleasures.
Therefore, having consecrated my eldest son in the kingdom, I became intent on seeking the supreme Dharma in the four directions.
Thus, I caused a proclamation to be made by means of a bell: "Whoever shall bestow the supreme Dharma upon me and explain its meaning..."
"I would become his servant. At that time, there was a rishi who said this to me: "Great King, there is a sūtra called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which is the supreme exposition of the Dharma."
"Therefore, if you agree to enter into servitude, then I shall cause you to hear that Dharma.
Having heard the words of that seer, I was thrilled, delighted, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and cheer; I then approached where that seer was.
Approaching him, he said, "I shall perform whatever service is to be done by a slave for you.
Having thus accepted the state of servitude to that seer, I performed the duties of a servant, such as gathering grass, wood, water, bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like,
until I even became the gatekeeper.
Having performed such work during the day, I would hold his feet for him as he lay on his couch at night;
neither physical fatigue nor mental weariness came upon me.
As I acted in this manner, a full thousand years passed by.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, elucidating this very meaning, spoke these verses:
"I recollect past eons when I was a righteous King of Dharma."
I exercised sovereignty for the sake of the Dharma, and not for the sake of sensual desires, but for the sake of the supreme Dharma.
"I made this proclamation in the four directions: 'I shall enter into servitude to whoever would preach the Dharma.
At that time, there was a wise seer who was a proclaimer of the sutra named *Saddharma*."
He said to me, "If you have a longing for the Dharma, enter into servitude; from me, I shall proclaim the Dharma.
Hearing those words, I was delighted and then performed whatever work was suitable for a servant.
"May neither physical nor mental exhaustion touch me, having become a servant for the sake of the True Dharma.
At that time, my vow shall be for the sake of sentient beings, not for the sake of myself, nor for the sake of sensual desires."
At that time, he was a king of unshakable heroism, whose activities in the ten directions were focused on nothing else;
for a full thousand kalpas, without weariness, he practiced until he obtained this sūtra named "Dharma."
What do you think, monks, was that king at that time and on that occasion someone else?
Indeed, it should not be viewed in this way.
And for what reason?
At that time, on that occasion, I was that king.
Furthermore, monks, you might think that the seer at that time, on that occasion, was someone else;
however, it should not be viewed in this way.
At that time, on that occasion, this very Devadatta was the monk-ṛṣi.
Monks, Devadatta is indeed my spiritual friend;
it is by relying on Devadatta alone that I have fulfilled the six perfections.
Great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity;

the thirty-two marks of a great man, the eighty minor marks, the golden-colored skin, the ten powers, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four means of attraction, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the power of great supernormal transformations.
The deliverance of beings in the ten directions—
all this is due to the transgression of Devadatta.
I declare this to you, monks.

I declare this: this monk Devadatta, in a future time after immeasurable and incalculable aeons, shall become the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Devarāja, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Blessed One, in the world-system called Devasopānā.
Furthermore, monks, the lifespan of that Tathāgata Devarāja will be twenty intermediate aeons.
And he will teach the Dharma in detail;
beings as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges will realize arhatship through the abandonment of all afflictions,
and many beings will resolve their minds toward pratyekabodhi.
And beings as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā will resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and will attain the patient acceptance of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, monks, after the Tathāgata Devarāja has passed into parinirvāṇa, his True Dharma will remain for twenty intermediate eons.
Furthermore, his body shall not be divided by the separation of its constituent elements;
rather, his body shall become a single solid mass, having entered a stūpa made of the seven precious gems.
And that stūpa shall be six hundred yojanas in height.
It will be forty yojanas in length;
and all the gods and humans there will perform worship with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, and flags,
and they will praise it with verses.
And those who shall circumambulate that stūpa or pay it homage—

some among them will realize the supreme fruit of arhatship, some will attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, and inconceivable and immeasurable gods and humans, having generated the resolve for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, will become irreversible.

Then the Blessed One addressed the community of monks once again: "Monks, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family in a future time shall hear this chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra,
and having heard it, shall neither doubt nor be perplexed,"
With a purified mind, he will develop resolute faith;
by that, the doors to the three miserable destinies will be closed, and he will not fall into rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, or the world of Yama.
Having been reborn in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions, he will hear this very sutra in birth after birth.
Furthermore, having been reborn in the worlds of gods or humans, he will attain a distinguished station.
And in whichever Buddha-field he is reborn, he will be born spontaneously upon a lotus made of the seven precious gems, in the very presence of the Tathāgata.

Then, at that very moment, a bodhisattva named Prajñākūṭa, who had come from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna in the direction below, said this to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna: "Blessed One, let us go to our own buddha-field.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, said this to the bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa: "Wait a moment..."
"Wait a moment, son of good family, until you have engaged in some determination of the Dharma together with my Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; afterwards you shall go to your own Buddha-field.
Then, at that very moment, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta appeared upon a thousand-petaled lotus the size of a chariot wheel.
Seated and surrounded by a multitude of bodhisattvas, he emerged from the palace of Sāgara, the nāga king, out of the midst of the ocean;
traveling through the air above by way of the sky, he approached the presence of the Blessed One on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, having descended from his lotus, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One Śākyamuni and the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and proceeded to where the bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa was.
Having approached, he exchanged various greetings and pleasantries with the bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa, and after engaging in polite conversation, sat down to one side.
Then the bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said this to the crown prince Mañjuśrī: "Mañjuśrī, while you were in the midst of the ocean, how many beings were disciplined by you?
Mañjuśrī replied, "Many, immeasurable, and incalculable beings have been disciplined."
They are immeasurable and incalculable, such that they cannot be made known by speech nor conceived by the mind.
Wait for a moment, noble son, until you see the preliminary sign.
As soon as these words were spoken by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, [the sign appeared].
At that moment, many thousands of lotuses emerged from the midst of the ocean and rose into the air above.
Upon those lotuses sat many thousands of bodhisattvas.
Then, by that very path through the sky, those bodhisattvas approached Vulture Peak Mountain.
Having approached, they were seen standing above in the air;
and all of them had been led by Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Among them were those bodhisattvas who had previously set out in the Mahāyāna.
They praise the six perfections, which are the qualities of the Mahāyāna;
whereas those bodhisattvas who were formerly śrāvakas praise only the Śrāvakayāna,
and all of them [agree that] all phenomena are empty.
They perceived the virtues of the Mahāyāna.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa: "Noble son, while I was in the midst of the ocean, I performed this entire discipline of sentient beings."
And this very one is seen.
Then the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa questioned Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta with a song of verses:
"O Greatly Auspicious One, named Hero by wisdom, those who have been disciplined by you today are incalculable."
"O God among men, tell me this when you are asked: to whom do these beings belong, and whose power is this?"

What Dharma have you taught, or what Sūtra providing instruction on the path to enlightenment, hearing which these beings have conceived the thought of awakening and have attained firm certainty regarding omniscience? (Saddhp 11.48)
Mañjuśrī said, "In the midst of the ocean, he preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra and no other.
Prajñākūṭa said, "This sūtra is profound, subtle, and difficult to perceive;
there is no other sūtra whatsoever that is equal to this sūtra."
"Is there any being who would honor this jewel of a sutra in order to understand it and to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?

Mañjuśrī replied, "There is, noble son; the daughter of Sāgara, the Naga King, is eight years of age by birth, possesses great wisdom, has sharp faculties, and is endowed with bodily, vocal, and mental actions preceded by knowledge, capable of grasping the words and meanings spoken by all the Tathāgatas."
She had attained the dhāraṇīs; she acquired in a single instant thousands of samādhis that concentrate upon all phenomena and sentient beings.

She was irreversible from the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) and possessed vast vows. She followed the same love for herself toward all sentient beings and was capable of generating virtues, never falling away from them.
With a smiling face, endowed with supreme excellence of beautiful complexion, possessing a mind of loving-kindness, she spoke words of compassion;
she was capable of realizing perfect, complete enlightenment.
The Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa said: "I have seen the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, when he was striving for enlightenment as a bodhisattva and performed manifold meritorious deeds."

For many thousands of eons, he never slackened his vigor. Within the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, there is not a single spot of ground even as small as a mustard seed where his body was not laid down for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings;
only after that did he fully awaken to enlightenment.
"Who could believe that she is able to realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in a single moment?
At that very moment, the daughter of Sāgara, the Naga King, appeared standing before them.
Having bowed her head at the feet of the Blessed One, she stood to one side.
At that moment, she spoke these verses:
"Merit, merit, and the profound—it radiates in every direction."
The subtle body is adorned with the thirty-two marks.
Endowed with the secondary marks and honored by all beings,
he is accessible to all beings, just like a marketplace.
"According to my wish, may I attain perfect enlightenment; the Tathāgata is my witness in this matter.
I shall teach the extensive Dharma that brings liberation from suffering."

Then, at that time, the venerable Śāriputra said this to the daughter of Sāgara, the Naga King: "Noble daughter, you have indeed conceived the thought of awakening, and you possess irreversible and immeasurable wisdom; yet, the state of perfect enlightenment is difficult to attain."
Noble daughter, there is a woman who does not slacken her vigor,
and for many hundreds of eons and many thousands of eons she performs meritorious deeds and fulfills the six perfections.
And yet, even now, she does not attain Buddhahood.
What is the reason?
There are five states that a woman has not yet attained.

What are the five? The first is the station of Brahmā; the second is the station of Śakra; the third is the station of a Great King; the fourth is the station of a Cakravartin; and the fifth is the station of an irreversible Bodhisattva.
Then, at that very moment, the daughter of the Naga King Sāgara possessed a single jewel,
which was worth the entire great trichiliocosm;
and that jewel was given by the daughter of the Naga King Sāgara to the Blessed One.
He was accepted by the Blessed One out of compassion.
Then the daughter of the Sāgara Naga King addressed the Bodhisattva Prajñākūṭa and the Elder Śāriputra, saying: "Was this jewel which I gave to the Blessed One accepted by the Blessed One quickly?"
The Elder said: "It was given by you quickly, and it was accepted by the Blessed One quickly.
The daughter of the Sāgara Naga King said: "Venerable Śāriputra, if I possessed great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), I would have awakened to perfect enlightenment even more quickly."
And there would be no one to receive this jewel.

Then, at that moment, before the eyes of the entire world and in the presence of the Elder Śāriputra, the daughter of the Naga King Sāgara’s female organ disappeared and a male organ appeared, and she manifested herself as a Bodhisattva.
At that time, he set out toward the southern direction.
Now, in the southern direction, there is a world-system named Vimalā.
There, at the foot of a Bodhi tree made of the seven precious gems, he manifested himself as having sat down and attained perfect awakening.
Bearing the thirty-two marks and possessing a form endowed with all the secondary characteristics, he pervaded the ten directions with his radiance while teaching the Dharma;
and all the beings in the Sahā world-system beheld that Tathāgata.
He was being venerated by all the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, humans, and non-humans, and he was delivering a discourse on the Dharma.
And all those beings who heard the Dharma discourse of that Tathāgata became irreversible from unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
That world-system Vimalā and this Sahā world-system shook in six ways;
and among the circles of the assembly of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, three thousand living beings attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
And three hundred thousand living beings received the prophecy of their attainment of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Prajñākūṭa and the Elder Śāriputra remained silent.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Manifestation of the Stūpa," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
(Vaidya 162) Saddhp_12: The Chapter on Encouragement. Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāpratibhāna—
Surrounded by a retinue of two million bodhisattvas, they addressed these words to the Blessed One in his presence: "May the Blessed One be free from concern regarding this matter.
O Blessed One, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, we shall teach and proclaim this Dharma discourse to sentient beings."
Moreover, Blessed One, although at that time there will be deceitful beings—

those with meager roots of merit, full of conceit, dependent on gain and honor, practicing unwholesome roots, difficult to tame, devoid of resolve, and abounding in lack of resolve— nevertheless, Blessed One, we shall demonstrate the power of patience and recite this sutra at that time.
"We shall uphold it, we shall teach it, we shall write it down, and we shall honor, revere, esteem, and worship it.
O Blessed One, even at the cost of our bodies and lives, we shall proclaim this sutra.
May the Blessed One be free from anxiety."

Then, in that assembly, about five hundred monks—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—said this to the Blessed One: "We too, Blessed One, are able to [uphold] this Dharma-discourse; however, Blessed One, it is rather in other world-systems [that we shall do so].
Then, as many of the Blessed One’s disciples, both those in training and those beyond training, as had been prophesied by the Blessed One for unexcelled perfect enlightenment, [spoke likewise].
Eight thousand monks, all of them extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One be of little concern;
we too shall proclaim this Dharma-discourse in the future time, in the final age, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, though it be in other world-systems."
For what reason?
Blessed One, because the beings in this Sahā world-system are arrogant, possess few roots of merit, are constantly malevolent in mind, deceitful, and of crooked nature.

Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, the Blessed One’s maternal aunt, together with six thousand bhikṣuṇīs—both those still in training and those beyond training—rose from her seat, joined her palms toward the Blessed One, and stood gazing up at the Blessed One.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī: “Gautamī, why do you stand there looking at the Tathāgata with a troubled mind?”
"I have not been proclaimed or predicted for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
rather, Gautamī, you have been predicted by means of a prediction for the entire assembly.
Furthermore, Gautamī, from this point forward, in the presence of thirty-eight hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Buddhas..."

Having performed honor, reverence, respect, worship, veneration, and homage, you shall become a Dharma-preacher, a bodhisattva mahāsattva. These six thousand bhikṣuṇīs, both those in training and those beyond training, together with you, shall also become bodhisattvas in the presence of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones.

They will become Dharma-preachers. Thereafter, having further perfected the conduct of a bodhisattva, you will appear in the world as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, and an unsurpassed one.

He is the charioteer who tames men, the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. And that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, Gautamī, will grant the sequential prophecy of these six thousand bodhisattvas for unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment.
Then, it occurred to the nun Yaśodharā, the mother of Rāhula: "My name has not been proclaimed by the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the nun Yaśodharā, said this to the nun Yaśodharā: "I announce to you, Yaśodharā."
I declare this to you:
you too, having performed honor, reverence, respect, worship, veneration, and adoration toward ten thousand koṭis of Buddhas, will become a Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher.
And having gradually fulfilled the conduct of a Bodhisattva, you will become a Tathāgata named Raśmiśatasahasraparipūrṇadhvaja.

"You shall become an Arhat, a perfectly enlightened Buddha in the world, endowed with conduct and practice, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One, in the world-system Bhadrā.
And the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Raśmiśatasahasraparipūrṇadhvaja, will be immeasurable."
Then indeed, the nun Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, accompanied by a retinue of six thousand nuns, and the nun Yaśodharā,

accompanied by a retinue of four thousand nuns, having heard their own prophecy for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment from the presence of the Blessed One, were struck with wonder and amazement; at that moment, they spoke this verse:
O Blessed One, you are the trainer, you are the guide, and you are the teacher of the world together with its gods;
you are the giver of consolation, honored by humans and devas, and today, O Protector, we too have been satisfied.
Then, having spoken this verse, those bhikṣuṇīs said this to the Blessed One: "We too, Blessed One, are eager to proclaim this Dharma-discourse in the future time, in the final age;
however, it shall be in other world-systems."

Then the Blessed One turned his gaze toward those eight hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas— bodhisattvas who had attained the dhāraṇīs and who set in motion the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
Thereupon, as soon as they were gazed upon by the Blessed One, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas rose from their seats.
Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, they thought: "The Blessed One exhorts us to proclaim this Dharma discourse.

Having reflected thus, they were deeply moved and said to one another: "O sons of good family, how shall we act when the Blessed One exhorts us regarding this Dharma discourse for the sake of the future?"
"For the purpose of fully illuminating this sound?

Then those sons of good family, out of reverence for the Blessed One and by virtue of their own former conduct and vows, roared a lion’s roar in the presence of the Blessed One: "Blessed One, in a future time, we [shall uphold] this Dharma-discourse."

After the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, we shall go in the ten directions and cause all sentient beings to write it down, recite it, reflect upon it, and proclaim it through the very power of the Blessed One;
and the Blessed One, remaining in another world-system, will provide us with protection, shelter, and defense.
Then those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, in unison, addressed the Blessed One with these verses:
“O Blessed One, you may remain free from anxiety; after you have entered parinirvāṇa, we ourselves shall proclaim this supreme sūtra during that most terrifying final age. (Saddhp 12.2)
O Leader, we shall endure and patiently accept the insults, threats, and even the brandishing of sticks by those who are foolish.
In the terrible final age, there will be those of evil intellect, crooked, deceitful, childish, and conceited; they will perceive what has not been attained as already attained.
Living in the forest and wearing patched rags, those of evil mind will say, "We are practitioners of the austere life. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 12.5)
Greedy for and attached to flavors, they will teach the Dharma to householders and will be honored just like those who possess the six supernormal powers.
Cruel-minded and wicked, preoccupied with their homes and wealth,
they will enter the seclusion of the forest only to revile us.
And those dependent on gain and honor will say of us: "Alas, these monks are heretics; they teach their own poetic compositions! (Saddhp 12.8)
Having composed sūtras themselves for the sake of gain and honor, those who mock us speak in the midst of the assembly. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 12.9.
Among kings, princes, or royal ministers, as well as among brahmins, householders, and other monks as well.
"They will speak ill of us and attribute our words to the doctrines of the heretics;
we shall endure all of this out of respect for the great seers."
And those evil-minded ones who will revile us at that time— [we shall think],
"These ones will become Buddhas," and we shall endure it in every way.
In this terrible and greatly fearsome time of the world’s dissolution, many monks in the form of yakṣas will revile us.
Out of reverence for the Lord of the World, we venture to perform what is extremely difficult;
having girded ourselves with the armor of patience, we shall proclaim this sutra.
O Leader, we have no desire for our bodies or our lives;
we desire only enlightenment, acting as the keepers of your entrusted deposit.
The Blessed One alone knows what kind of evil monks will exist in the future time— those who do not understand the intentional language (*saṃdhābhāṣya*). (Saddhp 12.16)
One must endure all frowns and repeated denials of recognition;
one may be expelled from monasteries and subjected to various forms of imprisonment and beatings.
Remembering the command of the Lord of the World, O Kāli, in the future age we shall fearlessly proclaim this sūtra in the midst of the assembly.
"Furthermore, O Leader, we shall go again and again to those who are seekers of this [teaching] here in cities and villages, and we will deliver this deposit to them for you."
"O Great Sage, Lord of the World, we shall carry out your command;
therefore, be free from anxiety, for you have attained peace and are perfectly at ease."
And all the illuminators of the world who have come from the ten directions—
our truthful words you understand, as well as our resolute faith.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "Encouragement," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 166) Saddhp_13: The Chapter on the Abiding in Bliss.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, it is difficult, most difficult, that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas have endured for the sake of the Blessed One."
“Blessed One, how should this Dharma-discourse be proclaimed by these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in the future time, in the final age?

When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Mañjuśrī, the Youthful: “Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva established in four qualities should proclaim this Dharma-discourse in the future time, in the final age...”
It should be proclaimed at the proper time.
At which four [times]?
Here, Mañjuśrī, this Dharma-discourse should be proclaimed by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is established in proper conduct and sphere of activity during the final period, in the final age.
And how, Mañjuśrī, does a bodhisattva mahāsattva become established in right conduct and sphere of activity?
When, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is patient, self-controlled, having reached the stage of self-control, with a mind that is neither terrified nor trembling, and free from envy.
And when, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not course in any dharma whatsoever,
and observes the specific characteristic of dharmas as it truly is—
this indeed is the non-investigation and non-conceptualization regarding these dharmas.
This, Mañjuśrī, is called the conduct of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
And what, Mañjuśrī, is the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
It is when, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not associate with kings.

He does not associate with, honor, attend upon, or approach princes, royal ministers, or royal officials; nor does he associate with, honor, or attend upon followers of other sects— such as Carakas, Parivrājakas, Ājīvakas, or Nirgranthas— nor does he associate with, honor, or attend upon beings who are devoted to the study of poetic treatises.
He does not associate with, honor, or attend upon those who uphold the mantras of Lokāyata nor the Lokāyatas themselves,
nor does he cultivate intimacy with them.
He does not [associate with] outcastes, wrestlers, pig-breeders, poultry-keepers, deer-hunters, meat-sellers, actors and dancers, cymbal-beaters, or boxers.
He does not frequent other places of pleasure and amusement belonging to others, nor does he cultivate intimacy with them; however,
when they do come to him, he speaks the Dharma to them from time to time.
And he speaks that [Dharma] without being dependent on it;
furthermore, he does not serve, associate with, or attend upon the monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor does he cultivate intimacy with them.
Nor does he come into their company, whether on the walking-path or in the monastery;
however, when they approach him, he speaks the Dharma to them from time to time,
and he speaks it without being dependent [on them].
Mañjuśrī, this is the sphere of activity of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not repeatedly teach the Dharma to women by grasping at any sign of attachment toward them, nor does he desire to see women frequently,
nor does he frequent their households.
He does not consider it appropriate to frequently address a girl, a maiden, or a young wife,
nor does he exchange greetings with them;
nor does he teach the Dharma to a paṇḍaka.
He does not cultivate intimacy with him, nor does he exchange greetings;
he does not enter among the houses alone for the sake of alms, except while cultivating the recollection of the Tathāgata.
If, however, he teaches the Dharma to women,
he does not teach the Dharma even with a passion for the Dharma, let alone with a passion for women.
He does not even show his row of teeth, much less make a coarse facial expression;
nor does he address a male novice, a female novice, a monk, a nun, a young boy, or a young girl.
He does not cultivate intimacy with them, nor does he engage in conversation with them; rather,
he values solitary seclusion above all else.
And he frequently resorts to solitary retreat;
this, Mañjuśrī, is called the first range of activity of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena as empty—
phenomena that abide according to reality, remaining non-erroneously, established as they truly are, immovable, unshakable, irreversible, and unchanging;
always abiding as they truly are, having the nature of space, devoid of verbal expression and conventional usage, unborn, non-existent, and unoriginated.
They are unconditioned, without continuity, expressed through the verbalization of non-existence, abiding in a state free from attachment, yet appearing through the perversion of perception.

It is in this way, Mañjuśrī, that a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells constantly contemplating all phenomena; dwelling by means of this dwelling, the bodhisattva mahāsattva becomes established in his proper sphere of activity.
This, Mañjuśrī, is the second sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, demonstrating this very matter more extensively, at that time spoke these verses:
“If a bodhisattva should desire, in the extremely dreadful future age, to proclaim this sūtra, being undaunted and confident— ” *Saddhp* 13.1.
One should guard one's conduct and sphere of activity, remaining unattached and pure;
one should always avoid intimacy with princes and kings.
Furthermore, one should not cultivate intimacy with royal officials, nor with outcasts, boxers, drunkards, or with any kind of heretics whatsoever.
One should not associate with those who are conceited, even if they are established in the Vinaya and the Āgamas;
one should avoid monks who are considered Arhats but are actually of immoral conduct.
One should always avoid a nun whose sphere of activity consists of laughter and idle chatter;
one should also avoid female lay devotees who remain in public display.
Those female lay followers who seek liberation in this present life—one should avoid intimacy with them; this is called proper conduct. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 13.6)
And whoever approaches him to ask about the Dharma for the sake of supreme enlightenment,
the wise one should always speak to them, being neither discouraged nor dependent [on anything].
One should avoid intimacy with those beings who are women or eunuchs; one should also avoid [interacting with] young wives and maidens within families. (Saddhp 13.8)
One should never seek to please them by inquiring about their skill in joking;
one should avoid intimacy with those who raise pigs and sheep.
Furthermore, one should avoid associating with those who would harm various living beings for the sake of profit and sell meat at a slaughterhouse.
One should avoid intimacy with those beings who support women,
as well as with actors, wrestlers, boxers, and other people of that sort.
One should not serve courtesans or others who live by sensual pleasures;
one should completely avoid socializing with them in every way.
And when a wise man teaches the Dharma to women,
he should not enter there alone, nor should he remain in a state of jesting.
Even when he enters a village repeatedly seeking food,
he should seek out a second monk or keep the Buddha constantly in mind.
For this is the first sphere of conduct that I have shown,
by which those possessed of wisdom dwell while upholding a sūtra such as this.

When one does not engage with phenomena that are inferior, superior, or intermediate, nor with the conditioned or the unconditioned, nor with the real or the unreal in any respect; ||| Saddhp_13.16 |||
The wise one does not act with the thought "this is a woman," nor should he conceptualize "this is a man";
because all phenomena are unborn, even when searching, he does not perceive them.
For this conduct of the bodhisattvas has been taught in its entirety; now listen as I reveal what their sphere of activity is like.
These dharmas have been revealed as non-existent; they have not appeared, nor are they born, all being empty and devoid of activity, abiding eternally. This is said to be the domain of the wise.
These have been conceptualized by those with perverted perceptions; for what is non-existent has been imagined as existent, and what is unreal as real.
These dharmas, which are unarisen and unborn, have been falsely conceptualized as having arisen and being real.
For one whose mind is single-pointed and always concentrated, remaining as firm as the peak of Mount Sumeru—
staying thus, he indeed beholds all these phenomena as being like space.
Always regarding all phenomena as having a core equal to space—unmoving and free from conceit—to dwell thus at all times is said to be the domain of the wise. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 13.22)
Any monk who, after I have entered parinirvāṇa, protects my deportment and proclaims this sūtra in the world, for him there shall be no shrinking back whatsoever.
Or, reflecting at the proper time, the wise one, having entered his dwelling and likewise composed himself,
should contemplate this entire Dharma thoroughly and, rising up with an undaunted mind, teach it.
In this world, kings provide protection for him, as do the princes who hear the Dharma;
moreover, other householders and brahmins also stand surrounding him on all sides.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, during the final period, the final time, when the true Dharma is in the process of disappearing, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who desires to proclaim this Dharma-discourse remains established in happiness.
Abiding in comfort, he speaks the Dharma, whether it be contained in his own body or in books;
and while teaching it to others, he does not become excessively prone to finding fault,
nor does he disparage other monks who are preachers of the Dharma.
He does not speak dispraise,
nor does he utter dispraise; nor does he, having mentioned the names of other monks belonging to the Śrāvaka vehicle, speak dispraise of them.
Nor does he spread dispraise, nor does he perceive them as adversaries.
For what reason?
For instance, because he abides in a state of ease,
he teaches the Dharma to those who come to hear it, supporting them with kindness and without envy.
Without disputing, and when asked a question, he does not answer by means of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
rather, he answers in such a way that one awakens to the knowledge of a Buddha.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The wise one always remains in comfort; thus seated in comfort, he teaches the Dharma, having prepared a magnificent seat upon a clean and pleasing spot of earth. (Saddhp 13.26)
Having put on a clean robe, well-dyed with excellent colors, and having likewise fastened the black shoulder-cloth and donned a large undergarment, he— *Saddhp_13.27* —
Having sat upon the seat provided with a footstool, which was well-spread with various fine cloths,
he ascended it with his feet well-washed, and with a head and face that were smooth and radiant.
And having sat here upon the Dharma-seat while beings of one-pointed mind have assembled,
he should offer many diverse discourses to the monks and the nuns alike.
