That wise one should always speak sweet words of manifold meaning to laymen and laywomen, as well as to kings and princes, without ever being envious.
Even when questioned by them at that time, he would explain the meaning in accordance with the questions;
and he would teach that collection of meanings in such a way that, having heard it, they might become attainers of awakening.
Having abandoned weariness and not giving rise to a sense of exhaustion,
the wise one should cast off all discontent and cultivate the power of loving-kindness toward the assembly.
That wise one shall preach the supreme Dharma day and night with millions of billions of parables;
he shall gladden and satisfy the assembly, yet he shall never at any time desire anything for himself.
He should not think of food, soft fare, as well as drinks, garments, beds, seats, or robes; nor should he request any medicine for the sick from the assembly. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 13.34.
Elsewhere, the wise one should always think: "May I become a Buddha, and may these beings [do likewise].
This is my provision for all happiness—that I proclaim the Dharma for the benefit of the world.
And whichever monk, free from envy, should proclaim this after I have entered parinirvāṇa—
for him there shall be no suffering, nor any obstacle, and never shall there be grief or despair.
No one should cause him fear, nor should they strike him, nor speak ill of him;
nor should they ever expel him, for he is thus established in the power of patience.
When the wise one is thus established in happiness, abiding exactly as I have described,
there arise many hundreds of millions of virtues that cannot be fully told even in a hundred eons.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa and the final period of the disappearance of the True Dharma is occurring, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds this sūtra becomes free from envy, free from deceit, and free from guile;
he does not speak dispraise of other persons belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle.
He does not revile them, nor does he disparage them;

nor does he instill remorse in other monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen—whether they belong to the vehicle of the hearers (*śrāvakayāna*), the vehicle of the solitary buddhas (*pratyekabuddhayāna*), or the vehicle of the bodhisattvas (*bodhisattvayāna*)—by saying: "O sons of good family, you are far from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
You do not appear worthy of it;
you dwell in extreme negligence.
"You are not capable of fully awakening to that knowledge"—
in this way, he does not instill regret in anyone belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle,
nor does he take delight in disputes over the Dharma.
He does not engage in disputes over the Dharma, nor does he abandon the power of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings;
and toward all Tathāgatas, he conceives the perception of them as his father.
He conceives the notion of the Teacher toward all bodhisattvas;
and those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who exist in the worlds of the ten directions, he constantly pays homage to them with resolute intention and reverence.
And while teaching the Dharma, he teaches the Dharma neither deficiently nor redundantly, with an impartial love for the Dharma;
and while proclaiming this Dharma-discourse, he does not show greater favor to anyone, even through his love for the Dharma.

Mañjuśrī, endowed with this third quality, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while proclaiming this Dharma discourse during the final period when the True Dharma has come to an end after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, dwells in a state of pleasant contact.
He proclaims this Dharma discourse without being harassed,
and he has companions who assist him in the communal recitation of the Dharma.
And there will arise for him listeners of the Dharma who shall hear this Dharma-discourse, have faith in it, accept it, retain it, master it, write it down, and cause it to be written down.
And having committed it to writing, they will honor it, revere it, respect it, and worship it.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, further spoke these words: "The preacher of the Dharma, having completely abandoned deceit, pride, and guile..."
Likewise, a wise person who desires to proclaim this sutra should never harbor envy.
One should never speak disparagement of anyone, nor should one ever engage in disputes regarding views;
one should never give rise to a basis for remorse, otherwise you shall not attain unsurpassed knowledge.
Always upright and gentle, and patient, such is the son of the Sugata;
in repeatedly proclaiming this Dharma again and again, he never experiences weariness.

Those bodhisattvas who wander in the world throughout the ten directions out of compassion for sentient beings—all of them are my teachers; a wise person should generate profound reverence toward them.
Remembering the Buddhas, the supreme among bipeds, one should always regard the Jinas as fathers;
having abandoned all notions of pride, no obstacle shall arise for him then. (Saddhp 13.43)
Having heard such a Dharma as this, the wise person should then protect it;
thus, being concentrated, they dwell in happiness and are well protected by millions of living beings.

Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, when the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa and the final period of the decline of the True Dharma is occurring, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to uphold this Dharma-discourse must dwell at a great distance, far removed from both householders and those who have gone forth.
One should dwell in the abiding of loving-kindness,
and one should conceive a sense of longing toward all those beings who have set out for enlightenment.
And he should generate this thought: "Alas, these beings are of a nature characterized by great lack of wisdom,
in that they do not hear, do not know, do not understand, do not inquire about, do not believe in, and do not resolve upon the Tathāgata’s skill in means and his intentional speech."

Furthermore, although these beings do not penetrate or understand this Dharma-discourse, nevertheless, after I have fully awakened to this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, I shall [guide] whoever may be established in whatever state.
I shall win him over by the power of my supernatural faculties right there; I shall cause him to have faith, I shall lead him to enter [the path], and I shall bring him to full maturity.

Mañjuśrī, by being endowed with this fourth quality as well, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who proclaims this Dharma discourse after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa will be free from affliction and will be honored, revered, esteemed, and worshiped by monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen; by kings, princes, royal ministers, and high officials of the court; by merchants and country folk; and by brahmins and householders.
Furthermore, the faithful deities who dwell in the atmosphere will follow behind him to listen to the Dharma.
The sons of the gods will always follow him for his protection, whether he has gone to a village or to a monastery;
they will approach him day and night to inquire about the Dharma,
and they will become satisfied, elated, and joyful by his explanations.
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, this Dharma discourse is empowered by all Buddhas.
Mañjuśrī, this Dharma discourse has been eternally empowered by the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
Mañjuśrī, the sound, the resonance, or even the hearing of the name of this Dharma discourse is difficult to encounter in many world systems.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as if there were a king, a wheel-turning monarch of power, who by his might conquers his own kingdom;
thereafter, his adversaries, enemies, and rival kings enter into conflict with him.
Now, that king, a wheel-turning monarch of power, has various kinds of warriors;
they fight with those enemies.
Then, seeing those warriors fighting, the king becomes pleased and joyful in mind.
Joyful and elated, he bestows various gifts upon those warriors;
that is to say, he gives villages or village lands, or he gives cities or city lands.

He gives garments, head-wraps, hand-ornaments, foot-ornaments, neck-ornaments, ear-ornaments, golden threads, necklaces and half-necklaces, as well as silver, gold, jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, and even elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, female slaves, and male slaves.
He gives vehicles and palanquins,
but he does not give his crest-jewel to anyone.
For what reason?
For that crest-jewel alone resides upon the head of the king;
yet when, Mañjuśrī, the king gives away even that crest-jewel, then the entire fourfold army of the king becomes struck with wonder and filled with amazement.

In the same way, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, the Lord of Dharma, the King of Dharma, exercises his righteous sovereignty over the triple world by means of the Dharma— righteousness won by the strength of his own arms and won by the power of his merit. Yet Māra, the Evil One, assails that triple world.
Furthermore, the noble warriors of the Tathāgata also fought against Māra.

Then, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of Dharma, and the King of Dharma, seeing those noble warriors fighting, spoke hundreds of thousands of various sūtras for the sake of gladdening the fourfold assembly.
He bestowed upon them the city of Nirvana, the great city of Dharma,
and enticed them with that final liberation;
yet he did not speak this kind of Dharma discourse.

In this regard, Mañjuśrī, just as that powerful universal monarch, being amazed by the great manly valor of those warriors as they fought, subsequently gives them his crest-jewel— the very last of all his possessions— which is beyond the belief of all the world and a source of wonder;
and just as, Mañjuśrī, that crest-jewel of that king has been long protected and remained upon his head.

In the same way, Mañjuśrī, when the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— the King of Dharma who rules by Dharma over the triple world— sees the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas fighting against the Māra of the aggregates or the Māra of the afflictions; and when, through fighting with them, the destruction of passion, hatred, and delusion is achieved, the departure from the entire triple world is realized, and the great heroic feat of vanquishing all Māras is accomplished, [he rejoices].

Then the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, having been pleased, preached to those noble warriors this very Dharma discourse— which is contrary to all the world, not to be believed by all the world, never before spoken, and never before taught.
The Tathāgata bestowed upon his disciples that which brings about omniscience for all, like a great crest-jewel.

For this, Mañjuśrī, is the supreme teaching of the Dharma of the Tathāgatas; this is the final Dharma-discourse of the Tathāgatas. Among all Dharma-discourses, this Dharma-discourse is the most profound and is contrary to the entire world.
"Mañjuśrī, just as this crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi), which has been long protected by the Tathāgata, was today released by that very same Wheel-Turning King of Power and given to his warriors;

even so, Mañjuśrī, the Tathāgata has likewise today fully revealed this secret of the Dharma, which has been long guarded, which stands at the summit of all Dharma-discourses, and which is to be understood only by a Tathāgata."
Then, indeed, the Blessed One, wishing to demonstrate this very matter more extensively, at that time spoke these verses:
"Always displaying the power of loving-kindness and always feeling compassion for all sentient beings,
one should proclaim such a Dharma as this distinguished sutra praised by the Sugatas."
Whether they be householders or those who have gone forth, whatever bodhisattvas there may be in that final age—
he shall indeed manifest the power of loving-kindness toward them all, lest they should reject the Dharma upon hearing it.
But when I have attained awakening and am established in the state of a Tathāgata, then, employing skillful means, I shall lead others [to it] and cause them to hear of this supreme enlightenment.
Just as a powerful universal monarch, being pleased, might give various kinds of gold to his warriors, and bestow upon them elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, as well as cities and villages.
Delighted, he gives hand-ornaments, silver, and gold thread;
pearls, gems, shells, stones, and coral, as well as various kinds of servants—delighted, he gives them all.
But when he is amazed there by someone through a supreme feat of strength,
and realizing that "this is a marvelous deed performed," he removes his crown and gives him the jewel.
In the same way, the Buddha is the King of Dharma, possessing the power of patience and a vast treasury of wisdom;
out of compassion and pity for the welfare of others, he governs this entire world through the Dharma.
Then, seeing sentient beings being afflicted, I preach thousands of millions of sūtras,
having understood the prowess of those living beings who are pure-souled here and destroyers of the afflictions.
Then the King of Dharma, the great physician, speaking through hundreds of millions of discourses,
and knowing that beings were possessed of strength, the Knower taught this sūtra as if it were a crest-jewel.
This is the final sutra I proclaim in the world; it is the foremost among all my sutras.
It has been guarded by me and never before spoken; today I shall cause it to be heard—listen, all of you!
These four qualities of such a kind are to be practiced by those who, after my parinirvāṇa, seek the supreme, foremost enlightenment and perform service for me. (Saddhp 13.55)
He has neither sorrow nor any obstacle, nor does he suffer from poor complexion or illness;
his skin does not become dark, nor does he dwell in an inferior city.
That great seer is always lovely to behold, like a Tathāgata worthy of worship;
those young sons of gods constantly serve as his attendants.
Neither weapon nor poison shall ever affect his body, nor even staff or clod of earth;
the mouth of whoever should utter even a word of abuse against him would be closed up.
He becomes a kinsman to living beings here on earth and wanders the world as one who has brought forth light,
dispelling the darkness for many millions of creatures, he who upholds this sutra after I have entered parinirvāṇa.
In his dreams he sees auspicious forms; he sees monks and nuns, and he sees his own person seated upon a lion throne, proclaiming the Dharma in many ways.
To the gods, yakṣas— as numerous as the sands of the Gaṅgā— and to the various kinds of asuras and nāgas,
he preaches the supreme Dharma while they all stand with palms joined in reverence within his dream. (Saddhp 13.61)
In his dream, he sees the Tathāgata teaching the Dharma to many millions of living beings,
emitting thousands of rays of light— the Lord of golden hue, with a beautiful voice.
And there he stands with palms joined in reverence, praising the Sage, the supreme among bipeds;
and that Jina, the great physician, proclaims the supreme Dharma to the fourfold assembly.
Having heard this, he becomes overjoyed and, filled with gladness, performs worship;
and in his dreams, he attains the dhāraṇīs, quickly touching the irreversible gnosis.
And having understood his intention, the Lord of the World prophesied for him the state of being a bull among men:
"Noble son, you too shall here in the future time attain unsurpassed, auspicious gnosis."
Your field, too, shall be vast, and you shall have four assemblies just like mine;
they will listen to the vast, untainted Dharma with reverence and with palms joined in salutation.
Furthermore, he sees that very person cultivating the Dharma in mountain caves;
having cultivated the Dharma and realized its true nature (dharmatā), he attains samādhi and beholds the Jina.
Having seen in a dream one of golden hue, endowed with the marks of a hundred merits, he hears the Dharma;
having heard it, he proclaims it to the assembly—such indeed is his dream. (Saddhp 13.68)
Even in a dream, having abandoned his entire kingdom, the inner apartments, and likewise his circle of kinsmen,
he went forth, renouncing all desires, and approached the seat of awakening.
Seated there upon the lion throne at the foot of that tree, seeking awakening, he will,
after the passing of seven days, attain the wisdom of the Tathāgatas.
Having attained awakening and emerged from that state, he set in motion the stainless wheel;
for inconceivable billions of thousands of eons, he taught the Dharma to the fourfold assembly.

Having revealed the Dharma there that is free from outflows, and having extinguished many millions of living beings, he himself enters extinction like a lamp when its fuel is exhausted; such is this dream.
And there will always be many and infinite benefits for him who, in the final age, shall proclaim this foremost dharma-sūtra well-taught by me— O Mañjughoṣa.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Chapter on Dwelling in Happiness," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 179) Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra, Chapter 14: The Emergence of the Bodhisattvas from the Earth.
At that time, eight bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, who had come from other world-systems, rose up from within that assembly.
They were present.

Joining their palms in reverence and facing the Blessed One, they paid homage to the Blessed One and said this to him: "If the Blessed One would grant us permission, we too, O Blessed One, would proclaim, recite, write down, and worship this Dharma-discourse in that Sahā world-system after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa."
"And may we apply ourselves to yoga in this Dharma-discourse. Therefore, it would be well if the Blessed One would also authorize us in this Dharma-discourse.
Then the Blessed One said this to those bodhisattvas: "Enough, sons of good family!"
"What business do you have with this?
Here in this Sahā world-system of mine, there are thousands of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers, which constitute the retinue of a single bodhisattva.
And of such bodhisattvas as these, there are likewise thousands of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers."
Each of those bodhisattvas shall have such a retinue that, after I have entered final nirvana, in the future time, in the final age, they will uphold, recite, and proclaim this Dharma discourse.
As soon as these words had been spoken by the Blessed One,

this Sahā world-system split open and burst asunder on all sides. And from within those fissures, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas emerged, their bodies golden in color and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
Those who were dwelling beneath this great earth in the realm of space,

relying upon this very Sahā world-system, indeed heard such a sound from the Blessed One and rose up from the earth; each one of those bodhisattvas was accompanied by a retinue of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of sixty Ganges rivers, a great assembly, a vast multitude, a leader of a host.

There were hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the sands of sixty Ganges rivers— leaders of such bodhisattvas, great leaders, and teachers of assemblies— who were emerging from the fissures in the earth here in this Sahā world-system;
what need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who had retinues of bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of fifty Ganges rivers?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of forty Ganges rivers?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of thirty Ganges rivers?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas numbering twenty?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of ten Ganges rivers?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of five, four, three, or two Ganges rivers?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of a single Ganges river?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of half a Gaṅgā River?

What need is there to mention those who have retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to one-fourth, one-sixth, one-eighth, one-tenth, one-twentieth, one-thirtieth, one-fortieth, one-fiftieth, one-hundredth, one-thousandth, one-hundred-thousandth, one-ten-millionth, one-billionth, one-trillionth, one-quadrillionth, one-quintillionth, or even those with retinues of bodhisattvas equal in number to the sands of a Gaṅgā River?
What need is there to mention the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have retinues of many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas?
What need is there to mention the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who have retinues of one koti?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with retinues of a hundred thousand?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with retinues of a thousand?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas with retinues of five hundred?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of four hundred, three hundred, or two hundred [bodhisattvas]?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of one hundred [bodhisattvas]?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of fifty bodhisattvas? And so on.
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have retinues of forty, thirty, twenty, ten, five, four, three, or two bodhisattvas?
What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are accompanied by only one other? What need is there to mention those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who dwell alone without a retinue?
Neither their number, nor their calculation, nor their comparison, nor even their measure can be apprehended—
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who here in this Sahā world-system were emerging from the fissures of the earth;
and having emerged one after another, they proceeded toward that great jeweled stūpa which was stationed in the sky, suspended in mid-air.

They approached that place where the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha— who had entered parinirvāṇa— was seated upon a lion throne together with the Blessed Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Having approached and bowed their heads at the feet of both Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, they also paid homage to all those emanations of the Lord Śākyamuni Tathāgata— those forms of the Tathāgata who had assembled from throughout the various world-systems in the ten directions.
Seated upon lion thrones at the foot of various jewel-trees,

they all paid homage and prostrated to them; having circumambulated those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas hundreds of thousands of times, and having praised them with various kinds of bodhisattva hymns,
they stood to one side.

With palms joined in reverence, they paid homage directly to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and to the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Furthermore, at that time, as those bodhisattva mahāsattvas emerged from the fissures in the earth, prostrating to the Tathāgatas and praising them with various kinds of bodhisattva hymns, fifty full intermediate kalpas passed by.

And for those fifty intermediate kalpas, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha remained silent. Those four assemblies likewise remained in silence for those same fifty intermediate kalpas.
Then, the Blessed One performed such a feat of supernatural power (ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra) as this:
By means of such a miraculous feat (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) performed, those four assemblies perceived that very single afternoon meal;
and they saw this Sahā world-system, encompassed by hundreds of thousands of leagues of space and filled with bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, within that great assembly of bodhisattvas, that great multitude of bodhisattvas, there were four bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Those who were the leaders were as follows: the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Viśiṣṭacāritra, and the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Anantacāritra.
The bodhisattva mahāsattva named Viśuddhacāritra and the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Supratiṣṭhitacāritra—
these four bodhisattva mahāsattvas were the leaders of that great host of bodhisattvas, that great multitude of bodhisattvas.

Then indeed, four bodhisattva mahāsattvas, standing at the head of that great assembly of bodhisattvas, that great multitude of bodhisattvas, and having joined their palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "Is it well with the Blessed One? Is he free from affliction, free from illness, and dwelling in comfort?"
"Are beings, O Blessed One, of good disposition, easy to instruct, easy to discipline, and easy to purify?
May they not cause weariness to the Blessed One?"
Then those four bodhisattva mahāsattvas addressed the Blessed One with these two verses:
“Are you dwelling in happiness, O Lord of the World, Illuminator? Are you free from illness, and is your body at ease, O Sinless One? (Saddhp 14.1)
Those beings are of good character, easy to discipline, and easy to purify;
may they not cause weariness for the Lord of the World as he speaks.

Then the Blessed One addressed these words to four bodhisattva mahāsattvas who were the leaders of that great host of bodhisattvas, that great multitude of bodhisattvas: "It is so, sons of good family; it is so.
I am dwelling in a state of pleasant contact, with little affliction and slight illness."
These beings of mine are of good character; they are easy to instruct, easy to discipline, and easy to purify.
Furthermore, they do not cause me weariness while being purified.
For what reason?
For these sons of good family, O noble ones, are my very own beings who have performed their preparatory practices under previous perfectly enlightened Buddhas;
for by the mere sight and hearing of me, O sons of good family, they gain resolute faith and enter into and plunge into the Buddha-knowledge.

Even those who had previously performed their service on the level of a śrāvaka or on the level of a pratyekabuddha have now been introduced by me to the knowledge of the Buddha-dharma and have been made to hear the ultimate truth.

Then, at that time, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas spoke these verses: “Excellent, excellent, O Great Hero! We rejoice in this, because by it sentient beings are well-formed, easily disciplined, and easy to purify. (Saddhp 14.3)
And those who hear this profound knowledge of yours, O Leader, and having heard it, develop faith and cross over, O Leader. (Saddhp 14.4)

When this had been said, the Blessed One gave his approval to the four bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who were at the head of that great host of bodhisattvas, that great multitude of bodhisattvas: "Excellent, excellent, sons of good family! You who thus rejoice in the Tathāgata."

Then, at that time, this thought occurred to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and to another eight hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges: "Never before have we seen such a multitude of great Bodhisattvas, such a mass of great Bodhisattvas."

And these bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, who have never been heard of before, having emerged from the fissures of the earth, stand before the Blessed One and honor, revere, respect, and worship him, and exchange greetings with the Blessed One— whence indeed have these bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, come?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, perceiving within himself doubt and uncertainty,

and knowing with his own mind the mental reflections of those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Bodhisattvas who were like the sands of the river Gaṅgā, at that moment joined his palms in reverence and questioned the Blessed One regarding this very matter by means of verses:
"O Supreme among Men, tell us of those unprecedented Bodhisattvas— many thousands, nayutas, and infinite kotis."
From where do these beings of great supernatural power come, or how? From where does the arrival of these ones with such vast bodies and forms originate?
All these great seers are steadfast and possessed of mindfulness;
they are pleasing to behold in form—whence have they come?
And for each wise Bodhisattva, O Lord of the World,
there is an immeasurable retinue, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
The retinue of the Bodhisattva consists of sixty full assemblies, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; all of them are illustrious and have set out for enlightenment.
Of such heroes, who possess assemblies and are protectors,
there are exactly sixty times the number of grains of sand in the Ganges.
And there are many others even more numerous than these, with infinite retinues—
fifty, forty, and thirty [times the number of] Ganges rivers.
Their retinues on all sides were twenty times that of the Ganges;
there were others even more numerous than these, numbering ten and five [times as many].
For each and every son of the Buddha, the Protector, there is a retinue;
O Leader, from where has such an assembly come today?
Each one has a retinue of four, three, or even two times as many as the sands of the Ganges,
who follow their training and act as their companions.
There are yet others far more numerous than these, whose number is infinite;
one would not be able to provide even an analogy for them throughout thousands of millions of eons.
The retinue of those heroic, protecting Bodhisattvas consists of half [the number] of Gaṅgā-sands, a third part, and parts of ten and twenty. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 14.16.
There are others even more numerous than these; their measure cannot be found even by one counting them for hundreds of millions of aeons.
But there are many others even more numerous than these, with infinite retinues— ten million, a hundred million, a billion, and likewise half a billion. (Saddhp 14.18)
And there were others, even more numerous than those counted,
great seers who were Bodhisattvas of great wisdom, all standing there with reverence.
Their retinue consists of one thousand and five hundred;
there is no counting them even in hundreds of millions of eons.
Twenty, ten, five, then four, three, and likewise two;
such is the retinue of these heroes, yet their number is beyond calculation.
Those who wander alone and find peace by themselves—
there is no counting those who have assembled here today.
Even if a person were to take a counting-stick in hand and count for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, they would never reach the end.
And from where does the birth of all these great-souled ones come— from those heroic Bodhisattvas, the protectors who possess such valor?
By whom was the Dharma taught to them? By whom were they established in enlightenment? To whose teaching do they take pleasure, and who are the upholders of that teaching?
For having split the entire earth on all four sides,
those of great wisdom, possessed of supernatural powers, and discerning, emerge from it.
O Sage, this world-system has been made dilapidated on all sides by these confident bodhisattvas who are emerging from it.
"Indeed, we have never before seen these at any time.
O Guide, tell us the name of that world-system."
For we have indeed searched the ten directions again and again,
yet we have never at any time seen these bodhisattvas.
"Not even a single son of yours has ever been seen by us before; today these have suddenly appeared. Tell us their history, O Sage! (Saddhp 14.30)
Hundreds, thousands, and nayutas of bodhisattvas,
all filled with curiosity, gaze upon the Supreme among Bipeds.
Explain it, O Great Hero, O Immeasurable One free from substrate:
from where do these courageous Bodhisattvas, confident and fearless, come?

Furthermore, at that time, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who had come from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other world-systems— those who were teaching the Dharma to sentient beings in various other world-systems— took their places before the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni.

Those who were seated cross-legged upon great jeweled lion-thrones at the foot of jewel-trees all around the eight directions from the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One—

those personal attendants of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones also saw that great assembly of bodhisattvas, that vast multitude of bodhisattvas, emerging from the fissures of the earth on all sides and established in the realm of space.
Filled with wonder, they said this to their respective Tathāgatas: "Lord, from where do these immeasurable and incalculable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas come?
When this was said, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones said to their respective attendants: "Wait a moment, noble sons!
This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Maitreya has been prophesied by the Lord Śākyamuni for supreme, perfect enlightenment immediately following him."
He asks this matter of the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha;
and this Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, will explain it,
so that you shall hear it from him.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Excellent, excellent, Ajita!
This matter you ask me about, Ajita, is sublime.
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas: 'Therefore, sons of good family, all of you must be diligent.'"
"Be well-armored and firm in your resolve, for this entire assembly of bodhisattvas is present.
Sons of good family, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha, is now fully revealing the vision of the wisdom of the Tathāgata."
The bull-like majesty of the Tathāgata, the activity of the Tathāgata, the sport of the Tathāgata, the display of the Tathāgata, and the prowess of the Tathāgata.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Be diligent, O sons of good family! I shall release all these words which are not otherwise.
Do not fall into despair here, O wise ones; the wisdom of the Tathāgatas is inconceivable. (Saddhp 14.33)
"Having become steadfast, mindful, and all fully composed, remain attentive;
today you must hear a Dharma never heard before, for it is truly a marvel among the Tathāgatas."
"Do not entertain any doubt at all, for I shall establish you all.
I am a Guide who speaks nothing otherwise; my knowledge is such that it admits of no measure."
The profound dharmas awakened by the Sugata are beyond reasoning; there is no measure for them.
Today I shall reveal those dharmas; listen to me as to what they are like and how they are.
Then, having spoken these verses, the Blessed One at that time addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya: "I announce to you, Ajita;
I declare to you: These bodhisattvas, Ajita, who are immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, incomparable, and beyond reckoning—"

Ajita, all these bodhisattva mahāsattvas whom you have never seen before and who have now emerged from the fissures of the earth, were all, after I had awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment in this Sahā world-system, inspired, encouraged, and gladdened by me.
They have been dedicated toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And these sons of good family, Ajita, have been matured, established, settled, firmly grounded, introduced, awakened, and purified by me in this bodhisattva-dharma.
Furthermore, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas dwell in this Sahā world-system, occupying the space within the realm of empty space below.

These sons of good family, O Ajita, are engaged in the study of the scriptures, their instruction, reflection, and wise attention; they delight in solitude, rejoice in non-association, do not cast off their burden, and have initiated heroic effort.
These sons of good family delight in seclusion and rejoice in seclusion;
these sons of good family do not dwell depending upon gods or humans, for they rejoice in the practice of non-association.
These sons of good family, delighting in the garden of the Dharma, are devoted to the wisdom of the Buddha.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

"These immeasurable and inconceivable bodhisattvas, for whom there is no measure, are endowed with supernatural powers, wisdom, and learning; they have practiced in knowledge for many millions of eons."
"All these have been ripened by me for enlightenment; they dwell within my very own field.
All these have been ripened by me alone; these bodhisattvas are indeed my sons."
All these, devoted to the ascetic practice of forest-dwelling, always avoid places of social contact;
moving without attachment, my sons follow and train themselves in my supreme conduct.
These heroic attendants dwell beneath this field within the expanse of space;
striving for this supreme enlightenment, they are diligent and heedless neither by day nor by night.
All of them have initiated vigor and possess mindfulness; they abide in immeasurable power of wisdom.
Confident, they preach the Dharma, and all these radiant ones are my sons.

And having attained this supreme enlightenment there at the foot of the tree in the city of Gayā, I turned the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma and brought them all to maturity for this supreme enlightenment.
This word of mine is true and free from outflows; having heard it, all of you should have faith in me.
Thus, after a long time, I have attained supreme enlightenment, and all of you have been brought to maturity by me alone.

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and those many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas were struck with wonder, filled with amazement, and overcome by astonishment, thinking: "How is it that by this Blessed One, through this dwelling in a single moment and in such a short interval of time, these so many incalculable Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas have been brought to maturity for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?"
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how is it that the Tathāgata,

while still a youth, having departed from the Śākya city of Kapilavastu and having gone to the supreme and excellent seat of awakening not far from the city of Gayā, fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment?"
“Blessed One, it has been more than forty years since that time.
How then, Blessed One, has the Tathāgata performed this immeasurable work of a Tathāgata within such a short interval of time?
By the Tathāgata, the bull-like power of a Tathāgata and the prowess of a Tathāgata have been exercised.”
"Blessed One, this assembly of bodhisattvas, this multitude of bodhisattvas, has been inspired toward and matured for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment over such a long period of time.
Blessed One, even if one were to count this assembly of bodhisattvas, this multitude of bodhisattvas, for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons, their end would not be found.
Thus, Blessed One, these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are immeasurable."

Thus, they were incalculable in number, having long practiced the holy life, planted roots of merit under many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and reached perfection over many hundreds of thousands of eons.

It is just as if, Blessed One, some man were young, youthful, a mere child with black hair, endowed with the first stage of life, being twenty-five years of age by birth; yet he were to point out sons who were a hundred years old and say, "These noble sons are my sons."
And those men, being a hundred years old, might say: "This is our father, our progenitor.
Blessed One, that statement of that man would be unbelievable to the world, difficult for the world to believe.
In the very same way, Blessed One, you have not long since fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

And these bodhisattva mahāsattvas are numerous and immeasurable; they have practiced the holy life for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, having long since made their firm resolve.

They were skilled in entering and emerging from hundreds of thousands of gateways of meditative concentration within the wisdom of a Buddha; they were perfected through the cultivation of the great superknowledges (*mahābhijñā*), having completed the preparatory exercises for the great superknowledges;
they were wise regarding the stage of a Buddha, and they were skilled in the harmonious recitation of the Tathāgata’s teachings.
They are a marvel and wonder to the world, having attained great heroism, strength, and power;
yet the Blessed One speaks of them thus: "From the very beginning, these were inspired by me, encouraged, matured, and directed toward this stage of a bodhisattva."
"By me, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, this entire exertion of vigor and prowess has been performed.
Furthermore, Blessed One, although we shall accept the word of the Tathāgata with faith— thinking, "The Tathāgata speaks nothing other than the truth"—
the Tathāgata alone should know this matter.
Furthermore, Blessed One, bodhisattva mahāsattvas who have newly set out in the vehicle will fall into doubt;
when the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa, upon hearing this Dharma discourse, they will not believe it, will not have faith in it, and will not resolve upon it.
Consequently, Blessed One, they will be possessed of the formative action that leads to the ruin of the Dharma.
Therefore, O Blessed One, please teach this very matter so that we may become free from doubt regarding this Dharma,
and so that in the future, sons of good family or daughters of good family belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle, upon hearing it, shall not fall into uncertainty.
Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One with these verses:

"When you were born in the place called Kapila, the dwelling of the Śākyas, and having gone forth, you attained enlightenment in the city named Gayā; O Lord of the World, this time [since then] has been short indeed."
And these noble ones, O Lord, are many and confident; they have practiced for millions of eons and form a great assembly.
Established in the power of supernatural faculties, they are unshakable; well-trained, they have reached mastery in the power of wisdom.
Unstained like a lotus by water, those who have come here today having pierced through the earth—
all these sons of the Lord of the World stand with mindfulness, full of reverence and with palms joined.
"How shall those bodhisattvas believe in such a wonder as this?
Speak for the sake of destroying their doubt; teach it yourself exactly according to its meaning."

For just as if there were some man here who was very young, a mere child with black hair, and who, being twenty or even more years of age by birth, would show sons born a hundred years ago; ||| Saddhp_14.48 |||
Covered with wrinkles and grey hair, they would say, "This is our progenitor.
O Lord of the World, it would be difficult for people to believe that such sons could belong to one so young.
In the same way, the Blessed One is young in age, and these wise bodhisattvas are endowed with mindfulness, confident through their wisdom, and well-trained for many billions of eons.
They were all steadfast, wise, and discerning; gracious and pleasing to behold;
confident in the definitive determination of the Dharma, and highly praised by the leaders of the world.
Moving without attachment like the wind, always dwelling in the realm of space without dependence,
the sons of the Sugata exert their vigor as they seek this stage of Buddhahood.
How indeed could this be credible once the Guide of the World has entered final nirvana?
We have no doubt at all; let us hear it from the presence of the Lord of the World himself.

Lest these bodhisattvas, having harbored doubt regarding this matter, should fall into an evil rebirth, please explain it correctly, O Blessed One: how have these bodhisattvas been brought to maturity?
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Emergence from the Cleft of the Earth," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
(Vaidya 189) Chapter Fifteen: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One addressed the entire assembly of bodhisattvas: "Believe me, sons of good family!"
"Have faith in the true words spoken by the Tathāgata.
For a second time, the Blessed One addressed those bodhisattvas: "Believe me, sons of good family; have faith in the true words spoken by the Tathāgata."
For a third time, the Blessed One addressed those bodhisattvas: "Believe me, sons of good family; have faith in the true words spoken by the Tathāgata.
Then that entire assembly of bodhisattvas, placing the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya at their head, joined their palms in reverence and said this to the Blessed One: "Please speak!"
"May the Sugata speak!
We shall have faith in what the Tathāgata has spoken.
A second time, that entire assembly of bodhisattvas said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One speak on this very matter."
"May the Sugata speak!
We shall have faith in what the Tathāgata has spoken.
For a third time, that entire assembly of bodhisattvas said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One speak on this very matter!"
"May the Sugata speak;
we shall have full faith in what the Tathāgata has spoken."
Then the Blessed One, having understood their request for a third time, addressed those bodhisattvas: "Therefore, noble sons, listen to this very matter.

Noble sons, it is that which this world—with its gods, humans, and asuras—perceives thus: 'Just now, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, having gone forth from the Śākya clan, has reached the supreme and excellent seat of awakening at the great city named Gayā.'"
"It has been realized as unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment"—
it should not be viewed in this way.
Rather, sons of good family, it has been many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons since I realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Sons of good family, it is as if, for example, there were as many atoms of the earth-element as there are in five million billion nayutas of world-systems; suppose then a certain man were to appear,
who, taking a single atom-dust, would cross over five million incalculable hundreds of thousands of world-systems in the eastern direction and deposit that single atom-dust there.

In this manner, for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, that man would empty all those world-systems of their earth-element, and by this method and this mode of depositing, he would cast all those atoms of the earth-element toward the eastern direction.
What do you think, noble sons— is it possible for anyone to conceive of, count, weigh, or perceive those world-systems?

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya and that entire host of Bodhisattvas, that multitude of Bodhisattvas, addressed the Blessed One: "Blessed One, those world-systems are incalculable; they are beyond counting and have transcended the plane of the mind.
Blessed One, even by all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, through noble wisdom, it is not possible to conceive of them, nor to count them, nor to weigh them, nor to discern them."
"Even for us, O Blessed One, who are bodhisattva mahāsattvas established on the stage of non-retrogression, the range of our minds does not operate regarding this matter.
O Blessed One, those world-systems would indeed be immeasurable."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "I announce to you, sons of good family;
I declare to you."
O son of good family, however many world-systems there may be— in those into which that man has placed those atoms, as well as those into which he has not placed them—
in all those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of world-systems, O son of good family, there do not exist even that many atoms.
O sons of good family, for as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons as it has been since I attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment—
ever since I have been teaching the Dharma to sentient beings in this Sahā world-system and in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other world-systems—
Furthermore, noble sons, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas beginning with the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara whom I have proclaimed here in the interim,

as well as the parinirvāṇas of those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas— these, noble sons, were all produced by me alone through the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma by means of skillful means.
Furthermore, sons of good family,
the Tathāgata, having observed the diversity of the faculties and vigor of beings as they arrive, proclaims his own name in this or that [form],
and proclaims his own parinirvāṇa in this or that [form].
In such and such ways, he satisfies sentient beings through various discourses on the Dharma.

In this regard, noble sons, for those beings who have diverse inclinations, who possess few roots of merit, and who are burdened with many secondary afflictions, the Tathāgata speaks thus: "O monks, I am young; I have recently gone forth from my home;
O monks, it has not been long since I attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Furthermore, noble sons,
when the Tathāgata— who has been thus awakened for so long— declares, "I have only recently attained awakening," it is for no other purpose than to bring sentient beings to maturity.
These Dharma-discourses were spoken for the purpose of leading [beings] into the path.
And all those Dharma-discourses, O sons of good family, were spoken by the Tathāgata for the sake of disciplining sentient beings.
Whatever words the Tathāgata speaks for the sake of disciplining sentient beings—whether by manifesting himself or by manifesting another—[they are all for that same purpose].
Whatever the Tathāgata declares, whether based on himself or based on another, all those Dharma-discourses spoken by the Tathāgata are true;
there is no falsehood in the Tathāgata regarding this.
For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata has seen the triple world as it truly is:
it is not born, it does not die, it does not pass away, it is not reborn, it does not transmigrate, and it does not enter final nirvana.
It is neither real nor unreal, neither existent nor non-existent, neither thus nor otherwise, neither false nor not false.
The Tathāgata does not perceive the triple world in the manner that foolish ordinary people perceive it;
for the Tathāgata, who has directly realized all phenomena, is indeed one whose nature is free from forgetfulness in this regard.
In that regard, whatever speech the Tathāgata utters,
all of it is true, not false, and not otherwise. Nevertheless,

for the sake of generating roots of virtue in beings who have diverse conducts, diverse intentions, and diverse patterns of perception and conceptualization, he utters various Dharma-discourses by means of various focal points.
For whatever must be done by the Tathāgata, O sons of good family, that the Tathāgata performs.
Having attained perfect awakening so long ago, the Tathāgata possesses an immeasurable lifespan and remains forever.
Although the Tathāgata has not passed into final nirvāṇa, he manifests final nirvāṇa for the sake of those to be trained.
Moreover, noble sons, even now my former bodhisattva conduct has not yet been fully perfected,
nor is the measure of my lifespan complete.
Indeed, noble sons, because the measure of my lifespan is still incomplete, there will yet be twice as many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons remaining for me.
Furthermore, noble sons, although I am not actually entering final nirvāṇa at this moment, I nevertheless announce my final nirvāṇa.
For what reason?

Noble sons, I bring sentient beings to maturity by this method: lest, while I remain for too long, sentient beings who have not yet cultivated roots of virtue, who are devoid of merit, impoverished, greedy for sense-pleasures, blind, and shrouded by the net of views, should— knowing that the Tathāgata remains— develop a calloused perception toward him through constant sight.
And they would not conceive the notion that a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter, thinking, "We are near to the Tathāgata.
They would not fail to initiate vigor for the sake of escaping from the triple world,
nor would they conceive the notion that a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
Then, O sons of good family, the Tathāgata, through his skill in means, spoke these words to those beings: "O monks, the appearance of a Tathāgata is difficult to encounter.
For what reason?
Because for those beings, even in many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, the sight of a Tathāgata [is rare].
Or perhaps they do not exist.
Therefore, noble sons, taking that as my basis, I say: "Monks, the appearance of Tathāgatas is indeed rare.
Having understood that the appearance of Tathāgatas is exceedingly rare, they will conceive a sense of wonder.
They will give rise to the perception of sorrow;
and not seeing the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Awakened Ones, they will become thirsty for a vision of the Tathāgatas.
Those roots of merit of theirs, consisting of mental attention directed toward the Tathāgatas as their object, will lead to their welfare, benefit, and happiness for a long time.
Having understood this matter, the Tathāgata, while not actually passing into parinirvāṇa, announces his parinirvāṇa out of consideration for the needs of those beings who are to be disciplined.
O sons of good family, this is the Tathāgata’s method of teaching the Dharma when he speaks in such a way;
there is no falsehood here on the part of the Tathāgata.
Sons of good family, it is just as if there were a certain physician who was learned, discerning, intelligent, and highly skilled in alleviating all diseases.
That man had many sons—ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, or even a hundred.
And that physician had gone abroad.
And suppose all of his sons were afflicted by either poison or venom;
they would be overwhelmed by painful sensations caused by that poison or venom,
and burning with that poison or venom, they would fall prostrate upon the earth.
Then their father, the physician, might return from his journey;
meanwhile, those sons of his would be afflicted by painful sensations caused by that emetic or poison,
and some among them would have distorted perceptions.
Some among them might have unperverted perceptions;
and all of them, being afflicted by that very suffering, would rejoice upon seeing their father and say this to him: "By good fortune, dear father, you have returned in safety and well-being!"
"Therefore, deliver us from this self-obstruction, or from the *gara* poison, or from the *viṣa* poison!
Grant us our life, dear father!
Then that physician, seeing his sons afflicted by suffering, overwhelmed by pain, burning with fever, and writhing upon the ground, [spoke thus].
Then, having procured a great medicine that was perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste,
he would grind it on a stone and give it to those sons to drink,
and speak to them thus: "Drink this, sons, this great medicine which is perfect in color, perfect in fragrance, and perfect in taste."
"O sons, by drinking this great medicine, you will quickly be liberated from this poison or venom;
you shall become healthy and free from disease.
Therein, those sons of that physician who possess unperverted perceptions, having seen the color of the medicine, smelled its fragrance, and tasted its flavor, would immediately consume it.
And by consuming those [medicines], they would all be completely and entirely freed from that affliction.

However, those sons of his who possessed perverted perceptions would welcome their father and say this to him: "By good fortune, dear father, you have returned in safety and well-being, you who are our physician!"
And they might speak these words,
yet they would not drink that medicine which was offered to them.
For what reason?
For it is because of their perverted perception that this medicine offered to them does not please them even in its color;
it does not please them in its fragrance, nor in its taste.
Then, indeed, that physician would think: "These sons of mine have developed a perverted perception due to this poison or venom."
Indeed, these sons do not drink this great medicine, yet they welcome me;
therefore, I shall cause these sons to drink this medicine through skillful means.

Then, that physician, desiring to have those sons drink that medicine through skillful means, would speak thus: "Sons of good family, I am worn out; I am aged and decrepit, and the time of my death has arrived."
And do not grieve, my sons; do not fall into exhaustion.
This great medicine has been brought to you by me.
"If you so desire, drink that very medicine.
Having thus instructed his sons through skillful means, he departed for another region of the country.
Having gone there, he would announce his own death to those sons who were ill;
at that time, they would grieve excessively and lament excessively, thinking: "Even our father, our protector, our progenitor, and our compassionate one, has indeed passed away."
Today they have become protectorless.
Indeed, perceiving themselves as having become protectorless and perceiving themselves as being without refuge, they would constantly be afflicted by grief.
And through that constant affliction by grief, their distorted perception would become non-distorted perception.

And they would perceive that medicine, endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, as being truly endowed with color, fragrance, and taste; then, at that time, they would consume that medicine, and by consuming it,
they would be completely freed from that affliction.
Then, indeed, that physician, knowing those sons to be freed from their affliction, would manifest himself once again.
What do you think, noble sons? Would anyone accuse that physician of falsehood for employing such skillful means?
They replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
"Certainly not, Sugata.

The Buddha said: "In the same way, sons of good family, I too have fully awakened to this unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment after immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of kalpas.
Nevertheless, sons of good family, from time to time I manifest such skillful means for the sake of training sentient beings."
And in this matter, there is no falsehood whatsoever on my part.
Then the Blessed One, further demonstrating this very course of events, at that time spoke these verses:
"Inconceivable are the thousands of millions of eons, the measure of which is never known; yet I attained this supreme enlightenment long ago, and I teach the Dharma at all times. (Saddhp 15.1)
I encourage many bodhisattvas and establish them in the wisdom of a Buddha;
for many millions of billions of eons, I bring many millions of billions of sentient beings to maturity.
I point out the ground of nirvāṇa; for the sake of disciplining sentient beings, I speak of skillful means.
Yet I do not enter nirvāṇa at that time; rather, right here I continue to proclaim the Dharma.
And even there, I manifest myself, as do all sentient beings;
yet those deluded men, possessed of perverted understanding, remain right there and do not see me.
Seeing my body as having entered final nirvāṇa, they perform various kinds of worship toward my relics;
and not seeing me, they give rise to longing, whereby their minds become upright. (Saddhp 15.5)
When those beings have become upright, gentle, and mild, and have cast off desire, then,
having formed a community of disciples, I manifest myself here on Vulture Peak.
And so, monks, I say this to them later: "At that time, I was not yet extinguished right here; this is my skill in means, by which I appear again and again in the world of the living."
Honored by other beings, I reveal my supreme enlightenment to them;
yet you do not hear my voice, for that Lord of the World has entered into parinirvāṇa.
I see beings being afflicted, yet I do not reveal my own form to them;
first, I cause those who thirst for the sight of me to long for it, and then I shall proclaim the True Dharma.
My constant empowerment has been such as this for inconceivable billions of eons;
yet I do not pass away from this Vulture Peak, nor do I ever leave it for millions of other dwellings and seats.
Even when sentient beings see this world-system and imagine it to be burning,
at that time my buddha-field remains completely filled with gods and humans.
Their play and delight become manifold: millions of gardens, palaces, and celestial mansions, adorned with mountains made of jewels, as well as trees endowed with flowers and fruits.
And from above, the gods strike musical instruments and let fall a rain of mandārava flowers;
they sprinkle them upon me, as well as upon my disciples and those other wise ones here who have set out for enlightenment.
And thus this field of mine remains forever as it is, yet others imagine it to be burning;
they see the world-system as most terrifying, afflicted, and strewn with hundreds of sorrows. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 15.14.
Furthermore, for many millions of eons, they have never even heard my name, nor that of the Tathāgatas, nor of the Dharma, nor of my assembly; such is the fruit of their evil karma.
But when beings who are gentle and mild are born here in the world of humans,
as soon as they are born through their wholesome karma, they see me proclaiming the Dharma.
And I have never before spoken to them of this unsurpassed activity such as this;
therefore, I am seen by him after a long time, and thus I speak to him, for the Jinas are very difficult to encounter.
Such is this power of my knowledge, luminous, of which there is no end; and my lifespan is long, acquired for infinite eons after I had previously practiced the conduct.
Do not harbor doubt in this matter, O wise ones; abandon all hesitation without remainder.
I speak these words as they truly are; my speech can never be false.
For just as that physician, skilled in expedient means, might say "I am dead" for the sake of his sons who possess perverted perceptions, a wise person would not accuse that physician of falsehood.
I alone am the Father of the world, the Self-Existent One, the physician, and the Lord of all beings;
having recognized that children are deluded and perverted, though not yet entered into Nirvana, I manifest as one who has attained Nirvana.
For what reason? Because of seeing me constantly, the ignorant and the unknowing become faithless;
they become confident in sensual pleasures and heedless, and by reason of that heedlessness, they fall into an evil destiny.

Constantly knowing their conduct at all times, I speak to sentient beings in such and such a way: "How indeed may I lead them toward awakening? How may they become attainers of the Buddha-dharmas? (Saddhp 15.23)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Lifespan of the Tathāgata," in the Dharma discourse of the Noble White Lotus of the Good Dharma.
Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra, Chapter 16: The Exposition of the Modes of Merit.
Furthermore, while this exposition on the measure of the Tathāgata’s lifespan was being taught, benefit was brought to immeasurable and incalculable beings.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Furthermore,

Ajita, while this Dharma discourse on the exposition of the Tathāgata’s lifespan was being taught, the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) arose in hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Bodhisattvas, equal in number to the sands of sixty-eight Ganges rivers."
A thousand times more than these were those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who attained dhāraṇīs;
and other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a thousandfold world-system, upon hearing this Dharma discourse, attained unimpeded eloquence;
and other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms of a two-thousandfold world-system, attained the dhāraṇī that revolves hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of times.
Furthermore, other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a three-thousandfold world system, having heard this Dharma discourse, set in motion the irreversible wheel of Dharma.
And other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a medium-sized world system, having heard this Dharma discourse, set in motion the wheel of stainless radiance.

Furthermore, other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms in a minor world system, having heard this Dharma discourse, became bound to no more than eight births before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; and other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, equal in number to the atoms in four sets of four-continent world systems, having heard this Dharma discourse, became bound to no more than four births before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in three or four world-systems of four continents, having heard this Dharma discourse, became bound to [only] three more births before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. And other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in two world-systems of four continents, having heard this Dharma discourse, became bound to [only] two more births before attaining unexcelled [perfect enlightenment].
Regarding perfect enlightenment:

other bodhisattva mahāsattvas, as numerous as the atoms in a single four-continent world system, having heard this Dharma discourse, became bound to only one more birth before attaining unsurpassed [enlightenment];

and by bodhisattva mahāsattvas as numerous as the atoms in eight thousand three hundred thousand great trichiliocosm world systems, having heard this Dharma discourse, the resolve for unsurpassed perfect enlightenment was generated.
Then, immediately after the Blessed One had taught this establishment in the realization of the Dharma for these bodhisattva mahāsattvas,
at that very moment, a rain of māndārava and mahāmāndārava flowers fell from the sky above in the air.

And in those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of world-systems, those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddhas who had come and were seated upon lion-thrones at the foot of jewel-trees—
And they all scattered them, showered them down, and strewed them about.

They scattered and showered offerings over the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and over that Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who had entered parinirvāṇa and was seated upon the lion throne.
They scattered [them],
and they strewed and showered them upon that entire assembly of bodhisattvas and those four groups of followers.
They scattered [flowers] all around;
divine powders of sandalwood and agallochum rained down from the sky;
and above, in the atmosphere, great celestial drums resounded without being struck, with sounds that were pleasing, sweet, and deep.
Hundreds of thousands of divine pairs of fine garments fell from the sky above;

necklaces, half-necklaces, pearl necklaces, jewels, and great gems hung down from the heights of the atmosphere in the sky, suspended on all sides in every direction; and thousands of jewel-encrusted censers of priceless incense moved of their own accord in every direction.

And for each individual Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas held a series of jeweled parasols in the sky above, reaching as far as the Brahma-world. In this manner, those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas held a series of jeweled parasols in the sky above, reaching as far as the Brahma-world, for all those immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas.
They praised those Tathāgatas individually with authentic hymns of praise, each employing distinct compositions of verses.

Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya spoke these verses: “It is a marvelous teaching proclaimed by the Sugata, never before heard by us! Such is the greatness of the Leaders, and their lifespan is indeed infinite. (Saddhp 16.1)
And thus, having heard today this Dharma being analyzed by the Sugata in his very presence,
thousands of millions of living beings— those who are the heart-born sons of the Guide of the World— are suffused with joy.
Some are established in irreversible supreme enlightenment; some are established in the excellent dhāraṇī;
some are established in unimpeded eloquence, and others in thousands of millions of dhāraṇīs.
Likewise, there are others who have set out for the supreme wisdom of a Buddha;
some will become Jinas of infinite vision after only eight births.
Some, having passed through four [lifetimes], and some through three or even two,
shall attain enlightenment— those who perceive the ultimate truth— having heard this Dharma of the Guide.
And those who, remaining for only one birth, shall become omniscient after one more existence—
having heard this lifespan of the Leader, they shall obtain such an outflow-free fruit. (Saddhp_16.6)
As many as there would be atoms in eight world-systems,
so many were the millions of beings who, having heard the Dharma, generated the supreme mind of enlightenment.
Such was the deed performed by the Great Seer as he revealed this awakening of a Buddha—
awakening which is infinite, without measure, and immeasurable like the realm of space.
A rain of māndārava flowers fell, and many thousands of millions of sons of gods—
as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, including Śakras and Brahmās— arrived from thousands of millions of buddha-fields.
Releasing fragrant powders and powders of sandalwood and aloe-wood,
they move through the sky like birds, scattering them according to ritual over the Lords of Jinas.
And above, in the sky, celestial drums resounded with sweet sounds without being struck;
thousands of millions of divine raiments were cast down and whirled about for the sake of the Leaders.
And thousands of millions of jewel-encrusted incense burners, filled with incense of priceless value,
moved about there on all sides by themselves for the sake of worshipping the Protector, the Lord of the World.

These wise bodhisattvas hold up infinite millions of billions of high, great parasols made of jewels, as well as floral garlands, reaching as far as the Brahma-world. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 16.13.
And with joyful hearts, the sons of the Sugata lowered beautiful victory banners belonging to the leaders, and praised them with thousands of verses. (Saddhp 16.14)
Today these leaders are seen, distinguished by such wonders, marvelous and diverse;
through this demonstration of the measure of their lifespan, all these beings have attained joy.
Today, a vast wealth has arisen in the ten directions, and the voice of the Leaders has resounded;
thousands of millions of living beings have been fully satisfied and endowed with the roots of goodness for enlightenment.

Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita, those beings who, while this Dharma discourse on the exposition of the Tathāgata’s lifespan was being taught, produced even a single thought of resolute faith,
or developed deep conviction— "
Listen to how much merit those sons of good family or daughters of good family produce; attend well and thoroughly to it. I shall speak as to how much merit they produce.

It is just as if, Ajita, some son of good family or daughter of good family, desiring unexcelled perfect enlightenment, were to practice the five perfections for eight hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of eons—

namely, the perfection of giving, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, and the perfection of meditation— while being devoid of the perfection of wisdom.

And, Ajita, compared to the accumulation of merit and the accumulation of wholesome roots belonging to that son of good family or daughter of good family who, having heard this Dharma-discourse explaining the lifespan of the Tathāgata, has produced even a single thought of resolute conviction or has established faith,
this former accumulation of merit and accumulation of wholesome roots [is not equal to it].

Connected with the five perfections and perfected over eight hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of aeons, it does not approach even a hundredth part [of this merit]; it does not approach even a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-nayuta-koṭi-th part; it does not admit of any calculation, fraction, reckoning, comparison, or likeness.

"Ajita, it is impossible that a son of good family or a daughter of good family endowed with such an accumulation of merit would turn back from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; such a case does not exist.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"And whoever, having undertaken the five perfections, abides here..."
Seeking this knowledge, the unsurpassed wisdom of a Buddha.
For eight thousand full millions of eons,
they repeatedly gave gifts to the Buddhas and their disciples.
Satisfying the Pratyekabuddhas and tens of millions of Bodhisattvas with various kinds of food and drink, as well as clothing, bedding, and seats.
In this world, one should cause dwellings and monasteries to be built of sandalwood,
as well as delightful groves adorned with places for walking meditation.
Having given such diverse and manifold gifts for thousands of millions of eons, one should dedicate them toward awakening.
Furthermore, one should maintain pure ethical discipline as praised by the Perfectly Awakened One— unbroken, commended by the wise— for the sake of attaining the wisdom of a Buddha.
Furthermore, established on the stage of self-control, one should cultivate patience; being steadfast and mindful, one should endure many insults.
And those beings who are critical and established in conceit—
he endures their abuse for the sake of the Buddha’s wisdom.
Always exerting oneself with vigor, dedicated to this [practice], and firm in mindfulness,
one should remain with a mind free of other intentions for ten million eons.
If one were to dwell in the forest, standing or walking upon the path of meditation, and having abandoned sloth and torpor, were to practice thus for ten million eons; 16.26.
And whoever is a meditator, a great meditator, delighting in meditation, and composed,
should remain in meditation for no fewer than eight thousand times ten million eons.
Through that meditation, that hero should aspire for supreme enlightenment, thinking, "May I become an omniscient one," having reached the perfection of meditation. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 16.28.
And whatever merit may belong to those who have practiced this rite for thousands of millions of eons, as was previously proclaimed— *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 16.29.
Whether it be a woman or even a man who, having heard my life-span, places faith in it for even a single moment, this merit is infinite. (Saddhp_16.30)
Having abandoned doubt, as well as wavering and conceit,
if one should have faith for even a moment, such will be the fruit thereof.
And those bodhisattvas who have practiced for tens of millions of eons do not tremble upon hearing this inconceivable lifespan of mine.
They pay homage with their heads bowed, thinking, "May I also become like this;
in a future time, may I deliver tens of millions of living beings."
Just as the Lord Śākyamuni, the Great Sage, the Lion of the Śākyas, having sat upon the seat of enlightenment, roared this lion’s roar: Saddhp_16.34.
In the future age as well, I too, honored by all embodied beings,
shall sit at the seat of awakening and teach such a lifespan.
Those persons who are endowed with resolute intention and who preserve what they have heard understand the intentional terminology; for them, no doubt exists.
Furthermore, Ajita, whoever, having heard this Dharma discourse that explains the measure of the Tathāgata’s lifespan, should enter into it, have faith in it, plunge into it, and understand it,
would produce an even more immeasurable accumulation of merit leading to the wisdom of a Buddha.

What need is there to mention one who would hear such a Dharma discourse as this, or cause others to hear it, recite it, uphold it, write it down, cause it to be written down, or honor it when it has been committed to a book?

If one should honor, revere, worship, or pay respect [to this], or offer flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, or oil lamps, ghee lamps, or scented-oil lamps,
one would generate a much greater accumulation of merit conducive to the wisdom of a Buddha.

And when, Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family, having heard this Dharma discourse— the exposition of the lifespan of the Tathāgata— resolves upon it with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), then these characteristics of his resolute intention are to be known: namely, he will see me on Vulture Peak Mountain teaching the Dharma, surrounded by a host of bodhisattvas, preceded by a host of bodhisattvas, and situated in the midst of the community of śrāvakas.

And this Buddha-field of mine, the Sahā world-system, he will see as consisting of lapis lazuli, with a level surface, laid out like a chessboard by golden threads, and adorned with various jewel-trees;
and there he will see Bodhisattvas dwelling in the enjoyment of gabled palaces.
Ajita, this should be understood as the characteristic of the resolute intention of a son or daughter of good family who is devoted with resolute intention.

Furthermore, Ajita, I say that even those sons of good family who, with resolute intention and conviction, hear this Dharma-discourse after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa and do not reject it, but rather rejoice in it further—
how much more so those who will uphold it or recite it?

Then, Ājita, that son of good family or daughter of good family who, having made this Dharma-discourse into a book, carries it upon their shoulder, carries the Tathāgata upon their shoulder. By that son or daughter of good family, no stūpas need be constructed for me,
nor do monasteries need to be built.
He does not provide medicinal requisites for the sick to the community of monks.
Why is that?
Because, Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family has already performed worship of my body with their own bodies.

And stupas made of the seven precious gems were constructed, reaching as high as the Brahma-world in height, with gradually tapering circumferences, provided with parasols, victory banners, bells, and caskets,
