and various honors were rendered to those reliquary stupas through diverse divine and human offerings.

With flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards; with various sweet, charming, and sharp sounds of *paṭaha*, *dundubhi*, and great *mahādundubhi* drums; with the resonant noise of musical instruments and cymbals;

and with many kinds of immeasurable songs, dances, and *lāsya* performances—through these many and limitless offerings, honor is rendered for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons.
Ajita, by upholding, reciting, writing down, and proclaiming this Dharma-discourse after I have passed into parinirvāṇa, one has also constructed vast and extensive monasteries;
one has taken possession of thirty-two palaces made of red sandalwood, eight stories high, serving as dwellings for a thousand monks.

They were adorned with gardens and flowers, provided with walking-paths and groves, furnished with beds and seats, and fully supplied with hard food, soft food, meals, drinks, and medicinal requisites for the sick; they were embellished with every kind of comfortable equipment,

and they were many and immeasurable— namely, a hundred, or a thousand, or a hundred thousand, or ten million, or a hundred ten-millions, or a thousand ten-millions, or a hundred thousand ten-millions, or even a hundred thousand nayutas of ten-millions.
And they have been offered by me directly to my community of disciples;
it should be understood that they have been consumed by me.
This applies to whoever, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, should uphold, recite, teach, write, or cause to be written this Dharma-discourse.

Therefore, Ajita, by this method I say this: after I have entered parinirvāṇa, one who has upheld this Dharma-discourse need not have stūpas for my relics constructed, nor perform worship of the Saṅgha;
what need is there to mention, Ajita, those who, while upholding this Dharma-discourse, would accomplish it through generosity, or morality, or patience, or vigor, or meditation?
or through wisdom— whether by means of generosity or wisdom—

that son of good family or daughter of good family would produce a far greater accumulation of merit, leading toward the knowledge of a Buddha, immeasurable, incalculable, and limitless. It is just as if, Ajita, the element of space were limitless in the eastern, southern, western, northern, downward, and upward directions, and in the intermediate directions.
In this way, that son of good family or daughter of good family will produce immeasurable and incalculable accumulations of merit conducive to the wisdom of a Buddha,
whether they themselves uphold, recite, teach, write, or cause to be written this Dharma discourse,
and remain dedicated to honoring the reliquaries of the Tathāgata.
He would speak in praise of the Tathāgata’s disciples and proclaim the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of virtues of the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas,
and he would reveal them to others.
One should accomplish through patience;
one should be possessed of ethical discipline,
be of virtuous character, pleasant to dwell with, and patient.
He should be self-controlled and free from envy;
his mind should be devoid of anger and free from malice; he should possess mindfulness and steadfastness, and he should be energetic and constantly diligent.

In the pursuit of the Buddha-dharma, he should be a meditator, one who values seclusion and abounds in seclusion, and one skilled in the analysis of questions, capable of resolving hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of inquiries.
Ajita, whatever bodhisattva mahāsattva, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, should uphold this Dharma-discourse, such qualities as these shall belong to him.

Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family should be known thus: "This son of good family or daughter of good family has set out for the seat of awakening; he is going to the foot of the Bodhi tree to fully awaken to awakening."
And wherever, Ajita, that son of good family or daughter of good family may stand, sit, or walk, there, Ajita, a shrine (caitya) should be erected in honor of the Tathāgata;
and it should be declared by the world together with its gods: "This is a stūpa of the Tathāgata."
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The mass of merit of one who would uphold this sūtra after the Leader of Men has entered nirvāṇa has been described by me again and again as being limitless. (Saddhp 16.37)
He has performed offerings for me and had reliquary stupas constructed—
made of jewels, diverse, beautiful to behold, and most magnificent.
Equal in height to the Brahma-world, they were adorned with rows of parasols; they were expansive, glorious, and equipped with victory banners.
Resounding with sharp bells and adorned with silk streamers,
the bells stirred by the wind shine beautifully upon the relics of the Jina.
And extensive worship was performed for them with flowers, perfumes, and ointments,
as well as repeatedly with musical instruments, garments, and drums.
Sweet musical instruments were played during those elements,
and lamps filled with fragrant oil were offered all around them.
Whoever should uphold this sutra and teach it during the age of decay has performed for me various kinds of manifold worship.
There were also many millions of excellent monasteries constructed of sandalwood,
as well as thirty-two palaces, eight stories high in elevation.
Supported by beds and seats, provided with various kinds of food and drink,
and furnished with thousands of dwellings arranged with exquisite rugs.
And gardens were given, adorned with flower gardens,
featuring many awnings and variegated with many forms.
Because he has performed various kinds of worship to the Saṅgha in my presence, whoever shall uphold this sūtra after the Guide has entered parinirvāṇa, [he shall obtain such merit].
If one should have faith as their core, they would indeed obtain much more merit than he who merely recites or writes down this sūtra. (Saddhp 16.48)
If any person should have this well-explained [sūtra] written down in a book, he should worship that book with perfumes, garlands, and ointments. (Saddhp 16.49)

Any person who performs such worship toward these books produces abundant merit, the measure of which cannot be known. (Saddhp 16.51)
Just as no measure can be found for the realm of space throughout the ten directions forever, so too is this mass of merit.
How much more so for one who is patient, self-controlled, concentrated,
virtuous, meditative, and whose sphere of activity is solitary retreat?
Free from anger and free from slander, established in reverence for this shrine, he is always humble toward the monks, neither arrogant nor lazy. (Saddhp_16.54)
Possessing wisdom and being steadfast, he does not become angry when questioned;
he teaches in accordance with the truth and maintains a mind of compassion toward all living beings.
If there should be anyone such as this who would uphold this sutra,
no measure can be found for their mass of merit.
If any person should see such a Dharma-preacher who upholds this sutra, they should indeed pay him honor.
One should scatter divine flowers and likewise cover him with divine garments;
having bowed one's head at his feet, one should conceive the thought that "this is a Tathāgata."
And having seen him, he thought at that time: "He will go to the foot of the tree;
he will awaken to supreme, auspicious enlightenment for the benefit of the world, including the gods."
Wherever that wise one walks, or wherever he stands or sits, or wherever that steadfast one prepares his bed, let him recite even a single verse from this sutra.

And in which [place] one should have a stūpa built for the Supreme among Men— variegated and beautiful to behold— and likewise cause various offerings to be made there, dedicated to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Guide.
That region of the earth has been enjoyed by me, and I myself have walked there;
wherever that son of the Buddha remains, I shall indeed be seated right there.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Merit," in the Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.
(Vaidya 205) Chapter Seventeen: The Exposition of the Merit of Rejoicing.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, if a son of good family, having heard this Dharma-discourse being taught, should rejoice in it..."
"Blessed One, how much merit would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce?
Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya spoke this verse:
"Whoever, after the Great Hero has passed into nirvāṇa, should hear such a sūtra as this..."
And having heard it, if one should rejoice, how much merit would there be? (Saddhp_17.1)
Then the Blessed One said this to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Ajita,

if any son of good family or daughter of good family— whether a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a wise man, or a youth— should hear this Dharma-discourse being taught and proclaimed after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,"
Or a young girl,
having heard it, should rejoice; yet if she, rising from that hearing of the Dharma, should depart, [she would incur such a fault].
Whether he has gone to a monastery, a house, a forest, a street, a village, or a country,

he should explain those causes, those reasons, and that Dharma— just as he has heard it, just as he has grasped it, and according to his ability— to another being, whether it be his mother, his father, or a kinsman.
Whether it be someone with whom he has been delighted, or another with whom he is well-acquainted,
if that person, having heard it, should rejoice in it, and having rejoiced, should in turn tell it to yet another;
If he, having heard it, should rejoice, and having rejoiced, should tell it to another, and that person too, having heard it, should rejoice;
In this manner, up to the fiftieth person in the succession;

then indeed, Ajita, as for that fiftieth person who rejoices by hearing [the teaching] through the succession, I shall describe the formation of merit associated with that rejoicing of even that son of good family or daughter of good family, Ajita.
Listen to that, and attend to it well and thoroughly;
I shall speak to you.

It is just as if, Ajita, there were all those beings existing and found within four hundred thousand incalculable world-systems, born into the six realms of existence—whether born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, or by spontaneous birth; whether possessing form or formless;
having perception, lacking perception, having neither perception nor non-perception; or whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed.
Or suppose that all beings included within the realm of sentient beings were to come together;

then, some man might arise who, desiring merit and desiring their welfare, would give to that assembly of beings all the desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing objects of pleasure, play, delight, and enjoyment they wished for. He would give to each single being an entire Jambudvīpa for the sake of pleasure, play, delight, and enjoyment.
He would give gold, fine gold, silver, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, stones, coral, horse-chariots, ox-chariots, and elephant-chariots; he would give palaces and gabled mansions.
In this manner, Ajita, that man, a lord of giving, a great lord of giving, would bestow gifts for a full eighty years.
Then, indeed, Ajita, that man, the lord of giving, the great lord of giving, would think: "All these beings have been made to play by me, made to rejoice, and made to live in happiness."
And these venerable beings are strong, yet they have gray hair; they are aged, decrepit, and advanced in years, being eighty years of age by birth;
and they are close to the time of their passing away.
"What if I were to cause these beings to enter and instruct them in the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata?
Then, Ajita, that man would exhort all those beings;
having exhorted them, he would cause them to enter and grasp the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata.
May those beings hear that Dharma from you;

and having heard it, may they all— in a single instant, a single moment, a single second— become stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and attain the fruit of non-returning, up to becoming arhats.

"Those whose outflows are exhausted, who are meditators, great meditators, and meditators on the eight liberations—what do you think, Ajita, would that man, the lord of donors, the great lord of donors, generate much merit on that account—an immeasurable and incalculable amount?
When this was said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya said this to the Blessed One: "So it is, Blessed One."
"So it is, Sugata! For this very reason, Blessed One, that man, the donor and great master of generosity, would produce much merit,
he who would give all the requisites for happiness to that many beings."
How much more so, then, if one were to establish them further in arhatship?
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Ajita: "I announce to you, Ajita; I declare to you:

suppose there were a man, a lord of gifts, a great lord of gifts, who, having fulfilled all the requirements for happiness of all sentient beings throughout four hundred thousand incalculable world-systems, established them in the state of Arhatship."

Whoever would produce merit by hearing even a single verse or a single word from this Dharma-discourse through a tradition of oral transmission reaching the fiftieth person, and whoever would rejoice in it—
that basis of meritorious action associated with that person’s rejoicing— [is greater than the former].
And as for that basis of meritorious action consisting of the gift associated with the state of arhatship established by that man, the lord of givers, the great lord of givers—
this alone is far more than that [of the former].
This is the case for this man who is the fiftieth.

Therefore, from this succession of persons, having heard even a single verse or even a single word from this Dharma-discourse, one should rejoice. Ajita, compared to this accumulation of merit and accumulation of roots of goodness associated with rejoicing, that former accumulation of merit— consisting of both the gift-associated and the establishment-in-arhatship-associated [merit]— is not even a fraction of it.
It does not approach even a hundredth part,

nor a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousandth part, nor a ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-ten-millionth part, nor a thousand-ten-millionth part, nor a hundred-thousand-ten-millionth part, nor even a hundred-thousand-billionth part.
It does not admit of calculation, nor of a fraction, nor of counting, nor of comparison, nor of analogy.

Thus, Ajita, that person— even the fiftieth in the succession of hearing— begets such immeasurable and incalculable merit by rejoicing even in a single verse or a single word from this Dharma-discourse.
What need is there to speak further, Ajita, of one who would hear this Dharma-discourse in my presence and,
having heard it, rejoice in it?
I declare, Ajita, that the accumulation of merit for such a person is immeasurably more and incalculably greater.
Furthermore, Ajita, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family should go forth from their own home and go to a monastery for the sake of hearing this Dharma-discourse,

and having gone there, should hear this Dharma-discourse for even a moment while standing or sitting— that being, by the accumulation and gathering of such a measure of merit performed, will, upon the cessation of that birth, in a second existence and in the acquisition of a second body, become a possessor of ox-carts.
He will become a recipient of horse-chariots, elephant-chariots, palanquins, bullock-carts, bull-vehicles, and even divine celestial mansions. Furthermore,
if he should sit there for even a single moment during that hearing of the Dharma and listen to this Dharma-discourse, or cause another to sit down, [he will attain these rewards].
Or he might share his seat with another being;
by that accumulation of merit, he will become a possessor of the thrones of Śakra, the thrones of Brahmā, and the thrones of the universal monarchs (cakravartin).
Furthermore, Ajita, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to say this to another person: "Come, O man!"
"Listen to the Dharma discourse named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

And if that person, having received such encouragement from him, should listen for even a mere moment, that being— by virtue of that encouragement and the roots of merit thus cultivated— will attain an encounter with Bodhisattvas who have acquired the dhāraṇīs."
He becomes non-dull, possessing sharp faculties and wisdom;
even throughout hundreds of thousands of births, his mouth does not become putrid nor foul-smelling.
Nor does he suffer from disease of the tongue,
nor does he suffer from disease of the mouth; nor do his teeth become discolored.
He does not have uneven teeth, nor yellowed teeth, nor ill-formed teeth, nor broken teeth, nor missing teeth, nor crooked teeth, nor protruding lips.
His lips are neither too protruding nor spread out; they are not torn, not crooked, not black, and not loathsome.
His nose is not flat, nor is it crooked.
He does not have a long face, he does not have a crooked face,
and he does not have a dark face.
His face is not unpleasant to behold;
moreover, Ajita, his tongue, teeth, and lips are subtle and well-formed,
his nose is prominent, his facial orb is exquisite, his eyebrows are beautiful, and his forehead is well-proportioned.
He attains the fully perfected marks of a great man,
he obtains the Tathāgata as his instructor and guide,
and he swiftly attains association with the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
Behold, Ajita, how much merit is produced even by merely encouraging a single sentient being;
what need is there to mention one who would listen with reverence, recite with reverence, or [practice] with reverence?
One should teach it; one should proclaim it with reverence.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "Listen to how much merit there will be for one who, with a clear and joyful mind, rejoices in even a single verse of this sutra heard fifty generations later in the succession. Listen to what that merit shall be. (Saddhp 17.2)
And that very man shall become a giver of gifts, constantly among billions of nayutas of beings;
he shall satisfy all those whom I previously described through similes for eighty years.
Seeing that old age had come upon them—wrinkles, broken teeth, and grey hair—he thought: "Alas! All sentient beings are indeed overcome by distress; what if I were to exhort them with the Dharma?"
He speaks the Dharma to them here, and afterwards he shall reveal the ground of nirvāṇa:
"All states of existence are like foam and a mirage; quickly become disenchanted with all existences! (Saddhp 17.5)
And all those beings, having heard the Dharma from the presence of that very man who gave it,
shall at one and the same time become Arhats, with outflows exhausted, bearing their final bodies.
If one hears even a single verse from this succession [of teachings] or rejoices in it, the merit of that person would be far greater;
compared to that mass of merit, the former [merit] does not even amount to a fraction.
Thus, the merit of such a person would be vast, infinite, and beyond measure;
how much more so for one who hears even a single verse through oral tradition, let alone one who hears it directly in person!

And whoever should speak to even a single being there, encouraging them, saying: "Go and listen to the Dharma! For this sūtra is very difficult to encounter in many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons. (Saddhp 17.9)
And if that being, encouraged by him, should listen to this sutra for even a moment, hear the fruit of that Dharma: he shall never suffer from diseases of the mouth.
His tongue never experiences pain, nor do his teeth ever fall out;
his lips never become dark, yellow, uneven, or loathsome.
His face is never crooked, nor dry, nor long, nor ever flat;
his nose is well-proportioned, as are his forehead, teeth, lips, and the circle of his face.
He is always pleasing to look upon by men, and his face never becomes distorted;
like a blue lotus here on earth, the fragrance of his mouth wafts forth perpetually.
Indeed, having gone from his home to a monastery, the wise man should go there to hear this sutra;
and having gone there, he should listen for even a moment—now hear the fruit for one whose mind is full of serene faith.
The physical form of that wise one becomes exceedingly bright, and he travels about in horse-drawn chariots;
mounting upon high elephant-chariots adorned with various jewels, he wanders about.
He shall obtain a decorated palanquin carried here by many men;
even having gone merely to hear the Dharma from him, such is the auspicious fruit that accrues.
Having sat there before the assembly by virtue of that white karma performed,
he becomes a possessor of the thrones of Śakra, the thrones of Brahmā, and the thrones of kings.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Merit of Rejoicing," in the Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.
(Vaidya 210) Chapter 18: The Benefits of the Dharma-preacher.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Satatasamitābhiyukta: "Noble son, whoever shall uphold or recite this Dharma-discourse..."
Or shall teach, or shall write it,
that son of good family or daughter of good family will obtain eight hundred qualities of the eye and twelve hundred qualities of the ear.
He will obtain eight hundred qualities of the nose, twelve hundred qualities of the tongue,
and eight hundred qualities of the body.
He will obtain twelve hundred qualities of the mind.
By means of these many hundreds of qualities, his collection of six sense faculties will become pure and thoroughly purified.
With such a purified faculty of sight—his ordinary fleshly eye produced from his mother and father—he will [see] the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system.

He will see that entire world-system, both inside and out, including its mountains, forests, and groves, from the great Avīci hell below up to the peak of existence above, all with his ordinary fleshly eye; and he will see whatever sentient beings have been born therein.
He will see them all and will know the ripening of their karma.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Listen to me regarding the virtues of one who would preach this sūtra in assemblies with confidence, proclaiming it without any hesitation. *Saddhp* 18.1.
There are eight hundred qualities in his eye in every respect,
by which his eye becomes stainless, pure, and unclouded.
With that fleshly eye, born of his mother and father,
he beholds this world-system with its mountains, forests, and groves.
He beholds Meru, Sumeru, and all the Cakravāla mountains;
he also sees other mountain ranges and the oceans.
As far as the Avīci hell below and the peak of existence above,
all that the wise one sees with such a fleshly eye is like this.
He has not yet attained the divine eye, nor has it even arisen;
such is the range of his physical eye.

Furthermore, Satatasamitābhiyukta, that son of good family or daughter of good family, while proclaiming this Dharma-discourse and causing others to hear it, will be endowed with twelve hundred qualities of the ear,
by which they can hear whatever various sounds issue forth within the triple-thousand great-thousand world system, down as far as the great Avīci hell.
And as far as the peak of existence, both internally and externally— namely, sounds of elephants, or sounds of horses, or sounds of camels, or sounds of cattle, or sounds of goats,
or sounds of people from the countryside, or sounds of chariots, or sounds of weeping, or sounds of lamentation, or terrifying sounds, or sounds of conchs, or sounds of bells.

or the sound of kettledrums, or the sound of drums, or the sound of play, or the sound of singing, or the sound of dancing, or the sound of musical instruments, or the sound of cymbals, or the sound of women,
or the sound of men, or the sound of boys, or the sound of girls, or the sound of Dharma, or the sound of non-Dharma, or the sound of happiness, or the sound of suffering, or the sound of fools.

Or noble sounds, or pleasant sounds, or unpleasant sounds; or the sounds of gods, or the sounds of nāgas, or the sounds of yakṣas, or the sounds of rākṣasas, or the sounds of gandharvas, or the sounds of asuras, or the sounds of garuḍas, or the sounds of kinnaras, or the sounds of mahoragas, or the sounds of humans, or the sounds of non-humans; or the sounds of fire, or the sounds of wind, or the sounds of water.
Whether they be sounds of villages, sounds of cities, sounds of monks, sounds of disciples, sounds of pratyekabuddhas,
sounds of bodhisattvas, or sounds of tathāgatas— whatever sounds whatsoever issue forth within and without the trichiliocosm, great trichiliocosm world-system—
He hears those sounds with that naturally pure faculty of hearing;
yet he has not yet produced the divine ear.
He understands the cries of those various sentient beings.
He discerns and analyzes them with that ordinary faculty of hearing;
as he hears the cries of those various beings, his faculty of hearing is not overwhelmed by all those sounds.
Such, Satatasamitābhiyukta, is the attainment of the faculty of hearing of that bodhisattva mahāsattva.
And yet, he has not yet brought forth the divine ear.
The Blessed One said this.
Having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
"His faculty of hearing becomes pure, unclouded, and even that which is natural."
For by means of this, he hears all various kinds of sounds here in this world-system without exception.
He hears the sounds of elephants, horses, chariots, oxen, goats, and sheep;
of kettledrums, clay drums, and sweet-sounding instruments; and of lutes, flutes, and harps.
The steadfast one hears pleasant and sweet songs, yet he does not become attached to them;
he hears the voices of millions of people, whatever they say, wherever they may be.
He constantly hears the sounds of the gods, as well as sweet and charming songs,
and also the voices of men and women, as well as those of boys and girls.
Those birds that dwell in mountain caves— the kalaviṅkas, cuckoos, and peacocks—
as well as the jīvakajīvakas: he indeed hears their beautiful songs.
Those who experience sensations in the hells utter most dreadful cries;
likewise, the hungry ghosts (preta) produce such sounds when they are tormented by the sufferings of hunger and thirst.
And whatever asuras dwell in the midst of the ocean, they emit sounds, some of which are directed at one another;
yet that Dharma-preacher, standing right here, hears all those sounds and is not overwhelmed by them.
Whatever cries there are among the animal wombs that convey mutual conversation,
he, remaining right here, hears those as well— various sounds of many kinds.
The gods who dwell in the Brahma-world, the Akaniṣṭha gods, and those Ābhāsvara gods—
whatever sounds they make to one another, he hears them all without exception.

Those monks who here engage in the private recitation of the scriptures, having gone forth in this teaching of the Sugata, and those who teach the Dharma in assemblies—he constantly hears their voices as well. (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra 18.16)
Those bodhisattvas here in this world-system who engage in mutual recitation and those who perform the communal chanting of the teachings— he hears their various sounds.
The Blessed One, the Buddha, the charioteer who tames men, proclaims the supreme Dharma among the assemblies;
and a bodhisattva who maintains this sutra hears that very Dharma at the same time.

All the many sounds produced by sentient beings within this triple-thousandfold world system— whether inside or outside, from the Avīci hell below up to the summit of existence above— are heard. (Saddhp 18.19)

He hears the sounds of all sentient beings, yet his field is not obstructed; with sharp faculties, he knows what is possible and impossible—even though his faculty of hearing is merely that of an ordinary person.
Yet he does not yet exert effort toward the divine; this ear remains established in its natural state.
For such are the qualities that belong to one who fearlessly upholds this sutra.

Furthermore, Satatasamitābhiyukta, for this bodhisattva mahāsattva who maintains, proclaims, recites, and writes down this Dharma-discourse, the faculty of smell becomes purified, endowed with eight hundred qualities.
With that purified faculty of smell, he perceives whatever various odors exist within and without the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system—
whether they be foul odors or pleasant odors, such as the scents of various kinds of *sumana* flowers,
namely, the fragrances of jasmine, *mallikā*, *campaka*, and *pāṭala*.
He smells those fragrances;
he also smells the various fragrances of water-born flowers, such as the fragrances of blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-lotuses, and white lotuses.
He smells the scents of the flowers and fruits of various flowering and fruit-bearing trees; that is to say, he smells the fragrant scents of sandalwood, *tamāla* leaves, *tagara*, and *agaru*.
Remaining in a single place, he smells all the hundreds of thousands of diverse varieties of perfumes and transformations of scent.
He also smells the various scents of sentient beings, such as the scents of elephants, horses, cattle, sheep, and other livestock;
he smells the bodily scents of various creatures belonging to the animal realm.
He smells the scents of the bodies of women and men;
he smells the scents of the bodies of boys and girls;
and he smells the scents of even grasses, shrubs, herbs, and trees situated at a great distance.
He smells the scents of beings,
yet he is not captivated by those scents, nor does he become deluded by them.
Remaining right here, he perceives even the scents of the gods;
that is to say, he perceives the scents of divine flowers such as the pārijātaka, the kovidāra, the māndārava, the mahāmāndārava, the mañjūṣaka, and the mahāmañjūṣaka;
he perceives the scents of divine agarwood powder and sandalwood powder.
He smells the fragrances of hundreds of thousands of various kinds of divine floral transformations,
and he recognizes their names;
he also smells the fragrances of the bodies of the sons of gods.
For example, one smells the fragrance of Śakra, the lord of the gods, and recognizes it— whether he is sporting, enjoying himself, and being entertained in the Vaijayanta palace,
or teaching the Dharma to the Trāyastriṃśa gods in the Sudharmā assembly hall of the gods, or whether he is in a pleasure grove.
As he was going out for sport,
he smelled the distinct scents of the bodies of other sons of gods.
He smells the scents of the bodies of even the daughters of the gods and the wives of the gods; he smells the scents of the bodies of even the young gods and the young goddesses.
And he is not captivated by those odors.
By this method, he smells even the bodily odors of beings born as far as the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*);
he smells the bodily odors of the sons of gods belonging to the Brahma-realm (*brahmakāyika*) and even those of the Great Brahmas (*mahābrahman*).
In this manner, he also smells the scents of the bodies of all the classes of gods;
he smells the scents of the bodies of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and tathāgatas;
and he also smells the scents of the thrones of the tathāgatas.
He also knows the place where those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas dwell;
yet his olfactory faculty is not obstructed by those various kinds of fragrances.
It is neither harmed nor oppressed;
and desiring it, he also explains those various fragrances to others.
And his mindfulness is not impaired.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"His faculty of smell becomes purified, and he perceives many various scents—whatever fragrant or foul odors there may be anywhere in this world-system. (Saddhp 18.22)
The fragrance of jasmine, as well as that of *mallikā*, *tamāla* leaves, and sandalwood;
the scent of *tagara* and also of *agaru*, as well as that of various flowers and fruits. *Saddhp_18.23*
Likewise, standing at a distance, he perceives the scents of beings—of men and women;
by their scent, he knows the location of boys and girls.
He knows of kings, of universal monarchs (cakravartin), of wheel-turning monarchs (balacakravartin), and of regional rulers;
likewise, by means of that fragrance, he knows their princes, ministers, and all those within their harems.
Whatever various kinds of precious objects for enjoyment and base metals are buried in the earth—
even those that have become like jewels among women— the Bodhisattva knows them by their scent.
Whatever ornaments they have, of various forms, worn upon their bodies— whether garments, garlands, or ointments— the Bodhisattva knows them by their scent. (Saddhp 18.27)

Whether standing, sitting, or likewise lying down, as well as all their play, delight, and supernatural power—the wise one who maintains this most excellent sūtra knows them all by the power of his sense of smell. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 18.28.

Likewise, whether standing still or moving, he knows and smells the fragrances of scented oils, various perfumes, and the scents of diverse flowers and fruits; he perceives these odors as being in such-and-such a place or in this very spot. (Saddhp 18.29)
Whatever many sandalwood trees are in flower there within the clefts of the mountains,
and whatever beings dwell therein— he perceives them all by their fragrance.
Those beings who dwell on the slopes of the Cakravāla mountains, those who live in the midst of the ocean,
and those creatures who inhabit the center of the earth— he discerns them all by means of their scent.
He knows the gods and likewise the asuras; he recognizes the daughters of the asuras;
he knows the play and the delight of the asuras—such indeed is the power of his sense of smell.
Whatever four-footed creatures there are in the forests— lions, tigers, as well as elephant-kings,
buffaloes, cattle, and gayals— he knows their dwelling place by means of his sense of smell.
And as for women who are pregnant, whether they carry a boy or a girl in their womb,
he knows what is there by the scent from their exhausted bodies.
He knows when she has conceived a being, and he knows when that which is subject to destruction is about to perish;
"This woman, her suffering removed, shall give birth to a son composed of merit. (Saddhp 18.35)
He discerns the many intentions of men, and likewise smells their scent of intention;
he smells the scent of those who are lustful, the wicked, and the deceitful, as well as the scent of those whose minds are tranquil.
Whatever treasures exist within the earth— be they bullion, gold, silver, or precious metals,
as well as chests and iron vessels completely filled with incense— the Bodhisattva smells them all.
He knows by scent all those necklaces and half-necklaces, as well as various jewels and pearls obtained at no small price, including their priceless names and their radiant qualities.
And likewise, even while remaining here, that steadfast one smells the flowers above among the gods— both the *mandārava* and the *mañjūṣaka*, as well as whatever flowers belong to the *pārijāta*.
Whatever celestial palaces there are— whether noble, inferior, or middling—
and whatever various forms they take wherever they may be located, he perceives them all here by the power of his sense of smell.

They likewise perceive the pleasure groves, as well as the Sudharmā assembly hall and the Vaijayanta palace; they also recognize the most excellent palaces where the sons of the gods take their delight.
Standing here, he smells their fragrance; by that fragrance, he knows the sons of gods—
wherever they perform their deeds, whether standing, lying down, walking, or wherever else they may be.
Wherever the daughters of the gods—adorned with many flowers, wearing garlands and ornaments, and beautifully decorated—dally or go, the Bodhisattva knows by their fragrance. *Saddhp_18.43*
Even the gods above, as far as the peak of existence— including Brahmā and Mahābrahmā who dwell in celestial palaces—
he perceives there by means of that fragrance, whether they are established in meditative concentration or have emerged from it.

He knows the sons of the gods in the Ābhāsvara heaven—those who have passed away, those who have been reborn, and those who were never there before—such is the olfactory faculty of the bodhisattva who upholds this sutra. (Saddhp 18.45)
Whatever monks there may be who are devoted to the teaching of the Sugata and stand firm in their practice,
and those monks who delight in the recitation and study of the scriptures— the Bodhisattva knows them all.
Those disciples who are sons of the Jina, some of whom always dwell at the foot of trees—the Wise One knows them all by their fragrance: "There, such-and-such a monk is staying."
Those bodhisattvas who possess mindfulness and meditate, who always delight in recitation and study,
and who proclaim the Dharma in assemblies— the Bodhisattva knows them by their fragrance.

In whichever direction the Sugata, the Great Sage, compassionate for the welfare of others, reveals the Dharma while being honored in the midst of the assembly of disciples— the World-Protector— he perceives that very place by means of his fragrance.
Furthermore, whatever beings hear his Dharma and, having heard it, become joyful in mind—
the Bodhisattva, remaining right here, perceives that entire assembly of the Jina there. (Saddhp 18.50)
Such is his power of smell, yet his sense of smell has not yet become divine;
rather, this serves as the precursor to his future divine and untainted (anāsrava) sense of smell.

Furthermore, Satatasamitābhiyukta, that son of good family or daughter of good family who maintains, teaches, elucidates, and writes down this Dharma-discourse shall obtain a faculty of the tongue endowed with those twelve hundred qualities of the tongue.
Whatever tastes he may taste with such a tongue-faculty,
or whatever tastes he may place upon his tongue-faculty, they all shall become a divine, great flavor.
And he will experience tastes in such a way that he will not experience any taste as unpleasant;
even those tastes which are unpleasant, when placed upon his faculty of the tongue, will release a divine flavor.
And whatever Dharma he shall proclaim while standing in the midst of the assembly, [it will be so].
Because of that, those beings will have their faculties gladdened; they will be satisfied, supremely satisfied, and filled with joy.
And from him there will issue forth a voice that is sweet, lovely, charming, deep, heart-piercing, and endearing.
Because of that, those beings will be satisfied and their minds will be uplifted.
And for those to whom he shall teach the Dharma,
having heard his sweet resonance— beautiful and pleasing— even the gods will think they must approach him to see him, to pay homage, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma;
even the sons of the gods and the daughters of the gods will think they must approach him to see him, to pay homage, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma.
Even the Śakras, the Brahmās, and the sons of the gods belonging to the Brahma-realm will think they should approach him to see him, to pay homage to him, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma.
Even the Nāgas and Nāga maidens will think they should approach him to see him, to pay homage to him, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma.
Even the Asuras and Asura maidens will think they should approach him to see him, to pay homage to him, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma.
Even the garuḍas and garuḍa maidens will think it necessary to approach him for the purpose of seeing him, paying homage, attending upon him, and hearing the Dharma;
as will the kinnaras and kinnara maidens,
and the mahoragas and mahoraga maidens.
Yakṣas and yakṣa maidens,
as well as piśācas and piśāca maidens, will think that they should approach him to see him, to pay homage to him, to attend upon him, and to hear the Dharma;
and they will show him honor.
They will show respect, honor, worship, veneration, and reverence [to them].
Monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen will also desire to see them.
Kings, princes, royal ministers, and royal high officials will also desire to see them.

Even kings who are powerful wheel-turners, as well as universal monarchs endowed with the seven jewels, together with their princes, ministers, and the retinues of their harems, will desire to see him and seek to pay him honor.
That Dharma-preacher will preach the Dharma so sweetly, exactly as it is and just as it was spoken by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, other brahmins, householders, merchants, and countryfolk will be constantly and continuously following after that Dharma-preacher until the end of their lives.
The disciples of the Tathāgata will also desire to see him;
the Pratyekabuddhas will also desire to see him;
and the Blessed Buddhas will also desire to see him.
And in whichever direction that son of good family or daughter of good family shall dwell,
in that direction they will teach the Dharma facing toward the Tathāgata,
and they will become a vessel for the Buddha-dharmas.
In this way, his deep and pleasing sound of the Dharma will issue forth.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The faculty of his tongue becomes preeminent; he never tastes inferior flavors. As soon as they are placed [in his mouth], they become divine, endowed with celestial flavor. (Saddhp 18.52)
He speaks with a beautiful voice, uttering words that are sweet, worth hearing, desirable, and delightful;
in the midst of the assembly, he always speaks with a deep resonance that inspires love.
And whoever hears the Dharma as he speaks it through many millions of billions of parables,
and generates supreme joy therein, performs for him an immeasurable and foremost worship.
Even the gods, nāgas, asuras, and guhyakas always desire to see him;
they listen to the Dharma with reverence, and all these qualities belong to him. (Saddhp 18.55)
And if he so desires, he could make himself understood by his voice throughout this entire world-system;
his voice is smooth and sweet, deep, melodious, and most lovely.
Kings who are sovereigns of the earth, seeking to pay him honor, approach him together with their sons and wives; joining their palms in reverence, they constantly listen to the Dharma.
He is always honored by the yakṣas, as well as by the nāgas and the hosts of gandharvas; he is highly esteemed, respected, and worshipped by both the piśācas and the piśācīs. (Saddhp 18.58)
Even Brahmā becomes subject to his power, as do Maheśvara, Īśvara, and the son of the gods;
likewise Śakra and other sons of the gods, as well as many daughters of the gods, approach him.

And those Buddhas who are compassionate for the welfare of the world, together with their disciples, having heard his voice, provide protection so that they may behold his face; and they become joyful as he speaks this Dharma.
Furthermore, Satatasamitābhiyukta, that bodhisattva mahāsattva, while upholding, reciting, proclaiming, teaching, or writing this Dharma discourse, shall obtain eight hundred qualities of the body.
His body will be pure and completely purified, with a complexion as clear as lapis lazuli.
He is pleasant to behold for all beings. When that physical body is completely purified, he will see the entire great trichiliocosm;
and he will see whatever beings in that great trichiliocosm pass away and are reborn.
Lowly and exalted,
beautiful and ugly,
in happy destinies and miserable destinies.
And whatever beings dwell upon the Cakravāla and Mahācakravāla mountains, and upon Meru and Sumeru, the kings of mountains;
and whatever beings dwell below in the Avīci hell and above as far as the peak of existence (bhavāgra)—
he will see them all within his own body.
And whatever śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, or tathāgatas dwell in this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system;
whatever Dharma those tathāgatas teach;
and whatever sentient beings attend upon those tathāgatas—
He will see the physical forms of all those beings within his own physical form.
Why is that?
Because this physical form is utterly pure.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The physical form of one who maintains this sublime sūtra becomes completely pure, just like a perfectly clear crystal. Such a person is always pleasing to behold by sentient beings. (Saddhp 18.61)
Just as one might see a reflection on the surface of a mirror, so too is this world seen within his body;
the Self-Existent One sees it himself, but other beings do not, for such is the purity of his body.
Whatever beings there are here in this world-system— humans, gods, asuras, or guhyakas—
and those in the hells, among the hungry ghosts, or in the wombs of animals, their reflections are seen there within that body.
The celestial palaces of the gods as far as the peak of existence, even the mountains and the Cakravāla range,
Himavat, Sumeru, and the great Meru— all these are seen entirely within his body.

Within his own body, he also beholds Buddhas together with their disciples, as well as the sons of the Buddhas and others—those bodhisattvas who dwell alone and those who dwell in a group, proclaiming the Dharma. *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* 18.65.
Such is his purity of body that the entire world-system is seen by him;
yet he has not yet attained the divine eye, for such is the nature of his physical body.
Furthermore, Satatasamitābhiyukta, when this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
upholds, teaches, proclaims, writes, or recites this Dharma-discourse, his faculty of mind will become completely purified, endowed with those twelve hundred qualities of mental attention.
With that purified faculty of mind, if he hears even a single verse, he will understand its manifold meaning;
having understood it, he will teach the Dharma for as long as a month on account of that cause.
He will teach the Dharma for four months or even for a year; and whatever Dharma he shall speak,
that will remain in his memory and shall not be lost.
Whatever worldly conventions there may be— whether discourses or mantras—
he will harmonize them all with the method of the Dharma.
And as for all those beings who, born within the six realms of existence, wander in transmigration throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, [he will lead them to liberation].
He will know the movements and fluctuations of the mental conduct of all those beings;
he will know and discern their stirrings, conceits, and conceptual proliferations.
And even before he has attained noble gnosis, his faculty of mind will be purified in such a manner.
Whatever definition of the Dharma he reflects upon before teaching the Dharma, all of that he will teach as it truly is;
he speaks everything spoken by the Tathāgata and everything set forth in the discourses of former Jinas.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"The faculty of his mind becomes purified, radiant, pure, and untroubled."
Thus, by means of that, he discerns various phenomena—those that are inferior, as well as those that are superior and middling.
Having heard even a single verse, the wise one understands its manifold meaning therein;
he always speaks what is consistent and true, whether for four months or likewise for a year.
And whatever beings dwell here in this world-system, whether inside or outside—
gods, humans, asuras, guhyakas, nāgas, and even those in the wombs of animals.
Whatever thought may arise for the beings dwelling in the six realms of existence, they all understand and know it in a single moment; having upheld this sutra, these are the benefits.
Whatever Dharma the Buddha, who possesses the marks of a hundred merits, proclaims throughout this entire world, he hears its pure sound; and whatever he speaks, that is grasped.
He contemplates many supreme dharmas and constantly speaks of many;
having retained this sutra, he never experiences delusion—these are the benefits.
He understands both the connections and the disconnections among all phenomena, as well as their diverse characteristics;
he discerns their meanings and etymologies, and speaks exactly as he knows them.
Whatever sūtra was spoken here over a long period of time by the former teachers of the world,
that Dharma he preaches at all times, without fear, in the midst of the assembly. (Saddhp 18.74)
Having retained and recited this sutra, his faculty of mind becomes such as this;
yet he has not yet attained unimpeded knowledge, for this [faculty] merely serves as its precursor.

For by upholding this sūtra of the Sugata, one comes to stand upon the level of a teacher and shall preach the Dharma to all sentient beings; one also becomes skilled in millions of modes of etymological interpretation.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Benefits for the Preachers of Dharma," in the Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.
(Vaidya 224) Chapter 19: Sadāparibhūta.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta: "By this [also]..."
To this extent, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, it should be understood by way of this analogy: that those who will reject such a Dharma-discourse as this,
and who will revile, abuse, and insult monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen who uphold such sūtras— [they shall suffer such consequences].
They will address them with false and harsh speech;
for them there will be such an undesirable ripening of karma that it cannot be fully described in words.
And those who shall uphold, recite, teach, master, and extensively proclaim this very sūtra to others—
for them there will be such a desirable maturation as I have previously described.
And they will attain such purification of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

In the past, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in a time long gone, more than incalculable, more than immeasurable, vast, and inconceivable eons ago— even further back than that— at that time and in that era, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, one perfected in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, lived in the aeon called Vinirbhoga in the world-system called Mahāsaṃbhavā.

Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, was teaching the Dharma in that world-system Mahāsaṃbhavā before the world with its gods, humans, and asuras.

That is to say, he taught the Dharma associated with the Four Noble Truths for the sake of the Śrāvakas— concerning the transcendence of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair, and culminating in Nirvāṇa— as the progression of dependent origination.
For the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, who are engaged in the six perfections, he taught the Dharma concerning unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, culminating in the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision.

Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, the lifespan of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, was forty million billion nayutas of koṭis of kalpas, equal to the number of sands in forty Ganges rivers.
After he had attained final nirvāṇa, the True Dharma remained for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of kalpas, equal in number to the atoms of Jambudvīpa;
the Counterfeit Dharma remained for hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of kalpas, equal in number to the atoms of the four continents.
Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, in that world-system called Mahāsaṃbhavā, belonging to the Blessed One Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja...
When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha had passed into parinirvāṇa, and when the semblance of the True Dharma had disappeared,

another Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja appeared in the world— one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans.
And for human beings, there was the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, through this succession, in that world-system Mahāsaṃbhavā, there were two hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja.
Therein, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, he who was the very first Tathāgata was the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, endowed with knowledge and conduct.
The Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Charioteer of men to be tamed, the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One—

when that Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, when the true Dharma had disappeared and the semblance of the true Dharma was vanishing, and when that teaching was overrun by monks of overweening pride,
there was a bodhisattva monk named Sadāparibhūta.
For what reason, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, is that bodhisattva mahāsattva called Sadāparibhūta?
Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, whichever monk, nun, layman, or laywoman that bodhisattva mahāsattva sees, he approaches each of them and says: "Venerable sirs, I do not despise you."
"You are not to be despised.
For what reason?
Because you all must practice the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"You shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
By this method, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while being a monk, did not give oral instruction nor did he engage in recitation.
Otherwise, whoever he sees—even if they have gone far away—he approaches them all and makes this proclamation to a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman;
approaching each one, he says: "Sisters, I do not hold you in contempt."
"You are not to be despised.
For what reason?
Because you must all practice the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"You shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Mahāsthāmaprāpta, at that time, whatever monk, nun, layman, or laywoman that bodhisattva mahāsattva thus addresses,
almost all of them become angry with him.
They harbored malice, gave rise to ill-will, reviled, and abused him, saying: "Why does this monk, when unasked, display such a mind free from contempt toward us?
By predicting our unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—something non-existent and undesired—he treats himself with contempt.
Then, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, many years passed while that bodhisattva mahāsattva was thus reviled and abused.
He does not become angry with anyone,
nor does he give rise to a mind of malice;
and even when those who hear him proclaiming in this way throw clods of earth or sticks at him, [he remains unperturbed].
From afar, he made himself heard by raising his voice and declaring to them, "I do not despise you!
Because those arrogant monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen constantly and perpetually proclaimed this to him, he came to be known by the name Sadāparibhūta ("Always Despised").

Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, when the time of death had arrived and the moment of passing away was at hand, this Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was heard by that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta.
And this Dharma discourse was spoken by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, in twenty hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of verses.
It was so. And when the time of death had approached for that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta, he heard this Dharma discourse from a voice in the sky.
Having heard this voice from the sky uttered by someone or other, he took up this Dharma discourse.
He attained such purity of the eye, purity of the ear, purity of the nose, purity of the tongue, purity of the body, and purity of the mind.
Having attained these purities, he further sustained his own life-force for another two hundred quadrillion years and proclaimed this Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
And those conceited beings— monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—
who were previously addressed by him, "I do not despise you," and by whom this name "Sadāparibhūta" (Always Despised) was given to him;

Having seen his power, strength, and majesty of sublime supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*), his power, strength, and majesty of resolve and eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and his power, strength, and majesty of wisdom (*prajñā*),

everyone became his companions for the sake of hearing the Dharma. By him, as well as by others, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of living beings were inspired to attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, after that bodhisattva mahāsattva passed away from there, he propitiated two hundred billion Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all of whom bore the same name as Candra-svara-rāja.
And under all of them, he fully proclaimed this Dharma-discourse.

By means of those very same roots of merit from the past, he proceeded in due order and once again [encountered] Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, all of whom bore the same name as Dundubhi-svara-rāja.
He propitiated exactly twenty hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas;
and under all of them, he propitiated this very Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma and proclaimed it to the four assemblies.

By virtue of those very same roots of merit from the past, as well as through new ones, he again pleased twenty hundred thousand million Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, all of whom were named Meghasvararāja; and under them all, he mastered this very Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and proclaimed it to the fourfold assembly.
And in all these respects, he was endowed with such purity of the eye;
he was endowed with purity of the ear, purity of the nose, purity of the tongue, purity of the body, and purity of the mind.

Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, that bodhisattva mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta, having performed acts of honoring, revering, respecting, worshiping, adoring, and venerating so many hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Tathāgatas,
and having performed acts of honoring, revering, respecting, worshiping, adoring, and venerating many other hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of Buddhas,
And in all those [lifetimes], he encountered this very Dharma-discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
having encountered it, through that very same previously cultivated and ripened root of merit, he fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Now, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you might perhaps have some doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation, thinking that the Bodhisattva named Sadāparibhūta at that time and on that occasion was someone else.
Who was that mahāsattva who,
under the teaching of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja, was always regarded as "one who has never been despised" by the fourfold assembly,
and by whom those so many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas were propitiated?
Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you should not view it in this way.
Why is that?
It was I myself, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who at that time and on that occasion was the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sadāparibhūta.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, had I not previously taken up this Dharma discourse and retained it, I would not have so swiftly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, because I have maintained, recited, and taught this Dharma-discourse in the presence of former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones,
I have thus so quickly awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Furthermore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, those hundreds of monks who were [disciples] of that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sadāparibhūta—
Hundreds of bhikṣuṇīs, hundreds of upāsakas, and hundreds of upāsikās were made to hear this Dharma discourse in the teaching of that Blessed One: "I do not despise you;
may you all practice the conduct of a bodhisattva."
"You shall become Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas.
Those who gave rise to a mind of malice toward that Bodhisattva did not see a Tathāgata for twenty hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of kalpas."
Neither the word "Dharma" nor the word "Saṅgha" was heard by them;
for ten thousand eons, they experienced agonizing sensations in the great Avīci hell.
Yet, they were all completely liberated from that karmic obscuration.
They were matured for unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by that very Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
Now, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, you might perhaps have some doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation as to who those beings were at that time, on that occasion, who mocked and ridiculed that Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.

In this very assembly, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, five hundred bodhisattvas headed by Bhadrapāla, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs headed by Siṃhacandrā, and five hundred upāsikās headed by Sugatacetanā were all established in irreversibility regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

Thus, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, this retention, recitation, and teaching of this Dharma-discourse of great significance serves to bring about unexcelled, perfect enlightenment for bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas. Therefore, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, this Dharma-discourse must be constantly retained, recited, and taught by bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas.
"It should be fully elucidated."

Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses: "I recall the past, when there was a Jina named Bhīṣmasvara, a king of great majesty, honored by men and gods, the leader of humans, gods, yakṣas, and rākṣasas. (Saddhp 19.1)
When that Jina had entered parinirvāṇa and the true Dharma was falling into decline in the final age, there was then a monk who was a bodhisattva; by name he was called Sadāparibhūta.
Then, having approached other monks as well as nuns who held views based on apprehension, that monk said:
"I have never had any contempt for you; indeed, you should practice the conduct for the sake of supreme enlightenment."
And having thus constantly proclaimed this, they endured their insults and abuse;
when the time of death had arrived, he heard this sutra.
At that time, having fixed a lifespan of great length through his mastery of skillful means,
the wise one proclaimed this sutra within the teaching of that Guide.
And all of them, who were greatly attached to objective apprehension, were brought to maturity by him for enlightenment;
then, having passed away from there, that bodhisattva propitiated thousands of millions of Buddhas.
By that merit accumulated in succession, having constantly illuminated this sutra, that son of the Conqueror attained awakening; I myself was he at that time, Śākyamuni.
And those monks who were then attached to objective perception, the nuns, and the laymen and laywomen who were there at that time— to them all the wise one proclaimed awakening.
And they too have seen many millions of Buddhas, as well as these five hundred [disciples] without exception;
likewise, monks and nuns, and laywomen as well, have been in my presence.
I have caused all of them to hear the supreme Dharma, and I have brought them all to maturity;
even after I have entered nirvana, all these steadfast ones shall indeed uphold this supreme sūtra.
Throughout many hundreds of millions of inconceivable eons, such a Dharma as this has never been heard;
even when there are hundreds of millions of Buddhas, they do not proclaim this sutra.
Therefore, having heard this very kind of Dharma proclaimed by the Self-Existent One himself,
and having attained it, you should repeatedly reveal this sutra here after I have entered nirvana.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "Sadāparibhūta," in the Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma.

(Vaidya 229) Saddhp_20: The Chapter on the Supernatural Manifestation of the Tathāgata. Then, indeed, those hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas, equal in number to the atoms of dust in a thousandfold world-system, who had emerged from the fissures in the earth—
They all, having extended their joined palms toward the Blessed One, said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One,

after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, we shall [promote] this Dharma-discourse in all Buddha-fields— whatever Buddha-fields of the Blessed One there may be— and wherever the Blessed One shall have passed into parinirvāṇa."
We shall reveal it here and there.
O Blessed One, we are eager for this single, sublime Dharma-discourse, whether for its preservation, recitation, teaching, revelation, or writing.

Then indeed, many hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of bodhisattvas headed by Mañjuśrī— who were residents in this Sahā world-system, including monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—

as well as many bodhisattva mahāsattvas equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, said this to the Blessed One: "We too, Blessed One, shall proclaim this Dharma-discourse for the sake of the Tathāgata."

"O Blessed One, even after you have entered final nirvāṇa, we shall remain in the sky with our physical forms invisible and cause our voices to be heard; and for those beings who have not yet planted roots of merit, we shall cause them to plant roots of merit."

Then, at that time, the Blessed One addressed a certain leading Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Viśiṣṭacāritra— who was a leader of those former Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who were heads of groups, leaders of great groups, and teachers of groups— saying: "Excellent, excellent, Viśiṣṭacāritra!"
In this way, you must act for the sake of this Dharma discourse;
you have been brought to maturity by the Tathāgata.
Then indeed, the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, and that Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who had entered parinirvāṇa within the stūpa—
both seated upon their lion-thrones— manifested a smile and extended their tongues from within the openings of their mouths.
And by means of those two tongue-faculties, they reached as far as the Brahma-world.
From those two tongue-faculties, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of light rays issued forth.
And from each of those light rays, many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of bodhisattvas issued forth.
Golden-colored in body and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, they sat upon lion-thrones within the heart of lotuses.

Those bodhisattvas, having spread throughout hundreds of thousands of world-systems in the cardinal and intermediate directions, stood in the sky in all those directions and intermediate directions and taught the Dharma.

Just as the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, performs a miracle of supernatural power with his tongue-faculty, and just as the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, the Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, does likewise, so too do all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.

Those who had come from hundreds of thousands of myriads of millions of other world-systems and were seated individually on lion-thrones at the foot of jewel-trees performed a miracle of supernatural power with their tongue-faculties; then indeed the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha, and all those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, maintained that manifestation of supernatural power for a full hundred thousand years.
Then, after the passing of a hundred thousand years, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas withdrew those tongues once again;

and at one and the same time, in a single moment, an instant, and a brief duration, they all simultaneously made the sound of a great lion’s roar and produced the sound of a single snap of the fingers.

And by that great sound of clearing the throat and that great sound of the clapping of hands, as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields as there are in the ten directions were all shaken, trembled, and violently shaken; they quivered, quivered intensely, and quivered violently; they shook, shook intensely, and shook violently.

And in all those Buddha-fields, as many beings as there were— whether gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, or non-humans— they too, by the power of the Buddha, while remaining right where they were, beheld this Sahā world-system;
and they saw all those hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of Tathāgatas seated individually upon lion-thrones at the foot of jewel-trees.
And they saw the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha,

as well as the Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha who has entered parinirvāṇa, seated upon a lion throne within that great jeweled stūpa, sitting together with the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata. And those...
The three assemblies beheld [him], and having seen him, they were struck with wonder, filled with amazement, and overcome with joy.
And from the sky, they heard this voice: "Friends, beyond immeasurable and incalculable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems, there is a world-system named Sahā."
In that [world], there is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.

He is currently proclaiming to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas a Dharma discourse called the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, a sūtra of great vaipulya, an instruction for Bodhisattvas, and the protection of all Buddhas.
You should rejoice in this with a resolute intention,

and pay homage to that Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, and to that Blessed One Prabhūtaratna, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Then, having heard such a voice from the sky, all those beings, remaining right where they were, paid homage.
With palms joined in reverence, they addressed these words to the Blessed One Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One:
"We offer various flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards; we cast them toward this Sahā world-system.
We also cast various ornaments, necklaces, half-necklaces, and precious jewels."
For the purpose of making offerings to the Blessed One Śākyamuni and to the Tathāgata Prabhūtaratna, and for this Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*,

those flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, flags, and victory standards, as well as those necklaces, half-necklaces, jewels, and gems that were thrown, come into this Sahā world-system.

And with those heaps of flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and victory standards, as well as necklaces, half-necklaces, and precious jewels, they— along with those other hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of world-systems that had become one with this Sahā world-system— [filled it].
The Tathāgatas were seated upon them,
and above all of them, in the sky and mid-air, a great canopy of flowers was established all around.
Then the Blessed One addressed those bodhisattva mahāsattvas, headed by Viśiṣṭacāritra: "Noble sons, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones possess inconceivable power.

Noble sons, for the sake of entrusting this Dharma discourse, I could speak of many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of benefits through various primary teachings even for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons;
yet, while speaking, I would not reach the end of its virtues."

In brief, noble sons, I have taught in this Dharma-discourse the preeminence of all Buddhas, the secret of all Buddhas, and the profound domain of all Buddhas. Therefore, noble sons, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa, you must respectfully uphold, teach, write down, recite, proclaim, cultivate, and honor this Dharma-discourse.

And in whatever region of the earth, noble sons, this Dharma-discourse may be recited, or revealed, or taught, or written down, or contemplated, or spoken, or studied, or exists in the form of a book—
whether in a park, or a monastery, or a house, or a forest, or a city, or at the foot of a tree, or in a palace, or a lodging, or a cave— there...
On that spot of earth, a stūpa dedicated to the Tathāgata should be constructed.
Why is that? For that spot of earth should be known as the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) for all Tathāgatas.
And it should be known that on that spot of earth all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones have awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment;
and on that spot of earth the wheel of Dharma has been turned by all Tathāgatas; and on that spot of earth all Tathāgatas have entered final nirvāṇa.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Inconceivable is the nature of the Dharma of those who benefit the world, who are established in the knowledge of the superknowledges;
they display miraculous powers with infinite vision for the sake of bringing joy here to all embodied beings. (Saddhp 20.1)

Reaching as far as the Brahma-world with their tongues and emitting thousands of rays of light, these who have set out for supreme enlightenment display wonders here through their supernatural powers. (Saddhp 20.2)
The Buddhas even cause a coughing sound, or those who produce the sound of a single snap of the fingers;
they thus inform this entire world throughout the ten directions of this world-system.
Displaying these and other miracles through their virtues, those who are compassionate for the welfare of others—
how indeed will they, filled with joy at that time after the Sugata has entered parinirvāṇa, uphold this sūtra?
Even for many thousands of millions of eons, one could speak the praises of those sons of the Sugata who shall uphold this supreme sūtra after the Leader of the World has entered final nirvāṇa.
There would be no end to their virtues, just as there is no end to the directions within the realm of space;
inconceivable are the virtues of those who always uphold this auspicious sutra.
I have been seen, as have all these leaders, and this Leader of the World who has entered nirvāṇa;
and all these many bodhisattvas and the fourfold assemblies have been seen by him.
Today, I have pleased him here, and all these leaders have been pleased;
as has this Lord of Jinas who has entered nirvana, and those others who are in the ten directions.
The Buddhas of the future and the past, as well as those who currently abide in the ten directions—
all of them would be seen and perfectly honored by whoever upholds this sutra.
The secret knowledge of the Supreme Persons, which was contemplated at the seat of enlightenment—
that too one should quickly reflect upon, whoever would uphold this sutra, the true Dharma.
The eloquence of such a person shall also be infinite, just as the wind is never obstructed anywhere;
he who maintains this distinguished sūtra understands the Dharma, its meaning, and its etymological interpretation.
He always understands the underlying connections of the sutras spoken with intentional meaning by the Leaders;
even when the Guide has entered final nirvana, he knows the true meaning of those sutras.
Resembling the moon and equal to the sun, he shines, becoming a maker of light and illumination;
wandering here and there upon the earth, he inspires many bodhisattvas.
Therefore, those wise bodhisattvas who, having heard these ten benefits,
shall uphold this sutra after my parinirvāṇa— for them there will be no doubt regarding awakening.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Supernatural Manifestation of the Tathāgata," in the Dharma discourse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
(Vaidya 233) Chapter 21: The Dhāraṇī.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and—
Placing his right knee upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, how much merit would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce who should uphold this Dharma discourse, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?"
"Having committed it to memory or having written it down in a book?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja:

"Bhaiṣajyarāja, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family were to [venerate] hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas, equal in number to the sands of eighty Ganges rivers..."
One should honor, revere, respect, and worship them.
What do you think, Bhaiṣajyarāja, how much merit would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce on that account?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said: "Much, Blessed One."
"Much, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "I announce to you, Bhaiṣajyarāja;
I declare to you."

Bhaiṣajyarāja, if any son of good family or daughter of good family should uphold, recite, or master even a single four-line verse from this Dharma discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma, [they shall attain such merit].
And one should accomplish it through practice;
therefore, that son of good family or daughter of good family, Bhaiṣajyarāja, would generate much more merit on that account.
Then, at that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, we shall provide for those sons of good family or daughters of good family who have this Dharma-discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma committed to their bodies."
Or, for the sake of protection, defense, and guarding, these *dhāraṇī* mantra-words are set down in a book: namely—
*anye manye mane mamane citte carite same samitā viśānte mukte muktatame same aviṣame*.
Sama-same, jaye, kṣaye, akṣaye, akṣiṇe, śānte, samite, dhāraṇi, ālokabhāṣe, pratyavekṣaṇi, nidhiru, abhyantaraniviṣṭe,
abhyantarapāriśuddhimutkule, araḍe, paraḍe, sukāṅkṣi, asamasame, buddhavilokite, dharmaparīkṣite, saṃghanirghoṣaṇi, nirghoṇi, bhayābhayaviśodhani, mantre, mantrākṣayate.
In the rut, in skill in rutting, in the inexhaustible, in the state of being like an inexhaustible forest, in the vakula, in the valodra, in the state of non-conceit, svāhā!
“Blessed One, these mantra-dhāraṇī phrases have been spoken by Blessed Buddhas as numerous as the sands of sixty-two Ganges rivers.
All those Blessed Buddhas would be wronged by anyone who would transgress against such Dharma-preachers or such upholders of this sūtra.”
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyarāja!
You have acted for the benefit of sentient beings;
out of compassion for sentient beings, you have spoken these words of dhāraṇī."
Protection, defense, and guardianship have been established.
